For load-by-equal-steps, the failure dynamics are governed by the recursion Ut₊¹ = 1 − σ/Ut, yielding susceptibility χ = (σ꜀ − σ)⁻¹/² and relaxation time τ ∝ (σ꜀ − σ)⁻¹/₂, both diverging at the critical stress σ꜀ = 1/4. Plotting χ⁻² and τ⁻² versus stress produces linear fits that intersect the x-axis at σ꜀. 

In the overloaded case (σ = σ꜀ + ϵ), the breaking rate R(t) = dUt/dt exhibits a minimum at t₀(ϵ), which corresponds to halfway to complete collapse (t₀/t_f ≈ 1/2). Finally, energy emission distributions (acoustic emissions) show distinct power-law behaviors: slope −1 for below-critical stresses and −1·5 for over-critical stresses. The author concludes that all three scenarios provide distinct, observable, and predictable signatures of imminent failure measurable from single-system trajectories.

Research Context
The prediction of failure points is a major challenge in various fracture and breakdown scenarios from nano-materials to earthquakes. The fiber bundle model (FBM) has been proved to capture the essentials of failures in composite materials through simple geometry and clear-cut stress redistribution rules. The FBM is one of the few material failure models that can be solved analytically to some extent, making its statistical properties well-studied. While failure dynamics at constant load has been formulated through recursion relations, the practical question of predicting failure from precursors remains open. A precursor is defined as some prior indication of an upcoming incident, in this context the complete failure (collapse) of a fiber bundle under external load.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is: how can we predict the failure point of a loaded fiber bundle from available precursors? The paper hypothesizes that different loading conditions will produce distinct observable precursors that can be traced to a single system without disturbing the failure process. For quasi-static loading, the hypothesis is that burst size statistics will show a robust crossover near the failure point. For force-controlled loading, the hypothesis is that susceptibility and relaxation time will diverge with power laws near the failure stress. For the overloaded case, the hypothesis is that the breaking rate will show a characteristic minimum and energy burst statistics will differ below versus above criticality.

Methodological Details
The study uses the equal-load-sharing fiber bundle model with N elastic fibers clamped at both ends, all obeying Hooke's law with force constant set to unity. The bundle consists of N fibers with independent random breakdown thresholds xi associated with elongation. For simplicity, the cumulative distribution of thresholds is taken as a uniform distribution P(x) = x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1. The simulation is based on a single bundle containing N = 10⁷ fibers with uniformly distributed thresholds. The quasi-static loading is strain-controlled, stretching the bundle at each step until the weakest intact fiber fails. The force-controlled case involves increasing the load by equal stress increments at each step, governed by the recursion Ut₊¹ = 1 − σ/Ut. In the overloaded case, the initial stress σ = σ꜀ + ϵ is slightly above the critical value σ꜀ = 1/4. Energy emission En is calculated as 1/2 K ∑(xᵢ²) for a burst of size ∆, where each xi is the strength of a failing fiber.

Procedures And Architectures
The quasi-static procedure stretches the bundle incrementally; the expected force at elongation x is F(x) = N x (1 −P(x)), and failure occurs when dF/dx = 0 at x꜀. Burst statistics are obtained by recording the number of simultaneous fiber failures ∆ at each step, following the power law D(∆)/N = C∆⁻⁵/². The crossover test samples bursts occurring exclusively in the threshold interval (0.9x꜀, x꜀) to isolate near-failure avalanches. The average burst size ∆ₐᵥ is plotted against elongation x, and a power-law fit (∆ₐᵥ ∝ (x꜀ − x)⁰·⁹) is applied. For force-controlled loading, the recursion Ut₊¹ = 1 −σ/Ut is iterated from U₀ = 1 until Ut₊¹ = Ut, and the susceptibility χ = dU*/dσ and relaxation time τ are calculated from the differential form. In the overloaded case, the breaking rate R(t) = dUt/dt is computed as a function of step t, and its minimum t₀ is found for varying ϵ. Energy emission bursts are recorded at each redistribution step for below-critical (σ꜀ - 0.001, σ꜀ - 0.002), at critical (σ꜀), and over-critical (σ꜀ + 0.001, σ꜀ + 0.002, σ꜀ + 0.003, σ꜀ + 0.005) stress levels.

Key Results
The universal burst exponent for all avalanches in the FBM is ξ = 5/2, independent of the threshold distribution under mild assumptions. Near the failure point, the burst distribution exhibits a crossover from D(∆) ∝ ∆⁻⁵/² to D(∆) ∝ ∆⁻³/², as demonstrated in Figure 2. The average burst size follows ∆ₐᵥ(x) ∝ (x꜀ − x)⁰·⁹, and plotting Δₐᵥ⁻¹⁰/⁹ versus x yields a straight line touching the x-axis at x꜀, visible in a single system. The critical stress for the uniform distribution is analytically derived as σ꜀ = 1/4. The susceptibility and relaxation time diverge with exponent β = 1/2 and θ = 1/2, respectively, as σ approaches σ꜀ from below. In force-controlled simulations, plots of χ⁻² and τ⁻² versus stress show linear behavior near σ꜀, with the dotted best-fit lines intersecting the stress axis at σ꜀. In the overloaded case, the breaking rate R(t) has a minimum at t₀, and for varying ϵ, t₀/t_f all occur close to 1/2 when plotted as a function of the scaled variable. Energy burst distributions exhibit a slope of -1.0 for below-critical stresses and -1.5 for over-critical stresses, with many small bursts present below criticality that are absent above. The energy bursts in the overloaded case also attain a minimum value around halfway to complete collapse, consistent with previous findings.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The crossover from -5/2 to -3/2 in burst statistics is explained analytically and provides a criterion for the imminence of complete failure observable from outside the system. The power-law divergence of χ and τ means the failure stress σ꜀ can be predicted without approaching too close to the actual failure point, through extrapolation from lower stress. The symmetry of the breaking rate minimum at t/t_f = 1/2 in the overloaded case implies a temporal landmark for remaining time to collapse. The distinct energy burst exponents (-1 below vs. -1.5 above criticality) provide a qualitative and quantitative signature to determine the system's relative state. The fact that these signatures are observable in a single system and do not require ensemble averaging has strong potential for practical detection applications.

Contradictions And Limitations
The uniform threshold distribution P(x)=x is chosen for simplicity; results may vary for other distributions though the 5/2 exponent is generally robust. The prediction from average burst size extrapolation assumes a clean (xc - x)⁰·⁹ scaling near the endpoint, which may be noisy in small systems or near-critical data. The χ⁻² extrapolation is valid only near σ꜀; the linear regime may be narrow, limiting the range from which extrapolation can be performed. The paper reports results from a single bundle (N=10⁷), and while the author claims single-system observability, ensemble averaging would strengthen the statistical confidence. The overloaded case requires the system to be slightly above σ꜀, meaning a controlled over-stress must be applied, which may not always be practical in real material monitoring.

Claims
The crossover in burst statistics from -5/2 to -3/2 provides a detectable precursor to imminent failure in a single system. The burst distribution shows a crossover from D(∆) ∝ ∆⁻⁵/² to D(∆) ∝ ∆⁻³/² near x꜀ as demonstrated in Figure 2. This crossover is explained analytically and is observable in the threshold interval (0.9x꜀, x꜀). The crossover signal alone only warns of imminent failure but does not provide a precise failure point without further information. Any signature in burst statistics detectable without disturbing the failure process has wide scope of applicability.
The average burst size ϵav scales as (x꜀ − x)⁰·⁹, enabling linear extrapolation to predict x꜀ from a single system trajectory. ∆ₐᵥ ∝ (x꜀ − x)⁰·⁹ is demonstrated in Figure 3 for the same bundle as Figure 2. Plotting Δₐᵥ⁻¹⁰/⁹ versus x yields a straight line touching the x-axis at x꜀ in Figure 4. The linear fit is shown near x꜀, implying the approximation may break down further from the critical point. The failure point x꜀ can be predicted in advance by measuring the average burst size, making it a practical detection tool.
Susceptibility χ and relaxation time τ diverge as (σ꜀ − σ)⁻¹/², allowing prediction of σ꜀ via linear extrapolation of χ⁻² and τ⁻². β = 1/2 and θ = 1/2 are the derived exponents for susceptibility and relaxation time respectively. Plots of χ⁻² and τ⁻² versus stress show linear behavior near σ꜀ with the dotted best-fit lines intersecting at σ꜀ in Figure 5. The linear regime is only valid near the critical point, limiting the extrapolation range. One can predict the failure stress value without approaching too close to the failure point.
The breaking rate minimum in the overloaded case occurs at halfway to complete collapse, and energy burst exponents distinguish below-critical from over-critical states. The minimum in R(t) occurs at t₀/t_f close to 1/2 for varying excess stress levels ϵ. Energy burst distributions have slope -1 for σ < σ꜀ and -1.5 for σ > σ꜀. The energy burst minimum is noted as a very recent finding from another study [20], not established here. The different power laws provide a qualitative and quantitative signature to determine whether a system is below or above criticality.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The crossover in burst statistics is demonstrated by comparing all bursts with those in the interval (0.9x꜀, x꜀), showing the effect depends on the spatial range of threshold sampling. The 5/2 exponent is shown to be universal under mild assumptions (quadratic maximum in p(x)), suggesting robustness against threshold distribution changes. The overburden ϵ is varied at 0.001, 0.003, and 0.005 in the breaking rate study, confirming the 1/2 position is robust. The energy burst distributions are tested at σ꜀ ± 0.001 and σ꜀ ± 0.002 to confirm the -1.0 and -1.5 slopes.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the fiber bundle model of composite materials: N elastic fibers with thresholds xi, all obeying Hooke's law with force constant unity. Figure 2 compares the complete burst distribution (D(∆) ∝ ∆⁻⁵/²) with the near-failure interval (0.9x꜀, x꜀) showing the -3/2 power law, based on N = 10⁷ fibers. Figure 3 plots average burst size ∆ₐᵥ versus elongation x, showing the (x꜀ - x)⁰·⁹ scaling behavior. Figure 4 shows the inverse of average burst size Δₐᵥ⁻¹⁰/⁹ versus x, demonstrating the linear extrapolation reaching x꜀. Figure 5 plots χ⁻² and τ⁻² versus stress, with dotted linear best-fits intersecting the x-axis at σ꜀. Figure 6 shows the breaking rate R(t) versus step t (upper) and rescaled t/t_f (lower), with R(t) minimum at t/t_f ≈ 1/2 for ϵ = 0.001, 0.003, 0.005. Figure 7 displays energy emission En versus step number at σ꜀, σ꜀+0.001, and σ꜀-0.001, showing distinct burst patterns. Figure 8 shows the energy burst distribution D(En) for below-critical stresses with slope -1.0. Figure 9 shows the energy burst distribution D(En) for over-critical stresses with slope -1.5.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is demonstrating that the fiber bundle model, under equal-load-sharing with uniform thresholds, yields three distinct, single-system observable precursors to failure: burst size extrapolation near the crossover, power-law divergence of susceptibility and relaxation time, and breaking rate minimum in the overloaded case. 2. The strongest evidence is the single-bundle simulation (N = 10⁷ fibers) reproducing the predicted power-law crossovers, the (x꜀ − x)⁰·⁹ average burst size scaling with linear extrapolation to x꜀, the linear χ⁻² and τ⁻² fits to σ꜀, and the R(t) minimum at t/t_f ≈ 1/2. 3. The future path lies in applying these single-system, non-invasive crossover and divergence signatures to real-world composite material fracture monitoring, with the crossover and extrapolation methods providing practical, externally measurable detection tools.

summary.title: Critical Correlations for Short-Range Valence-Bond Wavefunctions on the Square Lattice
summary.authors: A. Fabricio Albuquerque, Fabien Alet
summary.field_subfield: Condensed Matter Physics / Quantum Spin Liquids / Valence-Bond States
summary.type_of_paper: Theoretical study using Monte Carlo simulations of valence-bond wavefunctions
summary.executive_summary: The authors investigate a family of nearest-neighbor valence-bond (NN-VB) wavefunctions on the square lattice, which are SU(2)-invariant and characterized by topological winding numbers w = (wx, wy). The wavefunctions are defined as equal-amplitude superpositions of all dimer configurations within a fixed winding sector. Using Monte Carlo simulations with an algorithm combining non-local dimer updates and spin-overlap updates, the authors find that NN-VB states exhibit short-range spin correlations with a correlation length ξ = 1.35(1) and no long-range spin order. Crucially, the four-point connected dimer-dimer correlators exhibit power-law decay at large distances: longitudinal correlations decay as r−α|| with α|| = 1.16(4), and transverse correlations decay as r−α⊥ with α⊥ = 2.53(5). These exponents are smaller than the corresponding classical dimer exponents αc|| = 2 and αc⊥ = 3, suggesting a stronger tendency toward valence-bond crystal (VBC) order. Furthermore, longitudinal correlations are spatially modulated by a wave-vector Q = (2π/L)(wy, wx) determined by the winding numbers, a modulation that cancels upon division by a phase factor cos(Q·r). The dimer order parameter histogram exhibits no angular structure, favoring a continuous U(1) symmetry over discrete columnar or plaquette VBC patterns. The authors conclude that the SU(2)-invariant Hamiltonian stabilizing these wavefunctions should exhibit gapped spin and gapless non-magnetic excitations, corresponding to a gapped U(1) or SU(2) spin liquid state. A similar unpublished study by Tang, Sandvik, and Henley was acknowledged as having parallel results.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
The authors investigate a family of nearest-neighbor valence-bond (NN-VB) wavefunctions on the square lattice, which are SU(2)-invariant and characterized by topological winding numbers w = (wx, wy). The wavefunctions are defined as equal-amplitude superpositions of all dimer configurations within a fixed winding sector. Using Monte Carlo simulations with an algorithm combining non-local dimer updates and spin-overlap updates, the authors find that NN-VB states exhibit short-range spin correlations with a correlation length ξ = 1.35(1) and no long-range spin order. Crucially, the four-point connected dimer-dimer correlators exhibit power-law decay at large distances: longitudinal correlations decay as r−α|| with α|| = 1.16(4), and transverse correlations decay as r−α⊥ with α⊥ = 2.53(5). These exponents are smaller than the corresponding classical dimer exponents αc|| = 2 and αc⊥ = 3, suggesting a stronger tendency toward valence-bond crystal (VBC) order. Furthermore, longitudinal correlations are spatially modulated by a wave-vector Q = (2π/L)(wy, wx) determined by the winding numbers, a modulation that cancels upon division by a phase factor cos(Q·r). The dimer order parameter histogram exhibits no angular structure, favoring a continuous U(1) symmetry over discrete columnar or plaquette VBC patterns. The authors conclude that the SU(2)-invariant Hamiltonian stabilizing these wavefunctions should exhibit gapped spin and gapless non-magnetic excitations, corresponding to a gapped U(1) or SU(2) spin liquid state. A similar unpublished study by Tang, Sandvik, and Henley was acknowledged as having parallel results.

Research Context
The quest for quantum spin-liquid (QSL) states of matter dates back to Anderson's proposal that strong quantum fluctuations could drive an antiferromagnet towards a disordered state with exponentially decaying spin correlations. In the context of cuprates, spin-singlets in a QSL were interpreted as pre-formed Cooper pairs that would superconduct upon doping. While major advances including classification of QSL states and explicit lattice realizations have been made, a complete characterization of QSL states is still missing. The absence of magnetic order does not exclude valence-bond crystal (VBC) states that break lattice symmetries, precluding unambiguous identification of experimental QSL realizations. Nearest-neighbor VB states on the square lattice were previously identified as non-magnetic, but the possibility of other types of order, such as VBC, had not yet been excluded.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is to characterize the nearest-neighbor valence-bond (NN-VB) wavefunctions on the square lattice, which are arguably the simplest SU(2)-invariant wavefunctions capable of accounting for spin-liquid behavior. The authors hypothesize that these NN-VB states, defined as equal-amplitude superpositions of dimer configurations within fixed topological winding sectors, will exhibit short-range spin correlations without long-range magnetic order. It is conjectured that the four-point connected correlators between dimers will exhibit power-law decay, reminiscent of the classical dimer problem, but with different critical exponents. The authors predict that longitudinal dimer-dimer correlations will be spatially modulated according to a wave-vector determined by the topological winding numbers w. A key prediction is that a spin Hamiltonian stabilizing these wavefunctions as its degenerate ground states should exhibit gapped spin and gapless non-magnetic excitations, corresponding to a gapped U(1) or SU(2) spin liquid.

Methodological Details
The study investigates nearest-neighbor valence-bond (NN-VB) wavefunctions on the square lattice, defined by contracting adjacent spins into singlets |i,j⟩ = (1/√2)(|↑i↓j⟩−|↓i↑j⟩). Dimer configurations are split into topological sectors on the torus, labeled by winding numbers w = (wx, wy) defined as differences in B←A and A→B dimers along reference lines. Each winding sector is characterized by an equal-amplitude superposition of VB configurations |cw⟩ with fixed w, in contrast to Sutherland's approach which considered all NN-VB states simultaneously. The overlap between two VB configurations is given by ±2^NL − 1, where NL is the number of loops in the transition graph. Monte Carlo simulations are performed with periodic boundary conditions (PBC) of system sizes up to L = 128 (N = 128 × 128 = 16384 sites). For the dimer order parameter analysis, the angular dependence on φ = arctan(Dy/Dx) is extracted from the histogram P(Dx, Dy) of dimer order parameter values. The data for L = 96 with w = (0, 0) is used to analyze the dimer order parameter histogram.

Procedures And Architectures
The MC algorithm combines non-local updates for underlying dimer configurations to ensure small autocorrelation times with spin updates that sample the overlap weight with unitary acceptance rate. The algorithm is adapted from a recently introduced method (Sandvik and Evertz, 2010) and relies on the ALPS libraries. Topological symmetry is enforced by starting from a configuration in a given winding sector and refusing all MC moves that change w. Expectation values are computed using the estimator ⟨O⟩w = Σ ⟨cw,1|O|cw,2⟩ / (⟨cw,1|cw,2⟩⟨cw,1|cw,2⟩), where the estimator is evaluated by analyzing loop structures in transition graphs. Four-point connected correlators Cijkl = ⟨(Si · Sj)(Sk · Sl)⟩−⟨Si · Sj⟩⟨Sk·Sl⟩ are defined for NN sites i,j and k,l, classified as longitudinal (parallel dimers) and transverse (perpendicular dimers). The dimer order parameter Dα = N⁻¹ Σ_r (−1)^rα Sr · Sr+eα is used to probe quasi-long-range dimer order.

Key Results
NN spin correlations ⟨Sr·Sr+eα⟩ converge to a universal value of −0.295953(7) in the thermodynamic limit for all winding sectors, with finite-size corrections vanishing as L⁻². The spin correlation length is found to be ξ = 1.35(1) for L = 128 and w = (0, 0), confirmed by an exponential fit of (−1)^r⟨S0·Sr⟩ versus distance. Longitudinal four-point connected correlators Cijkl∥ exhibit power-law decay with an exponent α∥ = 1.16(4) for all winding sectors. Transverse four-point connected correlators Cijkl⊥ exhibit power-law decay with an exponent α⊥ = 2.53(5). In the classical dimer problem, the corresponding exponents are αc∥ = 2 and αc⊥ = 3; the smaller exponents for NN-VB states suggest a stronger tendency toward VBC order. Longitudinal correlations are spatially modulated by a phase factor cos(Q·r) with Q = (2π/L)(wy, wx); dividing by this factor collapses all curves onto the dx = 0 curve. The dimer order parameter histogram P(Dx, Dy) for L = 96, w = (0, 0) shows no angular structure, consistent with a continuous U(1) symmetry and against discrete columnar or plaquette VBC patterns.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The algebraic decay of dimer-dimer correlations indicates that the NN-VB states encode critical quasi-long-range dimer order, analogous to the critical behavior of classical dimer models but with a slower decay rate. The smaller exponents (α∥= 1.16(4) < 2, α⊥= 2.53(5) < 3) relative to the classical case suggest that quantum fluctuations reduce the effective dimension or increase the tendency toward valence-bond crystal order. Each |Ψw⟩ is a degenerate ground state of the Cano-Fendley Hamiltonian on a torus, and standard arguments predict gapped spin and gapless non-magnetic excitations for such a model. The classification places the ground state as a gapped U(1) or SU(2) spin liquid, which is believed to be unstable for a generic local spin model.

Contradictions And Limitations
A sign problem precludes Monte Carlo simulations of NN-VB wavefunctions on geometrically frustrated lattices, limiting the current findings to bipartite lattices. The work concerns wavefunctions and not the full spectrum of a given Hamiltonian, so predictions about gapless excitations are based on standard arguments rather than direct spectral analysis. The gapped U(1) or SU(2) spin liquid is believed to be unstable for a generic local spin model, and its stability under perturbations is not established in this work. Similar work by Tang, Sandvik, and Henley was announced concurrently with preliminary results, indicating potential overlap or competition in results. The exact value of L at which finite-size effects in Fig. 4(a-c) become significant is not quantified, only stated to increase linearly with L.

Claims
NN-VB wavefunctions on the square lattice exhibit critical (algebraic) dimer-dimer correlations with exponents α∥ = 1.16(4) and α⊥ = 2.53(5). Longitudinal correlations decay as r−α∥ with α∥ = 1.16(4) for L = 128 across all winding sectors. Transverse correlations decay as r−α⊥ with α⊥ = 2.53(5) for L = 128. Data are consistent with power-law decay over many decades of distance. Small deviations from algebraic behavior are seen for large distances in Fig. 4(a-c). The authors note this as a finite-size effect rather than a breakdown of power-law decay. The slower decay relative to the classical case (αc∥=2, αc⊥=3) suggests increased tendency toward valence-bond crystal order. The results connect the NN-VB wavefunctions to the classification of QSL states as gapless gauge modes.
Longitudinal dimer correlations are spatially modulated by a wave-vector Q = (2π/L)(wy, wx) determined by the topological winding numbers w. Dividing Cijkl∥ by cos(Q·r) collapses all curves onto the dx = 0 curve for various dx values. The modulation is confirmed by quantitative analysis [31]. Fig. 3 shows modulation in Cijkl∥ for non-zero w sectors (0,1), (1,0), and (1,1).  The modulation reflects the non-trivial phase structure imposed by topological winding on the torus.
The NN-VB state does not break discrete translational or rotational symmetries; the dimer order parameter histogram favors continuous U(1) symmetry over columnar or plaquette VBC states. The histogram P(Dx, Dy) for L = 96, w = (0,0) shows no angular structure. Data are in favor of a continuous U(1) symmetry. Columnar states would show peaks at φ={0,±π/2,π} and plaquette at φ={±π/4,±3π/4}, neither of which appear. The authors note that no angular structure is evident in the L = 96 data, but do not explicitly rule out extremely subtle VBC patterns. This further supports the interpretation of the NN-VB state as a U(1) or SU(2) spin liquid.

Data And Code Availability
The MC codes are based upon the ALPS libraries (Troyer et al., 1998; Albuquerque et al., 2007). The work was performed using HPC resources from GENCI-CCRT and CALMIP, and supported by French ANR program ANR-08-JCJC-0056-01.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The results for NN spin correlations and dimer-dimer correlations are checked across all four winding sectors w = (0,0), (1,0), (0,1), (1,1). Virtually identical results are obtained for different L values (L = 16, 32, 48, 64, 80, 96, 112, 128) and winding sectors. Anisotropy in spin correlations is evident for sectors (1,0) and (0,1) at small L but converges in the thermodynamic limit. The longitudinal correlations are tested at various dx displacements up to the anti-nodal line with phase Q·r = π at dx = L/2.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1(a) shows the transition graph between two NN-VB configurations on the square lattice with sublattices A/B, showing winding numbers w = (1,0) and w = (0,1) and a loop winding in both directions. Figure 1(b) plots NN spin correlations versus L−1 for winding sectors w = (0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1), showing convergence to a common thermodynamic limit value. Figure 2(a) plots spin correlation (−1)^r⟨S0·Sr⟩ between origin and site r for L = 128, w = (0,0); Figure 2(b) shows exponential fit yielding ξ = 1.35(1). Figure 3 shows MC data for rCijkl for L = 16 for all four winding sectors, with line thickness proportional to Cijkl, indicating the strongest correlation directions. Figure 4(a) plots Cijkl∥ for w = (0,0) across various system sizes; Figure 4(b) shows Cijkl∥ for L = 128 across all winding sectors; Figure 4(c) shows Cijkl∥ divided by cos(Q·r) for w = (0,1) for various dx; Figure 4(d) shows transverse Cijkl⊥ for w = (0,0). Figure 5 shows the dimer order parameter histogram P(Dx, Dy) for L = 96, w = (0,0), used to extract the angular structure of the quasi-ordered state.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the systematic Monte Carlo characterization of NN-VB wavefunctions on the square lattice, establishing that they exhibit critical dimer-dimer correlations with exponents α∥ = 1.16(4) and α⊥ = 2.53(5), placing them between the classical dimer limit and fully ordered VBC states. 2. The strongest evidence is the collapse of longitudinal correlations divided by the phase factor cos(Q·r) for all winding sectors, confirming that spatial modulation is entirely accounted for by the topological winding numbers, and the dimer order parameter histogram favoring continuous U(1) symmetry. 3. The future path includes extending the analysis to d = 3 (simples cubic lattice, Coulomb phase) and geometrically frustrated lattices, although a sign problem precludes the same MC approach for the latter.

summary.title: A quantitative measure for the organization of a system, Part 1: A simple case
summary.authors: Georgi Y. Georgiev
summary.field_subfield: Physics / Systems Theory / Complexity Science
summary.type_of_paper: Theoretical framework with simple illustrative case
summary.executive_summary: This paper proposes a universal quantitative measure for the organization of any system, positing that organization is inversely proportional to the total physical action of the system's elements. Drawing on the principle of least action, which governs physical dynamics, the author derives an expression for organization and applies it to a simple limiting case: a closed, two-dimensional system with one free particle element and one internal constraint. Key assumptions include free particles with zero potential energy, no energy dissipation, isotropic medium, and the application of Hamilton's Principle. The author derives that for the one-element, one-constraint case, organization is proportional to the cube of the reciprocal of trajectory length. In a comparative illustrative example where the least-action trajectory in one state is twice the length of that in a second state, the model predicts the second state is twice as well-organized as the first. The author argues this provides a long-sought quantitative criterion applicable across natural and social sciences for analyzing and designing complex systems. Future parts of the paper are designated to extend the model to multiple elements and time-dependent closed and open systems. The significance lies in grounding organization in the fundamental physical principle that actually determines trajectories, thus obviating the need to explicitly model constraint states. The paper acknowledges its limitations as a single-element, nondissipative model and positions it as a building block for a generalized multi-element framework.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper proposes a universal quantitative measure for the organization of any system, positing that organization is inversely proportional to the total physical action of the system's elements. Drawing on the principle of least action, which governs physical dynamics, the author derives an expression for organization and applies it to a simple limiting case: a closed, two-dimensional system with one free particle element and one internal constraint. Key assumptions include free particles with zero potential energy, no energy dissipation, isotropic medium, and the application of Hamilton's Principle. The author derives that for the one-element, one-constraint case, organization is proportional to the cube of the reciprocal of trajectory length. In a comparative illustrative example where the least-action trajectory in one state is twice the length of that in a second state, the model predicts the second state is twice as well-organized as the first. The author argues this provides a long-sought quantitative criterion applicable across natural and social sciences for analyzing and designing complex systems. Future parts of the paper are designated to extend the model to multiple elements and time-dependent closed and open systems. The significance lies in grounding organization in the fundamental physical principle that actually determines trajectories, thus obviating the need to explicitly model constraint states. The paper acknowledges its limitations as a single-element, nondissipative model and positions it as a building block for a generalized multi-element framework.

Research Context
Measuring the level of organization has been a long sought criterion in all sciences to evaluate system structure. The study of organized systems has intensified recently due to the increasing complexity of society and advances in natural and social sciences. Previous attempts to quantify organization have primarily relied on information theory and entropy-based concepts. The principle of least action has been applied to chemical, ecosystem, biotechnical, and reliability systems to explain functioning. There is a gap in a universal, quantitative model that can be applied consistently across different types of systems.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is how to quantitatively calculate the amount of organization in a general system. The main hypothesis is that the measure of organization of a system is inversely proportional to the sum of actions of all its elements. The author hypothesizes that because the principle of least action determines actual paths, action is the most natural measure of a system's state. The predicted outcome is that the model will provide a quantitative comparison between different organizational states of the same system under varying constraint configurations. The author expects the model to empower all natural and social sciences to quantify organization in the systems they study.

Methodological Details
The system under study is a closed, two-dimensional system with only one element and one internal constraint. The element is defined as a free particle not subject to external forces, meaning potential energy is zero. The boundaries of the closed system form a square, and positions of constraints are not explicitly calculated. The start and end points of the trajectory are fixed at opposite corners of the square. The medium is assumed to be isotropic, meaning properties are identical in all directions. The element does not interact with the constraint, and the constraint cannot block the path completely. The speed of the element and the mass are both assumed to be constants. There is no energy dissipation in the system, so the Lagrangian is constant. Hamilton's Principle determines the actual trajectory as the one with least action in each configuration.

Procedures And Architectures
The fundamental equation sets the variation of the sum of actions of all elements to zero: delta(Sum(integral(L_i dt))) = 0. The Lagrangian is defined solely as kinetic energy T = (1/2)mv² because potential energy is zero. With constant mass and speed, the Lagrangian is constant, making the action integral proportional to the interval of time. The organization measure is defined as Org proportional to the reciprocal of the sum of actions: Org ∝ 1/(Sum(I_i)). For the one-element case, the constant of proportionality is set to unity for simplicity. The isotropic assumption allows substitution of time interval with trajectory length, since speed is constant: t = l/v. The action integral for the one-element system becomes C * (l/v), where C is the constant Lagrangian. The final organization expression for the one-element system is Org = Const / (C * l³ / v²), or Org = C' / l³. Two states with different constraint orientations (Fig. 2a and 2b) are compared to demonstrate quantitative differentiation.

Key Results
The organization of a system is found to be inversely proportional to the cube of the trajectory length for the one-element case. In state 1 (Fig. 2a), the least-action trajectory is twice the length of the trajectory in state 2 (Fig. 2b). The mathematical comparison between the two states yields the ratio of organizations as (l1/l2)³. In the example where l1 = 2 * l2, the organization of state 2 is quantitatively twice as well-organized as state 1. The same result can be expressed as a 50% difference between the two organization values. The model shows that a state with half the action of another state has double the amount of organization. The derivation shows that constraint positions do not enter the calculation directly as they are reflected in trajectory length.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The model grounds organization in the principle of least action, the fundamental physical principle governing actual motions. The inverse relationship between action and organization implies that systems minimizing action are optimally organized. The significance is that it provides a quantitative measure for comparing different levels of organization in the same system. The model is designed to be extended to open systems and multiple elements, providing a general framework. Measuring organization should facilitate the development of all natural and social sciences by providing a universal criterion.

Contradictions And Limitations
The model is limited only to closed, nondissipative systems with one free particle as the element. The assumption of no energy dissipation (constant Lagrangian) excludes systems with real-world dynamics. The free particle assumption (zero potential energy) limits the scope to conservative systems. The isotropic medium assumption restricts applicability to uniform environments. The constraint is assumed not to block the path completely, and the element does not interact with the constraint. The specific one-element, one-constraint case is a limiting illustration; the general case requires multiple elements and arbitrary constraints.

Claims
Organization of a system is inversely proportional to the total physical action of its elements, grounded in the principle of least action. The model explicitly derives Org ∝ 1/(Sum(I_i)) from the principle of least action. The illustrative case demonstrates a quantitative twice-better organization when action is halved. The model is restricted to a very narrow set of assumptions (one particle, nondissipative, free particle) that may not generalize easily. If validated, this provides a universal criterion for comparing organization across any system type.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The single-constraint, two-state comparison serves as a validation of the derived formula for the simplest non-trivial configuration. The author explicitly states limitations and assumptions in a dedicated list to qualify the model's scope.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 presents the boundaries of the closed system as a square and defines the initial and final points of motion. Figure 2 shows a cartoon representation of the two states (a and b) with different constraint orientations and corresponding least-action trajectories.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the derivation of an organization measure for systems that is inversely proportional to the total physical action of their elements, rooted in the principle of least action. 2. The strongest evidence is the explicit derivation of the organization ratio (l1/l2)³ and its verification in the illustrative case where half action yields double organization. 3. The future path involves extending the model to systems with an arbitrary number of elements (Parts 2 and 3) and to open systems with time-dependent organization.

summary.title: Statistical mechanics of two-dimensional foams
summary.authors: Marc Durand
summary.field_subfield: Condensed Matter Physics / Soft Matter Statistical Mechanics
summary.executive_summary: This paper develops a statistical mechanics framework to describe the equilibrium state of a two-dimensional foam under macroscopic agitation. The author introduces a new state variable, the total cell curvature κ_tot, which replaces surface energy as the thermodynamic potential analogous to energy in conventional statistical thermodynamics. A microcanonical ensemble (N_B, κ_tot, N_s) is defined based on the postulate that all accessible microstates of a given set of bubbles filling 2D space have equal probability under slow agitation. A grand-canonical ensemble approach is subsequently used to derive an analytical expression for the probability distribution of the number of sides for a cell of given area. The model yields a distribution p_A(n) that correlates topological disorder (side distribution) to geometrical disorder (size distribution). When simplified by assuming the elongation e(n) is nearly constant, the result matches semi-empirical expressions conjectured by prior work but with size-dependent parameters. Comparison with four experimental datasets from Quilliet et al. shows the theoretical distributions reproduce experimental data well. The topological-geometrical correlation in the thermodynamic limit scales as ∆n/⟨n⟩     ≈ 0.27 (∆A/⟨A⟩)^0.8, which is consistent with experimental observations. The model requires no free parameters in the thermodynamic limit, but one fitting parameter is introduced when comparing to finite-N experiments. The author notes limitations regarding the validity range 1 ≪ N*_B ≪ N_B and suggests the formalism can extend to 3D foams and coarsening systems.

Executive Summary
This paper develops a statistical mechanics framework to describe the equilibrium state of a two-dimensional foam under macroscopic agitation. The author introduces a new state variable, the total cell curvature κ_tot, which replaces surface energy as the thermodynamic potential analogous to energy in conventional statistical thermodynamics. A microcanonical ensemble (N_B, κ_tot, N_s) is defined based on the postulate that all accessible microstates of a given set of bubbles filling 2D space have equal probability under slow agitation. A grand-canonical ensemble approach is subsequently used to derive an analytical expression for the probability distribution of the number of sides for a cell of given area. The model yields a distribution p_A(n) that correlates topological disorder (side distribution) to geometrical disorder (size distribution). When simplified by assuming the elongation e(n) is nearly constant, the result matches semi-empirical expressions conjectured by prior work but with size-dependent parameters. Comparison with four experimental datasets from Quilliet et al. shows the theoretical distributions reproduce experimental data well. The topological-geometrical correlation in the thermodynamic limit scales as ∆n/⟨n⟩     ≈ 0.27 (∆A/⟨A⟩)^0.8, which is consistent with experimental observations. The model requires no free parameters in the thermodynamic limit, but one fitting parameter is introduced when comparing to finite-N experiments. The author notes limitations regarding the validity range 1 ≪ N*_B ≪ N_B and suggests the formalism can extend to 3D foams and coarsening systems.

Research Context
Foams, emulsions, biological tissues, and polycrystals serve as a paradigm for a wide range of physical phenomena. Quilliet et al. studied topological features of 2D soap froths under slow oscillatory shear and reported an equilibrium state. The number of sides of every cell evolves through T1 events during macroscopic strain. Prior approaches to describe foam properties using statistical thermodynamics have relied on strong assumptions. These prior models used ad-hoc interaction potentials or involved empirical laws correlating size and side distributions. Previous maximum entropy models have been subject to controversy. None of the previous models can account for the correlations between topological and geometrical disorders reported by Quilliet et al. The pioneering work of Edwards on granular matter showed statistical physics could be extended to athermal systems.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether the equilibrium state of a 2D foam under slow agitation can be described using statistical thermodynamics. The hypothesis is that energy is not relevant for describing the macroscopic state, and total cell curvature should be the appropriate state variable. All accessible microstates of a given set of NB bubbles filling 2D space have equal probability under slow macroscopic agitation. The paper predicts that the distribution of the number of sides for a cell of given area can be derived analytically. The model predicts a correlation between topological disorder and geometrical disorder within a foam. The model predicts that the semi-empirical expression conjectured by other authors is recovered in a certain limit.

Methodological Details
The study considers a given set of NB bubbles with prescribed areas {Ai} on time scales shorter than bubble coarsening. The foam is considered in the dry limit where liquid volume fraction is negligible. Physical constraints are derived from mechanical equilibrium: Plateau's laws (120 degree angles) and Laplace's law. The balance of gas pressures implies every edge is an arc of circle with curvature κij = Pj −Pi / γ. Topological requirements include Euler's rule relating NB, N_P, and N_v, giving NP = 3(NB − c). The Gauss-Bonnet theorem applied to an n-sided cell yields the sum of edge curvatures equals π(n −6)/3. The paper distinguishes between unbounded foams (infinite/periodic) and bounded foams (free cluster, cluster within foam, or enclosed). For an unbounded foam, Ns = 6(NB − c) and κtot = 0 are conserved quantities. Jiang et al. reported energy fluctuations less than 2% in 2D foams under shear. Graner et al. obtained energy values of different metastable states within 2% of the ground state. Kraynik et al. reported surface energy fluctuations below 4% for 3D foams.

Procedures And Architectures
The microcanonical ensemble (NB, κ_tot, Ns) assumes all accessible microstates are equally probable. An idealized foam description replaces the rest of the foam by a mean field of identical bubbles. The cell curvature of an n-sided regular cell with area A is given by equation (5). The elongation e(n) lies between 3.74 and 3.71. The grand-canonical ensemble (NB, β−1, µ) treats Ns and κ_tot as fluctuating internal variables. The probability for a microstate (n1, n2, ..., nNB) is proportional to e−βκ_tot+µNs. β−1 and µ represent the effective temperature and chemical potential of the reservoir. The probability for a cell of size A to have n sides is p_A(n) = χ−1(A)e−βκ(A,n)+µn. When e(n) is assumed constant at 3.72, the distribution simplifies to p_A(n) = χ′−1(A)e−β′(n−6)2+µ′(n−6). β′(A) = πβ/(3e√A) and µ′(A) = µ −2πβ/(e√A). In the thermodynamic limit, ⟨Ns⟩/NB → 6 and ⟨κ_tot⟩/NB → 0. The thermodynamic limit corresponds to NB → ∞ with total surface area A_tot → ∞ and ⟨A⟩ = A_tot/NB remaining finite.

Key Results
For a monodisperse foam p(A) = δ(A −A0), the distribution of side number tends to p(n) = δn,6. All bubbles of an unbounded monodisperse foam have hexagonal shape in the thermodynamic limit. The average number of sides n(A) increases with A. The model reproduces experimental data from the four distributions in Quilliet et al. well. In the inset of Figure 4, the power-law fit of the correlation gives a = 0.30 ± 0.03 and b = 0.74 ± 0.08. The linear fit for the same plot gives a = 0.30 ± 0.02 and b = 0.03 ± 0.01. The power-law fit can hardly be distinguished from a linear fit. The model contains no free parameters in the thermodynamic limit. One adjustable parameter is added when fitting to finite-size experimental data due to unknown κ_tot.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Total cell curvature κ_tot plays the role of energy in conventional statistical thermodynamics. The distribution p_A(n) explicitly depends on bubble size A through β′(A) and µ′(A). This size-dependence is necessary to reflect the correlations between bubble size and bubble shape. The formalism allows derivation of the side distribution directly from the size distribution p(A). The method extends to 3D foams and to coarsening and coalescing foams. The formalism can also be extended to concentrated emulsions and cell aggregates.

Contradictions And Limitations
The model requires the condition 1 ≪ N_B* ≪ N_B, which cannot be checked on available data. A free parameter is introduced for experimental comparison due to the indeterminacy of experimental κ_tot values. The power-law fit of the size-topology correlation is hardly distinguishable from a linear fit. The idealized foam approximation ignores the curvature sum rule and Euler-Plateau relation between adjacent bubbles. The assumption that the rest of the foam constitutes a reservoir of sides and curvature may not hold for finite systems.

Claims
The total cell curvature κ_tot, rather than surface energy, is the appropriate state variable for describing the equilibrium state of 2D foam under slow agitation. Energy fluctuations between different metastable states are less than 2%. Different arrangements of bubbles do not affect the energy very much. κ_tot = 0 is a conserved quantity for an unbounded foam. The constraint κ_tot = 0 has always been ignored in previous theoretical models. For bounded foams, N_s and κ_tot are fluctuating variables. A new thermodynamic potential analogous to energy is established. Previous theories using energy or maximum entropy need revision.
The topological distribution p(n) is uniquely determined by the geometrical distribution p(A) through the derived side-number distribution p_A(n). The derived expression allows to correlate topological disorder to geometrical disorder. The model reproduces the four experimental distributions from Quilliet et al. well. The average number of sides increases with bubble area A. The fitting requires one adjustable parameter because experimental κ_tot is unknown. The power-law vs linear fit is not clearly distinguishable. The size distribution fully constrains the side distribution under the model.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The model was compared with four experimental distributions from Quilliet et al. [5]. The comparison of the relative standard deviation ∆n/⟨n⟩ vs ∆A/⟨A⟩ tested the correlation robustness across four different foams. The power-law and linear fits yielded similar results, limiting the strength of the correlation claim.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 illustrates the four boundary conditions for 2D foams: infinite, free cluster, cluster within foam, and enclosed foam. Figure 2 shows the equivalence between the sum over vertices and the sum over cells for total curvature. Figure 3 contrasts a real foam under shear with the mean-field idealized foam description. Figure 4 compares the theoretical and experimental distributions p(n), with the inset showing the size-topology correlation. Table 1 provides a direct analogy between the statistical description of an ideal gas and a 2D foam.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the introduction of total cell curvature κ_tot as the thermodynamic state variable replacing surface energy, enabling a statistical mechanics treatment of 2D foam equilibrium. 2. The strongest evidence is the successful reproduction of all four experimental p(n) distributions from Quilliet et al. and the agreement of the size-topology correlation with experimental power laws. 3. The future path involves extending the formalism to three-dimensional foams, coarsening systems, and concentrated emulsions, and confirming the zero-free-parameter model with further experiments.

summary.title: POWERS OF IDEALS AND THE COHOMOLOGY OF STALKS AND FIBERS OF MORPHISMS
summary.authors: MARC CHARDIN
summary.field_subfield: Mathematics; Commutative Algebra; Castelnuovo-Mumford regularity
summary.executive_summary: This paper provides a short proof of a refinement of a theorem by Kodiyalam and Cutkosky, Herzog and Trung concerning the Castelnuovo-Mumford regularity of powers of ideals over a standard graded algebra. The central result (Theorem 1.1) establishes that for a positively graded Noetherian algebra A, a finitely generated graded A-module M, and a graded ideal I, the limit lim_{t→∞}(end(H^i_A+(ItM)) + i - td) exists for any i, where d is the smallest degree at which the power I^pM = I^{p+1}M holds. This result implies a conjecture of Huy Tài Hà and generalizes a result of Eisenbud and Harris concerning ideals primary for the graded maximal ideal. The author further compares the cohomology of stalks with the cohomology of fibers of a projective morphism, showing that the maximum regularity over fibers equals the maximum regularity over stalks under conditions of 'near-flatness' (Hilbert polynomials differing by at most a constant). A concrete geometric criterion is derived: reg((It)^sat) = dt + b for t ≫ 0 holds if and only if the projection from the closure of the graph of the map defined by minimal generators admits a fiber of positive dimension. The paper also establishes that for finite morphisms, there is no difference between the regularity of stalks and fibers, and provides conditions under which the maximum regularity of stalks bounds that of fibers. The work builds on results by Kodiyalam, Eisenbud, Harris, and Hà, and is motivated by remarks from Bernd Ulrich and Joseph Oesterlé.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper provides a short proof of a refinement of a theorem by Kodiyalam and Cutkosky, Herzog and Trung concerning the Castelnuovo-Mumford regularity of powers of ideals over a standard graded algebra. The central result (Theorem 1.1) establishes that for a positively graded Noetherian algebra A, a finitely generated graded A-module M, and a graded ideal I, the limit lim_{t→∞}(end(H^i_A+(ItM)) + i - td) exists for any i, where d is the smallest degree at which the power I^pM = I^{p+1}M holds. This result implies a conjecture of Huy Tài Hà and generalizes a result of Eisenbud and Harris concerning ideals primary for the graded maximal ideal. The author further compares the cohomology of stalks with the cohomology of fibers of a projective morphism, showing that the maximum regularity over fibers equals the maximum regularity over stalks under conditions of 'near-flatness' (Hilbert polynomials differing by at most a constant). A concrete geometric criterion is derived: reg((It)^sat) = dt + b for t ≫ 0 holds if and only if the projection from the closure of the graph of the map defined by minimal generators admits a fiber of positive dimension. The paper also establishes that for finite morphisms, there is no difference between the regularity of stalks and fibers, and provides conditions under which the maximum regularity of stalks bounds that of fibers. The work builds on results by Kodiyalam, Eisenbud, Harris, and Hà, and is motivated by remarks from Bernd Ulrich and Joseph Oesterlé.

Research Context
The Castelnuovo-Mumford regularity of the power I^t of an ideal over a standard graded algebra was known to be eventually a linear function in t, a result by Kodiyalam and Cutkosky, Herzog and Trung. This result was first obtained for standard graded algebras over a field, then extended by Trung and Wang to algebras over a Noetherian ring. Cutkosky provided examples showing hectic behavior of ai(t) := end(H^i_{A+(It)}) as t varies, pointing out that the limit's existence does not imply all such functions are eventually linear. Eisenbud and Harris proved that for standard graded algebras over a field, for an ideal generated in a single degree and A+-primary, the constant term in the linear function is the maximum regularity of the fibers of the defined morphism. Huy Tài Hà generalized this result to the a*-invariant, conjecturing that a similar result holds for the regularity itself. The gap was the lack of a short proof and the comparison between stalk and fiber cohomology for non-finite or non-flat morphisms.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether the limit lim_{t→∞}(end(H^i_{A+(ItM)}) + i - td) exists and what it represents for positively graded Noetherian algebras. The paper aims to provide a very short proof of the refinement of the Kodiyalam-Cutkosky-Herzog-Trung theorem. The hypothesis is that this limit equals the maximum of the end degree of the i-th local cohomology of the stalks of the projection from the closure of the graph to its image, for ideals generated in a single degree. A corollary explores whether reg((It)^sat) = dt + b holds eventually and under what geometric conditions. The paper also investigates whether the maximum of regularities over stalks and fibers agree for families of projective schemes close to being flat.

Methodological Details
The setting is a positively graded Noetherian algebra A over a commutative ring R. M is a finitely generated graded A-module, and I is a graded A-ideal. The value d is defined as the minimum µ such that (I^≤µ)I^pM = I^{p+1}M for some p. The Castelnuovo-Mumford regularity is defined using end(H^i_{S+(M)}) and Tor-based invariants. Regularity over a scheme is extended by defining ai(F) := sup_{y∈Y} ai(F ⊗ O_{Y,y}) for a locally free sheaf F. The closure of the graph of the map defined by minimal generators is constructed as a key geometric object. Local cohomology and the torsion functor commute with localization on the base ring R. The notion of regularity over a scheme generalizes the usual definition with reference to a polynomial extension.

Procedures And Architectures
The proof of Theorem 4.1 constructs a bigraded S-module from J = I≤d and writes J = (g_1, ..., g_s) with deg g_i = d. The bigraded into map RJ → RI makes M_R_I a finitely generated bigraded S-module. Equality of graded A-modules H^i_{S+(M_R_I)}(∗,t) = H^i_{A+(M_R_I)}(∗,t) shows H^i_{S+(M_R_I)}(µ,t) = H^i_{A+(M_I t)}(µ) = H^i_{A+(I^t M)}(µ)+td. Proposition 5.1 uses flat base change and the fact that local cohomology commutes with localization to express the limit as a maximum over Proj(B'). Theorem 5.3 applies Proposition 5.1 by setting J = I and M = A. The comparison of stalk and fiber cohomology uses Lemma 6.2, which gives two converging spectral sequences with same abutment. Proposition 6.3 uses descending recursion on ℓ to compare regularity over a ring and its residue field. Lemma 6.4 proves equivalence between dimension of Tor and Hilbert polynomial differences using the Dedekind-Mertens lemma.

Key Results
Theorem 4.1: The limit lim_{t→∞}(ai(ItM) + i - td) exists for any i, and is at least equal to the initial degree of M for some i. Theorem 5.3: In the equal degree case, lim_{t→+∞}(ai(It) −dt) = ai(Γ), where Γ is the closure of the graph of the rational map. This proves the conjecture of Huy Tài Hà that the limit is the maximum of the a*-invariant on the stalks. Corollary 1.2: The limit lim_{t→∞}(reg((It)sat) −dt) exists, and the limit is non-negative iff the projection π admits a fiber of positive dimension. Theorem 6.9 (i): lim_{t→+∞}(reg((It)sat) −dt) = max_{i≥2}{ai(Γ) + i}. Theorem 6.9 (ii): If π admits a fiber Z of dimension i −1, then lim_{t→∞}(ai(It) + i −td) ≥ ai(Z) + i ≥ 0. Theorem 6.9 (iii): a_{δ+1}(It) − td = a_{δ+1}(Γ) for all t≫0, where δ is the maximal fiber dimension. Theorem 6.9 (iv): If π: Γ→W is finite, then reg(It) = a_1(It) + 1 = freg(Γ) + td for all t≫0. Theorem 6.9 (vi): If A is reduced and Hilbert quasi-polynomials of fibers differ by a periodic function, then reg(It) = freg(Γ) + td for all t≫0. Lemma 1.3: For a local ring (R, m, k) and S = R[X_1, ..., X_n], H^d_S+(M) ⊗ Rk → H^d_{S+(M ⊗ Rk)} is an isomorphism, and H^i_{S+(M)} = 0 for i > d.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The result implies that at least one of the functions ai(t) is eventually linear in t, though not necessarily all. The geometric criterion reg((It)sat) = dt + b holds if and only if there exists a subvariety V of the closure of the graph contracted in its projection. For a polynomial ring with n+1 variables, any graded ideal generated by n forms of same degree d satisfies reg((It)sat) = dt + b for t≫0 with b≥0. The same result holds if the analytic spread of the ideal is at most n. The comparison between stalk and fiber cohomology provides results covering those of Eisenbud-Harris and Huy Tài Hà. The work introduces regularity over a scheme as a key ingredient, generalizing the polynomial extension definition. The regularity of stalks bounds above the one for fibers under a weaker hypothesis (Hilbert polynomials differ at most by a constant).

Contradictions And Limitations
The existence of the limit does not imply that all ai(t) are eventually linear functions of t; only at least one is. For morphisms that are not finite or flat, the situation is more subtle, and Proposition 6.3 addresses this specific case. The equality in reg(M) = max{ai(M)+i} holds only when reg(M) < ∞, for instance if R is Noetherian and M is finitely generated. Lemma 6.4 requires R to be reduced and S to be standard graded; Remark 6.5 notes modifications for non-standard grading. The equivalence in Proposition 6.3 (ii) requires cd(Tor^1_R(M, k)) ≤ ℓ+1 for one direction and ≤ℓ for the other.

Claims
The limit lim_{t→∞}(ai(ItM) + i - td) exists for any i and is at least the initial degree of M for some i. Theorem 4.1 directly states the existence of the limit for any i. The lower bound is given as the initial degree of M for some i. The proof uses the bigraded S-module structure and Theorem 2.1 to bound ai(MIt). Cutkosky's examples show that not all ai(t) are eventually linear, only at least one. This implies the conjecture of Huy Tài Hà on the regularity of powers of ideals. It generalizes the result of Eisenbud and Harris for ideals primary for the graded maximal ideal.
reg((It)sat) = dt + b for t≫0 holds if and only if the projection π admits a fiber of positive dimension. Corollary 1.2 states the equivalence between non-negative limit and positive dimension fiber. The geometric criterion is stated as the existence of a subvariety V contracted in its projection. A simple example is given for n forms of degree d in n+1 variables. The condition is dim(π(V)) < dim V; if the projection is injective on V, the criterion is not met. The same result holds if the analytic spread of the ideal is at most n.
The maximum regularity over stalks equals the maximum regularity over fibers for families of projective schemes close to being flat. Theorem 6.9 provides conditions (i)-(vi) relating reg((It)sat) to fiber invariants. The Hilbert polynomial difference condition (differ at most by a constant) ensures agreement. For morphisms that are not finite or flat, the situation is more subtle, as noted in Proposition 6.3. This provides a collection of results covering Eisenbud-Harris and Huy Tài Hà.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The proof of Theorem 4.1 explicitly notes that only JIpM = I^{p+1}M for some p is needed, implying the result holds for all p sufficiently large. Lemma 6.1 (ii) provides the specific hypothesis cd(Tor^1_R(M, R/m)) ≤ 1 needed for the regularity equivalence. Remark 6.5 describes the modification needed for non-standard grading in Lemma 6.4.

Key Figures Tables
The paper does not contain figures or tables; it is a purely theoretical algebraic geometry paper.

Executive Summary
This paper constructs two N = 1 supersymmetric frameworks that accommodate the KF-type Lorentz-symmetry violating electrodynamics, characterized by the CPT-even tensor Kµνκλ with non-zero vacuum expectation value. The authors propose two different superfield backgrounds: a chiral superfield and a vector superfield. In the chiral case, the background is determined by a complex scalar S, which when linearly dependent on xµ, yields a constant K-tensor with a specific form not previously discussed in the literature. In the vector case, the full θ-expansion of a vector superfield Ξ is used to exactly reproduce the K-tensor as defined by the Kostelecký ansatz. Both constructions show that a constant background breaking Lorentz symmetry necessarily breaks supersymmetry, as the fermionic partners of the background acquire non-zero values under SUSY transformations. The authors provide explicit component-field actions including bosonic, fermionic, and coupled terms for both cases. A key physical prediction is that the auxiliary field D becomes non-trivially fixed by the gauge field strength Fµν even without matter coupling, and minimally coupled charged scalars may acquire a magnetic dipole moment. No numerical results or experimental bounds are reported; the work is purely a theoretical construction. The authors state that the exact time ordering of SUSY and Lorentz-symmetry breaking remains undecided, but they argue that Lorentz-violation signals SUSY-violation. Future work includes analysis of photon-photino mass splitting, propagator pole identification for the four gauge superfield components, and construction of a model where SUSY and Lorentz-symmetry break contemporaneously through vacuum condensation.

Research Context
The Standard Model Extension (SME) provides the natural framework for investigating Lorentz-violation properties. The SME has been used to establish bounds on photon mass, radiative corrections, and CPT-odd terms. A Planck-scale anisotropic vacuum has drawn attention from particle and field theorists. String theories suggest that Lorentz-symmetry and CPT invariance might be spontaneously broken. Very recently, a CPT-violating neutrino mass-squared difference order of magnitude less than the quark sector bound gave support to Lorentz-violation. The authors adopt the viewpoint that Lorentz-symmetry breaking may be triggered by vacuum condensation of a tensor field. At the scale of Lorentz-symmetry breaking, supersymmetry or its imprints may still be present. The authors state they lack elements to decide whether SUSY breaking precedes Lorentz-symmetry breaking, though the latter signals the former. Katz and Shadmi discussed vacuum expectation values violating Lorentz symmetry as a possible route to SUSY breaking.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether and how the KF-type Lorentz-symmetry violating K-tensor can be accommodated within an N = 1 supersymmetric framework. The authors hypothesize two possible venues for this construction: a chiral superfield background and a vector superfield background. They expect that in the chiral case, the background vector must be the gradient of a complex scalar, yielding a special form for the K-tensor. In the vector case, they expect to exactly reproduce the standard K-tensor ansatz with all its degrees of freedom. A key predicted outcome is that a constant Lorentz-violating background will necessarily break supersymmetry. They predict the auxiliary field D will be non-trivially fixed by the gauge field strength Fµν.

Methodological Details
The study uses a covariant superspace-superfield formulation to construct the Lorentz-symmetry violating actions. Both proposals utilize the minimal extension form (DαΩ)Wα(ḊαΩ)W for the chiral case and (DαΞ)Wα(ḊαΞ)W for the vector case. The standard Wess-Zumino gauge is adopted for the gauge superfield Wα. The background superfields are fixed; no Wess-Zumino gauge can be taken for the background Ξ as it is not a gauge super-potential. For the chiral proposal, the superfield Ω has dimension of mass to −1 and its maximum spin component is restricted to s = 1/2. For the vector proposal, the full θ-expansion of Ξ is used, including all components up to θ2θ¯2. Ref. [31] was used for the component-wise action calculations. The tensor Kµνκλ is assumed to be CPT even and satisfy specific symmetry and tracelessness conditions.

Procedures And Architectures
The K-tensor is defined by Kµνκλ = 1/2 (ηµκ˜κνλ − ηµλ˜κνκ + ηνλ˜κµκ − ηνκ˜κµλ) with ˜κµν being a traceless tensor. The chiral proposal uses the superfield Ω with component expansion S(x) + √2θζ(x) + iθσµ¯θ∂µS(x) + θ2G(x) + i√2θ2¯θ¯σµ∂µζ(x) − 1/4θ2¯θ2□S(x). The vector proposal uses Ξ with full θ-expansion including constant background components C, χ, M, ξµ, ψ, B. In the chiral case, the auxiliary field D is determined by D = −8κi∂µS∂νS∗Fµν/16 + 32κ∂µS∂µS∗ when ψ = 0 and G = 0. For the vector case, constant background SUSY transformations are derived with δC, δχ, δM, δξ, δψ, δB relations. The gauge-invariant action (7) is formulated as κ Z d4x d2θ d2¯θ / n (DαΩ)Wα(ḊαΩ)W + h.c. The vector superfield V in Wess-Zumino gauge is VWZ = θσµ¯θAµ + θ2¯θλ + ¯θ2θλ + θ2¯θ2D. The second vector proposal (action 30) uses (DαΞ)(DαΞ)WβWβ and automatically yields the ξλξλF² term.

Key Results
In the chiral proposal, the K-tensor is completely fixed by the gradient of the complex scalar: ˜κµν = κ [ (∂µS∂νS∗ + ∂νS∂µS∗)/2 − (∂λS∂λS∗)ηµν/4 ]. The chiral K-tensor satisfies Kµνµν = 0 and depends exclusively on the scalar gradient, with no ζ or G dependence. A constant ∂µS ensures constancy of Kµνκλ as anticipated. The chiral action reproduces the bosonic term κ/4 [ 1/2ξµξνFµκFκν + 1/8ξλξλFµνFµν ] plus additional fermionic and coupled terms. The vector proposal exactly reproduces the action (1) with the K-tensor defined by the Kostelecký ansatz equations (3) and (4). In the vector proposal, the bosonic part contains terms proportional to ξλξµFµκFκλ, ξλξλFµνFµν, and i/4ξλξµελτρκFτρFµκ. The auxiliary field D is non-trivially fixed even if V is not coupled to matter: D = −8κi∂µS∂νS∗Fµν/16 + 32κ∂µS∂µS∗. In the vector case, the background carries ξλ ̸= 0, fixing D by the gauge field strength Fµν. The fermionic partner content is richer in the vector case than in the chiral case.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The K-tensor form in the chiral case is a natural consequence of the assumption that a chiral superfield carries the Lorentz-breaking background. The automatic appearance of the ξλξλF² term in the chiral supersymmetrization is not a coincidence but an irreducible representation fact. The charged scalar particles (selectrons) may acquire a magnetic dipole moment given by ∇μ = ∇S × ∇S∗. The breaking of the Lorentz-symmetry by a constant background signals that SUSY is not an invariance of the background. The appearance of the ξλξλF² term in the vector case arises from the full θ-expansion of the vector superfield background. The important physical question is the influence of the Lorentz-violating background on the spectrum and the avoidance of tachyons and ghosts.

Contradictions And Limitations
The authors explicitly state they have no elements to decide whether SUSY breaking occurs before or after Lorentz-symmetry violation. The full SUSY-preserving nature of the action is not guaranteed; the backgrounds Ω and Ξ are not invariant under SUSY transformations. The authors acknowledge that their two proposals do not cover all possibilities; a second vector superfield action (30) exists but is not exploited. No propagator pole analysis has been performed; the authors note that getting the four gauge superfield propagators demands special technicalities not pursued in this work. The relation between SUSY and Lorentz-symmetry breaking is not established; the authors only note that Lorentz-violation signals SUSY-violation. The Wess-Zumino gauge choice for Wα is taken as usually done, but no such gauge can be applied to the background superfields.

Claims
A chiral superfield can accommodate the KF-type Lorentz-violating K-tensor with a specific form determined by a complex scalar gradient. The K-tensor is expressed as ˜κµν = κ [ (∂µS∂νS∗ + ∂νS∂µS∗)/2 − (∂λS∂λS∗)ηµν/4 ] and Kµνµν = 0. The bosonic action reproduces the expected K-type terms plus the automatic ξλξλF² term. The maximum spin of the background is restricted to s = 1/2, which may limit the generality of the Lorentz-violation description. The constancy of the K-tensor is guaranteed by the linear dependence of S on xµ. The K-tensor depends exclusively on the scalar gradient with no ζ or G dependence.
A vector superfield can accommodate the KF-type K-tensor exactly as defined in the Kostelecký ansatz. The vector proposal exactly reproduces the action (1) with the K-tensor defined by (3) and (4). The bosonic action contains terms proportional to ξλξµFµκFκλ and ξλξλFµνFµν. The vector case requires the full θ-expansion and no Wess-Zumino gauge choice can be made for the background superfield. The fermionic partner content is richer in the vector case, including mixing of χ and Ψ. The vector case introduces an additional term i/4ξλξµελτρκFτρFµκ not present in the chiral case.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The authors note that the supersymmetrization of action (6) instead of (1) does not yield higher-spin components in the background. The vector case contains an additional second way to build the supersymmetric extension using a different action (30) which is not exploited.

Key Figures Tables
No figures or tables are included in the provided paper text.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the construction of two distinct N = 1 supersymmetric frameworks (chiral and vector) that accommodate the KF-type Lorentz-symmetry violating K-tensor, revealing a specific form for the K-tensor in the chiral case not previously discussed. 2. The strongest evidence is the explicit derivation of component actions showing the K-tensor is fixed by the scalar gradient (chiral) or the vector background (vector), both naturally breaking SUSY and fixing the auxiliary field D. 3. The future path includes propagator pole analysis for the four gauge superfield components, photon-photino mass splitting investigation, and construction of a model with contemporary SUSY and Lorentz-symmetry breaking.

summary.title: B-Mode auto-bispectrum due to matter bounce
summary.authors: Rahul Kothari, Debottam Nandi
summary.field_subfield: Cosmology / Early Universe Physics
summary.executive_summary: This paper analytically derives and numerically evaluates the B-mode auto-bispectrum of the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) generated by a matter bounce Universe and compares it with the signal from standard slow-roll inflation. The authors motivate their work by noting that while the B-mode power spectrum is identical for both inflation and matter bounce at the end of both paradigms, their higher-order correlation functions—specifically the bispectrum—exhibit characteristic differences due to differing behavior of perturbations outside the horizon (freezing during inflation versus growth during bounce). The B-mode auto-bispectrum is formulated in terms of primordial tensor perturbations (gravity waves) in a minimally coupled Einstein frame. The analytical expression for the matter bounce bispectrum involves Wigner 3j and 9j symbols, leading to a sum over intermediate indices Li subject to selection rules derived from the triangle and parity conditions of the 9j symbol. The numerical evaluation requires resolving four (or five) integrals over momentum and configuration space variables. To compute this, the authors develop a binary search method for n-tuple storage to avoid repetitive integral evaluations and utilize the Rasch algorithm and open-source software (fgsl, wigxjpf) for Wigner symbol evaluation. Key quantitative results include: the highest bispectrum value for inflation is ∼6 × 10⁻¹¹ at (l₁, l₂, l₃) = (2, 15, 16), while for matter bounce it is ∼5 × 10⁻²³ (about 12 orders of magnitude smaller). The signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) at tensor-to-scalar ratio r = 0.01 and l_max = 100 is ∼10⁻⁵ for inflation, but only ∼10⁻¹⁸ for matter bounce, making the bounce signal ∼10⁻¹³ times smaller. The shape functions (normalized to unity) show stark differences across squeezed, folded, and equilateral limits. The authors also provide a new binary search algorithm for n-tuple retrieval that they believe has applications beyond bispectrum calculation.
