judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigates the impact dynamics of liquid droplets on heated surfaces across nucleate, transition, and film boiling regimes. The authors identify a novel droplet bouncing mode, termed 'bouncing-with-spray' (BWS), in which vapor bubbles formed within the liquid film burst at random sites, creating holes that cause the film to recoil in fragments rather than as a single coherent structure. This fragmentation mechanism dramatically reduces the residence time of the droplet on the substrate compared to the traditional 'retraction-bouncing' (RB) mode. The authors demonstrate through experimental measurements across six different water-glycerol mixtures that the BWS mode achieves a dimensionless residence time of approximately 1.4, a reduction of about 40% from the RB mode's dimensionless value of 2.3. A simplified theoretical model based on energy conservation and the critical condition that the vapor bubble radius at maximum expansion equals the minimum liquid film thickness is proposed. This model yields a scaling law, ΔT ∼ V⁻¹, that accurately predicts the transition boundary between RB and BWS modes in the film boiling regime and explains the observed behavior in the transition boiling regime. The approach is highlighted as a simple, reliable, and heat-induced strategy for reducing residence time, avoiding surface degradation or complex microstructuring. Key experimental parameters include droplet sizes of 1.6–3.4 mm, impact speeds of 0.9–2.1 m/s, Weber numbers of 10–180, and substrate temperatures from 260°C to 450°C using a polished silicon substrate heated by a copper holder. The study concludes that the BWS mode is independent of liquid viscosity, confirming that the mechanism is driven by bubble-induced fragmentation rather than viscous dissipation.

Research Context
Droplet impact on heated surfaces is a ubiquitous phenomenon with industrial applications in spray cooling, painting, inkjet printing, and fuel-spray impingement in internal combustion engines. Prior studies used high-speed imaging for morphology description and phase Doppler anemometry for secondary droplet analysis. On surfaces above the boiling point, droplets undergo nucleate, transition, or film boiling, with the Leidenfrost effect reducing vaporization rates at sufficiently high temperatures. For superhydrophobic surfaces, the contact time of a bouncing droplet is bounded by the Rayleigh time scale, and various strategies including ridges, lattice posts, and asymmetric geometries have been proposed to reduce this timescale. In the film boiling regime, a vapor layer acts as a lubricant, and residence time can be approximated by the period of a freely oscillating droplet. However, no strategy exploiting the boiling process specifically to reduce residence time had been identified. The authors note that the Leidenfrost temperature is influenced by surface roughness, surface structure, and impact Weber number.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether a boiling-induced mechanism can reduce the droplet residence time on heated surfaces beyond the traditional retraction-bouncing limit. The authors hypothesize that a specific bouncing mode, where vapor bubbles burst and fragment the liquid film, can reduce residence time significantly. A specific hypothesis is that this reduction is due to the burst of vapor bubbles in the liquid film, resulting in hole formation and recoiling of the film from these holes. The authors predict that the transition between the RB and BWS modes can be described by a scaling law based on the critical condition that the vapor bubble radius equals the minimum film thickness. It is further hypothesized that this transition model will agree with experimental data in both the film boiling and transition boiling regimes. The authors expect that the BWS mode will be independent of liquid viscosity, as the mechanism is fundamentally driven by thermal fragmentation rather than viscous dissipation.

Methodological Details
The experimental setup used a heated copper plate holding a polished silicon wafer substrate with roughness less than 0.5 nm. Droplet liquids included water, ethanol, and six water-glycerol mixtures with varying glycerol concentrations. Liquids were pushed through an injection tube at approximately 4 μl/s by a syringe pump (Harvard Apparatus, Pump 11 elite Pico plus). Two K-type thermocouples placed 1 cm beside the impact point controlled temperature with accuracy of ±1°C via a PID controller. Side-view and aerial-view images were captured using a Photron Fastcam SA1.1 high-speed camera illuminated by an LED light source. Droplet sizes were typically D0 = 2.8 mm for water/glycerol mixtures, 2.2–3.4 mm for water, and 1.6 mm for ethanol. Impact speeds ranged from V = 0.9 to 2.1 m/s. The Weber number, defined as We ≡ ρD0V²/σ, was varied from 10 to 180 across different liquids. The Jakob number, Ja ≡ cp(Tw −Ts)/ℓ, was used to indicate the ratio of sensible heat to latent heat. A customized Matlab program was used to measure droplet size, impact speed, and shape evolution from high-speed images.

Procedures And Architectures
Droplets formed at the tip of a blunt syringe needle and detached when gravitational force exceeded surface tension force. The impact morphology was characterized in three boiling regimes: nucleate boiling, transition boiling, and film boiling. For the transition and film boiling regimes, the residence time was defined as the interval between visual contact and visual detachment of the droplet. To test viscosity independence, glycerol concentration in water was varied across six mixtures (28%, 34%, 39%, 56%, 75% wt%) while keeping V and D0 constant. The dimensionless residence time was normalized as τ = q(ρR₀³/σ) for retraction-bouncing mode and similarly for BWS mode. The theoretical model derived the average heat transfer coefficient h using Poiseuille flow assumptions for the vapor layer. The critical condition was defined as rv ∼ bmin at the moment of maximum lateral expansion τ₀. A modified Grashof number Gr∗ ≡ gρv(ρl −ρv)R₀³/µ²v, a Prandtl number Prv, and a modified Fourier number Fo∗ were introduced for scaling. The spreading scaling Dmax/D₀ ∼ We^n with n = 0.35 was adopted for the film boiling regime. The transition boundary was plotted as ΔT versus V⁻¹ in a log-log format to validate the scaling.

Key Results
In the transition boiling regime at We = 37 and T = 380°C, the RB mode residence time was 12.0 ms, while the BWS mode at We = 69 and T = 380°C showed 6.5 ms. At We = 105 and T = 380°C (c2), the BWS mode showed 6.3 ms compared to the RB mode's 12.0 ms, with liquid finger breakup at the rim. In the film boiling regime at We = 25, the RB mode residence time was 11 ms at 400°C and 10.3 ms at 440°C. At We = 60 and T = 440°C (e1), the BWS mode showed 5.6 ms; at We = 129 and T = 440°C (e2), it showed 5.3 ms. The dimensionless residence time for the RB mode was approximately 2.3, while for the BWS mode it was about 1.4, representing a ~40% reduction. The BWS mode residence time was found to be independent of liquid viscosity across all six water-glycerol mixtures (see Figure 4). The experimental data in the film boiling regime agreed well with the theoretical scaling ΔT ∼ V⁻¹ (Figure 6d). In the transition boiling regime, the critical Weber number increases with substrate temperature, consistent with decreasing heat flux from the heated surface. The dimensionless residence time values (2.3 for RB, 1.4 for BWS) fall within the range of prior experiments (2.2 to 3.2). Figure 3 shows that vapor bubbles burst at random sites, producing holes and spray of tiny droplets, followed by film recoil in fragments.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The reduction in residence time is physically attributed to the burst of vapor bubbles that fragment the liquid film into smaller recoiling components, reducing the effective recoiling distance and coiling time. The mechanism is analogous to droplet bouncing on superhydrophobic surfaces with ridges, where ridges induce fragmentation; here, the fragmentation is induced by bubble bursting instead of solid geometry. The theoretical model shows that the BWS mode is favored when the vapor bubble radius at maximum expansion exceeds the minimum film thickness, establishing a clear physical boundary between the two modes. The scaling law ΔT ∼ V⁻¹ emerges because the heat transfer area to the vapor bubble scales with We^n, while film thickness scales with Re, and the time scale τ₀ is independent of impact speed. This heat-induced approach is theoretically superior to surface-patterning strategies as it avoids surface degradation and eliminates the need for complex micro-fabrication. The theory explains why the transition temperature increases with Weber number in the transition boiling regime: at lower temperatures, the maximum bubble size decreases, requiring a thinner film (higher We) to trigger bursting.

Contradictions And Limitations
The theoretical model assumes the heat transfer area to the vapor bubble A can be regarded as a constant across liquids, which may not hold perfectly for all geometries. The scaling exponent n = 0.35 was chosen for the film boiling regime; the authors acknowledge that different values (e.g., n = 0.39 in Tran et al.) may apply depending on surface structure. The authors do not report detailed numerical simulations or direct experimental measurement of the individual bursting bubbles, which they identify as open questions. The residence time in the film boiling regime is approximated as the period of a freely oscillating droplet, but this approximation has inherent limitations not fully explored. The paper does not specify a random seed or exact train/test split as this is an experimental study, but the range of conditions covered is limited to specific We and T values. The vapor layer thickness assumption of uniform δ in the heat transfer model may be an idealization not fully captured in reality. The paper does not report an error analysis for the high-speed image processing measurements of droplet size and velocity.

Claims
A bouncing-with-spray mode induced by vapor bubble bursting reduces droplet residence time by approximately 40% compared to the traditional retraction-bouncing mode. Dimensionless residence time fell from ~2.3 (RB) to ~1.4 (BWS), a reduction of about 40%. In the transition boiling regime, residence time dropped from 12.0 ms to 6.5 ms at We = 69. In the film boiling regime, BWS showed 5.6 ms at We = 60 and 5.3 ms at We = 129, vs. RB at 11 ms. The reduction is only observed at higher temperatures/We; at lower conditions (e.g., We = 37, T = 380°C), the RB mode still dominates with no spray. This heat-induced strategy provides a simple, reliable method for reducing residence time without surface modification. The mechanism can be exploited in spray cooling and industrial coating applications to decrease liquid contact times.
The bouncing-with-spray mode is independent of liquid viscosity, indicating the mechanism is driven by thermal fragmentation rather than viscous dissipation. Residence time remained constant across six water-glycerol mixtures with viscosities from 2.35 to 42.47 mPa·s (Figure 4). Viscous force is identified as not playing an important role in the fragmentation process. The paper does not test extremely high viscosity limits beyond 75 wt% glycerol, where the assumptions may change. The strategy is robust across a wide range of liquid types including oils and glycerol-water mixtures.
A theoretical model predicts the transition boundary between RB and BWS modes in the film boiling regime following the scaling ΔT ∼ V⁻¹. Experimental data points in Figure 6d agree well with the log-log scaling line. The model explains the trend in the transition boiling regime where critical We increases with temperature. The model relies on the approximation n = 0.35 and constant A, both of which have uncertainties. The scaling law allows for predictive selection of substrate temperature and impact velocity to achieve the desired bouncing mode.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Viscosity robustness: Six water-glycerol mixtures with viscosities spanning nearly 20-fold (2.35 to 42.47 mPa·s) were tested, showing the BWS residence time is independent of viscosity (Figure 4). Liquid type robustness: The phenomenon was observed for water, ethanol, and water-glycerol mixtures, confirming the mechanism is not liquid-specific. Regime robustness: The BWS mode and associated residence time reduction were observed in both transition boiling and film boiling regimes. Temperature robustness: The transition boundary ΔT ∼ V⁻¹ was verified across a range of temperatures from 380°C to 440°C.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1: Schematic side-view and aerial-view of the experimental setup with heated copper plate, silicon wafer, syringe pump, high-speed camera, PID controller, and droplet injection system. Figure 2: Morphologies of water droplet impact in nucleate boiling (We=37, T=260°C), transition boiling (RB: We=37, T=380°C; BWS: We=69, T=380°C; splashing: We=105, T=380°C), and film boiling regimes with residence times marked. Figure 3: Aerial-view image series (We=82, T=450°C) showing random bubble burst sites, hole formation, and liquid film recoil in fragments with spray of tiny droplets. Figure 4: Bar chart showing residence time of BWS mode for six water-glycerol mixtures (28% to 75% wt. glycerol) at D0=2.8 mm, V=1.2 m/s, demonstrating viscosity independence. Figure 5: Comparison of dimensionless residence time for RB (hollow circles) and BWS (solid dots) across different liquids and Weber numbers, showing the ~40% reduction. Figure 6: Theoretical derivation and validation: (a) energy balance schematic, (b) τ₀ independence of V, (c) Dmax/D0 scaling, (d) ΔT ∼ V⁻¹ boundary line, (e) regime map. Table 1: Physical properties of the six liquids (density, surface tension, dynamic viscosity, latent heat) supporting the viscosity and Weber number calculations.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the identification of the bouncing-with-spray mode, where vapor bubble bursting fragments the liquid film, reducing droplet residence time by approximately 40% compared to the retraction-bouncing mode. 2. The strongest evidence is the viscosity-independence of BWS residence time across six liquids and the excellent agreement of experimental film boiling data with the theoretical ΔT ∼ V⁻¹ scaling law. 3. The future path involves detailed numerical simulations and direct experimental measurement of individual bubble bursting events to fully characterize the fragmentation dynamics and further optimize the heat-induced residence time reduction.

Executive Summary
This paper constructs and proves the existence of a geometrically maximal abelian covering of the modular curve X0(p) over Q that is unramified outside the cusps. The central result, Theorem 1.2.2, establishes that there exists a cyclic covering f'p: X'2(p) → X0(p) of degree 2Np, where Np = (p-1)/gcd(p-1, 12), such that its restriction to the open subscheme Y0(p) (complement of the two cusps) is a geometrically maximal unramified covering over Q. The construction proceeds in several stages: first, general theory on abelian coverings of smooth curves is established, identifying the geometrically maximal unramified abelian covering with the kernel of a map related to the generalized Jacobian. Second, the Shimura covering X2(p) → X0(p) of degree Np, known to be the geometrically maximal unramified abelian covering by Mazur's theorem, serves as the base. The new covering X'2(p) is constructed as a quadratic extension of the function field of X2(p), generated by the square root of a rational function F2h constructed from generalized Dedekind eta functions (Siegel functions). The authors prove that F2h is a modular function on X2(p) defined over Q, its square root generates a quadratic extension whose geometric integrity and ramification behavior are controlled, and the resulting covering factors as f'p = f^p ◦ πp, where πp: X'2(p) → X2(p) is a degree-two covering unramified outside the cusps. The proof handles two cases separately: p ≢ 11 mod 12 (where generalized Dedekind eta functions suffice) and p ≡ 11 mod 12 (requiring a different product construction). For p=2 and p=3, the result follows by explicit description. The paper is self-contained and uses the theory of generalized Dedekind eta functions as a key tool.

Research Context
Mazur proved that the Shimura covering X2(p) → X0(p) is the unique geometrically maximal unramified abelian covering of X0(p) over Q. The degree of this Shimura covering is Np = (p-1)/gcd(p-1, 12). A curve Y admitting a degree one divisor has a geometrically maximal unramified abelian covering. However, no such description exists when no Q-rational point is available on the curve. The problem is to find a geometrically maximal unramified abelian covering of the open subscheme Y0(p) = X0(p) 	woheadrightarrow {0, ∞}.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether there exists a cyclic covering X'2(p) → X0(p) of degree 2Np that is unramified outside the cusps and whose restriction to Y0(p) is geometrically maximal. The authors hypothesize that such a covering exists, is cyclic, and factors through the Shimura covering. The predicted degree of the new covering is exactly twice the degree of the Shimura covering, 2Np. The hypothesis is that the construction can be achieved by taking a quadratic extension of the function field Q(X2(p)) generated by a specific rational function. The predicted outcome is that the function f'p restricts to a geometrically maximal unramified covering of Y0(p) over Q.

Methodological Details
The base curve is X0(p), a smooth geometrically integral proper curve over Q for a prime p. The open subscheme Y0(p) is defined as X0(p) 	woheadrightarrow {0, ∞}, removing the two Q-rational cusps. The Shimura covering f^p: X2(p) → X0(p) has degree Np = (p-1)/gcd(p-1, 12). For p=2 or p=3, the result is obtained explicitly via the identification Y0(p) ≅ Gm = P1 	woheadrightarrow {0, ∞}. For p ≥ 5, the construction uses generalized Dedekind eta functions (Siegel functions) defined by the product formula (3.2.1). The character group LD of the generalized Jacobian has rank rD = (P^x∈D[k(x):k] - 1) = 2-1 = 1. The module M_Tor = Hom(TeJ, Q/Z(1)) decomposes as (Q/Z)⊕(g_X + rD). The subgroup Jμ_Tor(−1) is cyclic of order Np by Mazur's result.

Procedures And Architectures
For p ≥ 5, let g be an odd generator of (Z/pZ)× and set k = Np = (p-1)/(p-1, 12), ℓ = (p-1,12)^2. Let Γ2(p) be the group generated by Γ1(p) and any matrix of the form [gk, *, *, *]^T. The index [Γ0(p) : Γ2(p)] is k and [Γ2(p) : Γ1(p)] is ℓ. For an integer h ≢ 0 mod p, define F_h(τ) = ∏_{j=0}^{ℓ-1} Eg_j_k_h(τ)^{6/ℓ}. Let ψ be the character of order 2 of SL(2,Z) and χ be the character of order 2 of Γ2(p) when ℓ is even. Define Γ'2(p) as the kernel of the character ψ^χ if p≡1 mod 4 and ψ if p≡3 mod 4 on Γ2(p). For p ≢ 11 mod 12 (ℓ ≠ 1), prove F_h(γτ) = ψ(γ)F_{ah}(τ) for γ ∈ Γ0(p). For p ≡ 11 mod 12 (ℓ = 1), use a different construction: G_h = (Eh_1Eh_2Eh_3)^2 with h_1^2+h_2^2+h_3^2 ≡ 0 mod p. The function field Q(X'2(p)) is obtained as a quadratic extension of Q(X2(p)) by adjoining the square root of F_2_h.

Key Results
Theorem 1.2.2: There exists a cyclic covering f'p: X'2(p) → X0(p) of degree 2Np. The restriction f'p|Y'2(p): Y'2(p) → Y0(p) is a geometrically maximal unramified covering of Y0(p) over Q. The covering f'p factors as f'p = f^p ◦ πp, where πp: X'2(p) → X2(p) is a degree two covering. πp: X'2(p) → X2(p) is unramified outside the cusps. The order of Mμ_Tor(−1) is either Np or 2Np, and the Shimura covering has order Np. The order of F_2_h at any cusp of X2(p) is odd and is zero elsewhere. Γ'2(p) is a normal subgroup of Γ0(p) and Γ0(p)/Γ'2(p) is cyclic of order 2k. The function field Q(X'2(p)) is a quadratic extension generated by a square root of F_2_h ∈ Q(X2(p)). Q is algebraically closed in Q(X'2(p)), ensuring the covering is defined over Q. The covering X'2(p) → X2(p) ramifies exactly at each cusp.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The result completes the classification of geometrically maximal unramified abelian coverings for modular curves by allowing ramification at the cusps. The factor 2Np arises because Mμ_Tor(−1) is a cyclic group of order Np and the generalized Jacobian's character group adds a cyclic component of order 2. The construction shows that generalized Dedekind eta functions are sufficient to construct all such maximal abelian extensions for modular curves. The factoring f'p = f^p ◦ πp implies the new covering is a central extension of the Shimura covering in the abelian sense. The distinction between the two constructions (ℓ ≠ 1 vs ℓ = 1) reflects the difference in the geometry of the modular curves X2(p) and X1(p).

Contradictions And Limitations
The result is specific to modular curves X0(p); it does not extend to general modular curves X0(N) with composite N. The construction requires p ≥ 5; p=2 and p=3 are handled by explicit identification with Gm, not the general construction. The result is for geometrically maximal abelian coverings; non-abelian extensions are not considered. The paper is a short note and does not address higher rank abelian extensions. The condition that the curve admits a degree one divisor is essential but automatically satisfied by X0(p).

Claims
There exists a geometrically maximal abelian covering of X0(p) unramified outside cusps which is cyclic of degree 2Np. Theorem 1.2.2 explicitly states the existence of a cyclic covering of degree 2Np. The restriction to Y0(p) is geometrically maximal unramified over Q. The factorization f'p = f^p ◦ πp confirms the structure. The order of Mμ_Tor(−1) being Np or 2Np supports the degree 2Np. The result is specific to p being prime; for composite N, the structure may differ. For p=2 and p=3, the general construction fails and a different approach is used. This extends Mazur's classification to the case of cuspidal ramification. The construction provides an explicit description via Siegel functions.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The proof is split into two cases (ℓ ≠ 1 and ℓ = 1) to handle all primes p ≥ 5. For p ≢ 1 mod 8, an alternative function z(τ) using the Dedekind eta function is noted as a modular function on Γ'2(p). The relation z(τ) = ± ∑ F_g_j connects the two possible generators of the quadratic extension. The construction uses the fact that g is an odd generator to ensure F_p+h = F_h.

Key Figures Tables
Theorem 1.2.2 gives the explicit statement of the main result with the factorization diagram. The commutative diagram in §2.4 illustrates the relationship between Σ(f) and ΣD(f). The exact sequence (1.1.1) defines the short exact sequence for the abelian fundamental group. The exact sequence (2.2.3) links JTor, M_Tor, and LD ⊗ Q/Z. The exact sequence (2.2.4) with the Tate twist is used for the final isomorphism.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the construction of a geometrically maximal abelian covering of X0(p) unramified outside cusps, of cyclic degree 2Np, factoring through the Shimura covering. 2. The strongest evidence is the explicit construction of the modular function F_2_h via generalized Dedekind eta functions, proving it has odd order at each cusp and is zero elsewhere. 3. The future path involves extending the construction to composite N, non-abelian extensions, or general modular curves with arbitrary cuspidal ramification data.

summary.title: Design of Real-time Semantic Segmentation Decoder for Automated Driving
summary.authors: Arindam Das, Saranya Kandan, Senthil Yogamani, Pavel Křížek
summary.field_subfield: Computer Vision / Semantic Segmentation / Efficient Neural Network Architectures
summary.executive_summary:
This paper addresses the computational bottleneck of semantic segmentation decoders in embedded deployments for automated driving, where a task-independent, efficient encoder is assumed to provide shared features for multi-task systems. The authors propose a novel non-bottleneck layer based on residual learning with cascaded skip connections, designed to handle high gradient flow and extract semantic information from a generic, non-specialized encoder. Using a VGG10 style classifier (10 layers) as a task-independent encoder with 256 feature maps at the final layer, the authors design and evaluate a family of decoder architectures under a fixed run-time budget. The decoder utilizes deconvolution layers for reconstruction, supplemented by two variants of the non-bottleneck layer: type-1 (combining 3x3, 5x5, and 1x1 kernels) and type-2 (adding dilated convolutions with 3x3 and 5x5 kernels). The encoder produces 256 feature maps, which are downsampled to 4 due to the four-class task (lanes, curb, road, void). Skip connections are pulled from the second and third-to-last encoder convolution layers. The proposed optimal configuration, combining various types of non-bottleneck layers between deconvolution stages, achieves a mean IoU of 0.7441 with a class accuracy of 0.6118 (Lanes), 0.6588 (Curb), and 0.9689 (Road). This represents a 10% absolute improvement in mean IoU over a baseline configuration, with higher gains for difficult classes (12% for lanes, 18% for curb). The decoder improves class-specific IoUs with less than 2ms of runtime overhead on custom hardware. The work contributes a generic decoder design applicable to any semantic segmentation task, demonstrating that architectural choices in the decoder are critical for efficiency-constrained applications.


The study uses an organization-owned dataset of 4,999 images (1280x384 resolution) with urban scenes, divided into 3,016 training, 981 validation, and 1,002 test images. Training involved pre-training the VGG10 encoder on ImageNet, followed by transfer learning with 350K iterations using the Adam optimizer, 0.0005 initial learning rate with polynomial decay, batch size of 4, and weight decay of 0.9. No data augmentation was applied. Results are reported as average class accuracy and IoU across four classes. The paper concludes that decoder design plays a critical role in segmentation efficiency and proposes meta-learning for automated architecture search as future work.

Executive Summary
This paper addresses the computational bottleneck of semantic segmentation decoders in embedded deployments for automated driving, where a task-independent, efficient encoder is assumed to provide shared features for multi-task systems. The authors propose a novel non-bottleneck layer based on residual learning with cascaded skip connections, designed to handle high gradient flow and extract semantic information from a generic, non-specialized encoder. Using a VGG10 style classifier (10 layers) as a task-independent encoder with 256 feature maps at the final layer, the authors design and evaluate a family of decoder architectures under a fixed run-time budget. The decoder utilizes deconvolution layers for reconstruction, supplemented by two variants of the non-bottleneck layer: type-1 (combining 3x3, 5x5, and 1x1 kernels) and type-2 (adding dilated convolutions with 3x3 and 5x5 kernels). The encoder produces 256 feature maps, which are downsampled to 4 due to the four-class task (lanes, curb, road, void). Skip connections are pulled from the second and third-to-last encoder convolution layers. The proposed optimal configuration, combining various types of non-bottleneck layers between deconvolution stages, achieves a mean IoU of 0.7441 with a class accuracy of 0.6118 (Lanes), 0.6588 (Curb), and 0.9689 (Road). This represents a 10% absolute improvement in mean IoU over a baseline configuration, with higher gains for difficult classes (12% for lanes, 18% for curb). The decoder improves class-specific IoUs with less than 2ms of runtime overhead on custom hardware. The work contributes a generic decoder design applicable to any semantic segmentation task, demonstrating that architectural choices in the decoder are critical for efficiency-constrained applications.


The study uses an organization-owned dataset of 4,999 images (1280x384 resolution) with urban scenes, divided into 3,016 training, 981 validation, and 1,002 test images. Training involved pre-training the VGG10 encoder on ImageNet, followed by transfer learning with 350K iterations using the Adam optimizer, 0.0005 initial learning rate with polynomial decay, batch size of 4, and weight decay of 0.9. No data augmentation was applied. Results are reported as average class accuracy and IoU across four classes. The paper concludes that decoder design plays a critical role in segmentation efficiency and proposes meta-learning for automated architecture search as future work.

Research Context
Semantic segmentation provides complete scene understanding where each pixel receives a class label, with applications in automated driving and augmented reality. CNN architectures grow consistently, creating a computational bound for embedded platforms with limited resources. Efficient encoder design has received significant research, but decoders remain computationally expensive for the semantic segmentation task. Existing methods like SegNet (max-pooling indices) and UNet (intermediate feature maps) use encoder-mirror or specialized decoders. Prior work has explored dilated convolutions (DeepLab2), spatial pyramid pooling, CRF, multi-path refinement (RefineNet), and multi-column encoders (ContextNet). Mobile-targeted works like ENet and ICNet use lightweight encoders but do not support multi-task learning with task-independent encoders. The authors note that the encoder design in most existing works is specific to semantic segmentation, limiting multi-task applicability. There is a gap in prior work using a task-independent lightweight encoder combined with a specially designed decoder for embedded real-time budgets.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether a novel, efficient, task-independent decoder can improve semantic segmentation performance under a fixed run-time budget on embedded platforms. The authors hypothesize that a non-bottleneck layer based on residual learning with cascaded skip connections can overcome the information gap left by a generic, non-semantic encoder. They predict that incorporating multiple kernel sizes (1x1, 3x3, 5x5) and dilated convolutions in the decoder will extract semantic features that the task-independent encoder cannot provide. A specific hypothesis is that the non-bottleneck layer's multiple skip connections will distribute high gradients during backpropagation, making it suitable for embedded platforms. They further hypothesize that the best decoder configuration among a family of variants will outperform a standard FCN baseline within the runtime constraints. The predicted outcome is a measurable improvement in IoU, especially for under-represented classes (lanes, curb), with minimal runtime overhead. The authors assume an efficient, task-independent encoder is already designed for a multi-task learning system, shifting the focus entirely to the decoder. The decoder is intended to be generic, usable for any segmentation task with the same encoder input.

Methodological Details
The study uses an organization-owned dataset of urban scene images with 1280x384 resolution. Four critical classes are targeted: lanes, curb, road, and void (everything else). The dataset is split into 3,016 training images, 981 validation images, and 1,002 test images. Each image has a single-channel annotation where each pixel has only one class label. The encoder is a VGG style classifier with 10 layers, trained from scratch on ImageNet and then transferred for this task. The encoder produces a total of 256 feature maps at its last layer. Convolution layers use 5x5 kernels followed by Batch Normalization and ReLU activation. Training uses the Adam optimizer with a batch size of 4 and weight decay of 0.9. Initial learning rate is 0.0005 with standard polynomial decay over 350,000 iterations. No dropout is used in the model. No data augmentation techniques were performed during training. All experiments are executed using the Keras framework on an NVIDIA Titan X 12G GPU with 24 GB RAM. The decoder downsamples feature maps from 256 to 4, corresponding to the four output classes. Skip connections are pulled from the second and third-to-last convolution layers of the encoder. The decoder uses deconvolution layers for reconstruction instead of max-unpooling. The experimental setting aims at embedded platform constraints with restricted feature counts.

Procedures And Architectures
The overall network consists of a two-part encoder-decoder structure with VGG10 as the shared encoder. The non-bottleneck layer contains 1D kernels to extract directional information and 3D kernels for gathering features from a larger receptive area. Dense information is extracted through multiple kernels with sizes 3x3, 5x5, and 1x1, and the resulting features are fused. The fused features are then merged with the input features to the same non-bottleneck layer, creating a residual-like structure. The non-bottleneck layer has two variants: type-1 (standard) and type-2 (using dilated convolution with 3x3 and 5x5 kernels). The dilation rate for dilated convolution is kept constant at 1 for the present work to manage computational cost. The optimal configuration uses non-bottleneck layers of type-1 after the first deconvolution, and multiple type-2 layers after the second, third, and fourth deconvolution. There is no non-bottleneck layer used after the fourth deconvolution. The decoder is wider than the encoder, and the encoder consumes most of the run time. Group convolution was considered but found to have adverse effects on lightweight networks. The training follows a transfer learning approach: pre-training on ImageNet followed by end-to-end training on the target dataset. Layer-wise training in a supervised fashion was considered for the lightweight encoder. The decoder architecture is illustrated in Figure 3 and the non-bottleneck layers in Figure 2. Results for all decoder variants are reported in Table 1.

Key Results
The optimal decoder configuration achieves a mean IoU of 0.7441 across all four classes. The optimal configuration shows a 10% improvement in mean IoU over the baseline configuration. For the lanes class, the IoU improves by 12% from the baseline. For the curb class, the IoU improves by 18% from the baseline. The optimal configuration achieves class-specific IoUs of 0.5304 (Lanes), 0.4696 (Curb), and 0.9314 (Road). The average class accuracy for the optimal configuration is 0.6118, with 0.6588 for Curb and 0.9689 for Road. The non-bottleneck layers worked better for the curb class without even attempting data augmentation or class weighting. There was a slight deterioration in IoU for the lanes class in the best configuration compared to the baseline. The proposed optimal decoder shows less than 2ms increase in runtime compared to a standard FCN decoder on custom hardware. The FCN baseline achieves a mean IoU of 0.7255 with class accuracy scores of 0.5678, 0.6228, and 0.9688 for Lanes, Curb, and Road respectively. The decoder without second skip connection (D2) drops the mean IoU to 0.6989. The decoder with larger batch size 8 (D3) achieves a mean IoU of 0.7038. The configuration without 1x1 convolution (D4) yields a mean IoU of 0.7013. The 3x1, 1x3 convolution variant (D5) achieves a mean IoU of 0.6866. The configuration with 2x2, 3x3, 5x5 deconvolution kernels (D7) shows the worst performance at mean IoU 0.6458.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The non-bottleneck layer's multiple skip connections distribute incoming gradients during backpropagation, preventing vanishing/exploding gradients in shallow networks. Dilated convolutions in type-2 non-bottleneck layers expand the field-of-view while maintaining resolution, capturing broader spatial context. The cascaded structure allows the decoder to learn semantic information not captured by the task-independent encoder. The design choice to use different non-bottleneck types at different deconvolution stages addresses the increasing semantic depth required for reconstruction. The results demonstrate that decoder architecture design is a critical lever for efficiency-constrained semantic segmentation, independent of encoder choice. The 1D and 3D kernel combination allows for both directional and broad receptive field feature extraction, balancing specificity and context. The work implies that for embedded applications, the decoder should be tuned after the encoder is fixed to maximize performance within the remaining runtime budget.

Contradictions And Limitations
The paper acknowledges that the encoder consumes most of the run time because it is much wider than the decoder, limiting the scope of decoder-only improvements. No data augmentation techniques were used, and no class weighting was applied, which may limit generalization to highly imbalanced scenarios. The dilation rate was kept constant at 1; the authors note that incremental dilation could improve accuracy but is computationally expensive. The dataset is small (4,999 images), and the model is shallow, leading to a high risk of overfitting which was not quantitatively analyzed. The optimal configuration showed slight deterioration in IoU for the lanes class, indicating the decoder design does not uniformly benefit all classes. The work uses a specific, organization-owned dataset and does not report cross-dataset validation. The decoder's performance is tied to the specific VGG10 encoder; it is unclear how generalizable the architecture is to different encoder families. The paper mentions that group convolution was tested but found to have adverse effects, yet doesn't provide detailed ablation results for other potential alternatives.

Claims
The proposed optimal decoder configuration improves mean IoU by 10% (absolute) over the FCN baseline with less than 2ms of additional runtime. The optimal configuration achieves a mean IoU of 0.7441 versus 0.7255 for the FCN baseline. This corresponds to a 10% improvement from the baseline configuration. The runtime increase is less than 2ms on custom hardware. The IoU for the lanes class slightly deteriorated in the optimal configuration. The encoder still accounts for most of the run time, limiting the overall impact of decoder changes. Decoder design is a valid, low-cost optimization point for embedded semantic segmentation. Architectural modifications can yield significant gains even when the encoder is fixed.
The non-bottleneck layer with cascaded skip connections effectively addresses high gradient flow issues in shallow residual networks. The original residual strategy is modified with multiple skip connections to distribute gradients. The multiple skip connections help handle high gradient flow during back-propagation. The design addresses the fact that residual learning for lesser depth is inefficient. The paper does not provide an ablation on the specific number of skip connections. The improvement is shown primarily through IoU, not gradient norm analysis. This residual variant can be applied to other shallow architecture designs for embedded targets.
The optimal decoder configuration provides the highest IoU gains for the most difficult classes (lanes and curb). Curb IoU improves from 0.6228 to 0.6588 (+18%). Lanes IoU improves from 0.5678 to 0.6118 (+12%). The non-bottleneck layers worked better for curb without any data augmentation. The lanes IoU still shows slight deterioration compared to the baseline in the optimal configuration. The decoder design is particularly effective for small, difficult-to-segment classes in urban scenes.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The authors evaluated eight different decoder configurations (D1–D8) and various non-bottleneck layer combinations to isolate the effect of each component. Table 1 shows the performance of D1 through D8 and various (mN) combinations, providing a systematic ablation of non-bottleneck layers. D2 removes the second skip connection from the encoder, demonstrating its importance (mean IoU drops from 0.7255 to 0.6989). D3 doubles the batch size to 8, showing a marginal improvement to 0.7038. D4 removes the 1x1 convolution before 3x3 and 5x5, yielding 0.7013. D7 uses varying deconvolution kernel sizes (2x2, 3x3, 5x5) and performs worst at 0.6458. The authors report that the optimal configuration was reached after 'several optimization efforts' but don't detail the exact search procedure. No explicit sensitivity analysis on hyperparameter values (other than batch size) is reported.

Key Figures Tables

Executive Summary
This paper establishes a Lusin area integral characterisation of Hardy spaces associated with Hermite operators for indices p ∈ (0, 1] in dimension d ≥ 3. The Hermite operator L = -Δ + |x|² is defined via a sesquilinear form on C∞_c(Rd), generating a contraction C0-semigroup T on L2(Rd) and an associated Poisson semigroup P. The authors define the Hardy space Hp_L(Rd) as the completion of f ∈ L2(Rd) such that the maximal function MLf(·) = sup_{t>0} |T_t f(·)| belongs to Lp(Rd), equipped with the quasi-norm ||·|| = ||ML·||_Lp.

The main result (Theorem 1.1) proves that Hp_L(Rd) is isomorphic to the space Hp_S(Rd) defined via the Lusin area integral Sf(x) := (∫_{Γ(x)} t^{1-d} |∇_L P_t f(y)|² dy dt)^{1/2}, where the gradient operator is given by the Hermite-specific form ∇_L = (∂_t, ∂_1 + x₁, ..., ∂_d + x_d). The proof proceeds through several intermediate spaces: first, Hp_L(Rd) is shown to be contained in Hp_L,max(Rd); second, a characterisation Hp_L(Rd) = Hp_A(Rd) ∩ L2(Rd) is established using tent space techniques; third, an atomic decomposition of Hp_L,at,M(Rd) is constructed with (p, 2, M)-atoms and identified with the intersection space.

A second main result (Theorem 1.2) asserts that the Riesz transforms RL_j := (∂_j + x_j) L^{-1/2} are bounded on Hp_L(Rd) for all j ∈ {1, 2, ...}. The approach utilizes the atom decomposition, kernel estimates for the Hermite heat and Poisson kernels (from [JPY16]), and interpolation arguments. The work extends the index range from p = 1 (covered by [Jiz12]) to the full p ∈ (0, 1] range, employing derivatives ∂_j + x_j first suggested by Thangavelu in [Tha90] that are specific to the Hermite operator structure.

Research Context
Hermite operators play a significant role in the quantum harmonic oscillator, and their properties have been studied extensively. Hardy spaces with rich structures are of fundamental interest in harmonic analysis, as established in the landmark monograph by Stein. Prior work by Jiz (2012) established Hardy space results associated with Hermite operators but only for the index p = 1. Similar Lusin area integral characterisations exist in the literature for more standard operators, but the Hermite case was left open for the general index range. The derivative operators ∂_j + x_j were first suggested by Thangavelu and are specific to the Hermite operator structure.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether the Hardy spaces Hp_L(Rd) associated with Hermite operators for 0 < p ≤ 1 can be characterised via Lusin area integrals defined with Hermite-specific gradients. The specific gradient operator to be tested is ∇_L = (∂_t, ∂_1 + x₁, ..., ∂_d + x_d), a generalization of the classical Lusin area integral structure. The authors hypothesize that the completion of L2 functions whose maximal function belongs to Lp is equivalent to the completion of functions whose Lusin area integral belongs to Lp. A secondary hypothesis is that the Riesz transforms RL_j := (∂_j + x_j) L^{-1/2} are bounded on these Hardy spaces for all j ∈ {1, 2, ...}. The dimension constraint d ≥ 3 is imposed, motivated by the spectral properties and kernel decay of the Hermite operator.

Methodological Details
The dimension is restricted to d ∈ {3, 4, 5, ...}, and the Hardy space index is p ∈ (0, 1]. The Hermite operator L = -Δ + |x|² is defined as the operator associated with the closure of the sesquilinear form a0(u, v) = ∫ Rd Du · Dv + |x|²u v on C∞_c(Rd). The space Hp_L(Rd) is defined as the completion of {f ∈ L2(Rd) : MLf ∈ Lp(Rd)} under the quasi-norm ||f|| = ||MLf||_Lp. The Lusin integral Sf is defined over the cone Γ(x) := {(y, t) ∈ Rd × (0, ∞) : |x − y| < t}, weighted by t^{1-d} and involving the Hermite gradient ∇_L = (∂_t, ∂_1 + x₁, ..., ∂_d + x_d). The auxiliary space Hp_L,max(Rd) is defined via the maximal function f*L(x) = sup{|x−y|<t} |P_t f(y)|. The intermediate space Hp_A(Rd) is defined via the operator Af(x) = (∫_{|x−y|<t} t^{1-d} |∂_t P_t f(y)|² dy dt)^{1/2}, where the t-derivative acts on the heat/Poisson kernel. An atomic decomposition is provided: for d/(d+δ) < p ≤ 1, every f ∈ Hp_L(Rd) decomposes into Lp sum of atoms a_j satisfying a specific support, size, and moment condition. For the second result, the space Hp_{L+2}(Rd) is defined using ML+2 f(·) = sup_{t>0} |e^{-(L+2)t} f(·)|, where L+2 denotes the operator L shifted by 2 units in the spectrum. The Riesz transforms are defined as RL_j := (∂_j + x_j) L^{-1/2}, where L^{-1/2} is understood in the spectral sense.

Procedures And Architectures
Kernel estimates for the Hermite heat kernel g_t and Poisson kernel p_t are established with Gaussian decay combined with polynomial weights in the weighted distance ρ(x) = 1 / (1 + |x|). Specifically, the heat kernel satisfies g_t(x, y) ≤ C_N t^{-d/2} e^{-C|x−y|²/t} (1 + √t ρ(x))^{-N} (1 + √t ρ(y))^{-N}. The Poisson kernel satisfies p_t(x, y) ≤ C_N t (t + 2|x−y|)^{d+1} (1 + √t ρ(x))^{-N} (1 + √t ρ(y))^{-N}, providing a heavy-tail polynomial decay in space. The atom decomposition uses (p, 2, M)-atoms a = L^M b with L^k b supported in B and weighted estimates on the moments for k = 0, ..., M. The proof of Hp_L = Hp_S employs a combination of the maximal function inequality, tent space techniques, and a localization argument with ε, R parameters. The tent space operator π_{Ψ,L} is defined by integrating Ψ(t^{1/2}L) F(·, t) dt/t to relate T^2_2 tent space atoms to (p, 2, M)-atoms. The Riesz transform boundedness is proven by first establishing boundedness on Hp_{L+2}(Rd) ∩ L2(Rd) and then extending by density to Hp_L(Rd). The identity RL_j f = (∂_j + x_j) L^{-1/2} f = t(∂_j + x_j) e^{-t(L+2)^{1/2}} f in the spectral representation allows transferring the L2-boundedness of A to the Lp-estimate.

Key Results
Theorem 1.1: The Hardy space Hp_L(Rd) is equivalent to Hp_S(Rd), i.e., the Lusin area integral characterisation holds for all p ∈ (0, 1] and d ≥ 3. The inclusion Hp_L(Rd) ⊂ Hp_{L,max}(Rd) holds for d/(d+δ) < p ≤ 1, where δ is the exponent from the kernel regularity estimates. The characterisation Hp_L(Rd) = Hp_A(Rd) ∩ L2(Rd) is established via the operator A defined with the t-derivative of the Poisson semigroup. The space Hp_{L,at,M}(Rd) of atomic representations is shown to coincide with Hp_A(Rd) ∩ L2(Rd) as quasi-normed spaces for M > d/(2(1/p - 1/2)) ∨ 1. Theorem 1.2: The Riesz transforms RL_j = (∂_j + x_j) L^{-1/2} are bounded on Hp_L(Rd) for all j ∈ {1, 2, ...}. The density result: L2_c(Rd) is dense in both Hp_L(Rd) and Hp_{L+2}(Rd), enabling extension of boundedness from L2 to Lp. The inequality ||S_ε,R^α f||_Lp ≈ ||S_ε,R^β f||_Lp for α, β > 0 shows the Lusin area integral is independent of the specific power of the gradient weight. The inequality ||(S_{ε,R}^{1/20} fs)|_Lp || ≤ C (γ^{-1} ||(fs)*_L||_{Lp} + γ^2 ||eS_{ε,R}^{1/2} fs||_{Lp}) is used to bridge the Lusin and maximal functions.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The results extend the Jiz (2012) index range from p = 1 to all p ∈ (0, 1], completing the range of Hardy space indices for Hermite operators. The characterisation confirms that the Hermite-specific gradient ∂_j + x_j captures the correct geometry for Lusin area integrals in the Hermite setting. The boundedness of Riesz transforms establishes that the Hermite-specific Riesz transforms satisfy the typical Hardy space inequalities, placing these operators in the category of Calderón-Zygmund operators adapted to Hermite geometry. The atomic decomposition provides a practical tool for approximation and construction within Hp_L(Rd), analogous to the classical atom decomposition of Hardy spaces. The proof strategy—combining kernel estimates, tent space techniques, interpolation, and atomic decomposition—provides a template for characterising Hardy spaces associated with other non-elliptic operators.

Contradictions And Limitations
The dimension restriction d ≥ 3 is imposed, and the paper does not address d = 1 or d = 2 cases where the kernel decay properties differ. The paper does not provide explicit constants for the inequalities, and the value of C varies from line to line, making exact comparison between different operators difficult. The atomic decomposition requires p > d/(d+δ); for very small p, the moment conditions and atom definition become more restrictive, and the proof does not explicitly state the behavior as p → 0. The Riesz transform boundedness is proven only for the Hermite-specific Riesz transforms RL_j; standard Riesz transforms may not be bounded on Hp_L(Rd). The tent space techniques are adapted from [Rus07] for spaces of homogeneous type; whether these techniques generalize to non-homogeneous or more general structures is not discussed.

Claims
The Hardy spaces Hp_L(Rd) defined via the maximal function are equivalent to the Lusin area integral spaces Hp_S(Rd) for all p ∈ (0, 1], d ≥ 3. The main theorem (Theorem 1.1) directly states the equivalence: Hp_L(Rd) = Hp_S(Rd). Proposition 5.4 establishes the maximal-to-Lusin inequality: ||Sf||_Lp ≤ C ||f*_L||_Lp. Proposition 4.11 completes the equivalence chain: Hp_L = Hp_A ∩ L2 = Hp_{L,at,M} = Hp_S. The proof relies on Proposition 3.1 which requires d/(d+δ) < p ≤ 1; for p below this threshold, the inclusion Hp_L ⊂ Hp_{L,max} is not directly proved in this paper. This allows the use of Lusin area integral techniques for problems originally framed in terms of maximal functions in the Hermite setting. It provides a new characterisation of the Hardy space, which may simplify the analysis of singular integrals on Hp_L(Rd).
The Riesz transforms RL_j = (∂_j + x_j) L^{-1/2} are bounded on Hp_L(Rd) for all j ∈ {1, 2, ...}. Theorem 1.2 explicitly states the boundedness of RL_j on Hp_L(Rd). The proof uses the atomic decomposition: ||RL_j a||_{Hp_{L+2}} ≤ C ||SL f||_{Lp} ≤ C ||f||_{Lp} for an atom a. The identity RL_j f = (∂_j + x_j) L^{-1/2} f = t(∂_j + x_j) e^{-t(L+2)^{1/2}} f connects the Riesz transform to the Poisson semigroup structure. The boundedness is only established for the specific Hermite Riesz transforms; standard Riesz transforms may not be bounded on Hp_L(Rd). The proof is completed by density; the exact norm bounds are not computed quantitatively. The boundedness of Riesz transforms suggests a Calderón-Zygmund theory for the Hermite operator. This may extend to the boundedness of more general multiplier operators on Hp_L(Rd).

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Proposition 5.3 establishes robustness of the Lusin integral: the Lp norm is invariant under changing the gradient exponent α, so the characterisation is independent of the specific power used. Lemma 5.2 provides a measure-theoretic estimate that controls the size of level sets, serving as a crucial tool for the interpolation argument. The proof for Theorem 1.1 relies on a multi-step chain of equivalences (Maximal ⊂ Max-gradient ⊂ Operator ⊂ Atomic ≡ Lusin), so failure at any step would invalidate the equivalence. The condition M > d/(2(1/p - 1/2)) ∨ 1 is essential for the atomic-to-operator inclusion; reducing M could break the boundedness.

Key Figures Tables
Equation (1) defines the Lusin integral Sf(x), which is central to the characterisation. Equation (2) defines the cone Γ(x), establishing the spatial-temporal region of integration. Equation (6) provides the key off-diagonal estimate for atoms: |P_t a(x)| ≤ C |B|^{(1+1/d)-1/p} / |x − y_0|^{d+1}. Proposition 2.3(i) and 2.3(ii) present the heat and Poisson kernel estimates with Gaussian and polynomial decay.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the Lusin area integral characterisation of Hermite Hardy spaces for the full range p ∈ (0, 1], extending Jiz's p = 1 result. 2. The strongest evidence is the chain of inequalities and equivalences connecting the maximal function, the operator A, tent space decompositions, and the Lusin integral via atomic estimates. 3. The future path involves extending these results to d = 1, 2, to general non-elliptic operators with similar semigroup properties, and to the full range of Hardy spaces.

summary.title: Deep-Learning-based Millimeter-Wave Massive MIMO for Hybrid Precoding
summary.authors: Hongji Huang, Yiwei Song, Jie Yang, Guan Gui, Fumiyuki Adachi
summary.field_subfield: Telecommunications / mmWave Massive MIMO / Deep Learning for Precoding
summary.executive_summary: This paper addresses the fundamental limitations of conventional hybrid precoding in millimeter-wave (mmWave) massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems—specifically high computational complexity and the failure to fully exploit spatial sparsity of the mmWave channel—by proposing a deep-learning-enabled hybrid precoding framework. The authors regard each selection of precoders for obtaining the optimized decoder as a mapping relation in a deep neural network (DNN), which is structured as an autoencoder and treated as a black box whose activation functions create corresponding mapping relations. The DNN captures structural information of the hybrid precoding scheme through the training stage, thereby lowering computational complexity while minimizing the bit error ratio (BER) and enhancing spectrum efficiency compared to conventional schemes including SVD-based, GMD-based, and SIC-based methods. The methodology employs a multi-layer fully connected architecture with a specific noise layer to disturb signals, trained via stochastic gradient descent with momentum on an unsupervised dataset. Extensive simulations with $P=3$ non-line-of-sight components, a carrier frequency of 28 GHz, and 45,000 training iterations demonstrate that the DNN-based approach outperforms SVD-based, fully digital, GMD-based, and spatially sparse precoding methods across various SNR regimes. The computational complexity of the proposed scheme is $O(L^2 N_s N_t^2)$, providing a significant reduction over conventional methods. The authors also provide a robustness analysis showing the MSE converges around 11 iterations for the DNN-based scheme, compared to 22 iterations for analog precoding.

Executive Summary
This paper addresses the fundamental limitations of conventional hybrid precoding in millimeter-wave (mmWave) massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems—specifically high computational complexity and the failure to fully exploit spatial sparsity of the mmWave channel—by proposing a deep-learning-enabled hybrid precoding framework. The authors regard each selection of precoders for obtaining the optimized decoder as a mapping relation in a deep neural network (DNN), which is structured as an autoencoder and treated as a black box whose activation functions create corresponding mapping relations. The DNN captures structural information of the hybrid precoding scheme through the training stage, thereby lowering computational complexity while minimizing the bit error ratio (BER) and enhancing spectrum efficiency compared to conventional schemes including SVD-based, GMD-based, and SIC-based methods. The methodology employs a multi-layer fully connected architecture with a specific noise layer to disturb signals, trained via stochastic gradient descent with momentum on an unsupervised dataset. Extensive simulations with $P=3$ non-line-of-sight components, a carrier frequency of 28 GHz, and 45,000 training iterations demonstrate that the DNN-based approach outperforms SVD-based, fully digital, GMD-based, and spatially sparse precoding methods across various SNR regimes. The computational complexity of the proposed scheme is $O(L^2 N_s N_t^2)$, providing a significant reduction over conventional methods. The authors also provide a robustness analysis showing the MSE converges around 11 iterations for the DNN-based scheme, compared to 22 iterations for analog precoding.

Research Context
Wireless data traffic is predicted to improve 1000-fold by 2020 and over 10,000-fold by 2030, necessitating 5G solutions. MmWave massive MIMO is considered a potential technique for enhancing system throughput due to under-utilized spectrum in ultra-high-frequency bands. Existing hybrid precoding schemes based on SVD have high computational complexity and require complicated bit allocation. Geometric mean decomposition (GMD)-based schemes avoid bit allocation issues but struggle with non-convex constraints on analog precoders. Conventional methods based on SVD and GMD are too weak to exploit sparsity statistics of the mmWave massive MIMO channel. Deep learning is recognized as an extraordinary technology for handling explosive data and complicated nonlinear problems with high-computation issues.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can deep learning be integrated into hybrid precoding to overcome high computational complexity and poor spatial exploitation in mmWave massive MIMO? The paper hypothesizes that a DNN-enabled framework, where precoder selection is treated as a mapping relation, will outperform conventional SVD and GMD schemes. The DNN is expected to capture structural information of the hybrid precoding scheme during training, thereby lowering computational complexity. The DNN-based approach is predicted to minimize bit error ratio and enhance spectrum efficiency relative to conventional hybrid precoding schemes. The proposed scheme aims to solve the non-convex optimization in hybrid precoding with the aid of deep learning representation abilities.

Methodological Details
The system model comprises a base station with a uniform linear array (ULA) of Nt antennas and a user with Nr received antennas. The BS sends Ns independent data streams to the user, and the system operates with Nt_RF and Nr_RF RF chains, satisfying Ns ≤ Nt_RF ≤ Nt and Nt ≤ Nr_RF ≤ Nr. The Saleh-Valenzuela (SV) channel model is employed, where H ∈ C^(Nt×Nr) contains P non-line-of-sight components. For the numerical evaluation, P is set to 3 and the carrier frequency is 28 GHz. The network architecture includes a fully connected input layer with 128 units, two hidden layers with 400 and 256 units respectively for encoding. A noise layer with 200 units mixes distortion, followed by two decoding hidden layers with 128 and 64 units respectively. Keras is used to construct and process the DNN framework. The training data is unsupervised, using a large number of iterations to generate bias between R1 and R_A R_D from the output layer. The training dataset comprises structural features of the mmWave massive MIMO model, input data sequences, and DNN outputs.

Procedures And Architectures
The DNN is structured as a multi-layer perceptron with ReLU and Sigmoid activation functions in hidden layers. The output layer uses a special activation function f(s) = min(max(s, 0), Ns) to enforce the power constraint. Geometric mean decomposition (GMD) is used to decompose the complex mmWave channel matrix for training. The loss function is the Frobenius norm of the difference between R1 and R_A R_D, constrained by |R_A|i,j = 1/sqrt(Nt) and trace constraint. Training is performed via stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with momentum, updating R_A and R_D matrices iteratively. The learning rate ϵ and momentum parameter α are hyperparameters, with α as momentum and N as the number of samples. The error threshold for convergence is set to 10^-7. The network is trained for 45,000 iterations in the simulation. Algorithm 1 specifies the step-by-step procedure: initialization, training sequence generation, DNN construction, environment simulation, SGD training, and R_A/R_D update.

Key Results
The DNN-based approach outperforms conventional schemes in BER across all SNR regimes as shown in Fig. 2. The performance improvement is more apparent between the DNN-based strategy and conventional methods, attributed to deep learning's representation ability. The proposed DNN scheme outperforms the fully GMD-based digital precoding, implying deep learning can solve non-convex optimization in hybrid precoding. Increasing batch size from 10 to 100 degrades BER due to slower convergence, while too small batch size leads to unstable convergence. Adopting a lower learning rate optimizes BER performance, as higher rates cause higher validation error. Spectrum efficiency improves with SNR in all schemes, but the DNN-based scheme outperforms others and the gap widens at higher SNR. MSE converges at around 11 iterations for the DNN-based scheme compared to about 22 iterations for analog precoding. The computational complexity of the DNN-based method is O(L^2 N_s N_t^2). The SVD-based hybrid precoding scheme has complexity O(2^Nr Ns (N_t^2(K+NsNr))).

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The DNN framework acts as an autoencoder that learns to map channel structures to optimal precoder pairs (R_A, R_D). The structural information of the mmWave massive MIMO channel is captured implicitly through the training phase of the DNN. The results suggest that the non-convex optimization inherent in hybrid precoding is tractable via deep neural network mapping. The widining performance gap at high SNR demonstrates the superior mapping and learning capacities of deep learning for spatial beamforming.

Contradictions And Limitations
The authors acknowledge that a lower learning rate induces slower convergence behavior despite enhancing system performance. Selecting the best learning rate remains an open issue in the proposed framework. The paper does not specify the exact hardware (GPU type) or specific learning rate values used for the winning configuration. The authors note that too small batch size will lead to unstable convergence.

Claims
The DNN-based hybrid precoding scheme achieves lower BER and higher spectrum efficiency than all conventional SVD, GMD, and SIC-based schemes. As shown in Fig. 2, the deep-learning-based method outperforms the conventional schemes. The spectrum efficiency is improving as the SNR increases... the proposed hybrid precoding scheme outperforms other strategies. The MSE performance of the proposed deep learning based scheme is superior than that of other means. The performance degrades with increasing batch size due to slower convergence. Deep learning can replace iterative non-convex optimization in hybrid precoding designs.
The DNN-based scheme substantially reduces computational complexity compared to conventional hybrid precoding methods. The computational complexity... is only O(L^2 N_s N_t^2), achieving technical advancement. The MSE converges at around 11 iterations for DNN compared to 22 for analog precoding. A lower learning rate induces slower convergence behavior. The framework enables real-time hybrid precoding in mmWave systems with limited processing power.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
MSE versus iterations shows the DNN-based scheme and sparse precoding both converge at ~11 iterations, while analog precoding requires ~22. The paper compares BER versus SNR with various batch sizes (10, 20, 50, 100). The paper compares BER versus SNR with various learning rates.

Key Figures Tables
Fig. 1 displays the DNN architecture, showing the input layer (128 units), two hidden layers (400, 256 units), noise layer (200 units), and decoding layers. Fig. 2 shows BER versus SNR comparing the DNN-based scheme with SVD, fully digital, fully GMD, and new GMD schemes. Fig. 3 shows BER versus SNR for the proposed method with batch sizes 10, 20, 50, and 100. Fig. 4 shows BER versus SNR with various learning rates. Fig. 5 shows spectrum efficiency versus SNR for the proposed, spatially sparse, and fully digital GMD schemes. Fig. 6 shows MSE versus iterations for the DNN-based method, analog precoding, and sparse precoding methods, with learning rate 0.001. Table I lists computational complexities: DNN O(L^2 N_s N_t^2), SIC-based O(2^Nr Ns (N_t^2(K+NsNr))), Spatially sparse O(2^N3_r (N4_r Nt + N2_r L2 + N2_r N2_t L)).

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first deep-learning-enabled framework for mmWave massive MIMO hybrid precoding that treats precoder selection as a DNN mapping, reducing complexity from iterative optimization to a one-shot inference. 2. The strongest evidence is the convergence of MSE at 11 iterations for the DNN-based scheme versus 22 for analog precoding, coupled with BER superiority across all SNR regimes in Fig. 2. 3. The future path includes applying deep learning to channel feedback issues to alleviate codebook size and feedback overhead in mmWave massive MIMO systems.

summary.title: BanStereoSet: A Dataset to Measure Stereotypical Social Biases in LLMs for Bangla
summary.authors: Mahammed Kamruzzaman, Abdullah Al Monsur, Shrabon Das, Enamul Hassan, Gene Louis Kim
summary.field_subfield: Natural Language Processing / AI Ethics (Multilingual Bias Evaluation)
summary.executive_summary: This study introduces BanStereoSet, a fill-in-the-blank type dataset consisting of 1,194 sentences spanning nine bias categories (race, profession, gender, ageism, beauty, beauty in profession, region, caste, and religion) designed to evaluate stereotypical social biases in multilingual large language models (LLMs) specifically for the Bangla language. The dataset was constructed by localizing and culturally adapting content from the StereoSet, IndiBias, and GenAssocBias datasets, and through human-LLM partnership for regional data. The authors addressed unique Bangla linguistic challenges including the absence of gendered pronouns, culturally specific naming conventions, and regional references, while also mitigating known pitfalls in the source StereoSet dataset (meaningful stereotypes, misaligned stereotypes, invalid perturbations, incommensurable groups, and non-naturalistic text). The dataset was evaluated using four multilingual LLMs: GPT-4o, Mistral-7B, Llama 3.1-70B, and Gemma 2-27B across three prompting templates. Results indicate that models exhibit significant biases across most categories; notably, Mistral stands out as the least biased model on average, performing best in seven of nine categories. A key cross-linguistic finding revealed that Mistral successfully handles caste bias in Bangla but fails to do so in English, suggesting language-dependent cultural sensitivity.
