Executive Summary
This paper introduces and demonstrates a theoretical and experimental framework for three-dimensional (3D) topological valley photonics with a complete photonic bandgap. Previous valley photonics studies were restricted to 2D, suffering from out-of-plane losses and limited to planar light manipulation. The authors develop a 3D FCC-lattice photonic crystal (a = 20 mm) with diamond-like geometry composed of PEC spheres and rods. By breaking inversion symmetry (∆D ≠ 0), the nodal lines at W_α± valleys gap out to form a complete photonic bandgap, hosting triple pairs of valleys characterized by valley Chern vectors (VCV) instead of scalar valley Chern numbers. 

The vectorial valley-contrasting physics is verified by pump-probe measurements using a vectorial chiral source array, where clockwise (counterclockwise) phase windings at 13.8 GHz produce −32.9° (+32.9°) outcoupling angles corresponding to W_y− (W_y+), while the X-point coexisting states yield 0°. The authors derive a k·p Hamiltonian for each valley, showing valley-chirality locking. By covering the (001) surface with a metallic plate and tuning a boundary sphere (D3 = 4 mm, h = 6.25 mm), they achieve a chiral surface state with linear dispersion and flat isofrequency contours, resulting in diffractionless canalization along the +y direction. 

Unlike prior 3D topological photonic insulators where surface states appear on only specific surfaces, the 3D VPC supports chiral valley surface states on all (100), (010), and (001) surfaces simultaneously. The propagation direction is locked to each valley, forming closed loops around the sample geometry. A fundamental right-hand-thumb rule relates the direction of VCVs to the circulating propagation of surface states across all surfaces. The concept is demonstrated at microwave frequencies but the authors note the framework is transferable to terahertz and optical regimes using all-dielectric diamond-like structures.

Research Context
Valley photonics exploits the valley degree of freedom to manipulate light, supplementing amplitude, phase, polarization, and frequency. Previous valley photonic crystal studies were limited to 2D systems where the third dimension confinement is non-topological. 2D valley systems suffer from out-of-plane losses and can only manipulate light in planar geometries. Topological valley photonics avoids breaking time-reversal symmetry or using synthetic spin-orbital coupling, making them experimentally feasible. Valley photonic crystals are versatile across broad frequency ranges and suitable for lasers, on-chip communication, and quantum optics. Full confinement and control of light flow require a complete photonic bandgap, which has remained a significant challenge.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether 3D valley photonics with a complete photonic bandgap and vectorial valley physics can be realized theoretically and experimentally. The authors hypothesize that a 3D FCC lattice with broken inversion symmetry will host triple pairs of valleys characterized by valley Chern vectors rather than scalar Chern numbers. It is predicted that the vectorial nature of Berry curvature will enable vectorial bulk valley vortices and canalized chiral valley surface states. A specific hypothesis is that the valley Chern vectors and surface state propagation direction are intrinsically governed by the right-hand-thumb rule. The authors posit that 3D VPCs can support chiral surface states on all sample surfaces, a capability not previously achieved by any 3D photonic topological insulators.

Methodological Details
The study uses a 3D FCC photonic crystal with lattice constant a = 20 mm. The lattice vectors are defined as a1 = (a/2, a/2, 0), a2 = (0, a/2, a/2), and a3 = (a/2, 0, a/2). The structure is a photonic diamond with nearest-neighbor spheres of diameters D1 and D2 connected by PEC rods. Each nearest-neighbor sphere is connected by PEC rods with diameter B1 = 2.4 mm. Next-nearest spheres are connected by PEC rods with diameter B2 = 1.2 mm to suppress high-order modes. The band structure is computed numerically for two cases: ΔD = 0 (D1 = D2 = 5 mm) and ΔD ≠ 0 (D1 = 6.4 mm, D2 = 3.6 mm). The k·p method yields an effective Hamiltonian near each valley with group velocity vD and mass term m = (ω1−ω2)/2. The vectorial chiral source array consists of four sources at (0,0,0), (−a/2, −a/2, 0), (−a/2, 0, −a/2), and (0, −a/2, −a/2). For Wy± selective excitation, relative phase delays are set to (0, ±π/2, ±π, ±3π/2) in the x-z plane. The (001) surface is modified with a metallic plate and a boundary sphere of diameter D3 = 4 mm. The gap between the metallic plate and the boundary sphere is set to h = 6.25 mm. The metallic plate features perforations with a hole interval of a/2 for source and probe insertion.

Procedures And Architectures
Numerical simulations use the full-wave eigenvalue equation for the 3D FCC diamond lattice geometry. Band structure calculation compares the inversion-symmetric case (ΔD=0) with nodal lines to the broken-symmetry case (ΔD≠0) with complete gap. The six valleys at W_α± positions are identified in the 3D Brillouin zone: (±π/a, 2π/a, 0), (0, ±π/a, 2π/a), and (2π/a, 0, ±π/a). Effective k·p Hamiltonians are derived near each valley for the lower band. Valley Chern vectors are calculated by integrating the vectorial Berry curvature Ω = (Ωx, Ωy, Ωz) over planar regions around each valley. The boundary condition HΦ = ωΦ with ˆzτ = M(σy sinθV + σz cosθV) is imposed on the (001) surface. The condition θV = π/2 is required for chiral surface states with linear dispersion. Pump-probe measurements selectively excite chiral Bloch modes at specific valley-locked polarizations. Fourier-transformed spectrum analysis maps surface dispersion around the Wx− valley. Far-field radiation patterns are measured for outcoupling verification. Right-hand-thumb rule is experimentally tested by positioning the source at the (001) center and measuring fields on all surfaces.

Key Results
At ΔD ≠ 0 (D1 = 6.4 mm, D2 = 3.6 mm), the nodal lines gap out to form a complete photonic bandgap. The Berry curvature at Wz± has a nonzero component only in the kx-ky plane, verifying vectorial valley-contrasting physics. Measured outcoupling at 13.8 GHz for clockwise phase winding shows a direction of −32.9° and for counterclockwise +32.9°, corresponding to Wy− and Wy+ respectively. The case without phase winding shows a direction of 0°, corresponding to the X-point coexisting states. The valley Chern vectors are calculated as (±1/2, 0, 0), (0, ±1/2, 0), and (0, 0, ±1/2) for Wx±, Wy±, and Wz± respectively. Measured surface transmission maintains high value within the complete photonic bandgap while bulk transmission is substantially lower. The surface state exhibits nearly-linear dispersion in the bandgap at 14.6 GHz. The surface states propagate diffractionlessly along the +y direction, confirmed experimentally and numerically. The chiral valley surface states are observed on all (100), (010), and (001) surfaces, with propagation direction locked to each valley. At the sharp bend, the surface state passes smoothly with high transmission, continuing to the (010) surface. The right-hand-thumb rule is confirmed: VCV (−1/2, 0, 0) at Wx− valley with clockwise circulation on the y-z plane.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The vectorial nature of Berry curvature in 3D introduces a vectorial valley-contrasting physics perspective beyond the 2D scalar case. The valley-chirality locking property means each valley state can be selectively excited using a chirality-matched source array. Canalization stems from the flat isofrequency contours, where the surface dispersion is independent of the wavevector vertical to propagation. The orbital moments of 3D valley states provide a means to control the angular momentum of light. The right-hand-thumb rule is an intrinsic relation between VCVs and valley surface states both determined by the bulk Hamiltonian. The concept can be extended to higher frequencies, including terahertz and optical ranges, using all-dielectric diamond-like 3D photonic crystals.

Contradictions And Limitations
The demonstration is at microwave frequencies, and extrapolation to optical requires all-dielectric realizations. The specific boundary parameters (D3 = 4 mm, h = 6.25 mm) are tuned for the (001) surface; applicability to other surfaces isn't quantified numerically. The metallic plate modification is specific to the (001) surface; achieving similar boundary conditions on other surfaces via on-site potential modification may be more complex. The source and probe insertion requires perforations in the metallic plate with hole interval a/2, introducing practical fabrication constraints. The paper does not report specific noise levels, thermal noise, or random seed values for the numerical band structure calculations.

Claims
The 3D VPC hosts triple pairs of valleys with vectorial Berry curvature, enabling vectorial bulk valley vortices and canalized chiral valley surface states. The three pairs of valleys are at Wx±, Wy±, and Wz± positions in the 3D Brillouin zone. VCVs are (±1/2, 0, 0), (0, ±1/2, 0), and (0, 0, ±1/2), showing vectorial contrast. Simulated Berry curvature components show non-zero values in specific planes, verifying vectorial nature. The Berry curvature at Wz± only has a nonzero component in the kx-ky plane, limiting the vectorial demonstration to specific projections. Vectorial valley states provide additional control over light angular momentum beyond 2D systems.
The right-hand-thumb rule intrinsically relates the direction of VCVs to the circulating propagation direction of valley surface states across all surfaces. Experimentally, Wx− with VCV (−1/2, 0, 0) yields clockwise circulation on the y-z plane. The rule applies to all three pairs of valleys and all sample surfaces. The relation is intrinsic, determined by the bulk Hamiltonian.  The rule provides a predictive design principle for 3D topological valley photonic devices.
Chiral valley surface states on the 3D VPC propagate diffractionlessly and can be observed on all sample surfaces simultaneously. Surface transmission is high within the gap while bulk transmission is substantially lower. States propagate along +y on (001) and -z on (010) without intervalley scattering at the bend. Flat isofrequency contours produce canalization, which was confirmed both experimentally and numerically. The demonstration relies on a specific on-site boundary condition modification with a metallic plate, which may affect sample isotropy. Canalization presents opportunities for imaging and lensing in 3D photonic devices.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The next-nearest-neighbor rods (B2 = 1.2 mm) are added specifically to suppress high-order modes and obtain a clean band structure. The comparison between ΔD = 0 (D1 = D2 = 5 mm) and ΔD ≠ 0 (D1 = 6.4 mm, D2 = 3.6 mm) demonstrates the topological transition from nodal lines to gapped phase. The outcoupling directions at 13.8 GHz are compared to theoretical predictions (32.9°, 0°, −32.9°) to verify the valley-locking. The isofrequency contours are shown both numerically and measured (Figure 3(h)) for consistency check.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1(a) shows the 3D FCC cubic cell geometry with lattice constant a, lattice vectors, and rod diameters B1, B2. Figure 1(b) displays the band structure comparing ΔD = 0 (5 mm spheres) and ΔD ≠ 0 (6.4 mm, 3.6 mm spheres) cases. Figure 1(c) illustrates the 3D Brillouin zone with six valleys and nodal line paths. Figure 1(d) shows simulated electric field profiles at Wz± with Poynting vector arrows and phase colors. Figure 2(d) reports measured outcoupling field directions of −32.9°, 0°, and +32.9° at 13.8 GHz for selective valley excitation. Figure 3(e) displays measured surface transmission versus frequency, identifying the complete photonic bandgap region. Figure 3(g) and 3(h) show measured and simulated surface dispersion and isofrequency contours at 14.6 GHz. Figure 4(b) shows the field distribution before and after the bend on the (001) and (010) surfaces. Figure 4(c) displays measured transmission before and after the bend, showing the surface state persists.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first realization of 3D topological valley photonics with a complete photonic bandgap and vectorial valley physics, going beyond 2D scalar valley Chern number frameworks. 2. The strongest evidence is the experimental verification of the right-hand-thumb rule: Wx− with VCV (−1/2, 0, 0) yielding clockwise circulation on the y-z plane, confirmed across surfaces and after a sharp bend. 3. The future path includes extending this framework to terahertz and optical frequencies using all-dielectric diamond-like crystals, and leveraging canalized states for 3D imaging and lensing applications.

summary.title: From Words to Wheels: Automated Style-Customized Policy Generation for Autonomous Driving
summary.authors: Xu Han, Xianda Chen, Zhenghan Cai, Pinlong Cai, Meixin Zhu, Xiaowen Chu
summary.field_subfield: Autonomous Driving / Reinforcement Learning / Natural Language Processing
summary.type_of_paper: Research paper introducing a new framework with experimental validation
summary.executive_summary: Words2Wheels addresses the limitation of uniform driving styles in autonomous vehicles by providing a framework that automatically generates customized driving policies from natural language user commands. Current approaches either rely on predefined styles requiring expert input or data-driven methods like Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) that require specific driving data difficult to obtain in scenarios like Robotaxis. Furthermore, these methods cannot generalize to new user commands not represented in pre-existing style data. Words2Wheels introduces a Style-Customized Reward Function (Style Reward) that bridges the gap between natural language commands and a Style-Customized Driving Policy (Style Policy) through an RL-based optimization loop. The framework leverages large language models (LLMs) with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to retrieve, adapt, and generalize driving styles from a Driving Style Database, which stores both data-driven and human-designed reward functions as code and their corresponding pre-trained policies. A Statistical Evaluation module ensures alignment with user preferences by comparing policy statistics against natural driving behavior on a reserved test set using metrics such as speed, acceleration, jerk, spacing, and time headway. The system operates in a fully automated pipeline: upon receiving a command, the LLM selects relevant rewards, generates new reward functions when no match is found, and trains new policies via Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), all in parallel. Results demonstrate superior performance over the Intelligent Driver Model (IDM) in human preference tests (72% preference rate) and validate the system's ability to generate entirely new, aligned styles when no similar styles exist in the database. The framework also includes a fuzzy memory function for recalling styles from semantically similar previous commands, with nearly all test cases successfully matched. The paper concludes that Words2Wheels is the first framework to automatically customize style-aware driving policies from natural language, opening new possibilities for user-centric AV design.

Executive Summary
Words2Wheels addresses the limitation of uniform driving styles in autonomous vehicles by providing a framework that automatically generates customized driving policies from natural language user commands. Current approaches either rely on predefined styles requiring expert input or data-driven methods like Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) that require specific driving data difficult to obtain in scenarios like Robotaxis. Furthermore, these methods cannot generalize to new user commands not represented in pre-existing style data. Words2Wheels introduces a Style-Customized Reward Function (Style Reward) that bridges the gap between natural language commands and a Style-Customized Driving Policy (Style Policy) through an RL-based optimization loop. The framework leverages large language models (LLMs) with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to retrieve, adapt, and generalize driving styles from a Driving Style Database, which stores both data-driven and human-designed reward functions as code and their corresponding pre-trained policies. A Statistical Evaluation module ensures alignment with user preferences by comparing policy statistics against natural driving behavior on a reserved test set using metrics such as speed, acceleration, jerk, spacing, and time headway. The system operates in a fully automated pipeline: upon receiving a command, the LLM selects relevant rewards, generates new reward functions when no match is found, and trains new policies via Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), all in parallel. Results demonstrate superior performance over the Intelligent Driver Model (IDM) in human preference tests (72% preference rate) and validate the system's ability to generate entirely new, aligned styles when no similar styles exist in the database. The framework also includes a fuzzy memory function for recalling styles from semantically similar previous commands, with nearly all test cases successfully matched. The paper concludes that Words2Wheels is the first framework to automatically customize style-aware driving policies from natural language, opening new possibilities for user-centric AV design.

Research Context
Current autonomous vehicles suffer from uniform driving styles that fail to reflect user preferences. 52.46% of AV crashes involved rear-end collisions, 1.6 times the rate of conventional vehicles, indicating a need for gentler braking. Early driving style approaches relied on classification or calibration of predefined styles requiring heavy expert input and frequent manual adjustment. Data-driven approaches using clustering and Inverse Reinforcement Learning derive policies from behavior data but require specific driving data difficult to obtain in Robotaxi scenarios. Existing methods cannot customize styles based on new user needs, leading to the generalization problem where no pre-existing style aligns with the command. Recent foundation model approaches adjust specific behaviors like speed but fall short in adjusting overall driving policy at the style level. Furthermore, involving the foundation model in most decision loops raises reliability and efficiency concerns.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can a framework automatically generate customized driving policies aligned with natural language user commands without prior driving data? Can an LLM-powered reward design approach generalize to new commands and styles through zero-shot generation capabilities? Will a Driving Style Database containing both data-driven and human-designed rewards enable efficient retrieval and continuous enrichment? Can a Statistical Evaluation module objectively measure alignment between generated policies and user commands against natural driving benchmarks? The authors hypothesize that a Style-Customized Reward Function serves as a low-complexity policy index enabling efficient retrieval and generation. They predict that newly generated policies will outperform existing ones and that the framework will generalize to out-of-distribution commands.

Methodological Details
The framework was evaluated in a car-following scenario representing a significant portion of driving behavior. Data was sourced from the HighD dataset, collected by a 4K resolution camera mounted on a drone. Data extraction and kinematic modeling for car-following behavior were based on FollowNet. 15% of the HighD data was reserved as a test set for the Statistical Evaluation module to prevent overfitting. User commands were categorized into three levels based on directness: Level I (Direct), Level II (Indirect with strong hints), and Level III (Indirect with mild hints). The Driving Style Database was initially populated with 8 styles: some data-driven via clustering and IRL, others human-designed. The base LLM was GPT-4o-2024-08-06 with temperature set to 0.3 for deterministic output. The selection parameter was set to k = 3 relevant styles and n = 2 statistical metrics in Statistical Evaluation. For PPO training, each reward function was run 5 times with different seeds, selecting the policy with the highest reward. Human evaluation involved 10 volunteers with valid driving licenses testing 20 events per command across 5 commands, totaling 1,000 events.

Procedures And Architectures
The framework uses a Markov Decision Process formulation where the reward function R(s, a) serves as the policy index. Upon receiving a command, the LLM applies RAG principles to select the top k relevant style rewards from the Driving Style Database. If a matched command exists in fuzzy memory, the existing Style Policy is reused; otherwise, the LLM generates m new reward functions. Style Reward generation produces Python code for reward functions, which are then trained via Proximal Policy Optimization. Training runs are parallelized; the temporary selected style provides an immediate solution while new policies train. The Statistical Evaluation module uses Chain-of-Thought prompting: (1) select top n metrics, (2) select best reward function by comparing to natural data, (3) output in JSON. Statistical metrics include speed, time headway, relative speed, acceleration, jerk, spacing, and time headway. The Driving Style Database stores Style Rewards as programming code, Style Policies as pre-trained neural networks, and analytical data in JSON. Analytical data and style policies can be embedded as high-dimensional vectors for LLM retrieval. The Statistical Evaluation module also supports custom test sets and spatio-temporal filtering for finer analysis.

Key Results
In basic adaptation tests (Aggressive/Normal/Conservative), the aggressive style showed higher speeds and greater acceleration, while the conservative style maintained larger gap and relative speed. The aggressive style unexpectedly showed larger time headway and the normal style higher jerk, attributed to LLM metric prioritization. In the generation-only experiment (no aligned styles provided), 'I'm going to be late' generated higher speed, acceleration, and jerk. For 'Safety first. I have plenty of time', the generated style showed greater spacing, time headway, and relative speed. In human preference tests, 72% of participants judged Words2Wheels better than IDM across all 5 command types. Specific command preferences: Safety first at 79.5% for Words2Wheels vs 17% for IDM; Drive as fast as you can at 72.5% vs 19% for IDM. IDM was preferred in only 9.2% of events, with 18.8% ties. Across 40 case studies, the rational priorities metric was 97.5%, rational metrics 95%, rational retrieval 92.5%, and rational generation 85%. The system correctly handled all Level I commands (100% rational priorities/metrics/retrieval). In fuzzy memory tests, all test cases were successfully recalled except one case: 'It's snowing and visibility has decreased'. Table II shows 200 tested events per command, with a total of 1,000 events.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The results demonstrate that the reward function as a policy index allows for a more compact and retrievable representation of driving styles. The zero-shot generation capability suggests that LLMs can reason about driving behavior without direct supervision data, opening paths to open-domain style customization. The alignment between generated statistics and user commands confirms that natural language can be mapped to quantitative driving metrics. The framework shows that combining RAG-based retrieval with RL-based policy generation creates a dual-path (cached/generated) architecture that balances reliability and novelty. The success in generation-only settings validates that the method does not rely on simply selecting the 'closest' existing style but can synthesize new behavior.

Contradictions And Limitations
The aggressive style unexpectedly showed larger time headway, contradicting the intended behavioral change, possibly because the LLM did not prioritize all metrics equally. The normal style showed higher jerk than expected, indicating sub-optimal metric weighting in the reward function. In Case 19, the LLM misinterpreted 'You are allowing a large gap' and in Case 26 it intentionally selected the highest jerk as a counterexample. When acceleration and jerk values were negative, the LLM's understanding conflicted with human intuition. The fuzzy memory test had one failure: 'It's snowing and visibility has decreased' was not recalled. The experiments were limited to car-following scenarios; more complex behaviors like lane changes or merging are not validated. The training process was run 5 times, but individual variability between seeds may affect reliability of specific style policies.

Claims
Words2Wheels is the first framework to automatically customize style-aware driving policies from natural language user commands. The paper explicitly states this to the best of their knowledge. The Statistical Evaluation module uses Chain-of-Thought to select metrics, rewards, and policies objectively. Experiments show 72% human preference over IDM across multiple commands. The authors note occasional misinterpretations in case studies (e.g., Case 19, Case 26). The negative jerk/acceleration values conflicted with human intuition in some cases. This opens the door for truly personalized AV experiences that can adapt instantly to driver mood or environmental context. It reduces the reliance on expert-curated style libraries.
The framework can generate novel driving styles that do not exist in the database, validating generalization beyond pre-existing examples. In generation-only tests, aggressive commands produced high speed and acceleration styles from a pool of only conservative/normal styles. Fuzzy memory recall succeeded in all but one case, indicating robust generalization of semantic meaning. The Statistical Evaluation module's metrics-based comparison provides objective verification of the generated style. The snowy/visibility case failed fuzzy recall. Some generated styles showed unintended metric behaviors (large headway, high jerk). New driving styles can be synthesized on-the-fly, enabling support for long-tail user preferences not captured in offline data collection.

Data And Code Availability
Code and demo are available at https://yokhon.github.io/Words2Wheels/. Experimental records available at https://bit.ly/4giYhB7. The Driving Style Database format and Statistical Evaluation prompts are partially described in the paper.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
PPO training was run 5 times with different seeds for each style policy, selecting the best performer to mitigate RL instability. The generation-only experiment (limiting initial styles to 4) isolated the synthesis capability from simple retrieval. Commands were run 5 times each and averaged to ensure robustness across repeated trials. 10th and 90th percentiles normalization was used for metric data to facilitate fair comparison across styles. The test set was reserved (15%) specifically to prevent the Statistical Evaluation module from overfitting to training distributions.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 illustrates the three-stage pipeline: User Command → Style Reward → Style Policy with LLM and RL components. Figure 2 depicts the three modules: Automated Policy Customization workflow, Driving Style Database structure, and Statistical Evaluation logic. Figure 3 shows the step-by-step execution of the RAG-based command cognition, style matching, and reward generation. Figure 4 exemplifies the Statistical Evaluation module's metric selection and reward comparison against natural data statistics. Figure 5 compares customized policies over style-aware metrics (speed, headway, jerk, etc.) for aggressive, normal, conservative styles. Figure 6 shows evaluation of generated policies when no pre-existing aligned style is provided in the database. Figure 7 displays the UI for the human-in-the-loop style comparison tool with anonymized clips. Table I categorizes user commands into three levels of directness with example commands. Table II reports human preference scores across 5 commands with 1,000 total events, showing 72% preference for Words2Wheels. Table III presents case study rationales across 40 commands, showing 97.5% rational priorities, 95% rational metrics, 92.5% rational retrieval, and 85% rational generation. Table IV summarizes fuzzy memory recall results for 3 experimental sets, showing successful recall for all but the snowy/visibility case.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is Words2Wheels: the first framework to automatically generate and customize style-aware driving policies from natural language user commands using a Style-Customized Reward Function bridged by LLMs and RL. 2. The strongest evidence is the 72% human preference rate over IDM across 1,000 events, and the generation-only experiment validating synthesis of novel styles not present in the database. 3. The future path includes expanding to complex scenarios beyond car-following, refining the Statistical Evaluation module, and incorporating a Feedback and Reflection module to improve reward functions.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper presents a comprehensive spectro-temporal investigation of the low-mass X-ray binary (LMXB) neutron star atoll source GX 9+9, based on a single archival AstroSat observation (Obs. ID: A09_018T01_9000003774) taken on July 25, 2020. Utilizing both the Large Area X-ray Proportional Counter (LAXPC) and Soft X-ray Telescope (SXT) instruments, the authors determined that GX 9+9 was in the soft/banana state (BS) with a disk-dominating energy spectrum between 0.7–25.0 keV. The flux was segregated into three levels (FL1: 450–570 cts/s; FL2: 570–650 cts/s; FL3: 650–770 cts/s) for flux-resolved spectral analysis. The best-fit spectral model was const*tbabs*(thcomp*diskbb), combining SXT and LAXPC data with 90% confidence level constraints. The source exhibited an average estimated inner-disk radius (Rin) of 16.57 ± 1.29 km (or 16.54 ± 1.78 km in the conclusion), consistent with prior estimates despite different distance and inclination assumptions. Total unabsorbed flux ranged from 5.94 × 10⁻⁹ to 7.30 × 10⁻⁹ ergs s⁻¹ cm⁻² over 0.01–100 keV, showing an increase across flux levels. In the temporal domain, LAXPC data revealed broad-band noise (BBN) centered at ~0.1 Hz, fitted with two Lorentzians; no QPOs were detected. Energy-dependent modeling using the Garg et al. propagative model formalism (reduced χ² ≈ 0.80) attributed the variability to simultaneous changes in the inner-disk temperature (δkTin ≈ 0.56 ± 0.10%) and fractional scattering (δfs ≈ 81 ± 32%), with a positive phase lag of 0.11 ± 0.08, indicating that perturbations propagate from the inner disk toward the coronal region.

Research Context
GX 9+9 is a neutron star low-mass X-ray binary identified during the Galactic center's sounding rocket mission. The source is an established atoll source tracing a 'C'-pattern in the hardness-intensity diagram, characterized by hard/island and soft/banana states. In the hard state Comptonization dominates, whereas the soft state is dominated by the accretion disk's thermal emission. The source was previously detected in a luminous soft state with ~220 mCrab X-ray flux in the 2–20 keV band. Previous spectral models have included power law, blackbody plus Comptonization, disk plus Comptonized blackbody, and double blackbody with a broad iron line. The source has 4.2-hour X-ray and optical waveband modulation and a distance estimated between 5 kpc and 10 kpc. While RXTE provided simultaneous X-ray and optical timing, AstroSat's LAXPC offers larger effective area and wider energy coverage for more precise time delays and spectral distribution. The source is not a well-studied source with previously reported but geometrically ambiguous spectral models.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central objective is to perform a spectro-temporal investigation of GX 9+9 using simultaneous AstroSat LAXPC and SXT data at different flux levels. The authors seek to identify the radiative origin of the observed variability by modeling energy-dependent temporal properties. The study aims to estimate various source characteristics including inner-disk radius, flux, and inner-disk temperature at multiple flux levels. A key hypothesis is that the source, previously observed in a luminous soft state, might show spectral parameter variations (e.g., decreasing kTe, increasing Tin) indicating a transition towards a softer state as flux increases. The authors compare the spectral and temporal analysis for constancy and relate obtained spectral parameters to physical source characteristics. The temporal analysis aims to detect QPOs or broad-band noise features and determine if the variability is driven by temperature fluctuations, optical depth changes, or propagation effects.

Methodological Details
The study used a single archival AstroSat observation (Obs. ID: A09_018T01_9000003774) taken on July 25, 2020. SXT was used for spectral analysis; only LAXPC was used for timing due to its microsecond-level timing resolution. LAXPC operates over 3–80 keV with three identical counters; however, counters 10 and 30 suffered abnormal gains since 2018, so only LAXPC 20 data were analyzed. SXT is an imaging instrument working in 0.3–8.0 keV. Good time interval data were extracted using the LAXPC software (version: Oct. 13, 2022), excluding South Atlantic Anomaly and Earth occultation periods. The SXT pipeline used was AS1SXTLevel2-1.4b, producing cleaned level-2 event files. SXT count rate exceeded the pileup threshold of 40 counts/sec, necessitating an annular extraction zone with outer radius 13 arcmin and inner radius 2 arcmin using XSELECT (V2.5b). A 2% model systematic error was incorporated for background uncertainty estimation. A gain fit was applied to SXT data with a slope of 1 and offset free, typically 0.02–0.09. Both LAXPC and SXT spectra were grouped optimally using ftool ftgrouppha. The HID plotted overall count rate in 3–20 keV against photon count ratio in 6–20 keV vs. 3–6 keV energy ranges, with 32s binning. The source was segregated into three flux levels: FL1 (450–570 cts/s), FL2 (570–650 cts/s), and FL3 (650–770 cts/s). Spectral analysis covered 0.7–25 keV using XSPEC (v.12.13.0c) and HEASOFT (6.31.1), with 90% confidence level for parametric errors. Strict simultaneous SXT and LAXPC data were used, with LAXPC 20 as base spectrum (constant fixed at 1) and SXT constant free for cross-calibration. The optical depth was frozen at 9, and edge models at 2.4 keV were added for instrumental features. For ThComp convolution, 1000 log bins were used with 'energies 0.01 500 1000 log'. For timing, PDS was generated for full flux in 3–20 keV over 0.003 Hz to 1 Hz, using the multi-Lorentzian approach. RMS and time lag spectra were obtained using LAXPC subroutine 'laxpc_find_freqlag' at centroid frequency ν₀ ≈ 0.04 Hz, with HWHM ≈ 0.09 Hz.

Procedures And Architectures
The best-fit spectral model adopted was const*tbabs*(thcomp*diskbb), where thcomp is the thermal Comptonization model (improved version of nThComp). The bbodyrad model was first tested but yielded reduced χ² > 2, failing to explain the data. The cross-calibration constant 'const' was used to align SXT and LAXPC; LAXPC 20 constant fixed at 1. Inner-disk radius Rin was calculated using Rin = k²(Ndbb / cosθ)^(1/2) * D10, with k = 1.7 (color-correction), θ = 60 degrees (disk inclination), and D = 10 kpc (source distance). Total unabsorbed flux was estimated using the 'cflux' model over 0.01–100 keV. The energy-dependent temporal modeling used the Garg et al. [29] propagative model based on a truncated disk and hot electron plasma (corona). The time lag was derived from phase lag as time lag = phase lag / 2πf, where f is the peak/central frequency (usually in milliseconds). The simplest temporal model varied inner-disk temperature (kTin) and fractional scattering (fs) with a time delay relative to fs. Combinations of heating rate and optical depth were also tested but produced insignificant χ² values (>2). The best-fit temporal model was Ktin w.r.t. fs variation with phase lag, yielding reduced χ² ≈ 0.80.

Key Results
The source was identified in the soft/banana state (BS) based on the HID, with the disk dominating the spectrum between 0.7–25.0 keV. The total unabsorbed flux across FLs was 5.94 × 10⁻⁹ ergs s⁻¹ cm⁻² (FL1), 6.51 × 10⁻⁹ ergs s⁻¹ cm⁻² (FL2), and 7.30 × 10⁻⁻⁹ ergs s⁻¹ cm⁻² (FL3) over 0.01–100 keV. The maximum flux of 7.30 × 10⁻⁹ ergs s⁻¹ cm⁻² is comparable to the 7.8 × 10⁻⁹ ergs s⁻¹ cm⁻² previously reported by Iaria et al. in the 0.1–100 keV range. The average inner-disk radius Rin was estimated at 16.57 ± 1.29 km (or 16.54 ± 1.78 km), consistent with the previously reported 27 ± 4 km by Iaria et al., though their estimate used θ ≈ 43° and D = 5 kpc. The spectral parameters showed a slight decrease in kTe (from 4.14 keV in FL1 to 3.69 keV in FL3) and an increase in Tin (from 1.87 keV in FL1 to 2.04 keV in FL3), suggesting a transition toward a softer state. No QPOs or prominent BBN features were detected in the discrete flux levels FL1, FL2, and FL3. In the full flux PDS (3–20 keV, 0.003 Hz–1 Hz), a BBN-like feature was observed centered at ν₀ ≈ 0.04 Hz with HWHM ≈ 0.09 Hz, yielding characteristic frequency νc ≈ 0.1 Hz. RMS at ~0.1 Hz increased with energy, while the phase lag showed a decreasing trend with energy (though error bars made it unreliable). The energy-dependent temporal model with Ktin variation relative to fs yielded reduced χ²/dof = 6.39/8, with δkTin = 0.56 ± 0.10%, δfs = 81 ± 32%, and phase lag = 0.11 ± 0.08. The positive phase lag indicates that the variation was initially introduced as a change in inner-disk temperature and moved toward the coronal region as a change in the fraction of seed photons being Comptonized.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The observed decrease in kTe and increase in Tin with rising flux supports the interpretation that the source is transitioning toward a softer state. The positive phase lag of 0.11 ± 0.08 (with δfs = 81 ± 32% and δkTin = 0.56 ± 0.10%) implies a propagative mechanism where a temperature perturbation originates at the inner disk and propagates toward the corona. The BBN-like feature at ~0.1 Hz is consistent with the broader variability patterns expected in neutron star LMXBs, even though no QPOs were detected. The spectral parameters (fs = 0.14–0.34, Tin = 1.87–2.04 keV) are comparable to those reported by Chatterjee et al. [16] for GX 9+9, validating the physical consistency of the model. The inner-disk radius of ~16.5 km, though smaller than Iaria's 27 km, arises from different geometrical assumptions (θ = 60° vs 43°, D = 10 kpc vs 5 kpc), highlighting the sensitivity of derived parameters to geometry. The success of the Garg et al. [29] model (reduced χ² ≈ 0.80) in reproducing the rms and lag spectra confirms the applicability of the truncated disk + corona coronal geometry for explaining stochastic variability in atoll sources.

Contradictions And Limitations
The paper explicitly states that GX 9+9 is not a well-studied source, and the study is constrained by poor data quality. The SXT count rate exceeded the pileup threshold of 40 counts/sec, requiring annular zone extraction which potentially limits signal-to-noise. The phase lag measurement shows a decreasing trend but the authors note they cannot rely on it because 'the error-bar are consistent within data points'. Combinations of heating rate and optical depth with the Ktin-fs model yielded insignificant χ² values (>2), limiting the scope of the temporal modeling. The inner-disk radius of 16.57 km is significantly smaller than the previously reported 27 km by Iaria et al., attributable to differing distance (10 vs 5 kpc) and inclination (60° vs 43°) assumptions. No QPOs or prominent BBN features were detected in the individual flux levels, limiting the statistical power of the temporal analysis per flux state.

Claims
GX 9+9 is in the soft/banana state during the AstroSat observation with a disk-dominated spectrum. The HID shows a form consistent with the banana state, and the source was detected in the soft state during observation. The best-fit model const*tbabs*(thcomp*diskbb) with a diskbb component gives good physical parameters. The HID shows the overall count rate in 3–20 keV plotted against photon count ratio in 6–20 keV vs 3–6 keV. The paper notes the source is not well-studied and the soft state detection is from a single observation. The soft state identification justifies the use of the diskbb + thcomp model over a pure blackbody model.
The inner-disk radius of GX 9+9 is approximately 16.5 km, consistent with prior neutron star LMXB estimates under different geometrical assumptions. The computed Rin is 16.57 ± 1.29 km from the spectral fitting. The unabsorbed flux of 7.30 × 10⁻⁹ ergs s⁻¹ cm⁻² is comparable to Iaria's reported 7.8 × 10⁻⁹. The reported value by Iaria et al. is 27 ± 4 km, which is substantially larger than 16.5 km. The difference is explained by differing distance (5 vs 10 kpc) and inclination (43° vs 60°) assumptions. The discrepancy highlights the dependence of derived physical parameters on geometric assumptions rather than intrinsic model failure.
The broad-band noise variability at ~0.1 Hz is driven by simultaneous inner-disk temperature and fractional scattering fluctuations propagating from disk to corona. The Ktin-w.r.t.-fs model with phase lag 0.11 ± 0.08 gave a reduced χ²/dof of 6.39/8. The positive phase lag indicates perturbations move from inner disk to coronal region. The Garg et al. [29] model formalism with reduced χ² ≈ 0.80 reproduces the rms and lag spectra. The phase lag error bars are consistent within data points, making the trend statistically weak. No QPOs or prominent BBN features were found in individual flux levels. This supports a propagative, two-component (truncated disk + corona) model for LMXB variability.

Data And Code Availability
The software used for data reduction includes LAXPC software (version: Oct. 13, 2022), AS1SXTLevel2-1.4b SXT pipeline, and XSELECT (V2.5b) for annular extraction. Spectral fitting was performed using XSPEC (version: 12.13.0c) of HEASOFT (6.31.1).

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The bbodyrad model was tested first but failed with reduced χ² > 2, justifying the switch to the diskbb-based model. Combinations of heating rate and optical depth were introduced to improve the temporal fit but produced insignificant χ² values (>2). The source was segregated into three discrete flux levels (450–570, 570–650, 650–770 cts/s) to test spectral parameter evolution. Only LAXPC 20 data were used, excluding counters 10 and 30 which suffered abnormal gains.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 displays the HID of the source with AstroSat data, showing count rate in 3–20 keV vs. photon count ratio in 6–20 keV and 3–6 keV, with 32s binning and flux levels color-coded. Figure 2 shows the best-fit spectrum of FL1, FL2, and FL3 from top to bottom in the 0.7–25 keV energy range, with red and black points representing SXT and LAXPC 20 data respectively. Figure 3 (left) presents the PDS fit with two Lorentzians at ν₀ ≈ 0.04 Hz, HWHM ≈ 0.09 Hz, and characteristic frequency νc ≈ 0.1 Hz. Figure 3 (right) shows the energy-dependent temporal modeling of fractional r.m.s. and phase lag for the representative FL1 segment. Table 1 presents best-fit parameters for spectral analysis across FL1, FL2, FL3, and full flux, along with energy-dependent temporal modeling parameters (δkTin, δfs, phase lag).

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a flux-resolved spectro-temporal characterization of the neutron star LMXB GX 9+9 using AstroSat, identifying a disk-dominated soft state and estimating an inner-disk radius of 16.6 km under a 10 kpc / 60° geometry. 2. The strongest evidence for a propagative variability mechanism is the energy-dependent temporal model with reduced χ² ≈ 0.80, yielding δkTin ≈ 0.56% and δfs ≈ 81% with a positive phase lag of 0.11 ± 0.08, indicating perturbations propagating from disk to corona. 3. The future path requires multi-mission observations (SXT + LAXPC + IXPE/future) of the poorly-studied GX 9+9 at various flux levels to resolve geometric ambiguities and confirm the proposed propagative variability mechanism.

summary.executive_summary: This paper introduces Dense-TSNet, an ultra-lightweight speech enhancement network designed for resource-constrained edge devices. Motivated by the observation that single-channel speech enhancement models with approximately 10,000 parameters are under-researched, the authors propose a novel Dense Two-Stage (Dense-TS) architecture that replaces dilated convolutions in the classic Two-Stage structure with densely connected Two-Stage modules to smooth the loss landscape of narrow lightweight models. The network incorporates a Multi-View Gaze Block (MVGB) composed of a Large Kernel Extractor (LKE), Learnable-Sigmoid Gate (LSG), and Channel Attention (CA), all implemented entirely with CNNs for efficient deployment. The model processes only the magnitude spectrum of the short-time Fourier transform (STFT) input. A significant contribution is the Consistency Magnitude Loss, which computes the minimum distance between the magnitude spectrum of twice-STFTed speech and the clean speech magnitude spectrum, avoiding complex-domain computations that lightweight models struggle to fit. Ablation studies on the VoiceBank+DEMAND dataset demonstrate that the MVGB components (LKE, CA, LSG) each contribute substantially to PESQ scores, with the full configuration achieving 3.05 PESQ, 4.51 CSIG, 3.58 CBAK, and 3.86 COVL. Comparisons reveal that Dense-TSNet achieves 3.05 PESQ with only 14,000 parameters—the first speech enhancement model at approximately 10K parameters—outperforming the classic TS baseline (2.96 PESQ) despite a narrower architecture. Further loss function studies reveal that while adding a Metric Loss (via PESQ discriminator) increases the PESQ score (up to 3.41 at P=200), it also increases spectral errors and introduces pseudohallucination distortions, leading the authors to default to only Consistency Magnitude Loss. The final model uses 14,000 parameters and 356M MACs, making it uniquely suited for deployment on smartphones and cameras.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper introduces Dense-TSNet, an ultra-lightweight speech enhancement network designed for resource-constrained edge devices. Motivated by the observation that single-channel speech enhancement models with approximately 10,000 parameters are under-researched, the authors propose a novel Dense Two-Stage (Dense-TS) architecture that replaces dilated convolutions in the classic Two-Stage structure with densely connected Two-Stage modules to smooth the loss landscape of narrow lightweight models. The network incorporates a Multi-View Gaze Block (MVGB) composed of a Large Kernel Extractor (LKE), Learnable-Sigmoid Gate (LSG), and Channel Attention (CA), all implemented entirely with CNNs for efficient deployment. The model processes only the magnitude spectrum of the short-time Fourier transform (STFT) input. A significant contribution is the Consistency Magnitude Loss, which computes the minimum distance between the magnitude spectrum of twice-STFTed speech and the clean speech magnitude spectrum, avoiding complex-domain computations that lightweight models struggle to fit. Ablation studies on the VoiceBank+DEMAND dataset demonstrate that the MVGB components (LKE, CA, LSG) each contribute substantially to PESQ scores, with the full configuration achieving 3.05 PESQ, 4.51 CSIG, 3.58 CBAK, and 3.86 COVL. Comparisons reveal that Dense-TSNet achieves 3.05 PESQ with only 14,000 parameters—the first speech enhancement model at approximately 10K parameters—outperforming the classic TS baseline (2.96 PESQ) despite a narrower architecture. Further loss function studies reveal that while adding a Metric Loss (via PESQ discriminator) increases the PESQ score (up to 3.41 at P=200), it also increases spectral errors and introduces pseudohallucination distortions, leading the authors to default to only Consistency Magnitude Loss. The final model uses 14,000 parameters and 356M MACs, making it uniquely suited for deployment on smartphones and cameras.

Research Context
Speech enhancement technologies aim to improve speech clarity in noisy environments for voice calls, video recording, and automatic speech recognition. Recent advancements in deep neural networks employ the Two-Stage (TS) architecture for deep feature extraction, inspired by TSTNN. The classic Two-Stage architecture reshapes and partitions spectral data to address spectral distribution characteristics but faces complexity issues. Narrow lightweight models encounter performance bottlenecks due to uneven loss landscapes, and advanced operators like Transformers or Mamba may lack practical deployment efficiency. Research on single-channel speech enhancement models with around 10k parameters is still limited, underscoring a gap for effective models at this scale. Previous methods for lightweight models often focus on complex spectrograms or phase estimation, which lightweight networks cannot fully fit due to parameter constraints.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether a densely connected Two-Stage architecture can address the uneven loss landscape issue inherent in narrow lightweight speech enhancement networks. The authors hypothesize that replacing dilated convolutions in the Dilated Dense Block with Two-Stage modules ensures more robust refinement of the objective function in later training stages. They propose that capturing features from global, channel, and local views through entirely CNN-based modules enables efficient and deployable feature extraction without Transformer or Mamba dependencies. The authors predict that a model with approximately 14,000 parameters can achieve competitive performance with much larger models, addressing the gap in 10k-parameter speech enhancement research. The hypothesis regarding loss functions posits that the Consistency Magnitude Loss, which operates directly in the magnitude domain, is more suitable for lightweight models than complex-domain or Metric Loss approaches.

Methodological Details
Experiments were conducted using the VoiceBank+DEMAND dataset, known for its high-fidelity utterances. Speech samples were segmented into two-second intervals for short-time Fourier transform. The STFT employed an FFT size of 400, window length of 400, and hop length of 100. The training process used a batch size of 2 with the AdamW optimizer. Training was carried out for up to 1,000,000 steps. The network inputs only the magnitude spectrum derived from the complex STFT. For the Dense-TSNet, the input channel count is limited (4 channels in the Dense-TS vs 6 channels in classic TS for similar parameter counts). The channel count for the classic TS framework used for comparison was 64, which is typical for larger models but limiting for ultra-lightweight variants. Evaluation metrics included PESQ (range -0.5 to 4.5), CSIG, CBAK, and COVL (range 1 to 5).

Procedures And Architectures
The Dense-TS structure replaces dilated convolutions in the Dilated Dense Block with Two-Stage modules, making the network composed entirely of densely connected Two-Stage modules. Features are mapped to high-dimensional space using 1×1 convolutions, and the dilated dense block is omitted in favor of direct Two-Stage feature extraction with dense connections. For each layer i, input channels Ci = dense channel × (i + 1) and output channels Cout = dense channel, with an additional convolutional layer (Adjust-Conv) to adjust channel count. The output of each TS-MVGB is a serial connection: TS-MVGBi(x) = freq-MVGB (time-MVGB (x)). Each Dense-TS layer incorporates dense connections (Concat(Adjust-Conv(TS-MVGBi(skipi−1)), skipi−1)) and an extra residual connection. The Multi-View Gaze Block (MVGB) consists of three sub-modules: Large Kernel Extractor (LKE), Learnable-Sigmoid Gate (LSG), and Channel Attention (CA). LKE uses pointwise convolutions, Simple Gate, large kernel depthwise convolutions, Instance Norm, and HardSwish to establish a global perspective. CA reallocates weights to each channel to focus on important features while suppressing less significant ones. LSG consists of depth-wise convolution, pointwise convolution, and Learnable-Sigmoid activation for local spatial perspective and high-frequency detail. Features undergo L-Sigmoid activation and 1×1 convolution to decode the magnitude spectrum mask before multiplying by the noisy magnitude spectrum.

Key Results
Dense-TSNet achieves 3.05 PESQ, 4.51 CSIG, 3.58 CBAK, and 3.86 COVL on the VoiceBank+DEMAND dataset. Compared to the classic TS baseline (2.96 PESQ) with similar parameter counts, Dense-TSNet improves PESQ by +0.09 absolute. The model size of Dense-TSNet is approximately 14,000 parameters, the smallest reported speech enhancement model at this scale. The computational complexity is 356M MACs for Dense-TSNet versus 388M MACs for the classic TS baseline. Ablation without LKE reduces PESQ from 3.05 to 2.79 (-0.26 absolute), demonstrating the critical importance of the global view. Ablation without CA reduces PESQ from 3.05 to 2.86 (-0.19 absolute), showing the contribution of the channel view. Ablation without LSG reduces PESQ from 3.05 to 2.97 (-0.08 absolute), indicating the local view has a smaller impact. Using only Consistency Magnitude Loss yields 3.05 PESQ, while the complex-only loss yields significantly lower 2.60 PESQ. In the loss function study, P=1 yields 3.28 PESQ, P=200 yields 3.41 PESQ, and P=400 yields 3.04 PESQ, with training failing at very high P. The training curves (Figure 4) show Dense-TS converges slower initially but achieves higher PESQ in later stages compared to classic TS.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The denser connections in the narrower model provide a smoother loss landscape, enabling the network to achieve better final performance despite having fewer parameters. The MVGB demonstrates that combining global, channel, and local perspectives within a pure-CNN framework can compensate for the lack of multi-domain complexity in ultra-lightweight models. The Consistency Magnitude Loss addresses the domain mismatch between STFT space and ISTFT speech space without requiring complex-domain operations that are intractable for small models. The finding that Metric Loss increases spectral errors while improving PESQ suggests that the PESQ discriminator may favor perceptually pleasing artifacts over signal accuracy, posing a tradeoff between subjective and objective fidelity.

Contradictions And Limitations
While Dense-TSNet achieves the best PESQ among tested configurations, the Metric Loss study reveals that increasing the Metric Loss weight (P > 1) simultaneously increases amplitude, phase, and complex spectrum errors. At P=200, a pseudohallucination distortion is introduced in the audio, negatively affecting perceptual quality despite the higher PESQ score. The model uses only the magnitude spectrum as input, ignoring phase information which may limit performance in environments with extreme phase-related artifacts. The comparison with other methods in Table I uses a different parameter count (e.g., TSTNN at 0.92M vs Dense-TSNet at 14K), making direct performance-per-parameter comparison nuanced. The random seed, train/test split details, and specific hyperparameter tuning procedure for the Dense-TS variant are not explicitly reported.

Claims
Dense-TSNet is the first speech enhancement model to achieve a parameter size of approximately 14,000, addressing the gap in 10k-parameter research. The paper states the model size is approximately 14K, the first to achieve speech enhancement at this scale. Table I confirms Dense-TSNet has 14K parameters compared to hundreds of thousands or millions in other methods. The authors acknowledge the parameter count is 'around 14K,' which is slightly above the 10K target mentioned in the introduction. This opens a new frontier for deployment on ultra-constrained edge devices like simple cameras and smart watches.
The Dense-TS architecture with MVGB components outperforms the classic Two-Stage baseline in the later training stages. Table I shows Dense-TSNet at 3.05 PESQ versus Classic TS at 2.96 PESQ. Figure 4 training curves confirm the Dense-TS framework achieves better later-stage performance. The classic Two-Stage structure converges faster in the early training stages. Denser connections mitigate the 'loss landscape smoothness' problem that plagues narrow lightweight models.

Data And Code Availability
Source codes will be released after paper acceptance, and audio samples can be found at the provided GitHub repository.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Table II presents ablation experiments for the MVGB module, testing removal of LKE, CA, and LSG individually. Table III explores the loss function by varying the Metric Loss weight P from 1 to 400. Training fails at P=400 when the Metric Loss weight is too large. The complex-only loss produces 2.60 PESQ, substantially lower than the Consistency Magnitude Loss at 3.05 PESQ.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 displays the overall architecture of both Classic Two-Stage and Dense-TS, including the TS-MVGB structure and internal block details. Figure 2 details the internal modules of LKE, LSG, and CA with specific convolution and activation sequences. Figure 3 illustrates the training criteria including Consistency Magnitude Loss and the Metric Loss formulation with the PESQ discriminator. Figure 4 shows the PESQ training curves comparing Dense-TS and Classic-TS, with Dense-TS demonstrating superior later-stage convergence. Figure 5 shows training curves with different P values, highlighting the pseudohallucination at P=200 and failure at P=400. Table I compares Dense-TSNet against TSTNN, PHASEN, MANNER-S-5.3GF, CCFNet(Lite), and DeepFilterNet on PESQ, CSIG, CBAK, COVL, Parameters, and MACs. Table II reports ablation results removing LKE, CA, LSG, or Consistency Loss, showing each component contributes significantly to the final scores. Table III studies the loss function with P varying from 1 to 400 and compares against complex-only loss.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the Dense-TSNet, which achieves the first reported speech enhancement model at approximately 14,000 parameters, outperforming the classic Two-Stage baseline with a narrower architecture. 2. The strongest evidence is the ablation study showing LKE (-0.26 PESQ), CA (-0.19 PESQ), and LSG (-0.08 PESQ) each make substantial contributions, and the loss function analysis demonstrating that Metric Loss introduces perceptual artifacts despite improving objective scores. 3. The future path involves exploring further model size compression and continuing to develop efficient CNN-only architectures for ultra-constrained environments without relying on heavier operators.

summary.title: Recurrent Interpolants for Probabilistic Time Series Prediction
summary.authors: Yu Chen*, Marin Biloš*, Sarthak Mittal†, Wei Deng, Kashif Rasul, Anderson Schneider
summary.field_subfield: Machine Learning / Probabilistic Time Series Forecasting
summary.executive_summary: This paper introduces Recurrent Interpolants for Probabilistic Time Series Prediction, a novel framework that blends the computational efficiency of recurrent neural networks (RNNs) with the high-quality probabilistic modeling of stochastic interpolants (SI), a generalization of diffusion and flow-based models. Standard probabilistic time series forecasting methods, such as RNNs or transformer-based models with parametric output layers, are limited by simple probability families, while generative approaches like diffusion or flow matching suffer from scalability issues because model size depends on both feature dimension and time window length. The authors extend the theory of stochastic interpolants to a conditional generation framework with extra control features, enabling the model to learn a joint distribution p(x_{t+1}, x_t | x_{t-P:t-1}) where x_t is the current observation, x_{t+1} is the prediction target, and x_{t-P:t-1} is the context window. An RNN encodes the context into a history prompt h_t, which condition the velocity and score functions of the SI module. The model is trained on 3-tuples (x_{t+1}, x_t, x_{t-P:t-1}) and inference proceeds by transporting x_t to x_{t+1} via a forward SDE. On synthetic 2D datasets (Circles, Moons, Rings, Swissroll, 8gaussians), SI achieves Wasserstein distances ranging from 0.007 to 0.359 across variants. On real-world multivariate datasets (Solar, Exchange, Traffic, Wiki), SI outperforms or matches DDPM, SGM, and FM-based baselines on three out of four tasks under the CRPS-sum metric, demonstrating competitive probabilistic forecasting capability. The authors also compare against Vec-LSTM, showing that generative modeling of the probability distribution is critical for large-dimension time series prediction.

claims.description: Recurrent Interpolants achieve state-of-the-art or competitive performance on multivariate probabilistic time series forecasting tasks.
The method reduces computational cost relative to pure generative models while maintaining high-quality probabilistic modeling.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper introduces Recurrent Interpolants for Probabilistic Time Series Prediction, a novel framework that blends the computational efficiency of recurrent neural networks (RNNs) with the high-quality probabilistic modeling of stochastic interpolants (SI), a generalization of diffusion and flow-based models. Standard probabilistic time series forecasting methods, such as RNNs or transformer-based models with parametric output layers, are limited by simple probability families, while generative approaches like diffusion or flow matching suffer from scalability issues because model size depends on both feature dimension and time window length. The authors extend the theory of stochastic interpolants to a conditional generation framework with extra control features, enabling the model to learn a joint distribution p(x_{t+1}, x_t | x_{t-P:t-1}) where x_t is the current observation, x_{t+1} is the prediction target, and x_{t-P:t-1} is the context window. An RNN encodes the context into a history prompt h_t, which condition the velocity and score functions of the SI module. The model is trained on 3-tuples (x_{t+1}, x_t, x_{t-P:t-1}) and inference proceeds by transporting x_t to x_{t+1} via a forward SDE. On synthetic 2D datasets (Circles, Moons, Rings, Swissroll, 8gaussians), SI achieves Wasserstein distances ranging from 0.007 to 0.359 across variants. On real-world multivariate datasets (Solar, Exchange, Traffic, Wiki), SI outperforms or matches DDPM, SGM, and FM-based baselines on three out of four tasks under the CRPS-sum metric, demonstrating competitive probabilistic forecasting capability. The authors also compare against Vec-LSTM, showing that generative modeling of the probability distribution is critical for large-dimension time series prediction.

Research Context
Autoregression models like RNNs and transformers are the de facto tools for multivariate time series forecasting in domains such as finance, biology, and medicine. Probabilistic output layers in standard recurrent models are confined within a simple probability family because the density needs to be parameterized by neural networks with differentiable loss. Recent works have explored generative modeling via diffusion, flow-based models, and latent neural SDEs for probabilistic time series imputation and forecasting. Generative model predictors suffer from scalability issues because the model size is related to both feature dimension and the size of the window, unlike recurrent models where size is proportional only to the number of features. A computational-friendly framework is needed for large-scale generative model-based time series prediction problems.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether combining an RNN for temporal encoding with a stochastic interpolant for conditional generation can achieve high-quality probabilistic time series prediction while maintaining computational efficiency. The authors hypothesize that initiating the prediction of a future time point's distribution with the current time point (rather than Gaussian noise) is more straightforward and yields better quality. The hypothesis is that the longer temporal dependency can be encoded by a recurrent neural network, with the embedded history passed to the generative model as guidance. The method extends the theory of stochastic interpolants to a more general conditional generation framework with extra control features, predicted to improve multivariate forecasting. The paper predicts that the conditional SI module will be computational-friendly and achieve high-quality modeling of the future time point's distribution.

Methodological Details
The method is tested on several synthetic two-dimensional datasets including Circles, Moons, Rings, Swissroll, and 8gaussians. For diffusion-like baselines, DPPM is implemented with both linear and cosine noise schedulers. The four real-world time series datasets are Solar, Exchange, Traffic (PEMS-SF), and Wiki. Preprocessing follows the steps in Salinas et al. (2019), with the gluonts package providing metric calculations. The probabilistic forecasting is evaluated using Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS-sum), Normalized Root Mean Square Error via the median of samples (NRMSE), and Normalized Deviance (ND). To make a fair comparison between models, the same neural networks are used for DDPM, SGM, FM, and SI baselines. All models are assigned to generate data in the same setting by mapping from standard Gaussian to the target distribution. The training dataset consists of tuples (x_{t+1}, x_t, x_{t-P:t-1}), where xt belongs to RD with D dimensions. Importance sampling using a Beta distribution with parameters (0.1, 0.1) is leveraged to handle the integral over diffusion time in the loss functions. The code will be publicly available for the camera-ready version.

Procedures And Architectures
The core architecture (Figure 2) consists of an RNN encoding context xt-P:t-1 into a history prompt ht, followed by the SI module performing conditional generation from xt. The training algorithm (Algorithm 1) iterates through samples, drawing s_i from Beta(0.1, 0.1), computing xs,i = alpha(si)xti + beta(si)xti+1 + gamma(si)zi, and passing xti-P:ti-1 through the RNN to get hi. The velocity function b(s, x, s, ξ) and score function s(s, x, ξ) are modeled by deep neural networks and trained by minimizing Lb and Ls, both weighted by 1/p(Beta(si)). For inference (Algorithm 2), the RNN encodes xt-P:t-1 into ht, and the forward SDE is integrated for s ∈ [0, 1] starting from ˜x0 = xt with condition h, outputting ˜x1 as the prediction of xt+1. The stochastic interpolant equation is xs = α(s)x0 + β(s)x1 + γ(s)z, where α, β, γ are schedule functions with boundary conditions α(0)=1, α(1)=0, β(0)=0, β(1)=1, γ(0)=γ(1)=0. The conditional SDE for inference is d˜xs = [b(s, ˜xs, h) + ϵ(s)s(s, ˜xs, h)] ds + √{2ϵ(s)} dw, where ϵ(s) ≥ 0 is the diffusion variance. For multi-step prediction, the step-by-step prediction is run recursively. The model supports different gamma schedules: square root γ(s) = √(2s(1-s)), quadratic γ(s) = t(1-s), and trigonometric γ(s) = sin(πt)^2. Theorem 1 formally extends stochastic interpolants to arbitrary joint distributions, showing ρ_t satisfies the transport equation ∂ρ_t + ∇⋅(b_tρ_t) = 0 with velocity b_t(x|ξ). The paper notes that loss values become larger when s is close to the ends, necessitating importance sampling.

Key Results
On the synthetic 8gaussians dataset, SI with trig-linear schedule achieves a Wasserstein distance of 0.15, while the best-performing SI variant achieves 0.13 on the Rings dataset. Table 1 shows Wasserstein distances between generated samples and true data: for Circles, SI achieves 0.15 (trig, linear) versus FM's 0.15, SGM's 0.14, and DDPM's 0.12 (cosine) or 0.24 (linear). For the Swissroll dataset in Table 1, SGM achieves a Wasserstein distance of 0.35, FM 0.14, SI (sqrt, linear) 0.22, and SI (sqrt, trig) 0.48, while DDPM (cosine) is 0.12. On the Moons dataset, SI achieves Wasserstein distances ranging from 0.16 to 0.25 across variants, with SGM at 0.32 and DDPM at 0.20 (cosine). In the Solar dataset (Table 2), SI achieves a CRPS-sum of 0.080 ± 0.007, outperforming FM (0.133 ± 0.002) and SGM (0.108 ± 0.026). For the Traffic dataset, FM achieves the best CRPS-sum of 0.084 ± 0.023, outperforming SI (0.083 ± 0.005). On the Exchange dataset, SI achieves 0.359 ± 0.06, matching DDPM (0.359 ± 0.061) and outperforming FM (0.419 ± 0.027). On the Wiki dataset, SI achieves 0.087 ± 0.041, while DDPM achieves 0.008 ± 0.001. The authors note FM cannot capture the data distribution on Wiki. Compared to the pure recurrent Vec-LSTM model, SI and SGM/DDPM get better performance, implying that carefully modeling the probability distribution is critical for large-dimension time series prediction. Figure 4 shows forecast paths on 6/137 variate dimensions of the Solar dataset, with median prediction, 50th, and 90th confidence intervals showing the model captures uncertainty even with varying dimension scales.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The integration of an RNN with a stochastic interpolant addresses the computational scalability of pure generative models by encoding history into a compact prompt, while the SI module provides high-quality probabilistic modeling beyond simple Gaussian assumptions. The conditional SI framework can be adapted for any condition type: simple categorical values, complex prompts, partial observations (inpainting/imputation), images, or text, following the design of diffusion models for image generation. Theorem 1 provides a continuous-time interpretation of stochastic interpolants, avoiding characteristic functions and making the analysis more friendly to users compared to the discrete-time approach in Albergo et al. (2023b). The score function gradient ∇log ρ_t(x) is optimized in a simple quadratic objective function, providing theoretical grounding for the training procedure. The authors conclude that stochastic interpolants are a strong candidate for conditional generation, specifically for multivariate probabilistic forecasting, due to their flexibility and performance.

Contradictions And Limitations
On the Traffic dataset, the FM-based model achieves better CRPS-sum than SI (0.084 vs 0.083), and the authors were unable to get satisfying results from a hyperparameter search over flow matching settings. On the Wiki dataset, the DDPM model achieves a CRPS-sum of 0.008±0.001, significantly better than SI's 0.087±0.041, suggesting DDPM is superior for this specific data distribution. The authors note that on Wiki data, FM cannot capture the data distribution, limiting generalizability across all generative methods. The paper does not report specific hardware used for training or inference, making reproducibility of exact runtimes and compute budgets difficult. The random seeds for experiments are not specified, which may affect reproducibility of stochastic training runs. The train/test splits for the real-world datasets are not explicitly detailed beyond referencing Salinas et al. (2019).

Claims
Recurrent Interpolants achieve state-of-the-art or competitive performance on multivariate probabilistic time series forecasting tasks. SI achieves 0.080±0.007 CRPS-sum on Solar, outperforming FM (0.133±0.002) and SGM (0.108±0.026). SI matches DDPM on Exchange (0.359±0.06) and outperforms FM (0.419±0.027). SI outperforms or matches other models on three out of four datasets. FM achieves a better CRPS-sum on Traffic (0.084±0.023 vs SI's 0.083±0.005). DDPM achieves significantly better performance on Wiki (0.008±0.001 vs SI's 0.087±0.041). The framework is a strong candidate for multivariate probabilistic forecasting, suggesting that generative modeling of the probability distribution is critical. The conditional SI module can be extended to other condition types, potentially broadening its applicability beyond time series.
The method reduces computational cost relative to pure generative models while maintaining high-quality probabilistic modeling. The RNN encodes the context into a history prompt h_t, making the model computationally friendly for large-scale prediction. Compared to pure recurrent models, the generative approach is argued to be more natural for time series prediction. The paper does not provide a quantitative computational complexity comparison (FLOPs, inference time per step) against pure RNNs or pure diffusion models. The combination of RNN temporal encoding and SI generative modeling offers a middle ground between purely recurrent and purely generative architectures.

Data And Code Availability
The authors state that the code will be publicly available for the camera-ready version. The synthetic datasets are referenced to Chen et al. (2021) and Lipman et al. (2022) with published code repositories.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The authors test four different gamma schedules for SI: sqrt, quadratic, trigonometric, and linear interpolants. Most gamma-interpolant function combinations achieve good results modeling the target distribution. Two different noise schedulers (linear and cosine) are evaluated for DPPM baselines. Additional metrics including Sliced Wasserstein Distance (SWD) and Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) confirm results consistent with CRPS-sum. A hyperparameter search over flow matching without satisfying results is mentioned as a reason for concluding SI is a strong candidate.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the alpha(s), beta(s), gamma(s) schedules of stochastic interpolants illustrating the interpolant path. Figure 2 illustrates the Recurrent Interpolants model diagram showing the RNN encoding context and SI performing conditional generation. Figure 3 shows examples of model generated samples for the synthetic two-dimensional datasets across all compared methods. Figure 4 demonstrates forecast paths on the Solar dataset with median prediction and 50th/90th confidence intervals on 6/137 variate dimensions. Figure 5 shows the Time-Grad model for conditional time series prediction architecture. Table 1 reports Wasserstein distances between generated samples and true data for Circles, Moons, Rings, Swissroll, and 8gaussians. Table 2 reports CRPS-sum results on the four real-world datasets: Solar, Exchange, Traffic, and Wiki.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a conditional stochastic interpolant framework that combines RNN-based temporal encoding with an SI generative module to achieve high-quality probabilistic time series prediction while maintaining computational efficiency. 2. The strongest evidence is the outperformance or matching of DDPM, SGM, and FM baselines on three out of four real-world multivariate datasets under the CRPS-sum metric, demonstrating that generative probabilistic modeling is critical for large-dimension time series. 3. The future path involves extending the conditional SI framework to more control features (images, text, complex prompts) and potentially applying it to other conditional generation tasks beyond time series forecasting.

summary.title: The properties of highly concentrated aqueous CH₃COOK/Na binary electrolyte and its use in sodium-ion batteries
summary.authors: Shahid Khalid; Nicolò Pianta; Simone Bonizzoni; Piercarlo Mustarelli; Riccardo Ruffo
summary.field_subfield: Energy Chemistry / Aqueous Electrolytes for Sodium-Ion Batteries
summary.type_of_paper: Experimental research paper with comprehensive physico-chemical characterization and proof-of-concept electrochemical testing
summary.executive_summary: This paper presents a comprehensive physico-chemical and electrochemical characterization of highly concentrated aqueous binary CH₃COOK/CH₃COONa electrolytes, targeting the development of water-in-salt (WISE) electrolytes for sodium-ion batteries. The authors prepared four binary solutions with a fixed CH₃COOK concentration of 20 mol kg⁻¹ and varying CH₃COONa concentrations (1, 2.5, 5, and 7 mol kg⁻¹), alongside a 1 M NaAc control. The series was characterized via Differential Scanning Calorimetry (-120 to 90 °C), rheology (viscosity vs. temperature), electrical impedance spectroscopy (conductivity), and linear sweep voltammetry (electrochemical stability window). Thermal analysis revealed that glass transition temperature (Tg) increases with salt concentration, correlating with the transition from salt-in-water to water-in-salt behavior; notably, the 7N20K composition (7 mol kg⁻¹ NaAc + 20 mol kg⁻¹ KAc) showed a low liquidus temperature (~0 °C), suggesting resistance to salt crystallization. Ionic conductivity followed Vogel-Tamman-Fulcher behavior across all compositions, with the most concentrated 7N20K solution maintaining 21.2 mS cm⁻¹ at 25 °C, comparable to organic-based systems. Rheological data classified the acetates as structure-making salts with Arrhenius viscosity-temperature dependence. Electrochemical stability window measurements showed suppression of hydrogen evolution at higher concentrations, with 7N20K reaching 3 V in ideal flooded-cell conditions. As a proof-of-concept, carbon-coated LiTi₂(PO₄)₃ (CLTP) NASICON was synthesized via a one-pot sol-gel route and cycled in 7N20K electrolyte vs. 1 M NaAc. CLTP demonstrated reversible Na⁺ insertion at -0.7 V vs. SHE with 85 mAh g⁻¹ first-cycle anodic capacity, 96% average charge efficiency, and 90% capacity retention over 60 cycles. Impedance spectroscopy revealed a low charge-transfer activation energy of 0.12 eV and a diffusion coefficient of ~10⁻¹³ cm² s⁻¹ at room temperature, confirming the kinetic feasibility of the NASICON/WISE interface for sodium-ion battery applications.

claims.description: Highly concentrated CH₃COOK/CH₃COONa binary electrolytes in the water-in-salt regime exhibit favorable physico-chemical properties for sodium-ion battery operation, particularly at 7 mol kg⁻¹ NaAc + 20 mol kg⁻¹ KAc.
