judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper presents a comprehensive physico-chemical and electrochemical characterization of highly concentrated aqueous binary CH₃COOK/CH₃COONa electrolytes, targeting the development of water-in-salt (WISE) electrolytes for sodium-ion batteries. The authors prepared four binary solutions with a fixed CH₃COOK concentration of 20 mol kg⁻¹ and varying CH₃COONa concentrations (1, 2.5, 5, and 7 mol kg⁻¹), alongside a 1 M NaAc control. The series was characterized via Differential Scanning Calorimetry (-120 to 90 °C), rheology (viscosity vs. temperature), electrical impedance spectroscopy (conductivity), and linear sweep voltammetry (electrochemical stability window). Thermal analysis revealed that glass transition temperature (Tg) increases with salt concentration, correlating with the transition from salt-in-water to water-in-salt behavior; notably, the 7N20K composition (7 mol kg⁻¹ NaAc + 20 mol kg⁻¹ KAc) showed a low liquidus temperature (~0 °C), suggesting resistance to salt crystallization. Ionic conductivity followed Vogel-Tamman-Fulcher behavior across all compositions, with the most concentrated 7N20K solution maintaining 21.2 mS cm⁻¹ at 25 °C, comparable to organic-based systems. Rheological data classified the acetates as structure-making salts with Arrhenius viscosity-temperature dependence. Electrochemical stability window measurements showed suppression of hydrogen evolution at higher concentrations, with 7N20K reaching 3 V in ideal flooded-cell conditions. As a proof-of-concept, carbon-coated LiTi₂(PO₄)₃ (CLTP) NASICON was synthesized via a one-pot sol-gel route and cycled in 7N20K electrolyte vs. 1 M NaAc. CLTP demonstrated reversible Na⁺ insertion at -0.7 V vs. SHE with 85 mAh g⁻¹ first-cycle anodic capacity, 96% average charge efficiency, and 90% capacity retention over 60 cycles. Impedance spectroscopy revealed a low charge-transfer activation energy of 0.12 eV and a diffusion coefficient of ~10⁻¹³ cm² s⁻¹ at room temperature, confirming the kinetic feasibility of the NASICON/WISE interface for sodium-ion battery applications.

Research Context
Conventional organic carbonate electrolytes for Li-ion batteries suffer from low flash points, high melting points, and high viscosities that render them useless at lower temperatures. The thermochemically unstable LiPF₆ salt degrades in moisture to produce HF, causing corrosion of battery components. The narrow electrochemical stability window of water (1.23 V) limits the energy density of aqueous electrolyte systems. Water-in-salt (WISE) electrolytes developed by Suo et al. achieved 3 V windows by dissolving LiTFSI in water up to 21 mol kg⁻¹, reducing water activity through ion-water coordination. Fluorinated salts like LiTFSI exhibit severe oral and dermal toxicity, skin issues, and chronic aquatic toxicity, posing environmental and economic challenges. Cost-effective, highly soluble alternatives such as LiCl, CH₃COONa, and CH₃COOK are identified as suitable for water-in-salt formulations due to their broad availability. NASICON compounds offer stable structures and large ionic channels for efficient ion insertion-extraction, making them ideal electrode materials for concentrated aqueous electrolytes. The knowledge gap lies in the fundamental understanding of thermal, rheological, transport, and electrochemical properties of binary aqueous acetate systems at concentrations above 20 mol kg⁻¹.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is how the physico-chemical and electrochemical properties of highly concentrated aqueous CH₃COOK/CH₃COONa binary electrolytes vary with salt composition. The authors hypothesize that increasing NaAc concentration in the 20 mol kg⁻¹ KAc framework will widen the electrochemical stability window by reducing water activity, while maintaining sufficient ionic conductivity and manageable viscosity. It is predicted that the most concentrated solution (7N20K) will offer the best compromise between transport properties (conductivity, viscosity) and electrochemical stability. The authors further hypothesize that NASICON-based electrodes can reversibly intercalate alkaline ions in such concentrated aqueous environments, with the carbon coating necessary to enable electrochemical performance. A specific testable prediction is that the WIS electrolyte will outperform the 1 M NaAc diluted solution in specific capacity and efficiency during sodium-ion battery cycling.

Methodological Details
Four binary electrolytes were prepared: 1 mol kg⁻¹ NaAc + 20 mol kg⁻¹ KAc (1N20K), 2.5 mol kg⁻¹ NaAc + 20 mol kg⁻¹ KAc (2.5N20K), 5 mol kg⁻¹ NaAc + 20 mol kg⁻¹ KAc (5N20K), and 7 mol kg⁻¹ NaAc + 20 mol kg⁻¹ KAc (7N20K), using 99% purity NaAc and KAc from Alfa Aesar. The salts were dissolved in Milli-Q water (σ = 6.7 μS cm⁻¹) under sonication, with a 1 M NaAc solution prepared as a diluted control. Carbon-coated LiTi₂(PO₄)₃ (CLTP) was synthesized using a one-pot sol-gel route: 1.78 g NH₄H₂(PO₄)₃ (phosphate precursor) in 40 mL ethanol, 3.51 g Ti(OC₄H₉)₄ (Ti source), 0.52 g CH₃COOLi·2H₂O (Li source), and 0.58 g C₆H₁₂O₆ (carbon source), stirred for 4 h at 55 °C. The precursor was dried under vacuum at 100 °C, ground, and calcined at 800 °C for 6 h under argon flow (50 mL min⁻¹) with a ramp rate of 5 °C min⁻¹. Pristine LiTi₂(PO₄)₃ (LTP) was synthesized identically without C₆H₁₂O₆ as a structural control. XRD analysis was performed using Rigaku Miniflex 600 with Cu Kα radiation, from 10° to 80° in 2θ, step size 0.02, scan speed 1 deg min⁻¹. SEM imaging was conducted with Zeiss® Gemini SEM 450. Viscosity was measured on MCR Rheometer 102 (Anthon Paar) with a parallel plate (50 mm) setup, shear rates 10–300 s⁻¹ at 10, 20, 30, and 40 °C. Thermal analysis used DSC 1Star® (Mettler Toledo) with STARe® software, from -120 to 90 °C, cooling at 1 °C min⁻¹, 5 min isotherm, heating at 1 °C min⁻¹, and TGA using Mettler Toledo TGA/DSC-1. Conductivity was measured by EIS using a dip probe cell with two Pt foils in glass, cell factor 1.04 cm⁻¹, frequency 1 Hz–200 kHz, amplitude 25 mV, under N₂ flux in a climatic chamber (Angelantoni). For electrode preparation, slurries (active material : PVDF : carbon black = 8:1:1) were cast on Al foils for organic electrolyte cells, and dip-coated onto carbon cloth current collectors for aqueous electrolyte cells. The active material loads were ~2.4 mg cm⁻², ~2.7 mg cm⁻², and ~1.7 mg cm⁻² for Li, Na, and K based organic cells; ~6 mg cm⁻² for aqueous dip-coated cells. ESW was estimated in flooded three-electrode cells with glassy carbon working, Pt mesh counter, and double-junction SCE reference. GCPL technique was used for cycling, starting with 10 cycles at 0.1 C, then 0.5 C, 1 C, 5 C, 10 C, and reducing back to 0.1 C. 1C corresponds to 136 mA g⁻¹ (two-ion insertion). EIS for kinetics was performed at 20–70 °C, 1 kHz–100 kHz, 50 mV amplitude under N₂ in a flooded cell within a Faraday cage.

Procedures And Architectures
The electrolyte solutions were prepared at a fixed KAc concentration of 20 mol kg⁻¹ with NaAc concentrations ranging from 1 to 7 mol kg⁻¹ to investigate the effect of added cation-source on the water-in-salt regime. The DSC protocol involved an equilibration at 30 °C for 30 min, cooling at 1 °C min⁻¹ to -120 °C, a 5 min isotherm, and heating at 1 °C min⁻¹ to 90 °C, with the 1 °C min rate chosen to allow structural relaxation without sacrificing sensitivity. Ionic conductivity was determined from the x-axis intercept of the high-frequency side in Nyquist plots under N₂ flux in a climatic chamber, with the bulk ohmic resistance extracted for each concentration. For the electrochemical cell, a flooded three-electrode configuration was used to minimize concentration gradients and isolate electrode-electrolyte interface effects, with glassy carbon as the working electrode to approximate ideal electrocatalytic conditions. The carbon coating on NASICON was applied via a one-pot sol-gel route using glucose as the carbon precursor to improve electronic conductivity while maintaining structural integrity. For impedance spectroscopy, the CLTP electrode was partially sodiated, and during de-sodiation, measurements were interrupted at the middle of the first plateau and collected at 10 °C increments from 20 to 70 °C. The diffusion coefficient calculation utilized the Warburg coefficient σ_W, surface area A, Faraday's constant F = 96485 C mol⁻¹, and the mobile-ion concentration C = 12930 mol m⁻³, with n = 1.7 mobile ions. The 7N20K solution served as the primary test electrolyte for sodium-ion battery proof-of-concept, while 1 M NaAc served as the benchmark diluted electrolyte.

Key Results
DSC thermograms revealed glass transition temperatures (Tg) below -70 °C, cold crystallization (Tc) below -20 °C, and melting endotherms (Tm) around 0 °C, with Tg shifting to higher temperatures as salt concentration increased, indicating growing interspecies interaction. The 1N20K and 2.5N20K solutions exhibited no cold crystallization or melting endotherms under the DSC protocol, remaining frozen in the glassy state, whereas 5N20K and 7N20K showed single cold crystallization events at -28.06 °C and -33.70 °C, respectively. Ionic conductivity followed Vogel-Tamman-Fulcher behavior across the temperature range, with the 7N20K solution yielding 21.2 mS cm⁻¹ at 25 °C, comparable to the 20 M KAc benchmark. Viscosity measurements classified the aqueous acetates as structure-making salts (none showed viscosity decrease with increasing salt) and confirmed Arrhenius behavior with activation energies increasing with concentration, in agreement with conductivity activation energies. The Walden plot (molar/ionic conductivity vs. fluidity η⁻¹) classified all electrolytes as quasi-ideal, and the 7N20K solution at 25 °C followed Kohlrausch's law of strong electrolytes (Λ₀ = 52.90 Ω cm² mol⁻¹) implying complete salt dissociation even at highest concentrations. Linear sweep voltammetry on glassy carbon showed suppression of hydrogen evolution with increasing NaAc, and the anodic decomposition potential was less affected than the cathodic side, in agreement with previous acetate-based studies. The CLTP electrode in 7N20K electrolyte demonstrated a first-cycle anodic capacity of 85 mAh g⁻¹ at -0.7 V vs. SHE, with a 90% capacity retention after 60 cycles and an average charge efficiency of 96%. At 1 C (136 mA g⁻¹) in 7N20K, CLTP provided an average anodic specific capacity of 68 mAh g⁻¹ with 99.0% average charge efficiency, significantly outperforming the 1 M NaAc case (96 mAh g⁻¹ anodic, 36 mAh g⁻¹ cathodic at 1 C). EIS revealed a charge-transfer activation energy of 0.12 eV at room temperature, indicating very good kinetic properties of the NASICON/7N20K interface. The diffusion coefficient at room temperature was approximately 10⁻¹³ cm² s⁻¹, consistent with literature, and a low diffusion activation energy of 0.48 eV suggested that diffusion improves with temperature. The sodium concentration in 7N20K (Na⁺ : K⁺) was 2.85 times lower than potassium, yet preferential sodium insertion occurred, with the first-cycle anodic and cathodic capacities of 104 and 84 mAh g⁻¹ yielding 80% charge efficiency in the WISE electrolyte. In the diluted 1 M NaAc solution, first-cycle capacities were 96 and 36 mAh g⁻¹ yielding only 40% charge efficiency, confirming the WISE electrolyte advantage.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The upward shift of Tg with salt concentration signals the transition from salt-in-water to water-in-salt behavior, where water molecules form subnanometer clusters strongly interacting with ions, reducing water activity and increasing kinetic overpotentials for water electrolysis. The structure-making behavior (monotonically increasing viscosity) signifies that cations and acetate anions, being strongly hydrated, contribute to molecular ordering and reduce free water activity, supporting the WISE mechanism. The quasi-ideal behavior on Walden plots suggests that despite high concentrations, the acetates maintain complete dissociation according to Kohlrausch's law, with the degree of fluidity related to the association of ions in solution. The low charge-transfer activation energy (0.12 eV) and the fact that the aqueous electrolyte improves alkaline-ion diffusion inside the electrode structure relative to organic counterparts indicate kinetic superiority of WISE systems. The fact that the carbon content does not affect the NASICON crystal structure implies that the larger K⁺ ion is preferentially accommodated in the framework, and the 7N20K electrolyte preferentially utilizes Na⁺ for the anode. The 7N20K solution provides a significant advantage for long-term cycling by preventing premature cell failure caused by salt crystallization, as its liquidus temperature (~0 °C) exceeds practical operating temperatures.

Contradictions And Limitations
The anodic ESW expansion was not as significant as the cathodic expansion, in agreement with prior acetate-based studies, suggesting the cathodic suppression of hydrogen evolution is the primary stability benefit. The LSV procedure for decomposition potentials involves a quasi-ideal electrocatalytic electrode with small surface area and a large electrolyte volume, which may overestimate decomposition limits. The ionic conductivity of sodium-containing samples is lower than or nearly equal to the 20 M KAc benchmark, reflecting the expected trade-off between concentration and transport. All electrolytes behave like Newtonian fluids, but the VTF equation could not be fully confirmed due to the limited temperature range accessible by the DSC instrument, leaving the VTF analysis as an interpretation. The study does not report a formal statistical treatment of cycling data (e.g., error bars on capacity retention) or multiple test cycles for the proof-of-concept battery. The diffusion coefficient was calculated with n = 1.7, which is an estimate; the exact number of mobile ions inside the structure is not directly measured. The comparison between WISE and 1 M NaAc is limited to the specific NASICON/carbon electrode and does not span all concentrations or materials.

Claims
Highly concentrated CH₃COOK/CH₃COONa binary electrolytes in the water-in-salt regime exhibit favorable physico-chemical properties for sodium-ion battery operation, particularly at 7 mol kg⁻¹ NaAc + 20 mol kg⁻¹ KAc. The 7N20K solution achieves 21.2 mS cm⁻¹ conductivity at 25 °C, comparable to organic electrolytes. The liquidus temperature of ~0 °C prevents salt crystallization at room temperature. The ESL extends to 3 V in flooded-cell conditions, suppressing hydrogen evolution. Ionic conductivity is lower in sodium-containing samples than in the KAc-only 20 M solution. The anodic stability window expansion is less pronounced than the cathodic suppression of hydrogen evolution. These electrolytes offer a non-toxic, cost-effective aqueous alternative to organic-based sodium-ion batteries with comparable power and safety characteristics. The water-in-salt regime can be accessed with readily available acetate salts, removing the dependence on expensive fluorinated salts.
The CLTP/7N20K interface enables reversible sodium-ion intercalation with good capacity, efficiency, and stability, demonstrating the viability of WISE electrolytes for sodium-ion batteries. CLTP shows 85 mAh g⁻¹ first-cycle anodic capacity and 96% charge efficiency in 7N20K. 90% capacity retention after 60 cycles confirms cycle stability in the WISE electrolyte. The low activation energy of 0.12 eV confirms fast charge-transfer kinetics at the NASICON/7N20K interface. Preferential sodium insertion is observed despite Na⁺ concentration being 2.85 times lower than K⁺ in 7N20K. The first-cycle anodic capacity of 85 mAh g⁻¹ is significantly lower than the theoretical capacity for NASICON. The low activation energy suggests that the interface kinetics could be further improved by temperature modulation or surface modification. The results validate the design strategy of coupling water-in-salt electrolytes with NASICON cathodes for alkaline-ion batteries.

Data And Code Availability
Supporting Information is available free of charge and includes shear stress vs. shear rate curves, XRPD patterns, SEM images, and additional electrochemical characterization of the NASICONs in organic electrolytes.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The carbon coating effect was isolated by synthesizing and testing pristine LTP without glucose as a control; both samples showed the same rhombohedral NASICON crystal structure. The WISE effect was isolated by comparing CLTP cycling in 7N20K (85 mAh g⁻¹ anodic, 96% efficiency) versus the same electrode in 1 M NaAc (96 mAh g⁻¹ anodic, 40% efficiency). The carbon-coated NASICON was dip-coated onto carbon cloth for aqueous testing to isolate electrode corrosion from the aqueous electrolyte. EIS was performed in a Faraday cage to eliminate environmental interference, and measurements were repeated at different temperatures (20–70 °C) to extract activation energies.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows DSC thermograms with endotherm direction bottom, illustrating Tg, Tc, and Tm shifts and the single crystallization events of 5N20K and 7N20K. Figure 2a displays temperature-dependent ionic conductivity showing Vogel-Tamman-Fulcher behavior; 2b shows conductivity versus concentration. Figure 3a shows Arrhenius viscosity-temperature dependence for all electrolytes; 3b shows viscosity versus temperature confirming Newtonian fluid behavior. Figure 4a presents the Walden plot (molar/ionic conductivity vs. fluidity η⁻¹) classifying all electrolytes as quasi-ideal; 4b shows Kohlrausch's law fit for 7N20K at 25 °C. Figure 5 displays LSV profiles vs. SHE for all electrolyte samples, showing the expanded electrochemical stability window. Figure 7a shows potential profiles of CLTP in 7N20K and 1 M NaAc illustrating preferential sodium insertion; 7b shows rate capability at different C-rates. Figure 8 displays EIS Nyquist plots at different temperatures on a partially sodiated CLTP electrode showing depressed semicircles. Figure 9 shows the Arrhenius plot of the charge-transfer resistance yielding 0.12 eV activation energy. Table 1 lists the four binary electrolyte compositions and their compositional parameters; Table 2 reports molar conductivities, activation energies, ionic conductivities, T₀, and Tg. Table 3 summarizes the cathodic and anodic decomposition potentials for all electrolyte samples.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a comprehensive physico-chemical and electrochemical characterization of highly concentrated aqueous CH₃COOK/CH₃COONa binary electrolytes, establishing the 7N20K composition as a viable water-in-salt electrolyte with 21.2 mS cm⁻¹ conductivity and a ~3 V stability window. 2. The strongest evidence for the water-in-salt behavior is the observed 0.12 eV charge-transfer activation energy at the NASICON/7N20K interface, the low liquidus temperature (~0 °C) of the most concentrated solution, and the quasi-ideal behavior on Walden plots confirming complete dissociation even at extreme concentration. 3. The future path involves scaling the WISE approach to multi-concentration sodium-ion cells, optimizing the carbonate-based electrolyte formulation for improved anodic stability, and extending the electrode-material scope beyond NASICON to evaluate broader sodium-ion battery compatibility.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper describes the development of a high-throughput screening (HTS) implementation of the freeze-float selection platform for detecting ice-nucleating entities (INEs) in aqueous droplets. Building upon a prior proof-of-concept system using a 1 cm² cuvette that accommodated up to 50 droplets of 1 μL volume, the authors expanded the system to accommodate 48 cryovials each containing up to 40 droplets, achieving a throughput increase by a factor of 38 (1,920 droplets per assay). Key methodological improvements included the integration of the Biomek 3000 robotic liquid handling system for automated droplet generation, which produced 1 μL droplets with 9.2% polydispersity, and the adoption of an Asymptote VIA controlled-rate freezer to overcome thermal uniformity limitations of silicone oil. The study reports that the robotic system could generate up to ~3,800 droplets in 96 wells in approximately 15 minutes. The controlled-rate freezer reduced well-to-well freezing temperature dispersion from p = 4.4×10⁻⁷ (constant temperature) to p = 0.31 (linear cooling) and from p = 0.31 (generic freezer linear cooling) to p = 0.83 (controlled-rate freezer), with a 36% overall reduction in dispersion. A major technical limitation identified was droplet instability and coalescence during physical transfer due to static electricity. The work establishes a functional HTS platform that retains freeze-float selection principles while improving accuracy through increased sample size and uniform cooling rates.

Research Context
The prior proof-of-concept freeze-float system used a 1 cm² cuvette geometry that accommodated up to 50 droplets at once. The low thermal conductivity of silicone oil prevented increasing the container footprint without introducing thermal lag. Attempting 10 cuvettes in parallel in the same freezer resulted in a difference of a few degrees between cuvettes, indicating non-uniformity. High-throughput screening using 3,456-well microtiter plates can perform over 100,000 assays per day at volumes under 5 μL. Droplet-based assays reported a million-fold reduction in reagent consumption and 300-fold increase in throughput over multi-well HTS. Polydispersity in droplet emulsions is detrimental to ice-nucleation studies because freezing temperature is proportional to the logarithm of droplet diameter. A 1 mm diameter versus a 0.1 mm diameter droplet leads to a 2.3 °C difference in mean freezing temperature. Interfacing microfluidics with multi-well plates used in HTS was not trivial, leading the authors to use automated pipetting instead.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central goal was to expand the freeze-float system to higher throughput and accuracy by implementing automated droplet generation and controlled cooling. The authors hypothesized that droplet freezing is a random nucleation process that can be accelerated in the presence of ice nucleators. The stochastic nature of freezing results in inherent distributions that make determination difficult from small sample numbers. Expanding the assay from 50 droplets in one cuvette to 48 cryovials of 40 droplets each was expected to increase throughput by a factor of 38. Controlled-rate cooling was expected to reduce the cell-to-cell thermal gradient and improve uniformity across multiple samples. Uniform droplet volume was identified as critical for quantitative detection of ice-nucleation events. More than 30 droplets per sample was determined to be sufficient for observing reliable freezing temperature via confidence interval analysis.

Methodological Details
Droplets were generated as 1 μL aqueous aqueous samples in silicone oil with a 1% silicone surfactant system. The Biomek 3000 robotic liquid handling system replaced manual repeat pipetting for droplet generation. At a standard dispensing rate of 1 droplet per 2 seconds, 40 uniform droplets were generated in 96 wells in approximately 15 minutes. The theoretical capacity was up to ~3,800 droplets in a 96-well plate. To confirm monodispersity, 60 droplets were prepared in a 12-well plate with fluorescein dye. Droplet diameters were measured using the Matlab automated circle detection program Droplet_Dispersion.m. The polydispersity was 9.2%, with a standard deviation of 2.86×10⁻⁵ divided by a mean radius of 3.10×10⁻⁴ m. Based on the polydispersity, the expected dispersion in nucleation temperature was no more than ±0.09 °C. An HFE-7500 cushion layer was placed at the bottom to prevent droplet contact with the plastic wall. The Auto-set Ion Pump discharged static electricity from the Biomek 3000 to prevent droplet coalescence. Wet filter paper was placed below the plastic plate during movement to minimize static electricity. For the validation, 30 droplets with 1 mg/mL Snomax colored with yellow fluorescein dye were prepared in a 96 deep well system. The Asymptote VIA freezer accommodated up to 48 cryovials each containing 50 μL HFE-7500, 1 mL silicone oil with 1% surfactant, and 40 droplets. Each cryovial contained 20 INA droplets (1 mg/mL Snomax) and 20 INA-free droplets (milli Q water with Coomassie Brilliant Blue). Statistical comparisons used a Python script KStest.ipynb implementing the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test.

Procedures And Architectures
The 96 deep well plate was tested first using the Biomek 3000 in a silicone oil buoyant layer with an HFE-7500 cushion layer. Droplets were dispensed into the silicone oil layer at a rate of 1 droplet per 2 seconds. The Asymptote VIA freezer was employed to provide constant rate cooling with high precision down to −0.5 °C/min. A custom-made glass lid was equipped on the freezer to enable automated image recording by a generic digital camera. The freeze-float validation used the commodity freezer employed in the previous publication to record droplets freezing and floating behaviour. The KStest.ipynb script compared cumulative distributions of freezing temperatures using the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test for p-value calculation. For the controlled-rate system, droplets with INA froze at −7.1 ±0.59 °C, while droplets without INA did not freeze until −12.3 °C. In the commodity freezer, the mean temperature for INA droplets was −7.5 ±0.97 °C. The metal cooling plate and sample holder in the Asymptote freezer achieved homogeneous cooling through the vials.

Key Results
The Biomek 3000 successfully generated 40 uniform droplets in 96 wells (~3,800 total) in approximately 15 minutes at the standard dispensing rate. Droplets generated by the robotic system showed similar freezing and floating behaviour to the previous report, validating the automated generation step. The polydispersity of the generated droplets was 9.2%, supporting the requirement for uniform volume in quantitative detection. The expected temperature dispersion due to polydispersity was no more than ±0.09 °C. The p-value for freezing temperatures in cells of the same 96 deep well plate at −28 °C constant temperature was 4.4×10⁻⁷, indicating significant thermal gradient. With linear cooling (−0.25 °C/min) in the generic freezer, the p-value improved to 0.31, but mean freezing times between cells differed (47.4 and 50.6 min). In the Asymptote controlled-rate freezer, droplets with INA froze at −7.1 ±0.59 °C compared to −7.5 ±0.97 °C in the commodity freezer. The well-to-well freezing temperature dispersion in the Asymptote freezer showed p = 0.83 with standard deviation 0.73, compared to p = 0.31 with standard deviation 1.6 in the 96 deep well system. The Asymptote system achieved an overall 36% lower dispersion in well-to-well freezing temperature compared to the 96 deep well system in the generic freezer. The freezing-time range significantly increased with linear cooling in the generic freezer, which was a drawback. The throughput was increased by a factor of 38 when moving from 50 droplets in one cuvette to 1,920 droplets in 48 cryovials.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The reduction in p-value from 4.4×10⁻⁷ to 0.31 with linear cooling supports the importance of a constant cooling rate in stochastic heterogeneous nucleation models. The 36% reduction in dispersion in the Asymptote freezer confirms that controlled-rate cooling improves the accuracy of the freeze-float selection platform for multi-sample screening. The similarity between the freeze-float behaviour of INA droplets generated by the Biomek and those from the previous manual system validates the robotic implementation. The polydispersity analysis confirms that robotic droplet generation achieves the required volume uniformity for quantitative nucleation temperature measurement. The system demonstrates that the freeze-float principle can be scaled to high-throughput formats without losing the qualitative selection ability of the original proof-of-concept.

Contradictions And Limitations
The droplet stability was not sufficient when the system needed to be transferred over distances, such as between laboratories, due to static electricity causing coalescence. Static electricity caused by friction led to droplet coalescing during transport, preventing successful combination of the droplet generation system with the downstream assay. Although linear cooling improved the p-value, it significantly increased the range of freezing time in the generic freezer, and mean freezing times between cells differed (47.4 vs 50.6 min). The paper notes that the 96 deep well plate geometry with silicone oil still made it difficult to avoid cell-to-cell thermal gradients even with linear cooling. The paper does not report a full statistical analysis of the INA-free versus INA droplets at the threshold concentration for the Asymptote system.

Claims
The freeze-float system can be expanded to high-throughput screening (HTS) by combining robotic droplet generation with a controlled-rate freezer. The Biomek 3000 generated 40 uniform droplets per well in 96 wells with similar behaviour to the manual system. The Asymptote freezer reduced well-to-well dispersion from p=0.31 (generic) to p=0.83 (controlled-rate). The throughput increased by a factor of 38 by using 48 cryovials. Droplet stability failed during laboratory-to-laboratory transfer due to static-induced coalescence. The Biomek-generated droplets could not be successfully combined with the downstream system for transport. The platform is suitable for screening thousands of droplets in a single assay session but requires static-electricity mitigation for transportation. Controlled-rate cooling is essential for minimizing thermal artifacts in multi-sample freeze-float experiments.
The Biomek 3000 robotic system produces droplets with sufficient volume uniformity (9.2% polydispersity) for quantitative ice nucleation temperature measurement. The measured polydispersity was 9.2% against the required monodispersity standard. The expected temperature dispersion was ≤ ±0.09 °C based on the calculated polydispersity. Droplet diameters were confirmed by Matlab automated circle detection. The paper states polydispersity is detrimental in ice-nucleation studies and Swanson's approximation still imposes a sensitivity limit of 2.3 °C between 1 mm and 0.1 mm droplets. Automated pipetting replaces manual repeat pipetting with equivalent or better reproducibility, enabling higher throughput.

Data And Code Availability
The Matlab source code for droplet dispersion analysis is provided as Source Code S1 (Droplet_Dispersion.m). The Python script for Kolmogorov-Smirnov test comparisons is provided as Source Code S3 (KStest.ipynb). The paper mentions a KStest.ipynb script but does not specify a repository or accession number for full data availability.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The thermal gradient effect was tested by comparing constant temperature (−28 °C) versus linear cooling (−0.25 °C/min) in the generic freezer. Well-to-well variability was quantitatively assessed using the KStest.ipynb script with p-values. Droplet size (1 μL) and count (30 per well) were kept consistent across validation experiments. The detection threshold of INA concentration was investigated to confirm accuracy but the specific concentration values are truncated in the provided text.

Figure 1 A-B shows the 96 deep well plate compatible with Biomek 3000 for droplet dispensing. Figure 1C shows fluorescent image of 60 droplets for monodispersity verification by ChemiDoc MP. Figure 1D-E displays droplet diameter distribution confirmed by Droplet_Dispersion.m. Figure 2 shows the freeze-float validation experiment with 30 Snomax droplets in a commodity freezer. summary.executive_summary: This study develops a continuous flow protocol for the organophotoredox-catalyzed [2+2]-cycloaddition of electron-rich alkenes, specifically vinyl carbazoles and styrenes, to synthesize dimeric cyclobutanes. judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study develops a continuous flow protocol for the organophotoredox-catalyzed [2+2]-cycloaddition of electron-rich alkenes, specifically vinyl carbazoles and styrenes, to synthesize dimeric cyclobutanes. The authors merge homogenous small-molecule organophotoredox catalysis (pyrillium-based) with a commercial off-the-shelf continuous flow platform to address the limitations of traditional batch organophotoredox dimerization, which often suffered from excessive reaction times, requirement of cryogenic temperatures, and relatively high catalyst loadings. The key synthetic application is the production of 1,2-transdicarbazylcyclobutane (t-DCzCB), a host material for blue electrophosphorescence and PhOLEDs, from vinyl carbazole using only 0.1 mol% catalyst in continuous flow. The work compares batch versus continuous flow outcomes across multiple substrates, demonstrating reduced reaction times (often under 1 h in flow versus days in batch), improved yields, and elimination of cryogenic requirements. The scope extends to brominated, chlorinated, methoxylated, and arylated vinyl carbazoles, as well as styrenic natural product precursors, including the synthesis of the anti-inflammatory lignan magnosalin from E-asarone. The continuous flow methodology also enables functionalization via palladium-mediated Suzuki coupling on the resulting brominated cyclobutanes, establishing a complete synthetic route. The study positions continuous flow as a scalable, environmentally beneficial alternative to batch photoredox chemistry for the production of photophysical materials and natural products.

Research Context
The dimerization of electron-rich alkene building blocks such as enamines and styrenes provides synthetic routes to valuable cyclobutane functional materials and natural products. Vinyl carbazole serves as a precursor for t-DCzCB, used as a host material for blue electrophosphorescence and PhOLEDs. Naturally occurring styrenes such as E-asarone can be seen as precursors of the anti-inflammatory lignan magnosalin through a biomimetic light-induced dimerization process. Cyclobutanes are synthesized via a radical cation-induced [2+2]-cycloaddition. Prior chemical oxidation methods used Fe(III) salts, and photochemical dimerization was first reported in 1965 using organophotosensitizers. Visible light photoredox catalysis using Ru- and Ir-complexes demonstrated effectiveness in synthesizing symmetrical and unsymmetrical cyclobutanes from electron-rich olefins. Nicewicz and coworkers reported dimerization of electron-rich alkenes using a pyrillium organophotoredox catalyst. However, reaction times for organophotoredox-catalyzed dimerizations were excessive in some cases, cryogenic conditions were required for certain substrate classes, and catalyst loadings (typically 3 mol%) were not as low as metal-based systems (0.025 mol%). The use of continuous flow technology has advantages in photoredox transformations, including more efficient irradiation of starting substrates leading to higher conversions. A heterogeneous photoredox fixed-bed flow process using polymeric carbon nitrides was reported as a scalable route to magnosalin through dimerization of E-asarone.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether merging homogenous organophotoredox catalysis with continuous flow technology can overcome the limitations of batch conditions for cyclobutane dimerization. The authors hypothesise that continuous flow will provide a convenient, environmentally beneficial methodology with advantages over conventional batch chemistry in terms of reaction efficiency and scalability. It was anticipated that batch versus continuous flow comparison on commercially available vinyl carbazole would provide a convenient synthetic route to t-DCzCB using continuous flow technology. The authors further hypothesised that the protocol could be extended to a new class of functional materials, specifically brominated, chlorinated, and arylated vinyl carbazoles, and styrenic natural product precursors. A specific hypothesis was that the continuous flow would reduce reaction times and catalyst loadings relative to batch conditions while eliminating cryogenic temperature requirements.

Methodological Details
The study compares batch versus continuous flow conditions on commercially available vinyl carbazole (VCZ) as the model substrate. A commercial off-the-shelf continuous flow platform was selected for its usability and improved availability. Batch synthesis of t-DCzCB was achieved using 3 mol% of the pyrillium organophotoredox catalyst under conditions of Nicewicz. Batch conditions required deoxygenated acetone, cryogenic temperatures, and extended reaction times. The batch reaction of VCZ gave t-DCzCB in 82% isolated yield. Optimization of the continuous flow synthesis was determined through HPLC analysis using p-terphenyl as an internal standard. Calibration of VCZ and t-DCzCB was performed, with full details in the supporting information. Continuous flow reactions were performed at 0.4 M (standard) or 0.2 M in acetone for more challenging substrates. A 10 mmol scale was used for the final catalyst loading optimization. Substrates were synthesized via the method of Obora and coworkers, providing vinyl carbazoles (12a-24a) in moderate to good yields. The only exception was 1-bromo-9-vinylcarbazole (15a), which could only be achieved in very low yields. For styrenic substrates, a substoichiometric amount of anthracene (0.25 eq.) was added as an electron relay to suppress undesired polymerization.

Procedures And Architectures
The continuous flow reactions used a commercial flow platform with variable flow rates, catalyst loadings, and irradiation wavelengths. Optimal flow conditions for t-DCzCB were established at a flow rate of 0.5 mL min⁻¹ (residence time τ = 20 min) with 2 mol% catalyst at 450 nm irradiation. Alternative wavelengths of 405 nm and 420 nm were probed and provided comparable yields. For more soluble substrates at 0.4 M, a flow rate of 0.2 mL min⁻¹ (τ = 50 min) was used to maintain residence time. The pyrillium organophotoredox catalyst (10) served as the homogenous catalyst in both batch and flow conditions. For the styrenic substrates, anthracene was added to the starting solution before introduction into the flow apparatus. The flow system was operated under deoxygenated conditions for the batch model, with adventitious oxygen noted as a cause of side reactions in extended residence times. The flow conditions were designed to emulate batch irradiation with the photochemical equivalent in flow, ensuring comparable photon flux across the reaction zone.

Key Results
Batch synthesis of t-DCzCB using 3 mol% catalyst gave 82% isolated yield requiring cryogenic temperatures. Continuous flow at optimal conditions (0.5 mL min⁻¹, 2 mol% catalyst, 450 nm) gave 98% isolated yield of t-DCzCB. Increasing catalyst loading to 4.5 mol% in flow resulted in a modest reduction in yield to 90%. Reducing catalyst loading to 1 mol% in flow gave 93% isolated yield. Lowering the flow rate from 0.5 mL min⁻¹ to 2 mL min⁻¹ (τ = 50 min) reduced yield to 79% (at 2 mol% catalyst) or 82% (at 1 mol% catalyst), indicating potential reversibility. At 0.1 mL min⁻¹ (τ = 100 min), the yield dropped to 53% with formation of carbazole by HPLC analysis, attributed to O₂ oxidation. At 10 mmol scale with 0.1 mol% catalyst, the flow protocol gave 79% isolated yield of t-DCzCB, matching Ru-based system efficiencies. For 3-bromo-9-vinylcarbazole (12a), batch dimerization gave 48% in 5 days; flow at 0.2 mL min⁻¹ (τ = 50 min) gave 64% in under 1 h. For 4-bromo-9-vinylcarbazole (14a), batch gave 31% while flow gave 71% in considerably shorter time. 3,6-dibromo-9-vinylcarbazole (16a) gave 65% in flow; 2,7-dibromo (17a) gave slightly lower yield where batch slightly outperformed flow. The 2-chloro-9-vinylcarbazole dimer 18b was isolated in 61% yield; 2-methoxy dimer 19b in 45%. 2-hydroxycarbazole vinylation gave bis-vinylated 20a in 62% yield; chemoselective dimerization gave 21b in 25%. 4-fluoroarylated vinylcarbazole 22a gave dimer 22b in 65% yield due to improved solubility. 3,6-di-tert-butylcarbazole gave dimer 23b in 57% yield. The 3,6-bisarylated product 24b was obtained in 50% yield. 4-methoxy styrene (27) with anthracene relay gave dimer 28 in 44%. Styrene (29) with diethylaniline relay gave pellucidin A in 22%. E-aserone (3) dimerized on 10 mmol scale with anthracene relay to give magnosalin (4) in 40% yield in flow without cryogenic temperatures. Suzuki coupling of 13b with 4-methoxybenzene boronic acid gave 25 in 75% yield; borylation gave 26 in 36%.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The reduction in yield at extended residence times (0.1 mL min⁻¹) was attributed to background oxidation of the vinyl carbazole by adventitious oxygen, forming N-formylcarbazole which hydrolyzes to carbazole. The pyrillium catalyst operates through a radical cation-initiated [2+2]-cycloaddition mechanism where the alkene radical cation intermediate undergoes addition with a second alkene equivalent. Continuous flow provides more efficient irradiation of the starting substrates compared to batch, leading to higher conversions and reduced reaction times. The elimination of cryogenic temperatures in flow for the styrenic substrates demonstrates the kinetic advantage of increased photon flux and steady-state conditions. The catalyst loading reduction from 3 mol% (batch) to 0.1 mol% (flow) brings the system into the regime of Ru- and Ir-photoredox catalysts. The Suzuki coupling on brominated products demonstrates the synthetic utility of the cyclobutane dimers as building blocks for further functionalization.

Contradictions And Limitations
For 1-bromo-9-vinylcarbazole (15a), no cyclobutane product was detected by ¹H NMR under either batch or flow conditions, representing a failure of dimerization. For 2,7-dibromo-9-vinylcarbazole (17a), the batch reaction conditions slightly outperformed the continuous flow conditions. The vinylation of 2-hydroxycarbazole gave only 25% dimer 21b, a modest yield, suggesting chemoselectivity issues. The 2-arylated vinylcarbazole 21a displayed poor solubility in acetone, limiting the yield of dimer 21b to 22%. E-aserone dimerization to magnosalin in flow achieved only 40%, which is modest compared to the 98% for t-DCzCB. The paper does not report the random seed for any computational checks (not applicable here). The train/test split is not applicable as this is a synthetic chemistry paper.

Claims
Merging organophotoredox catalysis with continuous flow technology provides a convenient synthetic route to cyclobutanes with reduced catalyst loadings and reaction times compared to batch conditions. Batch t-DCzCB required 3 mol% catalyst and cryogenic temperatures; flow required only 2 mol% at optimal conditions (98%) and 0.1 mol% at 10 mmol scale (79%). Flow reaction times were under 1 h for several substrates, whereas batch required days (e.g., 5 days for 12a). Continuous flow eliminates the requirement for cryogenic temperatures for styrenic substrates. For 2,7-dibromo-9-vinylcarbazole (17a), the batch reaction slightly outperformed the flow condition. 1-bromo-9-vinylcarbazole (15a) failed to dimerize under either condition. The methodology enables scalable production of photophysical host materials without metal catalysts. The protocol is directly applicable to natural product synthesis under continuous flow conditions.
The protocol is general enough to encompass a wide range of functionalized vinyl carbazoles and styrenic alkenes including natural product precursors. Dimers were obtained for bromo, chloro, methoxy, aryl, and tetra-alkyl substituted vinyl carbazoles. The protocol successfully synthesized magnosalin from E-aserone under continuous flow conditions. Yields varied considerably from 98% (t-DCzCB) to 22% (21b) and 40% (magnosalin), indicating substrate-dependent efficiency. The brominated products serve as synthetic building blocks for further palladium-mediated functionalization.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Reversibility was probed by reducing flow rate from 0.5 to 2 and 0.1 mL min⁻¹, observing yield decreases from 98% to 79% and 53% respectively. Wavelength dependence was tested at 405, 420, and 450 nm, showing comparable yields at 0.5 mL min⁻¹. Absence of catalyst (entry 9) and absence of irradiation (entry 10) both prevented dimerization. Introduction of anthracene (0.25 eq.) as an electron relay greatly improved product outcome for styrenic substrates. For E-aserone, dimerization was performed on a 10 mmol scale in continuous flow.

Key Figures Tables
Table 1 presents the optimization study of t-DCzCB with entries for flow rate, catalyst loading, wavelength, and isolated yield percentage (98%, 90%, 93%, 79%, 82%, 53%, 79%). Scheme 1 illustrates cyclobutane dimers as functional materials and natural products (t-DCzCB, magnosalin). Scheme 2 depicts the radical cation-induced [2+2]-cycloaddition mechanism with chemical (2A) and photochemical (2B) radical cation generation routes. Scheme 3 shows the merged organophotoredox and continuous flow protocol applied to t-DCzCB, novel analogues, and lignan natural products. Scheme 4 compares batch and flow synthesis of t-DCzCB from vinyl carbazole. Scheme 5 shows the synthetic route to brominated t-DCzCBs and the Obora vinylation method. Scheme 6 demonstrates palladium-mediated Suzuki coupling and borylation on brominated cyclobutanes. Scheme 7 shows the expansion to electron-rich styrenes under continuous flow with anthracene as an electron relay.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a continuous flow protocol merging pyrillium organophotoredox catalysis with a flow platform, enabling synthesis of t-DCzCB from vinyl carbazole at 0.1 mol% catalyst loading and a new class of functionalized cyclobutane materials. 2. The strongest evidence is the 98% isolated yield of t-DCzCB in flow compared to 82% in batch, combined with yield reductions at low flow rates confirming reversible pathways and the elimination of cryogenic requirements. 3. The future path involves applying this continuous flow photoredox protocol to more complex natural product syntheses, scalability of photophysical materials, and exploring further substrate scope in the cyclobutane domain.

summary.title: A New Organocatalytic Desymmetrization Reaction Enables the Enantioselective Total Synthesis of Madangamine E
summary.authors: Shinya Shiomi; Benjamin D A Shennan; Ken Yamazaki; Ángel L Fuentes De Arriba; Dhananjayan Vasu; Trevor A Hamlin; Darren J Dixon
summary.field_subfield: Synthetic Organic Chemistry / Total Synthesis
summary.type_of_paper: Experimental total synthesis with catalytic method development
summary.executive_summary: This paper reports the 30-step enantioselective total synthesis of madangamine E, a complex pentacyclic marine natural product, enabled by a novel organocatalytic desymmetrization reaction. The key transformation involves an intramolecular Michael addition of a prochiral 4-aminocyclohexanone-linked β,β'-disubstituted nitroolefin to a tethered nitroolefin, catalyzed by a bifunctional primary amine thiourea organocatalyst. This reaction concurrently establishes three stereogenic centers, including a quaternary carbon, in near-perfect enantio- and diastereo-selectivity (99% ee as single diastereomer). The catalytic cycle was computationally probed using DFT, revealing a cooperative push/pull mechanism stabilized by multiple hydrogen bonding interactions between the thiourea, nitro group, and enamine moieties. The synthetic sequence proceeds from commercially available 1,4-cyclohexanedione monoethylene acetal, constructs the bicyclic core via the desymmetrization, and completes the pentacyclic skeleton through oxidative lactamization, a two-step Z-selective olefination of a sterically hindered ketone, and two ring-closing metathesis (RCM) macrocyclizations. The study demonstrates that early catalytic desymmetrization can install all stereochemical information in a complex natural product, and the pathway was validated by X-ray diffraction and DFT. The scalability of the desymmetrization was demonstrated on a 5g scale, and the model nitroolefin was accessible on a 17g scale, supporting the practical utility of the strategy.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper reports the 30-step enantioselective total synthesis of madangamine E, a complex pentacyclic marine natural product, enabled by a novel organocatalytic desymmetrization reaction. The key transformation involves an intramolecular Michael addition of a prochiral 4-aminocyclohexanone-linked β,β'-disubstituted nitroolefin to a tethered nitroolefin, catalyzed by a bifunctional primary amine thiourea organocatalyst. This reaction concurrently establishes three stereogenic centers, including a quaternary carbon, in near-perfect enantio- and diastereo-selectivity (99% ee as single diastereomer). The catalytic cycle was computationally probed using DFT, revealing a cooperative push/pull mechanism stabilized by multiple hydrogen bonding interactions between the thiourea, nitro group, and enamine moieties. The synthetic sequence proceeds from commercially available 1,4-cyclohexanedione monoethylene acetal, constructs the bicyclic core via the desymmetrization, and completes the pentacyclic skeleton through oxidative lactamization, a two-step Z-selective olefination of a sterically hindered ketone, and two ring-closing metathesis (RCM) macrocyclizations. The study demonstrates that early catalytic desymmetrization can install all stereochemical information in a complex natural product, and the pathway was validated by X-ray diffraction and DFT. The scalability of the desymmetrization was demonstrated on a 5g scale, and the model nitroolefin was accessible on a 17g scale, supporting the practical utility of the strategy.

Research Context
The madangamine family, isolated from Xestospongia marine sea sponges, features an architecturally complex pentacyclic fused-ring system. Three rings constitute a diazatricyclic core common to all family members, while the D ring differs in each madangamine. Despite prior attention, only two total syntheses of madangamine family members have been reported, with a single formal synthesis of madangamine A. Previous strategies used late-stage tetracyclic intermediate construction via N-acyl-iminium cyclization and allene hydroboration. The authors identified that the AC bicyclic motif was suited for construction from a catalytic enantioselective desymmetrization reaction. Intermolecular Michael addition reactions with nitroolefins had been established, but intramolecular desymmetrizing variants concurrently establishing a quaternary carbon center were unreported.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question was whether a bifunctional primary amine thiourea organocatalyst could mediate an intramolecular desymmetrizing Michael addition of a β,β'-disubstituted nitroolefin to establish a quaternary carbon. The authors hypothesized that a previously reported desymmetrizing intramolecular Michael addition to α,β-unsaturated esters could be expanded to β,β'-disubstituted nitroolefins. The hypothesis was that the desymmetrization would install all stereochemical information in a single chirality-inducing step, simplifying the total synthesis of madangamine E. The predicted outcome was near-perfect enantio- and diastereo-selectivity, concurrently establishing three stereogenic centers, including a quaternary carbon stereocenter. The study aimed to demonstrate that catalytic desymmetrization could serve as a general strategy for converting achiral starting materials to high-value stereochemically-rich products.

Methodological Details
The model substrate methyl-substituted nitroolefin 7 was constructed in 3 steps from commercially available 1,4-cyclohexanedione monoethylene acetal using oxidative radical nitration. A range of chiral single enantiomer primary and secondary amine organocatalysts was investigated, including trans-cyclohexanediamine and proline-derived scaffolds. The catalytic screening was performed in dichloromethane at 20 mol% loading with benzoic acid as co-catalyst. Jacobsen's thiourea catalyst 9f, previously the best for α,β-unsaturated esters, provided the desired bicyclic Michael adduct 8 in 70% yield as a single diastereomer in 99% ee. A simplified bifunctional primary amine catalyst 9e yielded 8 in 51% yield as a single diastereoisomer in 96% ee. The relative and absolute stereochemical configuration of 8 was established by single-crystal X-ray diffraction analysis. Nitroolefin 17E was accessed via a new route: reductive amination of 1,4-cyclohexanedione monoethylene acetal with allylamine and N-tosylation (2 steps), oxidative cleavage, Henry reaction, dehydration (72% over 3 steps), and organo-zinc-copper Michael addition (90% yield, 17g scale). Selenoxide elimination for nitroolefin installation proceeded in 52% yield over 3 steps with E:Z = 3.8:1, optimized in Et2O:CH2Cl2 (2:1, 0.033M). The desymmetrization of 17E with 20 mol% catalyst 9f and 20 mol% benzoic acid provided bicyclic nitroalkane 18 in 95% yield, >99% ee, single diastereomer, on >5g scale. The total synthesis of madangamine E required 30 steps from commercially available materials.

Procedures And Architectures
The catalytic cycle begins with primary amine addition to the ketone substrate to form a hemiaminal intermediate Int1, followed by elimination of water to form imine Int2. Enamine Int3 is formed by tautomerization from imine Int2, and the key C-C bond-forming intramolecular Michael addition occurs. DFT conformational search identified 16 possible transition structures, with TS1 emerging as most favorable by ΔΔG‡ = 3.0 kcal mol⁻¹. The Michael addition is computed as highly exergonic (ΔGrxn = -19.4 kcal mol -1) furnishing iminium-nitronate species Int4. The mechanism is a cooperative push/pull-type, where the transition structure benefits from hydrogen bonding with the thiourea, nitro group, and enamine moieties. The pKa difference [pKa = 17 (nitro) < 20 (thiourea) < 30 (ester)] explains why the desymmetrization works for nitroolefins but not esters. Following the intramolecular protonation, the complex Int6 is hydrolyzed through hemiaminal Int7 to furnish the product. For the total synthesis, oxidative lactamization was performed using AZADO, copper chloride, 2,2'-bipyridine, DMAP, open to air for B-ring closure. Ring-closing metathesis for the D ring used Grubbs 1st generation catalyst in CH2Cl2 at 40 ºC under high dilution. Z-selective olefination of the sterically hindered ketone used (methoxymethyl)triphenylphosphonium chloride and NaHMDS, with a saturated NH4Cl quench at 60 ºC for 3 hours improving yield from 26% to 86%. The final macrocyclization employed Hoveyda-Grubbs 2nd generation catalyst in PhMe at 110 °C with co-catalytic p-benzoquinone and very high dilution.

Key Results
Jacobsen's thiourea catalyst 9f gave the model bicyclic adduct 8 in 70% yield in 99% ee as a single diastereomer. The simplified catalyst 9e gave adduct 8 in 51% yield in 96% ee as a single diastereoisomer. DFT computed the energy difference between the lowest and second-lowest TS at 3.0 kcal mol⁻¹, corresponding to 99% ee, in excellent agreement with the experimental 99% ee. The intramolecular Michael addition was computed as highly exergonic with ΔGrxn = -19.4 kcal mol⁻¹. Treatment of 17E with 20 mol% catalyst 9f and 20 mol% benzoic acid gave bicyclic nitroalkane 18 in 95% yield, >99% ee, single diastereomer, on >5g scale. The butenyl chain installation on the nitroalkane proceeded in 90% yield and proved highly scalable on 17g. Selenoxide elimination gave the nitroolefin in 52% yield over 3 steps with E:Z = 3.8:1. The Wittig homologation yield was improved from 26% to 86% (b.r.s.m 99%) by using a rigorous NH4Cl quench at 60 ºC for 3 hours. Ring-closing metathesis to give tetracyclic enone 26 proceeded in 82% yield. The final Z-configured skipped diene 28 was obtained in excellent yield and good Z-selectivity (90%, 4.3:1) using SOCl2 with DTBMP. The macrocyclization to diamide 30 gave 71% yield. The final double amide reduction gave synthetic madangamine E in 72% yield using excess LiAlH4 in Et2O. The total synthesis was completed in 30 steps.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The early desymmetrization strategy demonstrates that a single chirality-inducing step can set all stereochemical information in a complex natural product. The catalytic cycle is described as a cooperative push/pull-type mechanism where the transition state is stabilized by multiple hydrogen bonding interactions. The mechanism explained the narrow catalyst structure allowance: only bifunctional thioureas with specific geometries accommodate the substrate. The pKa differences between nitronate and enolate control the mechanism, explaining why this reaction does not work for α,β-unsaturated esters. The result highlights the potential of organocatalytic desymmetrization for the rapid and atom-economical generation of stereochemical complexity. The failure of the Amat Wittig approach underscored the importance of substrate geometry and flexibility in late-stage functionalization.

Contradictions And Limitations
The oxidative radical nitration route failed when translated to the butenyl-substituted substrate, necessitating a complete redesign of the nitroolefin access. The Wittig homologation initially gave only 26% yield, indicating that the standard protocol was insufficient for the hindered bicyclic substrate. The RCM of tertiary alcohol 27 failed to close the E ring, attributed to the distant spatial arrangement of the terminal alkenes. Amat's Wittig reaction of an octenoate phosphonium salt was largely unsuccessful on ketone 3 despite extensive experimentation. The triorganozincate reaction for tertiary alcohol 27 was described as highly capricious and sensitive to the quality of the organocerium reagent before finding a reproducible method. The paper does not report the specific random seeds, exact train/test splits (not applicable for synthesis), or detailed demographics (not applicable) that would be relevant in a computational or analytical study.

Claims
A new organocatalytic desymmetrization reaction converts a prochiral cyclohexanone-linked nitroolefin into a bicyclic nitroalkane with near-perfect enantio- and diastereo-selectivity. Model substrate 7 gave 8 in 70% yield, 99% ee, single diastereomer with catalyst 9f. Synthetic substrate 17E gave 18 in 95% yield, >99% ee, single diastereomer on >5g scale. DFT computed 3.0 kcal mol⁻¹ energy difference between lowest and second-lowest TS. X-ray diffraction confirmed the relative and absolute stereochemistry. Catalyst 9e gave lower selectivity at 96% ee vs 99% ee. Most tested catalysts (9a-9d, 9g-9k) gave complex product mixtures instead of cyclised product. The reaction establishes a new method for constructing stereogenic quaternary carbon centres. The approach is highly scalable, demonstrated at 5g and 17g scales.
The early installation of stereochemical information via catalytic desymmetrization enables the total synthesis of madangamine E in 30 steps. The 30-step synthesis was completed, giving synthetic madangamine E (1). Key steps included oxidative lactamization, Z-selective olefination, and two RCMs. Analytical data were highly consistent with reports by Chida and Sato and Andersen. The amide reduction gave only 72% yield. The Wittig homologation initially gave only 26% yield. Demonstrates the utility of catalytic desymmetrization in the synthesis of high-value saturated molecular scaffolds. Highlights potential for rapid and atom-economical generation of stereochemical complexity.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
A range of 10 chiral catalysts was screened, with only two giving the desired product, confirming the narrow catalyst structure allowance. The DFT study investigated 16 possible transition structures for the key C-C bond formation. Computational replacement of the nitro group with α,β-unsaturated ester confirmed the pKa-driven mechanistic divergence. The selenoxide elimination was tested in various solvent mixtures, finding Et2O:CH2Cl2 (2:1, 0.033M) optimal. The RCM of 29 was optimized with co-catalytic p-benzoquinone at very high dilution to minimise undesired isomerisation and dimerization. The amide reduction used excess LiAlH4 in Et2O, giving 72% yield.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A shows the pentacyclic fused-ring system of the madangamine family with the diazatricyclic core. Figure 1B shows the total synthesis of madangamine A by Chida and Sato. Figure 1C illustrates the retrosynthetic analysis of madangamine E. Figure 2A shows the previously reported desymmetrizing intramolecular Michael addition to α,β-unsaturated esters. Figure 2B shows the catalyst screening of 10 organocatalysts on model substrate 7. Figure 2C illustrates the computational DFT mechanism for the intramolecular Michael addition. Figure 3 presents the DFT energy surface of the key stereoselectivity-determining step. Figure 4A shows the restructured route to nitroolefin 17. Figure 4B shows the organocatalytic enantioselective desymmetrization of 17E to 18.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a new organocatalytic desymmetrizing intramolecular Michael addition that constructs a chiral bicyclic core with 99% ee, establishing three stereogenic centers including a quaternary carbon in one step. 2. The strongest evidence is the DFT-computational rationalization of the 3.0 kcal mol⁻¹ energy difference between TS1 and the next-best TS, which perfectly matches the experimental 99% ee, confirming the cooperative push/pull mechanism. 3. The future path is the application of catalytic enantioselective desymmetrization as a general strategy for rapidly generating stereochemical complexity in complex natural product synthesis, and expanding the scope to diverse substrates.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigates the dielectric response of molecular-scale nanocomposites comprising silver (Ag) inclusions embedded in a magnesium oxide (MgO) matrix, focusing on how nanoparticle morphology—size, shape, and orientation relative to an external field—tunes the dielectric permittivity. Using Car-Parinello Molecular Dynamics (CPMD) and the Modern Theory of Polarization implemented in Quantum Espresso (versions 6.0 and 6.6), the authors model polarization in eight Ag-MgO systems (three rod-like and five disk-like inclusions) with sizes ranging from 8 to 32 atoms. Key findings reveal that dielectric permittivity enhancements of 30-100% are achievable with inclusion sizes of 8 to 32 atoms. Multi-layer disk-like inclusions (disks 332, 432, 442) yield more than 70% enhancement in ε_r over the matrix permittivity at similar volume loadings, significantly outperforming rod-like counterparts. The mechanism is attributed to local field enhancements at the Ag-MgO interface: electrons in the silver nanoparticle polarize and shift charge density to the interface, creating induced electrostatic fields in the matrix. The 'reach' and intensity of these induced fields depend strongly on the nanoparticle's orientation—parallel alignment maximizes the effective polarizability while perpendicular alignment induces depolarization regions that can suppress the overall dielectric response. The Born effective charge tensor is used to map local charge density variations, revealing that the strongest interfacial effects are confined to within 3 angstroms of the inclusion edge. The study concludes that molecular-scale metal inclusions, due to their finite size and quantum nature, avoid the percolation and tunneling issues of bulk metallic nanoparticles while providing a tunable platform for high-κ dielectrics. The authors note that 2D nanoparticles (421, 441) show a decrease in polarization relative to the bulk in both directions because electrons are confined in the z-direction. Future directions include other matrix materials (SiO₂, HfO₂), diverse transition metal inclusions, and exploration of the perpendicular response limits.

Research Context
The demand for new high-κ dielectric materials is driven by energy storage and processing power limits of traditional single-phase materials. Nanocomposite materials combining dielectric matrices with high-κ inclusions offer tunable dielectric and mechanical properties for transistors, super-capacitors, and quantum computing. As processor chips approach few-nanometer sizes, significant current leakage and tunneling effects dominate, necessitating complex higher-permittivity materials like hafnium oxides or polymer-enriched oxides. Molecular nanoparticles (mNPs) with up to 100 atoms bridge the gap between single-atom dopants and traditional metallic nanoparticles, avoiding the low percolation thresholds of bulk metallic phases. Effective medium approximations and classical atomistic approaches do not encompass the quantum response and local field effects that dominate dielectric behavior in complex solid-state materials. A previous study by the authors on Ag₈/MgO NCs with spherical inclusions found that interfacial effects produced greater than expected polarization response.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is how the distribution and shape of molecular-scale silver nanoparticle inclusions alter the dielectric capacity of a metal-oxide material. The authors hypothesize that at nanoparticle scales of <30 atoms, the size, shape, and orientation of the inclusion greatly alter the behavior of inclusion electrons and thus the atomic-scale polarization. It is predicted that asymmetric inclusions will bring on a dielectric enhancement larger than expected based solely on volume ratios. Rod-like inclusions are expected to show orientation-dependent enhancement, with polarization along the z-axis producing a greater increase than perpendicular polarization. Disk-like inclusions are expected to exhibit exponential growth in polarization with increasing dimension, potentially reaching a metallic threshold.

Methodological Details
The NC systems consist of a magnesium oxide (MgO) matrix with silver mNP inclusions, chosen for its cubic crystal structure, isotropic polarization, and bulk dielectric constant of 8-9.8 with a bandgap of 7.8 eV. Three rod-like and five disk-like inclusions were modeled, built on an ideal Ag fcc lattice and allowed to optimize within the CPMD simulation. The matrix extended 2 MgO layers beyond the inclusion edge in each direction to prevent periodic image interaction while controlling cell loading. The %loading ratios of inclusions to matrix were kept between 3-5% in atom counts to ensure sufficient matrix separation between periodic images. Electronic structure calculations used Quantum Espresso versions 6.0 and 6.6 with a plane wave-basis set using the LDA functional. Mg atoms were described using Bachelet-Hamann-Schluter norm-conserving pseudopotentials, while O and Ag used Rappe-Rabe-Kaxiras-Joannopoulos ultra-soft pseudopotentials from MaterialsCloud. The total energy convergence criterion was set to 10⁻⁸, a force threshold of 10⁻⁴, a wavefunction cutoff of 50-60Ry, and a charge density cutoff of 560Ry. Electron masses were maintained at 300 a.u. then increased to 450 a.u. after initial damped minimizations to accelerate convergence. Calculations employed periodic boundary conditions with Brillouin zone sampling at the Γ point throughout all steps. No thermostat or temperature control was applied; test runs between 200 and 600 K showed negligible temperature effects on geometry due to high melting temperatures and rigid lattice. The polarization was calculated using a static field of 0.001 a.u. applied along the z-axis, following the method of Umari and Pasquarello. The Born effective charge tensor (BEC) was computed by calculating the difference in force experienced by each atom under zero-field and static polarization, normalized to the bulk matrix.

Procedures And Architectures
The CPMD procedure involves two major stages: structural structure relaxation followed by polarization calculation. Step 1: Initial electron minimization with Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization, followed by damped dynamics for full ion and electron minimization. Step 2: Lattice vector relaxation to remove residual stress from the cell due to the inclusion. Steps 3-6: The electronic structure was relaxed in a series of optimization steps, with the simulation cell continuously updated for stress minimization. Step 8: The electronic polarization and BECs were calculated in the clamped-ion step, where electronic response is coupled to ionic positions. Step 9: The fully relaxed static polarization was computed by releasing ionic clamps and allowing full relaxation while applying the static field. The low-frequency dielectric constant ε_r was calculated according to Equation 1: ε_r = 1 + 4π(P_ε_damped - P_ε_relax)/ε_field, representing the volume average of periodic systems. The reference polarization was the cell without applied field, and the electronic/ionic polarization was partitioned using damped dynamics. A mathematical correction for polarization jumps (nx×boxlength) was applied during post-processing to address the quantum of polarization effect where electrons shift into neighboring image cells. The BEC maps were interpolated and smoothed to visualize the spatial distribution of the local electrostatic field created by the NP polarization in the matrix.

Key Results
Dielectric permittivity enhancements of 30-100% were observed across the family of Ag-MgO NC systems with inclusion sizes varying from 8 to 32 atoms. The previous spherical Ag₈ mNP showed an ≈30% increase in ε_r with an ≈4% mNP volume ratio. The multi-layer disks (332, 432, 442) exhibited more than 70% enhancement in ε_r over the matrix permittivity at similar volume loadings to the rods. For Rod224, polarization along the z-axis (parallel to field) gave an increase of 9.23, while perpendicular polarization was significantly lower. Disk442, with twice the x,y dimensions of Rod223, had a polarization increase of more than twice in comparison. The 2D nanoparticles (421 and 441) showed a decrease in polarization when compared to the bulk in both directions, because inclusion electrons are not free to move in the z-direction. The local structural distortion ('stress') from inclusion embedding extended only to the nearest neighbors, within approximately 3 angstroms from the mNP edge. BEC plots revealed that the polarization field enhancement is strongly localized to two layers of matrix ions at the interface, while the weaker depolarization field is often extended over large regions of the cell. The perpendicular depolarization area only affects the interfacial atoms, whereas the parallel-oriented field 'reach' extends further and is stronger.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The dielectric enhancement mechanism is driven by the polarization of silver d-electrons that couple to the oxygen p-band at the interface. The shape of the nanoparticle determines the spatial reach and intensity of the induced field: parallel alignment maximizes effective polarizability by mobilizing electrons along the field axis, while perpendicular alignment creates screening rings and depolarization regions. As the inclusions behave as molecules rather than bulk metal, the electron dynamics are quantum-mechanically governed, providing a picture of induced fields that is not applicable to macroscopic metallic nanoparticles. The results suggest a threshold exists at larger sizes where the exponential growth of polarization changes as the inclusion behaves more metallic, though computational constraints prevented reaching this size. The induced fields in nanoscale composites provide a pathway to understand quantum materials behavior as devices are miniaturized, where local interfacial effects become the dominant dielectric contribution.

Contradictions And Limitations
The values calculated for ε_r are not 'true' dielectric constants for a real material because surface charge and edge effects are not accounted for; the result is a periodic volume average. Dielectric constants in real materials are volume and loading-dependent; the study only explored a limited range of loading between 3-5%. Maximum computational constraints limited the simulation to mNP sizes of 32 atoms, preventing investigation of the crossover to metallic behavior. The DFT/LDA functional is expected to yield bandgaps significantly lower than experimental values, though the authors argue that NP states near the Fermi level should mitigate this. The polarization jumps (quantum of polarization effect) require careful mathematical post-processing and vary with asymmetry, adding complexity to effective polarization extraction. The paper notes that sometimes the perpendicular response in the matrix dominates, and the calculated ε_r can be lower than for the pure matrix, requiring close control on direction. The paper was submitted as a preprint or in-progress manuscript with multiple placeholder references (e.g., "Ref. ?"), suggesting incomplete finalization.

Claims
Dielectric permittivity can be tuned by 30-100% by varying silver nanoparticle size, shape, and orientation in an MgO matrix. Dielectric permittivity enhancements of 30-100% were observed with inclusion sizes varying from 8 to 32 atoms. The multi-layer disks (332, 432, 442) exhibited more than 70% enhancement in ε_r over the matrix permittivity at similar volume loadings. The Ag₈ spherical inclusion produced an ≈30% increase in ε_r with ≈4% volume ratio. The 2D nanoparticles (421, 441) showed a decrease in polarization relative to bulk in both directions, showing that not all shapes enhance the dielectric constant. Perpendicular polarization can result in an ε_r lower than the pure matrix, depending on direction. This opens a design space for tunable high-κ dielectrics where morphology is as important as material composition. Device engineers can exploit shape-dependent enhancement for area-efficient capacitive designs.
The local field enhancement mechanism is localized at the Ag-MgO interface, with the strongest effects confined to the first two layers of matrix ions. Enhancement of the polarization field is seen in the matrix in regions adjacent to the NP poles in the direction of the applied field. The enhancement is strongly localized to two layers of matrix ions at the interface. The Born effective charge maps reveal the induced field resembles an induced field on the nanoparticle with moving electrons creating areas of higher and lower force. The depolarization field, while weaker, is often extended over large regions of the cell, not limited to the interface. For perpendicular polarization, the BEC converges to +2,-2 values of matrix in a very short distance, suggesting the effect is minimal. The interfacial region is the critical design parameter for performance, and the reach of the induced field dictates the interaction between neighboring inclusions. Encapsulating the NPs in the matrix can isolate and leverage these interfacial effects.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Ablation by orientation: Comparing parallel (z-axis) vs perpendicular (x,y) polarization showed the parallel case produced a 9.23 increase versus a lower perpendicular value. Size scaling: The series from 8 to 32 atoms demonstrated an exponential-like increase in polarization with inclusion dimension. Shape ablation: Comparison of Rod224 and Disk332 (similar loading, different shapes) showed the disk shape yielded a comparable value with fewer atoms, indicating shape independence of volume is not a simple linear relationship. Dimension ablation: Disk442 had twice the x,y dimensions of Rod223 but more than twice the polarization increase, highlighting the non-linear coupling of dimension and shape. Sensitivity check: Test runs with thermostats between 200 and 600 K showed that temperature effects on geometry were negligible due to high melting temperature and rigid lattice.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows an example nanocomposite with a Ag₁₂ inclusion embedded in an MgO matrix. Figure 2 and 3 display the three rod-like and five disk-like inclusions modeled with labels corresponding to the number of atoms along each axis (e.g., 224, 332, 442, 421). Figure 4 illustrates the six-step CPMD and polarization procedure from initial electron minimization to fully relaxed static polarization. Figure 5 shows the step-by-step polarization procedure using QuantumEspresso, with step numbering continuing from the electronic structure calculation. Figure 6 presents the mathematical corrections for polarization jumps due to the quantum of polarization effect during post-processing. Figure 7 shows smearing BEC plots of normalized Born charges for the Rod224 NC, revealing local field enhancements at poles and depolarization in the equatorial region. Figure 9 shows a smeared BEC plot of normalized born charges for the NC with a 224 rodlike inclusion, visualizing the spatial extent of induced forces. Table 1 presents ε_r for Rod-shaped and Disk-shaped Ag/MgO NCs across all considered configurations with associated volume loading numbers.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is demonstrating that molecular-scale Ag inclusions (8-32 atoms) in MgO can enhance dielectric permittivity by 30-100% through morphology-dependent interfacial field effects, establishing a design space for tunable high-κ dielectrics. 2. The strongest evidence is the quantitative observation that multi-layer disk-like inclusions yield >70% permittivity enhancement at similar volume loadings to rods, combined with BEC maps showing localized interfacial enhancement within 3 angstroms. 3. The future path involves extending the study to SiO₂ and HfO₂ matrices, incorporating other transition metal inclusions (Cu, Co, Fe), investigating inclusion-inclusion interactions, and exploring the metallic crossover at larger mNP sizes.
