summary.title: Low density interior in supercooled aqueous nanodroplets expels ions to the subsurface
summary.authors: Shahrazad M A Malek (Memorial University of Newfoundland); Ivan Saika-Voivod (Memorial University of Newfoundland); Styliani Consta (The University of Western Ontario)
summary.field_subfield: Computational Chemistry / Physical Chemistry; Supercooled Nanodroplets, Ion Solvation Structure
summary.executive_summary: This computational study investigates the spatial distribution of Na+ ions in supercooled aqueous nanodroplets (ranging from 100 to 1100 water molecules) compared to room-temperature droplets, revealing that supercooling-induced solvent structural changes fundamentally alter ion positioning. Using molecular dynamics simulations (GROMACS v4.6.1, TIP4P/2005 water model, OPLS-AA ion parameters), the authors demonstrate that at 200 K, supercooled nanodroplets develop an anomalous, inverted radial density profile characterized by a low-density, tetrahedrally coordinated core surrounded by a high-density, more disordered subsurface. The Na+ ion is expelled from this low-density core and resides within the subsurface region (within ~0.1 nm of the density peak), whereas at 300 K, the ion distribution is nearly uniform in the droplet interior. A novel reference analytical model is introduced, predicting that an ion in a deformable dielectric droplet experiences a harmonic electrostatic confinement potential centered at the droplet's center of mass, with the spring constant $K$ peaking at a relative dielectric constant of 2.73. The study finds that multiple ions (up to 8 Na+ in 1100 water molecules) exhibit a similar expulsion from the core at 200 K, forming two peaks at 0.52 nm and 1.5 nm, and that the Non-linear Poisson-Boltzmann equation fails to explain this supercooled behavior. Key findings include that the electrostatic confinement effect is dominated by geometric factors at room temperature for low charges, but the supercooled density inversion overrides this at 200 K. The study concludes that the solvent's heterogeneous structure—specifically the low-density tetrahedral core—is the driving mechanism for ion expulsion, and that the analytical model serves as a reference that holds at room temperature but cannot predict supercooled behavior. Applications to electrospray ionization mass spectrometry, Rayleigh fission, and atmospheric chemistry are suggested.

Executive Summary
This computational study investigates the spatial distribution of Na+ ions in supercooled aqueous nanodroplets (ranging from 100 to 1100 water molecules) compared to room-temperature droplets, revealing that supercooling-induced solvent structural changes fundamentally alter ion positioning. Using molecular dynamics simulations (GROMACS v4.6.1, TIP4P/2005 water model, OPLS-AA ion parameters), the authors demonstrate that at 200 K, supercooled nanodroplets develop an anomalous, inverted radial density profile characterized by a low-density, tetrahedrally coordinated core surrounded by a high-density, more disordered subsurface. The Na+ ion is expelled from this low-density core and resides within the subsurface region (within ~0.1 nm of the density peak), whereas at 300 K, the ion distribution is nearly uniform in the droplet interior. A novel reference analytical model is introduced, predicting that an ion in a deformable dielectric droplet experiences a harmonic electrostatic confinement potential centered at the droplet's center of mass, with the spring constant $K$ peaking at a relative dielectric constant of 2.73. The study finds that multiple ions (up to 8 Na+ in 1100 water molecules) exhibit a similar expulsion from the core at 200 K, forming two peaks at 0.52 nm and 1.5 nm, and that the Non-linear Poisson-Boltzmann equation fails to explain this supercooled behavior. Key findings include that the electrostatic confinement effect is dominated by geometric factors at room temperature for low charges, but the supercooled density inversion overrides this at 200 K. The study concludes that the solvent's heterogeneous structure—specifically the low-density tetrahedral core—is the driving mechanism for ion expulsion, and that the analytical model serves as a reference that holds at room temperature but cannot predict supercooled behavior. Applications to electrospray ionization mass spectrometry, Rayleigh fission, and atmospheric chemistry are suggested.

Research Context
The spatial distribution of ions in nanodroplets is critical for chemical reactivity in atmospheric aerosols and man-made spray-based ionization methods. Prior computational studies of ionic clusters have primarily focused on clusters at room or elevated temperatures. Relatively few studies have addressed supercooled clusters due to the challenge of equilibrating them. Earlier studies by Voth et al. investigated single ions in clusters of up to 100 water molecules, finding exclusion from the interior only below the freezing temperature. The distribution of multiple ions in supercooled nanodroplets remained completely unknown prior to this work. The low-density core observed in pristine supercooled water clusters had not been combined with ion distribution analysis in previous literature.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether the low-density, tetrahedrally ordered core that emerges at supercooling in aqueous nanodroplets alters the radial distribution of ions. The study investigates how this heterogeneous solvent structure affects both single-ion and multiple-ion (up to 8 Na+) positioning at 200 K compared to 300 K. The authors hypothesize that the low-density water core in supercooled droplets will differentiate the ion distribution from that at room temperature. The hypothesis extends to both single-ion exclusion and multiple-ion expulsion from the core region at 200 K. The analytical model aims to predict under what conditions electrostatic confinement dominates over geometric confinement. The model's predictions are expected to match room-temperature simulations but deviate at supercooling due to density inversion.

Methodological Details
The study simulates Na+ ions in aqueous nanodroplets at temperatures of 200 K, 260 K, and 300 K. Nanodroplet sizes range from 100 water molecules (diameter ≈ 1.8 nm) to 1100 water molecules (diameter ≈ 4.0 nm). Molecular dynamics simulations were performed using GROMACS v4.6.1 with the leap-frog algorithm and a 2 fs time step. Water molecules were modeled with the TIP4P/2005 transferable intermolecular potential model. Na+ ion parameters were taken from OPLS-AA with a charge of +1 e. Nanodroplets were placed in periodic cubic boxes with cutoff at L/2 to reproduce long-range electrostatic interactions. Simulations were carried out in the canonical ensemble (NVT) using the Nosé-Hoover thermostat with a time constant of 0.1 ps. Two separate initial conditions—ion at center vs. ion on surface—were used for N = 360 and N = 776 at 200 K to assess equilibration. Equilibration was confirmed when ion density profiles converged; for N = 776, convergence occurred after 400 ns. The mean number of molecules in the connected cluster, Nd, and relaxation time τ were computed from the neighbor correlation function.

Procedures And Architectures
The reference analytical model expresses the energy of a charged droplet as the sum of electrostatic energy and surface energy. The model predicts the ion is subject to a harmonic potential centered at the droplet's center of mass, defined as electrostatic confinement. The spring constant K(ε) was evaluated over a range of relative dielectric constants ε. The theoretical spring constant K(ε) reaches a maximum at ε ≈ 2.73. Single Na+ ions were placed at the surface for the majority of runs and at the center for specific N=360 and N=776 at 200 K runs. Multiple-ion simulations initialized with ions near the droplet center of mass. Water density ρ(r), Voronoi-based density ρv(r), tetrahedral order parameter qT(r), and distance to fifth neighbor d5(r) were computed as radial functions. The tetrahedral order parameter qi uses a cutoff of r_cut = 0.35 nm between oxygen atoms. qT(r) was averaged within spherical shells of width ∆r = 0.05 nm. The Non-linear Poisson-Boltzmann equation solution for a rigid spherical geometry was used as a reference for multiple-ion predictions. The NPB predicted an exponential decay of ion distribution toward the COM with decay constant λPB. For 776 water molecules, multiple Na+ (5 ions) at 300 K was fitted with 0.42 exp(-(1.14-x)/1.2), yielding λPB ≈ 1.2 nm. For 1100 water molecules, the fitting function gave λPB ≈ 1.3 nm.

Key Results
At high temperature (300 K), the water density ρ(r) is that of a typical liquid droplet with a flat interior decaying sigmoidally. At 200 K, significant layering is observed for all nanodroplet sizes, with an increase in density toward the surface. The Voronoi-based density ρv(r) at 300 K is monotonically decreasing or flat, confirming the subsurface is approximately 0.3 nm thick. At 200 K, ρv(r) shows a monotonic increase toward a subsurface peak, indicating the high-density subsurface structure. At 300 K, the Na+ radial distribution is approximately uniform in the interior, consistent with electrostatic confinement but limited by low charge. At 200 K, the Na+ peak is located within 0.1 nm of the ρv(r) subsurface peak for N ≥ 200. The single Na+ ion in supercooled droplets resides in the highest-density environment, confirming the expulsion from the tetrahedral core. For N = 100 at 200 K, the Na+ peak coincides with a local minimum in ρ(r), suggesting layering plays a role. In the N = 776 droplet at 200 K, the tetrahedral order parameter qT(r) shows a significant decrease coinciding with the subsurface density peak. The d5(r) distance to fifth neighbor also shows a more disordered structure in the vicinity of the subsurface peak at low temperature. In the 1100 H2O droplet with 8 Na+ at 200 K, two peaks appear at 0.52 nm and 1.5 nm. The lower peak at 0.52 nm corresponds to one ion, while the outer peak at ≈ 1.5 nm contains the remaining ions. At 300 K, multiple-ion distributions are almost uniform with an incipient broad maximum in outer layers. The NPB solution with dielectric constant of water equal to 75 yields λPB ≈ 0.8, qualitatively comparable to droplet radius.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The Na+ ion tends to reside in the highest density environment because for constant temperature and polarization, dielectric constant increases with density. While the surface layer is at very high density, it does not provide a good solvation environment for the ion. The ions, whether single or multiple, prefer the relatively disordered high-density subsurface to the relatively ordered low-density tetrahedral network of the core. The electrostatic confinement model can be extended by including ion size and hydrophobic effects. The supercooled density inversion provides a mechanism that the NPB equation cannot account for, as NPB assumes a uniform solvent. The results are in agreement with Voth et al. for the N = 100 cluster, but our work extends the findings to larger droplets where the tetrahedral core is fully formed. The finding has implications for electrospray ionization, as the low-density core may hinder the formation of conical deformations required for ion emission. The study provides a starting point for investigating supercooled droplets containing unstructured peptides and ion complexes.

Contradictions And Limitations
The N = 100 cluster does not form a tetrahedrally organized core, limiting the observation of the full expulsion mechanism in this size regime. The N = 100 cluster is subject to larger relative shape fluctuations, affecting the validity of the electrostatic confinement model. For N = 100 at 200 K, ρv(r) is approximately constant below 0.3 nm, yet Na+ is peaked just below 0.3 nm, a contradiction with pure electrostatic arguments. Layering effects in small droplets may complicate the interpretation of the true electrostatic/density preference. The NPB solution cannot be analyzed at 200 K, making it difficult to quantitatively test the theoretical prediction against simulations. The dielectric constant of water equal to 75 is a single-value assumption; real droplets may have spatially varying dielectric responses. The Rayleigh parameter constraint means droplets of interest are near the instability limit, introducing potential shape distortions. Sampling of the ion positions is noted as a challenge in such systems, requiring long simulation times.

Claims
Supercooled aqueous nanodroplets develop a low-density, tetrahedrally ordered core that expels Na+ ions to the high-density subsurface, a behavior not present at room temperature. The Na+ peak at 200 K is within 0.1 nm of the ρv(r) subsurface peak, while at 300 K it is uniform in the interior. The tetrahedral order parameter qT(r) shows a significant decrease coinciding with the subsurface density peak at 200 K. At 200 K, ρv(r) shows a monotonic increase toward a subsurface peak, unlike the monotonic decrease at 300 K. For N = 100 at 200 K, the Na+ ion is peaked just below 0.3 nm despite a constant ρv(r) interior, suggesting layering interference. The N = 100 cluster lacks a fully formed tetrahedral core, making the effect less pronounced in this size regime. This heterogeneous solvent structure provides a new physical mechanism for ion distribution in supercooled droplets. The result challenges the applicability of NPB-based theories in the supercooled regime.
An ion in a deformable charged dielectric droplet experiences a harmonic electrostatic confinement potential centered at the droplet's center of mass, with maximum confinement at ε ≈ 2.73. The analytical model predicts a harmonic functional form for the energy as a function of distance from the COM. The spring constant K(ε) plotted for 1000 water molecules shows a maximum at ε ≈ 2.73. At 300 K, the Na+ distribution is consistent with this EC effect. At 200 K, the density inversion overrides the electrostatic confinement, meaning the model does not capture supercooled behavior. For the low charge of single Na+, geometric confinement effects can dominate over the force toward the COM. The model provides the first analytical reference for electrostatic confinement in a fluctuating droplet. The model can be extended with ion size and hydrophobic effects for improved accuracy.
Multiple Na+ ions are similarly expelled from the supercooled core, with 8 ions in 1100 H2O molecules forming two distinct peaks at 0.52 nm and 1.5 nm. At 200 K in 1100 water molecules, two peaks are observed at 0.52 nm and 1.5 nm. The multiple ions show a maximum at the same location as the single ion at 200 K. The lower peak at 0.52 nm corresponds to a single ion exchangeable with the outer peak. At 300 K, multiple-ion distributions remain almost uniform in the interior, with only an incipient outer-layer maximum. The two-peak structure is size-dependent; for 776 water molecules, a single fitted exponential describes the decay. The ion expulsion is a collective effect of the solvent structure, not dependent on single-ion concentration. The two-peak structure does not indicate a metastable state, but rather a concentration gradient in the subsurface.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Two separate simulations with different initial ion positions were run for N = 360 and N = 776 at 200 K to verify equilibration convergence. Equilibration was empirically determined by monitoring convergence of the radial density profile between the two initial-condition runs. The N = 1100 equilibration time was estimated to be approximately twice that of N = 776 using the relaxation time ratio τ1100/τ776 ≈ 2. For multiple-ion runs, the assumption is that relaxation times are shorter than for single-ion runs. The 200 K runs were conducted at 260 K for N ≤ 200 to account for temperature-dependent behavior in smaller clusters. The tetrahedral order parameter qT(r) and d5(r) data were extracted from a previous study (Ref. 31), and their radial profiles were verified against the current density data.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 plots the spring constant K(ε) as a function of the relative dielectric constant, showing the maximum at ε ≈ 2.73. Figure 2 displays the distribution of the center of mass distance for a charged cyclic peptide in a 3.8 nm droplet with 8e+ charge. Figure 3 shows water density ρ(r), Voronoi-based density ρv(r), and Na+ density ρNa(r) at 200 K and 300 K for all droplet sizes. Figure 4 displays the detailed comparison of pure water structure and Na+ distribution for the N = 776 droplet, including multiple-ion (5 Na+) data. Figure 5 shows multiple-ion radial distributions for 776 and 1100 H2O molecules at 300 K and 200 K. Table 1 reports system sizes (N), mean connected cluster size (Nd), and relaxation times (τ) for all simulated nanodroplets. Figure S3 in the SI shows convergence of Na+ trajectories starting from the surface versus the COM at 300 K.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the discovery that supercooling induces a heterogeneous solvent structure in nanodroplets (low-density tetrahedral core, high-density disordered subsurface) that expels Na+ ions from the core, a mechanism absent at room temperature. 2. The strongest evidence is the quantitative coincidence of the 200 K Na+ peak with the ρv(r) subsurface density peak (within 0.1 nm) and the concurrent minimum in tetrahedral order qT(r) and d5(r) at the core location. 3. The future path lies in extending this model to supercooled droplets containing unstructured peptides and ion complexes, applicable to native mass spectrometry and atmospheric chemistry studies.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study demonstrates the application of the subgroup-discovery (SGD) artificial-intelligence approach to a hybrid experimental-plus-theoretical dataset to identify physicochemical design rules for selective oxidation catalysts. The authors synthesized and tested 120 SiO2-supported catalysts containing ruthenium (Ru), tungsten (W), and phosphorus (P) in the catalytic oxidation of propylene. DFT-calculated free-atom properties, combined with reaction temperature, served as 11 candidate descriptive parameters. The oxygenates yield (acrolein and acrylic acid) was used as the target in SGD. The identified SG rules—defining constraints on temperature (280 ≤ T ≤ 300 °C), phosphorus content (JK > 0.55), and composition-weighted electronegativity (3.910 ≤ VY < 4.002 eV)—isolated a subgroup comprising only 1.2% of the data (15 out of 1220 measurements) yielding an average oxygenates yield of 24.15%, five times the global average of 4.83%. These rules were subsequently used to design and test four-component (Ru-W-P-V) and five-component (Ru-W-P-Te-V) catalysts. The four-component Ru-W-P-Te catalyst achieved 60.19% yield, and the five-component Ru-W-P-Te-Ta catalyst achieved 59.60%, both nearly double the highest training yield of 26.85%. A second SGD on the four- and five-component data (746 points) yielded new rules: T ≥ 360 °C, LA+1 ≤ 1.001 Å, and VH < -1.593 eV. The study concludes that SGD can identify interpretable, chemically meaningful rules for exceptional catalytic performance that extend beyond the training data to substantially more complex and performant material compositions.

Research Context
Heterogeneous catalysis is governed by an intricate interplay of multiple surface reaction networks and dynamic restructuring, making design challenging. Explicit atomistic modeling of the full catalytic progression by first-principles methods is impractical for practical catalyst design. High-throughput experimentation (HTE) can test large amounts of materials but lacks a straightforward method to select the next promising candidates from the results. With practically infinite possible materials and very few good catalysts, the direct approach unlikely identifies the needed catalyst material. Detailed characterization of each material in large libraries is typically not feasible, leaving little structural information available. Global models trained by minimizing average prediction error may not capture the focused, exceptional behaviors necessary for identifying high-performance catalysts. The SGD approach, a local artificial-intelligence method, is applied to a hybrid dataset combining HTE reactivity with DFT-calculated descriptive parameters.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is how SGD applied to a hybrid HTE-DFT dataset can identify key physicochemical parameters and value constraints associated exclusively with outstanding catalytic performance. The hypothesis is that the SGD rules, derived from a three-component Ru-W-P catalyst space, can guide the design of four- and five-component catalysts achieving superior yields. The temperature, phosphorus content, and composition-weighted electronegativity were predicted to be the primary parameters describing high yields of acrolein and acrylic acid. The rule on temperature was expected to reflect intermediate conditions favoring oxygenate formation over combustion. The phosphorus content rule was expected to relate to the dilution of active metal sites on a phosphate matrix. The electronegativity rule was expected to balance ruthenium's ability to generate propylene conversion against its tendency to promote combustion.

Methodological Details
The study synthesized 120 SiO2-supported catalysts containing ruthenium, tungsten, and phosphorus in different proportions on a pseudo-liquid support. At each of the 120 catalyst compositions, several reaction temperatures between 200 and 400 °C were examined. All reactions were carried out in tubular, fixed-bed reactors with a common feed of Ar, H2O, N2, O2, and propylene. Molar feed rates were 4.015 mmol/h (Ar), 4.015 mmol/h (H2O), 104.40 mmol/h (N2), 20.08 mmol/h (O2), and 1.57 mmol/h (propylene). The target variable was the yield of oxygenates (acrolein and acrylic acid), defined as the ratio of oxygenate molar rates to the propylene molar rate in the feed. Eleven descriptive parameters were used in the SGD analysis, including temperature and ten composition-dependent physicochemical properties calculated from DFT. Properties were calculated for isolated atoms using DFT-PBEsol with the FHI-aims code. The per-element free-atom properties were converted into system-specific properties via composition-weighted averaging over all elements in the catalyst composition. Oxygen content was excluded from characterization because its exact proportion is unknown from the catalyst formulation and not measured for all materials. For the three-component materials, the molar content was calculated over three elements; oxygen was not included in the material characterization.

Procedures And Architectures
The SGD approach starts with the generation of a pool of propositions (π) that apply only to a portion of the data set. For continuous parameters, propositions are inequalities constraining their values. SGD identifies selectors (σ) formed by a number of propositions connected by the AND operator, selecting subgroups with the most outstanding distributions of target values relative to the whole dataset. The quality function in Eq. 3 combines a coverage term M(X, gh) and a Jensen-Shanson divergence term m/no(X, gh). The coverage term controls subgroup size to prevent selection of statistically insignificant small groups. The second term, a properly symmetrized Kulback-Leibler divergence, measures dissimilarity between distributions and favors subgroups presenting target values as unusual compared to the majority. Cross-validation was performed using randomly selected 90% of the data points to validate the robustness of the SG rules. Yields lower than 3% were excluded from training in a separate sensitivity analysis. Four-component materials were designed by fixing phosphorus at 0.60 and ruthenium at 0.05 and adding one of seven potential substitution elements. Substitution elements (Nb, Ta, Cr, Mo, Sn, Sb, Te) were selected based on octahedral coordination, atomic radius compatibility with tungsten (max difference 0.10 Å), and experimental precedent. Five-component materials were designed by fixing Te as the substitution element and evaluating Mo, Nb, Ta, and Sb as additional elements.

Key Results
50% of all measured materials and conditions resulted in less than 2% oxygenates yield, and only 41 out of 1220 measurements gave yields above 20%. The average oxygenates yield over the whole data set was 4.83%, with a maximum observed yield of 26.85%. The identified SG, selected for highest cumulative Jensen-Shannon divergence (0.693), contained only 15 data points, approximately 1.2% of the total dataset. The average yield of oxygenates in this SG was 24.15%, approximately five times higher than the global average. The SG rules for three-component catalysts were: 280 ≤ T ≤ 300 °C, JK > 0.55, and 3.910 ≤ VY < 4.002 eV. The four-component Ru-W-P-Te catalyst achieved 60.19% oxygenate yield at 400 °C, well within the VY SG rule window. The five-component Ru-W-P-Te-Ta catalyst achieved 59.60% oxygenate yield at 400 °C, with a VY value of 3.947 eV within the SG rule. For the four- and five-component SGD (746 data points), the highest-quality SG contained 18 data points, approximately 2.4% of the dataset, with a cumulative Jensen-Shannon divergence of 0.355. The rules for the four- and five-component SG were: T ≥ 360 °C, LA+1 ≤ 1.001 Å, and VH < -1.593 eV.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The temperature rule reflects that highest yields occur at intermediate temperatures, neither too low for reaction nor too high for combustion. The phosphorus content rule is interpreted as reflecting the dilution of highly active metal sites on a phosphate matrix at high phosphorus loadings. The electronegativity rule limits Ru content: Ru is needed for conversion, but excessive Ru promotes undesired combustion products. The SG rules not only describe the underlying processes associated with high performance but also guide the design of materials more complex than those in the training set. The finding that four- and five-component catalysts outperform three-component ones (yields ≥ 60% vs. max 26.85%) suggests that the SGD approach can identify materials significantly more performant than any observed in training. The SGD-HTE-theory approach circumvents explicit modeling of the full catalytic progression and reduces the need for extensive experimental characterization.

Contradictions And Limitations
The SG rule on temperature (280–300 °C for three-component) is not transferable to four- and five-component systems, which require temperatures ≥ 360 °C. The four- and five-component SGD identified different composition-dependent parameters (LA+1, VH) compared to the three-component SG (JK, VY), even though these are related by the equation VY = (LA+1) * VH. The SGD rules were developed under assumptions of low Ru content and tungsten-compatible substitution elements (similar atomic radii). It is unclear if the SG rules generalize to arbitrary Ru content or substitution elements with significantly different atomic radii compared to tungsten. The oxygen content is not included in characterization because it cannot be reliably determined from catalyst formulation or measured for all materials. The atomic structures of all tested catalysts are not known in detail; the catalysts are described as disordered or possibly amorphous. The comparison of five-component SG rules with three-component ones is noted to be affected by the much higher materials complexity of the test systems.

Claims
The SGD-HTE-theory approach identifies interpretable, chemically meaningful rules that define exceptional catalytic performance for selective oxidation. The three rules (T, JK, VY) correlate physically to known chemical processes: temperature window, phosphate dilution, and Ru/combustion balance. Cross-validation using 90% of data and excluding low-yield points yielded consistent SG rules, indicating robustness. The rules captured a 1.2% subgroup whose yield was five times the global average. The temperature rule failed to transfer from three-component to four-component systems, suggesting the mechanism changes with composition complexity. The SGD rules for the more complex systems required entirely different composition-dependent parameters (LA+1, VH vs. JK, VY). SGD rules can guide the design of catalysts containing up to five elements, enabling exploration beyond the training space. The approach circumvents the need for explicit kinetic modeling of reaction networks, making it applicable to reactions with complex pathways.
The SG rules derived from three-component catalysts correctly predict the performance of four- and five-component extensions with yields exceeding any training observation. The four-component Ru-W-P-Te catalyst achieved 60.19% oxygenate yield, falling within the VY rule window. The five-component Ru-W-P-Te-Ta catalyst achieved 59.60% with VY = 3.947 eV, also within the rule window. Both multi-component yields are nearly double the training maximum of 26.85%. The Ru content was intentionally kept low (0.05) to minimize combustion, limiting the scope of the prediction. The temperature rule was entirely inapplicable for the four-component extension. The method can detect materials that are significantly more performant than any observation used in training, enabling true catalyst discovery.

Data And Code Availability
The electronic supporting information (ESI) contains further calculation details, values for the elemental properties used, detailed SGD description, and Jensen-Shannon divergence formulations. Detailed preparation, characterization, and reactivity analysis for the catalysts is discussed in a separate contribution. The paper notes that detailed ESI contains further calculation values and SGD details, but no public repository link is provided in the main text.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Cross-validation with randomly selected 90% of data points produced consistent SG rules. Excluding data points with oxygenates yields lower than 3% produced similar SG rules, with minimal threshold variation. The variation in minimum and maximum thresholds when using 90% data was [3.882, 3.910 eV] and [3.989, 4.031 eV], confirming rule stability. A second SGD on the four- and five-component data (746 points) validated the approach on higher-complexity systems.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A shows the SGD workflow: generation of propositions, selectors with quality function maximization, and identification of rules. Figure 1B, 1C, and 1D depict the reaction schemes and catalyst structures: three-component materials, four-component design, and five-component design. Figure 2A and B show propylene conversion vs. oxygenates selectivity profiles and the distribution of oxygenates yield across the dataset. Figure 2C, D, F illustrate the three SG rules: temperature window, phosphorus content, and electronegativity. Figure 3B shows a ternary diagram illustrating how the electronegativity rule limits ruthenium content. Figure 4A presents the catalyst map for four-component materials with VY values, showing bolded/starred points satisfying the SG rule. Figure 4C and D show the oxygenate yields for the four- and five-component catalysts tested by HTE. Figure 5A and B display the HTE data for four- and five-component catalysts. Figure 5C, D, E, F present the SG rules for the four- and five-component dataset.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is demonstrating that SGD applied to hybrid HTE-DFT data can isolate small, high-performance catalyst subgroups and derive interpretable physicochemical design rules that extend to more complex material compositions. 2. The strongest evidence is the four- and five-component Ru-W-P-Te catalysts achieving yields of 60.19% and 59.60%, nearly double the training maximum of 26.85%, while remaining within the SG-predicted electronegativity windows. 3. The future path involves extending the SGD analysis to broader composition spaces (higher Ru content, different substitution elements) and applying the framework to reactions where explicit kinetic modeling is impractical.

summary.title: Mechanochemical synthesis of eco-friendly fertilizer from eggshell (calcite) and KH2PO4
summary.authors: Roger Borges; Amanda Soares Giroto; Rodrigo Klaic; Fernando Wypych (Universidade Federal do Paraná); Caue Ribeiro
summary.field_subfield: Agricultural Chemistry / Materials Science - Mechanochemical Synthesis
summary.type_of_paper: Experimental Research / Dataset and Method Development Paper
summary.executive_summary: This study reports a free-solvent, mechanochemical synthesis method for producing calcium phosphate bioceramics (potassium calcium phosphates) as eco-friendly soil conditioners, repurposing eggshell waste (calcite) and potassium dihydrogen phosphate (KH2PO4). Based on reverse logistics principles, the process applies mechanical energy via high-energy ball milling to drive a solid-state chemical reaction between eggshell waste and KH2PO4 without solvents or unwanted subproducts. XRD analysis identifies the formation of K3CaH(PO4)2 (PDF 22-1218) and CaKPO4 (PDF 33-1002) phases, with the transformation confirmed by TGA, DSC, and 31P NMR MAS. Solubility kinetics in 2% citric acid reveal that the milled phosphates delay the release of potassium and phosphorus compared to the KH2PO4 precursor, while simultaneously increasing the bioavailability of calcium relative to the CaCO3 precursor. Soil release essays confirm these findings: the 2 h/600 rpm sample achieved 45 mg/kg P release at 30 days (15% of total P), compared to 40% release for the KH2PO4 precursor, and demonstrated an intermediate P radial diffusion (22% slower than KH2PO4, 34% faster than struvite). Further, hydroxyapatite (Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2) formation was observed in situ, yielding 30.97 mg/kg bioavailable Ca at 30 days. The authors conclude that the mechanochemical bioceramic acts as a smart release fertilizer providing superior nutrient management for P, K, and Ca simultaneously.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study reports a free-solvent, mechanochemical synthesis method for producing calcium phosphate bioceramics (potassium calcium phosphates) as eco-friendly soil conditioners, repurposing eggshell waste (calcite) and potassium dihydrogen phosphate (KH2PO4). Based on reverse logistics principles, the process applies mechanical energy via high-energy ball milling to drive a solid-state chemical reaction between eggshell waste and KH2PO4 without solvents or unwanted subproducts. XRD analysis identifies the formation of K3CaH(PO4)2 (PDF 22-1218) and CaKPO4 (PDF 33-1002) phases, with the transformation confirmed by TGA, DSC, and 31P NMR MAS. Solubility kinetics in 2% citric acid reveal that the milled phosphates delay the release of potassium and phosphorus compared to the KH2PO4 precursor, while simultaneously increasing the bioavailability of calcium relative to the CaCO3 precursor. Soil release essays confirm these findings: the 2 h/600 rpm sample achieved 45 mg/kg P release at 30 days (15% of total P), compared to 40% release for the KH2PO4 precursor, and demonstrated an intermediate P radial diffusion (22% slower than KH2PO4, 34% faster than struvite). Further, hydroxyapatite (Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2) formation was observed in situ, yielding 30.97 mg/kg bioavailable Ca at 30 days. The authors conclude that the mechanochemical bioceramic acts as a smart release fertilizer providing superior nutrient management for P, K, and Ca simultaneously.

Research Context
Food industry wastes, particularly eggshells, are disposed in landfills with no pretreatment and produce odors due to microbial growth. The paper applies reverse logistics as an instrument of economic and social development for product lifecycle responsibility. Solid-state mechanochemical activation applies mechanical energy through friction and impact to promote chemical reactions from solid reagents. Existing literature reports hydroxyapatite synthesis from phosphoric acid solutions rather than powder phosphate salts. No mechanochemical process has been reported for production of K3CaH(PO4)2 and CaKPO4 from calcite by eggshell and KH2PO4.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether a solvent-free mechanochemical process can synthesize calcium and potassium phosphates from eggshell waste and KH2PO4 as a cost-effective soil conditioner. The authors hypothesize that the produced potassium calcium phosphates will act as smart release fertilizers by delaying the bioavailability of P and K while improving Ca bioavailability. The study predicts that the mechanochemical activation will produce K3CaH(PO4)2 and possibly CaKPO4 phases from CaCO3 and KH2PO4. The authors predict that the phosphate products will exhibit slower solubilization than KH2PO4 but faster than CaCO3. The hypothesis is that the reaction will require a threshold of time and milling speed to initiate phase transformation.

Methodological Details
Eggshells were collected by the authors in their homes, washed, and dried at room temperature, presenting a diameter between 1 and 10 mm. The KH2PO4 PA was supplied from Vetec. Milling was performed in a Fritsch Pulverisette 7 high-energy ball mill with a 250 ml zirconia bowl and 5 zirconia balls of 15 mm diameter. Weight ratio of 1:1 (w/w) of eggshell and KH2PO4 was used, corresponding to 0.75 mmol of KH2PO4 and 1 mmol of CaCO3. Time trials were performed at 15 min, 30 min, 1 h, 2 h, 3 h, 6 h, 12 h, and 24 h at 600 rpm. Speed trials were performed at 100, 200, 400, and 600 rpm for 2 h. Characterization included XRD with a Shimadzu XRD 6000, 31P NMR MAS with Bruker Avance III HD, TGA-Q500, and DSC Q100 with a 25°C-600°C range. Nutrient content was determined by acid digestion in H2SO4/H2O2 (8:1 v/v, 24 h at 250 °C), atomic absorption for K and Ca, and colorimetric for P. For citric acid release assays, pellets were pressed at 5 bar and standardized to 100 mg/L of P, with 1.2 mL aliquots collected from 15 min to 30 days. Soil release assays used Petri dishes of 8.6 cm diameter with 78 g of sieved 2.0 mm mesh soil to achieve density of 1.2 g.cm⁻³, at 75% water saturation. Soil experiments were performed at 3, 7, 15, and 30 days with a single pellet standardized to 300 mg of P per kg of soil.

Procedures And Architectures
The mechanochemical process operates on a solid-state, solvent-free principle using friction and impact forces to promote ion migration and new structure formation. The stoichiometry of the mixture was 0.75 mmol KH2PO4 to 1 mmol CaCO3, assuming eggshells are mainly composed of CaCO3. XRD data were collected with a Cu Kα incident beam (λ = 0.1546 nm) at 30 kV, 40 mA, and a scanning speed of 2° min⁻¹ across the 3-40° (2θ) range. TGA was performed under synthetic air (N2/O2) at 10 °C min⁻¹ heating rate across 20 to 900 °C using platinum crucibles.  NMR MAS was conducted at 10 kHz using the HPDEC sequence with ADP as the phosphate reference at 0.8 ppm. Nutrient release kinetics were fitted using pseudo-first order, pseudo-second order, and intraparticle diffusion models. P diffusion in soil was visualized using pre-treated paper and analyzed with GNU Image Manipulation Program v. 2.6.11 via thresholding and histogram area quantification. Phosphorus release was quantified by molybdenum blue colorimetry, and K and Ca were quantified by flame atomic absorption spectroscopy with a PerkinElmer PinAAcle 900T. Soil residues were extracted: K by 0.05 Mol/L HCl, Ca by 1 Mol/L KCl, and P by Mehlich 1 method. For in situ hydroxyapatite confirmation, milled samples at 600 rpm were suspended in water, dried, and characterized by XRD.

Key Results
XRD confirmed that milling at 2 h and 400 rpm produced a mixture of K3CaH(PO4)2 (PDF 22-1218) and CaKPO4 (PDF 33-1002). Below 2 h and 400 rpm, only reactant diffraction patterns were observed, indicating a threshold energy required for reaction. TGA of KH2PO4 showed a residual mass of 89%, consistent with theoretical 87% for KPO3 formation. Eggshell thermal degradation showed experimental residue of 56% vs theoretical 59% for CaCO3 decomposition. Milled samples at 600 rpm showed crystallization water loss at 280°C, structural water loss at 420°C, and final polycondensation at 710°C. At 420°C, milled samples converted to KCaPO4 (PDF 33-1002), confirming the dehydration of K3CaH(PO4)2. 31P NMR showed KH2PO4 at δ = 3.74 ppm, K3CaH(PO4)2 at δ = 3.28 and 2.82 ppm, and CaKPO4 at δ = 0.74 ppm and δ = -4.78 ppm. In citric acid (2% wt), K and P showed slower release for milled samples than KH2PO4, with pseudo-second order model providing best correlation. Calcium release was faster for milled phosphates than for CaCO3 eggshells, indicating increased Ca bioavailability. In soil, KH2PO4 released 40% of total P (107 mg/kg) at 3 days, while the 2 h/600 rpm sample released only 45 mg/kg (15% of total P) at 30 days. The P radial diffusion of the 2 h/600 rpm sample at 30 days was 22% slower than KH2PO4 (2.62 cm) and 34% faster than struvite (1.99 cm at 2 days). Bioavailable Ca in soil increased to 30.97 mg/kg after 30 days for the 2 h/600 rpm sample (8% recovery), compared to no increase for CaCO3 eggshells. Hydroxyapatite (PDF 9-432) was identified from 3 to 30 days in soil, explaining the slow-release behavior.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The produced phosphates are classified as smart release fertilizers due to the delayed bioavailability of P and K and enhanced Ca bioavailability. The mechanism of mechanochemical activation involves breaking reagent bonds and promoting solid phase ion migration under mechanical stress. The reticular energy of the phosphate structure is influenced by cation size and charge, governing solubility differences among the various metal-phosphate phases. The formation of hydroxyapatite in soil under pH 5 conditions accounts for the progressive nutrient release and long-term Ca/P availability. The results suggest that the bioceramic can substitute for conventional mineral fertilizers while reducing nutrient loss and improving P management.

Contradictions And Limitations
At 2 h/600 rpm, TGA showed the phosphate phase was unclear at the 280°C thermal treatment, requiring additional 420°C treatment for full conversion. The 31P NMR shift at δ = -4.78 ppm in the 2 h/600 rpm sample is attributed to pyrophosphate dimerization, marking an intermediate compound state. The P radial diffusion of the 2 h/600 rpm sample at day 2 (1.99 cm) is compared to struvite (no release) and KH2PO4 (2.62 cm), but the direct day 2 comparison with struvite is not numerically defined. K release in soil reached ~100% for both 2 h/600 rpm and KH2PO4, limiting the ability to quantify the delaying effect for potassium in the soil system. The paper notes that a single pellet was used for each soil release container, which may affect the reproducibility of the release profile. The soil chemical and physical properties are referenced to Table S2 in Supplementary Materials, which are not provided in the main text.

Claims
The mechanochemical process produces K3CaH(PO4)2 and CaKPO4 from eggshell and KH2PO4 without solvents, with the reaction initiated at 2 h and 400 rpm. XRD confirmed K3CaH(PO4)2 and CaKPO4 phases at 2 h and 400 rpm. No phase transformation was observed below 2 h or 400 rpm. TGA showed the 2 h/600 rpm sample converted to KCaPO4 at 420°C, confirming the mechanism. At 600 rpm, low-energy conditions do not fully degrade calcite to form the target phosphates. The method enables solvent-free production of novel phosphates with improved solubility profiles. The threshold energy requirement constrains the process parameters for industrial scaling.
The milled phosphates act as smart release fertilizers, delaying P and K release while enhancing Ca bioavailability compared to the precursors. Citric acid release showed slower K and P release for milled samples than KH2PO4. Ca release was significantly faster for milled phosphates than for CaCO3 eggshells. Soil assays confirmed 45 mg/kg P at 30 days for milled vs 107 mg/kg for precursor. Soil Ca increased to 30.97 mg/kg for milled vs no increase for eggshells. K release reached ~100% in soil for both, making the delaying effect less discernible in that nutrient. The P radial diffusion showed the milled sample was 22% slower than the extremely soluble KH2PO4, confirming only relative delay. The material can be used to improve nutrient use efficiency and reduce leaching in P-sensitive environments. Hydroxyapatite formation in situ provides a long-term release mechanism compatible with soil pH 5.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Milling parameters (time and speed) were varied systematically: 15 min-24 h at 600 rpm and 100-600 rpm at 2 h. Release assays in citric acid used a 2 wt% solution with single pellets standardized to 100 mg/L P, in triplicate. Soil release was conducted in plastic containers with 50 g of sandy soil at 75% water saturation, with triplicate or single-pellet design noted. A second experiment suspended 600 rpm milled samples in water, dried, and characterized by XRD to confirm in situ hydroxyapatite formation. Phosphorus diffusion was visually validated using pre-treated paper in Petri dishes, providing a complementary spatial release metric to the aqueous assays. The P radial diffusion was compared against both the precursor (KH2PO4) and struvite as a benchmark low-diffusion reference.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows XRD patterns of all milled samples, identifying the main phosphate phases and confirming the reaction threshold. Figure 2 presents TGA curves for KH2PO4, eggshell, and all milled samples, showing mass loss events and residual percentages. Figure 3 displays calcined samples at 280°C, 420°C, and 710°C to characterize the phase at each mass-loss step. Figure 4 presents 31P NMR MAS spectra showing characteristic shifts for each phosphate phase. Figure 5 shows phosphorus and potassium release kinetics in 2% citric acid for precursor and all milled samples. Figure 6 displays soil release kinetics for K and P in the 2 h/600 rpm sample versus the KH2PO4 precursor. Figure 7 shows in situ hydroxyapatite identification in soil from 3 to 30 days. Table S1 contains detailed nutrient content of all samples and precursors. Table S2 reports chemical and physical soil properties.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first reported solvent-free mechanochemical synthesis of K3CaH(PO4)2 and CaKPO4 from eggshell waste and KH2PO4, producing a smart-release calcium phosphate bioceramic for soil conditioning. 2. The strongest evidence is the multi-modal confirmation (XRD, TGA, 31P NMR, 2% citric acid, soil assays) that the 2 h/600 rpm milled sample delays P/K release (45 mg/kg vs 107 mg/kg at 30 days) while simultaneously releasing bioavailable Ca (30.97 mg/kg) and forming in situ hydroxyapatite. 3. The future path involves using these nanocrystalline bioceramics in composite formulations (e.g., with urea and starch) to further tune solubility, scaling up the reverse logistics model for industrial waste repurposing.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study addresses the "lab-to-fab gap" in organic solar cell (OSC) manufacturing by demonstrating slot-die coating of PM6:Y6 active layers in open-air using the green solvent o-xylene without additives. The work is conducted on flexible polyethylene terephthalate (PET) substrates using a homemade roll-coater platform, mimicking roll-to-roll conditions at laboratory scale. The research systematically optimizes three critical fabrication parameters: coating temperature, solution concentration (affecting active layer thickness), and the inclusion of a ternary fullerene component (PC61BM). The optimal coating temperature of 100 °C, matched across the slot-die head, syringe, drum, and tube, minimizes bimolecular recombination (S = 0.978) and yields an average PCE of 5.8% with a champion 6.3%. An active layer thickness of approximately 200 nm (217 nm experimentally) was identified as the optimum, balancing light absorption with charge transport, achieving the highest average PCE of 5.8%. The introduction of a small amount of PC61BM (ternary PM6:Y6:PC61BM) as a complementary acceptor further enhances performance, yielding an average PCE of 6.7% (champion 7.2%) with a 12% higher short-circuit current compared to binary devices and improved charge dissociation probability (96.3% vs 93.7%). Stability tests under ISOS-D-1 dark storage conditions show that ternary devices retain 99.4% of initial PCE after 1050 hours, and binary devices retain over 97% after more than 1500 hours, confirming the robustness of open-air, roll-platform processed flexible OSCs. The work demonstrates for the first time that PM6:Y6 devices can be fabricated with scalable techniques on flexible substrates in open-air while maintaining high efficiency and stability, without additives or hazardous solvents.

Research Context
The most commonly used fabrication technique for OSCs is spin-coating, which is incompatible with industrial upscaling due to its poor potential for roll-to-roll manufacturing and substantial material waste. While blade or slot-die coating are suitable for roll-to-roll manufacturing, only few studies have reported solar cells using these scalable techniques. For environmentally friendly upscaling, inks based on non-hazardous solvent systems are needed, yet scalable open-air processing remains a challenge. The PM6:Y6 material combination was chosen because PM6 absorption matches the highest spectral irradiance point while Y6 complements in the red region, making it a strong candidate for minimizing the lab-to-fab efficiency gap. Prior work reported over 15% efficiencies on rigid substrates using green solvents like o-xylene, but transferring these devices to roll-processing on flexible substrates using scalable techniques was not previously addressed. A further complication is that PM6 exhibits temperature-dependent aggregation (TDA) behavior, requiring the solution to be heated to remain liquid throughout the coating procedure.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether PM6:Y6 active layers can be successfully slot-die coated in open-air on flexible substrates using a green solvent without additives while achieving industrially competitive efficiencies. The authors hypothesize that fine-tuning of coating parameters—specifically drying temperature and solution concentration—will reveal an optimal processing window that minimizes material aggregation while maximizing charge carrier collection. It was further hypothesized that the introduction of a tertiary fullerene acceptor (PC61BM) would enhance electron mobility and balance charge transport, thereby improving short-circuit current and fill factor via an energy cascade effect. The study aimed to demonstrate that devices fabricated under roll-to-roll compatible conditions could maintain high stability under storage, addressing the long-term durability requirement for flexible PV applications. The authors expected that the PM6:Y6 system, with its complementary absorption, could serve as a baseline material for bridging the efficiency gap between lab-scale spin-coated devices and scalable roll-processed devices.

Methodological Details
The study used PM6 (batch YY19260CH100) and Y6 (batch DW7038S) purchased from 1-Material Inc. as the primary active layer materials. PC61BM (batch M111) was obtained from Ossila for the ternary devices. ZnO nanoparticle ink from Sigma-Aldrich and MoO3 pellets from Kurt J. Lesker Co. were used for transport layers. The flexible substrate was pre-patterned ITO-coated polyethylene terephthalate (PET) from FOM Technologies. Pure silver from Sigma-Aldrich was used for back electrode evaporation, and DuPont 5025 heat-curing silver paste was used for flexographic printing. The green solvent o-xylene (O-XY) with ≥98% purity from Sigma-Aldrich was used to prepare all active layer solutions. A homemade roll-coater was fabricated to mimic roll-to-roll conditions at a laboratory scale, equipped with a syringe pump, hot tube, and temperature-controlled drum. The active layer solution was prepared at a 1:1 D/A ratio, with concentrations varied across 12, 16, 20, 24, and 28 mg/mL. The ZnO ETL was coated at a substrate temperature of 75 °C with a 0.06 mL/min flow rate and a drum speed of 1.08 m/min, then annealed at 100 °C for 10 min in air. The active layer was coated at temperatures of 60, 80, 100, 120 °C with a drum speed of 1.5 m/min and flow rate of 0.12 mL/min. The head, syringe, drum, and tube were kept at the same temperature as the coating temperature for each condition. 10 nm of MoO3 (HTL) and 150 nm of Ag were thermally evaporated under vacuum at 2 x 10^-5 mbar. Up to 24 solar cells were fabricated per evaporation, with at least 8 devices encapsulated per run. The encapsulated devices had an approximate active area of 0.8 cm², while a shadow mask defined an aperture area of 0.3996 cm² for J-V measurements. The activation process applied a reverse bias current of -5 V with a maximum of 100 mA to stabilize J-V curves before encapsulation. Encapsulation used epoxy-based glue (bisphenol A diglycidyl ether and Chissonox 221) with UV curing for 5 min at 66 ± 0.5 °C.

Procedures And Architectures
The device architecture followed an inverted geometry: ITO/ZnO/PM6:Y6/MoO3/Ag on flexible PET. The slot-die coating head, syringe, drum, and a connecting hot tube were all maintained at the same temperature to ensure the PM6 remained liquid during processing. For the ZnO ETL coating, a substrate temperature of 75 °C, flow rate of 0.06 mL/min, and drum speed of 1.08 m/min were used, followed by 100 °C, 10-minute air annealing. For the active layer coating, the D/A ratio was fixed at 1:1, and the temperature (60, 80, 100, 120 °C) was varied while drum speed was held at 1.5 m/min and flow rate at 0.12 mL/min. The solution concentrations were screened at 12, 16, 20, 24, and 28 mg/mL, corresponding to AL thicknesses ranging from approximately 101 nm to 217 nm. The 10 nm MoO3 and 150 nm Ag electrodes were deposited via thermal evaporation using tungsten boats at 2 x 10^-5 mbar, monitored by an INFICON XTM/2 system. For the ternary devices, PC61BM was added to the PM6:Y6 blend at two ratios: [1:1:0.2] and [1:1.1:0.1] (D:A:fullerene molar ratios). J-V curves were measured using a Keithley 2400 source meter with 50 mV steps, under a solar simulator calibrated to 1000 W/m² (AM1.5G) with a Fraunhofer-certified silicon reference cell. EQE measurements were performed with a QEX10 system from 300 to 1100 nm (5 nm step size) calibrated with a Si photodiode. Light intensity dependence measurements increased simulator power from 62.14 mW/cm² to 147.33 mW/cm² to extract recombination parameters. Thickness was measured by DS95-50 AFM in noncontact mode over 5 × 5 µm² scans.

Key Results
The PCE showed a clear improvement trend with increasing coating temperature, saturating at 100 °C with an average PCE slightly higher than that at 120 °C. At the optimal 100 °C coating temperature, the devices yielded an average PCE of 5.8% with a champion of 6.3%, and a fill factor of 47.10%. Increasing the temperature above 100 °C induced faster solvent drying, causing material aggregation at both edges of the AL stripe and reducing the average FF to 42.2% at 120 °C. The bimolecular recombination parameter (S) was closest to unity at 100 °C (S = 0.978), indicating reduced bimolecular recombination relative to other temperatures. All open-circuit voltage recombination slopes were higher than kT/q, identifying trap-assisted recombination as the dominant mechanism across all temperature conditions. The average PCE increased from 5.8% at the thinnest AL (101 nm, 24 mg/mL) to its highest average value of 5.8% at the thickest AL (217 nm, 24 mg/mL), with a champion 6.3%. The short-circuit current density reached its maximum at 154 nm of AL thickness (17.3 mA/cm²) and decreased slightly at 217 nm. The fill factor improved from 42.0% at 101 nm to 47.1% at 116 nm and did not increase further with thicker layers, showing the system maintains high performance as thick layers. The 217 nm AL thickness showed the lowest charge-transport limited behavior with S = 0.987 in the thickness optimization study. The ternary [1:1:0.2] blend achieved a 12% higher average Jsc compared to binary devices coated at 100 °C with 24 mg/mL concentration in o-xylene. Short-circuit current values of up to 20 mA/cm² were measured on the [1:1:0.2] ternary devices. The average PCE for the ternary devices were 6.6% ([1:1:0.2]) and 6.7% ([1:1.1:0.1]), with a champion efficiency of 7.2%. The [1:1.1:0.1] ternary device achieved the highest average FF of 49.1% compared to 47.3% for the [1:1:0.2] device. Charge dissociation probability (ηdiss) improved from 93.7% for the binary device to 96.3% ([1:1:0.2]) and 95.7% ([1:1.1:0.1]) when PC61BM was added. Charge collection probability (ηcoll) improved from 69.6% for the binary device to 77.7% and 73.2% for the ternary devices. After 1050 hours of dark storage under ISOS-D-1, ternary devices retained 99.4% of their average initial PCE. Binary devices retained more than 97% of their initial average PCE after more than 1500 hours of storage.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The optimal coating temperature of 100 °C balances drying kinetics: higher temperatures induce premature aggregation at the AL stripe edges that degrades fill factor, while lower temperatures require extra thermal annealing to enhance polymer crystallinity. The reduced bimolecular recombination (S = 0.978) at 100 °C, combined with the absence of extra thermal annealing, identifies this temperature as the practical optimum for roll-to-roll manufacturing. The trap-assisted recombination mechanism, confirmed by open-circuit voltage slopes exceeding kT/q, is consistent with open-air processing without cleanroom or glovebox conditions. The active layer thickness optimization shows that PM6:Y6 maintains high performance as thick layers, a critical attribute for roll-to-roll robustness where pressure, bending, and stretching are present. The energy cascade effect provided by PC61BM, with its LUMO level between PM6 and Y6, generates energetically favorable donor/acceptor interfaces that enhance charge dissociation and collection. The 12% Jsc enhancement and improved ηdiss confirm that a small fullerene amount can fundamentally improve charge extraction in flexible OSCs fabricated by slot-die coating.

Contradictions And Limitations
The paper notes that some devices showed improved performance after storage time in the case of the ternary device, which deviates from the general degradation expectation and warrants further investigation. The open-circuit voltage recombination slopes did not show a clear temperature tendency, preventing a mechanistic assignment based on recombination type across the temperature range. The devices were fabricated in open-air without cleanroom or glovebox conditions, leading to high trap-assisted recombination that limits ultimate PCE compared to vacuum-processed counterparts. While the optimal AL thickness was around 200 nm, the highest average PCE (5.8%) was attained at the thickest 217 nm, suggesting the true optimum may lie slightly above 200 nm or require further concentration screening. The study only tested two ternary ratios, leaving the full composition space unexplored; further systematic PC61BM concentration screening is needed. The paper is a pre-print (ChemRxiv), meaning the results may not yet have undergone full peer review.

Claims
Slot-die coating PM6:Y6 in open-air using o-xylene without additives is a viable fabrication route for flexible OSCs with competitive efficiencies. The optimal PCE of 5.8% (average) was achieved on flexible PET substrates using o-xylene without additives. Open-air processing yielded 99.4% PCE retention after 1050 hours of dark storage. The champion PCE of 7.2% for ternary devices is still significantly below the >15% achievable on rigid substrates with green solvents. This opens a scalable path for industrial production of PM6:Y6 devices on flexible substrates using roll-to-roll compatible processes.
A ternary strategy with PC61BM improves both the current and fill factor of PM6:Y6 flexible devices. The ternary blend achieved a 12% higher average Jsc compared to binary devices at the same coating temperature. Dissociation probability increased from 93.7% to 96.3% ([1:1:0.2]) with PC61BM addition. Collection probability increased from 69.6% to 77.7% with the [1:1:0.2] ternary blend. EQE measurements do not show specific photocurrent maxima associated with PC61BM due to its weak and broad absorption. Confirming for the first time that a better charge extraction can be achieved with a small fullerene amount in OSCs on flexible substrates.
The optimal coating temperature for PM6:Y6 slot-die coating is 100 °C, matched across the substrate, drum, head, and tube. Bimolecular recombination is minimized at 100 °C with S = 0.978. Aggregation at both edges of the AL stripe appears above 100 °C, reducing FF to 42.2% at 120 °C. The PCE shows a clear improvement trend towards higher coating temperature that saturates around 100 °C. The FF at 120 °C (42.2%) is still substantially higher than at 60 °C (44.6%), suggesting a continuous, albeit non-monotonic, FF trend. This establishes a practical roll-processing protocol that eliminates the need for extra thermal annealing steps.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The coating temperature was systematically screened from 60 °C to 120 °C with four matching heating zones (head, syringe, drum, tube). The solution concentration was screened at five levels (12, 16, 20, 24, 28 mg/mL), corresponding to four AL thicknesses. Two ternary molar ratios ([1:1:0.2] and [1:1.1:0.1]) were tested to optimize the fullerene content. The ZnO ETL was coated at a single temperature (75 °C) with one flow rate and drum speed, fixing the bottom-layer parameters. The flow rate (0.12 mL/min) and drum speed (1.5 m/min) were held constant across all active layer coating trials. Averaging over 8 devices per condition provided statistical robustness for PCE and FF measurements. Light intensity dependence and open-circuit voltage recombination slope analyses provided complementary validation of recombination mechanisms. Activation step (-5 V, 100 mA max) was applied to all devices before encapsulation to stabilize J-V curves. J-V curves and EQE were measured separately from thickness and AFM measurements, cross-referencing morphology to performance.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1: Schematic of the device architecture showing the complementary absorption profiles of PM6 (green-yellow) and Y6 (red-NIR). Figure 2: J-V curves and EQE spectra for representative devices coated at different temperatures (60, 80, 100, 120 °C). Figure 3: Box plots of PCE and FF evolution of eight devices across the temperature series, showing the saturation at 100 °C. Figure 4: SEM or optical images of the dried active layer stripe showing edge aggregation above 100 °C. Figure 5: Box plots of PV parameters across the five concentration/thickness levels. Figure 6: J-V curves and EQE spectra for binary and ternary devices at the optimal 100 °C / 24 mg/mL condition. Figure 7: Box plot comparing main PV parameters of binary and ternary devices. Figure 8: Stability plot showing PCE vs. time (up to 1500+ hours) under dark storage. Figure 10: Timeline or schematic of the ISOS-D-1 stability protocol. Table 1: PV parameters (Jsc, Voc, FF, PCE) for PM6:Y6 devices at different coating temperatures (60-120 °C). Table 2: PV parameters for PM6:Y6 devices at different concentrations (12-28 mg/mL), showing 5.8% average PCE at 24 mg/mL. Table S2: Average PV parameters for the two ternary blend formulations. Table S3: Exciton dissociation (ηdiss) and charge collection (ηcoll) efficiencies for binary and ternary devices.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the demonstration that PM6:Y6 flexible OSCs can be slot-die coated in open-air using o-xylene without additives on a roll-platform compatible setup, yielding an average PCE of 6.7% (champion 7.2%) and 99.4% PCE retention after 1050 hours. 2. The strongest evidence is the systematic parameter optimization: 100 °C is identified as the temperature that minimizes bimolecular recombination (S = 0.978) while avoiding edge aggregation, and 24 mg/mL (217 nm) as the thickness that maximizes light absorption without degrading charge transport. 3. The future path involves scaling this roll-platform protocol to full production, optimizing the ternary PC61BM content further, and investigating the impact of different fullerenes or additional ternary components to push flexible, scalable OSC efficiencies toward the >10% threshold.

summary.title: Stable open-shell aromatic nitric acid radicals: accessing highly efficient photothermal conversion with restricted radiative decay
summary.authors: Zejun Wang, Jiawen Zhou, Yiheng Zhang, Weiya Zhu, Yuan Li
summary.field_subfield: Materials Chemistry / Photothermal Conversion / Organic Radical Chemistry
summary.executive_summary: This study reports the design and synthesis of a series of star-shaped aromatic nitric acid radicals (ANARs) that achieve highly efficient photothermal conversion via restricted radiative decay. The authors developed four radical species—TPA-TPA-O6, TPA-TPZ-O6, TPA-PY-O8, and Spiro-O8—synthesized via facile demethylation and air-oxidation of phenolic hydroxyl precursors without steric hindrance protection. These open-shell organic conjugated radicals exhibit rich resonance structures, including closed-shell nitro-like and open-shell nitroxide states with unpaired electrons delocalized across conjugated backbones, imparting both electrochemical and thermal stability. Characterization by UV-Vis-NIR, ESR, cyclic voltammetry (CV), and PLQY revealed that the demethylated radicals exhibit extremely high spin concentration (confirmed by ESR) and drastically reduced photoluminescence quantum yields (<1%, compared to moderate PLQY in methoxy precursors), indicating dominant nonradiative decay channels. The TPA-TPA-O6 variant demonstrated a black powder color with broadband absorption extending from 300 to 2000 nm in aggregated state, significantly red-shifted compared to its precursor. Under 808 nm laser irradiation at 0.8 W cm⁻², TPA-TPA-O6 temperature rose from 25 °C to ~210 °C within 60 s, exhibiting superior photothermal stability over ten cycles. In an interfacial evaporation system on PU foam, TPA-TPA-O6 achieved a solar-to-vapor efficiency of 89.41% and a water evaporation rate of 1.293 kg m⁻² h⁻¹ under 1 sun (1.0 kW m⁻²), representing top performance among pure organic small molecule photothermal materials. The system was further validated for seawater desalination, reducing all four primary ions below membrane-based method values. The study demonstrates that neutral, stable organic radical small molecules with high spin concentration provide a new design strategy for solar energy materials with low cost, simple synthesis, and competitive performance to inorganic or conjugated polymer alternatives.
