Executive Summary
This study reports the design and synthesis of a series of star-shaped aromatic nitric acid radicals (ANARs) that achieve highly efficient photothermal conversion via restricted radiative decay. The authors developed four radical species—TPA-TPA-O6, TPA-TPZ-O6, TPA-PY-O8, and Spiro-O8—synthesized via facile demethylation and air-oxidation of phenolic hydroxyl precursors without steric hindrance protection. These open-shell organic conjugated radicals exhibit rich resonance structures, including closed-shell nitro-like and open-shell nitroxide states with unpaired electrons delocalized across conjugated backbones, imparting both electrochemical and thermal stability. Characterization by UV-Vis-NIR, ESR, cyclic voltammetry (CV), and PLQY revealed that the demethylated radicals exhibit extremely high spin concentration (confirmed by ESR) and drastically reduced photoluminescence quantum yields (<1%, compared to moderate PLQY in methoxy precursors), indicating dominant nonradiative decay channels. The TPA-TPA-O6 variant demonstrated a black powder color with broadband absorption extending from 300 to 2000 nm in aggregated state, significantly red-shifted compared to its precursor. Under 808 nm laser irradiation at 0.8 W cm⁻², TPA-TPA-O6 temperature rose from 25 °C to ~210 °C within 60 s, exhibiting superior photothermal stability over ten cycles. In an interfacial evaporation system on PU foam, TPA-TPA-O6 achieved a solar-to-vapor efficiency of 89.41% and a water evaporation rate of 1.293 kg m⁻² h⁻¹ under 1 sun (1.0 kW m⁻²), representing top performance among pure organic small molecule photothermal materials. The system was further validated for seawater desalination, reducing all four primary ions below membrane-based method values. The study demonstrates that neutral, stable organic radical small molecules with high spin concentration provide a new design strategy for solar energy materials with low cost, simple synthesis, and competitive performance to inorganic or conjugated polymer alternatives.

Research Context
Open-shell organic radicals have attracted attention for optoelectronics, organic magnets, photothermal, thermoelectric, and spintronic applications due to their unique chemical and physical properties. Narrow optical band gaps are achievable through chemical modification, and the biocompatibility of radical materials has driven their development in photothermal conversion. Compared to inorganic, 2D framework, and conjugated polymer photothermal materials, organic small molecules have been relatively overlooked due to their perceived disadvantages. Inorganic materials contain nondegradable metals causing safety issues in vivo; 2D frameworks and conjugated polymers suffer from poor synthesis reproducibility, high cost, poor solubility, and performance decay. Previous organic small molecules such as porphyrins and cyanine dyes are limited by cumbersome synthesis and poor photothermal stability. Organic small molecules offer excellent structural definiteness and convenient preparation without heavy metal ion poisoning risk. Open-shell radicals with high photothermal efficiency and electrochemical stability have been rarely reported in previous work. Preparing airstable organic conjugated radicals is challenging due to intrinsic high reactivity with oxygen. Stable neutral radicals are the basis for radical chemistry theory and a prerequisite for multifunctional applications. Photothermal materials based on organic stable radicals convert near-infrared light into heat via nonradiative decay.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether neutral, stable organic small-molecule open-shell radicals can be designed and synthesized for highly efficient photothermal conversion via restricted radiative decay. The authors hypothesized that star-shaped aromatic nitric acid radicals (ANARs) synthesized without steric hindrance protection would exhibit rich resonance structures enabling high electrochemical, thermal, and light stability. It was predicted that the delocalized unpaired electrons across conjugated backbones would promote high spin concentration and enhanced nonradiative decay. The four tested cores—triphenylamine, triazine, pyrene, and spiro-fluorene—were predicted to yield differential photothermal performances based on their electron-donating capabilities and optical band gaps. The authors expected that the TPA-TPA-O6 variant, possessing the most donor-acceptor conjugation, would exhibit the widest NIR absorption and highest photothermal efficiency. The study aimed to demonstrate that these radicals could outperform traditional organic small molecules in solar-to-vapor efficiency and exhibit negligible photobleaching. The radicals were expected to show superior electrochemical reversibility compared to previously reported radicaloids which showed low electrochemical stability. The authors also proposed that this design concept would produce a large space for structural optimization comparable to previous high-performance organic materials.

Methodological Details
Four star-shaped ANAR materials (TPA-TPA-O6, TPA-TPZ-O6, TPA-PY-O8, Spiro-O8) were synthesized by introducing triphenylamine, triazine, pyrene, and spiro-fluorene cores respectively. The synthesis involved facile demethylation and consequent air-oxidation of phenolic hydroxyl precursors, in only 2 steps with high yield. Molecular structures were characterized by NMR, mass spectrometry, and elemental analysis (details provided in SI). Radical species and physical properties were studied by cyclic voltammetry (CV), UV-vis-NIR spectroscopy, and electron spin resonance (ESR). CV curves were measured over 15 cycles in dichloromethane solution containing 0.1 M nBu4NPF6 as supporting electrolyte at a scan rate of 0.1 V/s. Methoxy precursors were dissolved in dichloromethane at 5 mg/mL for CV measurements. Target radical compounds were coated on carbon-glass electrodes to form films during CV. Potential values used saturated calomel electrode as reference with Fc+/Fc couple (0.27 V) as internal standard. HOMO and LUMO energy levels were calculated based on CV curves. Photoluminescence quantum yield (PLQY) tests were conducted in dichloromethane solution and film for all precursors and radical products. ESR spectra were recorded at a test amount of 0.02 mmol for all radical species. For photothermal conversion, an IR thermal camera monitored temperature increments under irradiation. The interface heating system used a commercially available white polyurethane (PU) porous foam as support. The PU foam had a 2.0 cm diameter and 30 mg of TPA-TPA-O6 was loaded into the foam. TPA-TPA-O6 was loaded into PU foam by impregnating pure PU foam in solution and drying at 80 °C. Photothermal conversion was tested under 808 nm laser irradiation at energy powers of 0.8 W cm⁻² and 1.0 W cm⁻². Seawater desalination was verified by monitoring concentration reductions of Na⁺, Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺, and K⁺. Comparative data for water evaporation efficiency and rate were compiled from previously reported organic, inorganic, and polymer materials (Figure S17, Table S2).

Procedures And Architectures
The star-shaped ANAR architecture was designed to delocalize the unpaired electron across a wide conjugated backbone, minimizing steric hindrance. The radical character is manifested by a closed-shell nitro-like and open-shell nitroxide structure with unpaired electrons delocalized in conjugated backbones. The TPA-TPA-O6 radical powder exhibited a totally black color, consistent with broad absorption covering the visible region. Aggregation in the powder state further broadened the absorption spectrum from 300 to 2000 nm for TPA-TPA-O6. TPA-PY-O8 showed an absorption edge around 1000 nm, while TPA-TPZ-O6 showed an edge around 800 nm in film. Radical generation occurred upon easy oxidation of phenolic hydroxyl groups in air after demethylation. The high spin concentration (confirmed by ESR) and low PLQY indicate dominant nonradiative decay channels for photothermal conversion. TPA-TPA-O6 PLQY was 0.1%, TPA-TPZ-O6 0.9%, TPA-PY-O8 1.0%, and Spiro-O8 0.3%. TPA-TPA-O6 showed a fast photothermal conversion process with temperature rising from 25 °C to ~210 °C within 60 s under 0.8 W cm⁻² laser. Increasing laser power to 1.0 W cm⁻² raised TPA-TPA-O6 temperature to ~250 °C within 60 s. The temperature rose regularly with increasing laser irradiation power. After laser turn-off, the temperature decreased quickly to ambient. TPA-TPA-O6 exhibited excellent photothermal stability over ten cycles of laser irradiation on and off. The interface heating system was established by floating the PU+TPA-TPA-O6 foam on water. Continuous 1 sun irradiation (1.0 kW m⁻²) for 600 s achieved an equilibrium temperature of 81.2 °C for the PU+TPA-TPA-O6 foam. The bare PU foam under identical conditions reached only 36 °C. After 1 h continuous irradiation (1 kW m⁻²), the PU+TPA-TPA-O6 foam reached 45 °C, about 10 °C higher than bare PU.

Key Results
The absorption spectrum of TPA-TPA-O6 in film showed a typical and great red shift with a long absorption tail in the range 400-825 nm, indicating radical character. ESR signal intensity of TPA-TPA-O6 and Spiro-O8 were significantly enhanced compared to triazine and pyrene-core radicals due to stronger electron-donating capability. All demethylated ANARs showed highly reversible CV curves over 15 cycles with negligible change, indicating unexpected electrochemical stability. HOMO energy levels of TPA-TPA-O6, TPA-TPZ-O6, TPA-PY-O8, and Spiro-O8 were -4.90, -4.81, -4.97, and -4.84 eV respectively, all enhanced compared to methoxy precursors. TPA-TPA-O6 and Spiro-O8 showed superior ESR signal intensities due to lower bandgap and more obvious radical character. Conductivity of all demethylated counterparts was improved relative to methoxy precursors. The lower HOMO energy levels of TPA-TPZ-O6 and TPA-PY-O8 made them harder to oxidize by O₂, leading to weaker ESR signals. PLQYs of all radical products were lower than 1% after demethylation, indicating radical formation by quenching of precursors. TPA-TPA-O6 demonstrated a rapid temperature rise from 25 °C to approximately 210 °C within 60 s under 0.8 W cm⁻² laser. TPA-TPZ-O6 and TPA-PY-O8 temperature rose from 25 °C to only about 40 °C within 60 s under the same laser power. At 1.0 W cm⁻², TPA-TPA-O6 temperature reached approximately 250 °C within 60 s. TPA-TPA-O6 exhibited stable performance over ten laser cycles with no significant degradation. The PU+TPA-TPA-O6 foam achieved an equilibrium temperature of 81.2 °C under 1 sun continuous irradiation for 600 s. The bare PU foam reached only 36 °C under the same conditions. Water evaporation efficiency of TPA-TPA-O6 was 89.41% and water evaporation rate was 1.293 kg m⁻² h⁻¹ under 1 sun (1.0 kW m⁻²). The mass change data confirmed the 89.41% efficiency and 1.293 kg m⁻² h⁻¹ rate under 1 sun. Seawater desalination with TPA-TPA-O6 significantly reduced all four primary ions to concentrations lower than membrane-based methods. TPA-TPA-O6 is cheap and synthesizable via 2 steps with very high yield compared to previous organic photothermal materials.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The star-shaped ANAR design with rich resonance structures (closed-shell nitro-like and open-shell nitroxide) stabilizes the radical via unpaired electron delocalization across the conjugated backbone. The exceptionally high spin concentration, confirmed by ESR, drives highly nonradiative decay, which is the fundamental mechanism for photothermal conversion. The strong donor-acceptor conjugation effect simultaneously reduces the optical bandgap and determines the paramagnetic property of the radical materials. The black color and broadband absorption up to 2000 nm in the powder state enable efficient sunlight harvesting across the NIR region. The unexpected electrochemical reversibility (15 cycles) indicates that the star-shaped neutral radical architecture is fundamentally more stable than previously reported radicaloids. The TPA-TPA-O6 system demonstrates that neutral, stable organic small molecules can outperform both inorganic and conjugated polymer photothermal materials in a simple, low-cost, solution-processable design. The strategy of using neutral radical small molecules with restricted radiative decay opens a new avenue for designing photothermal materials with wide absorption and high thermal stability. The findings suggest that further structural optimization—increasing planarity and adjusting donor-acceptor strengths—will yield even more efficient ANAR materials for solar energy and organic electronics.

Contradictions And Limitations
TPA-TPZ-O6 and TPA-PY-O8 exhibited relatively poor photothermal performance (temperature to 40 °C vs 210 °C), attributed to lower radical spin concentration and potential partial protonation. The PLQY values of TPA-TPZ-O6 (0.9%) and TPA-PY-O8 (1.0%) are higher than TPA-TPA-O6 (0.1%), which may suggest slightly stronger radiative channels or lower radical content. The lower HOMO energy levels of triazine and pyrene-core ANARs made them harder to oxidize by O₂, resulting in weaker ESR signals and lower photothermal performance. The paper does not specify the exact random seeds, batch numbers, or demographic information for the manufacturing of precursors, though these are less critical for purely synthetic organic chemistry. The exact molecular weight and purity percentages of the purified radical products are not explicitly stated in the main text. The supporting information (SI) contains detailed synthetic schemes and characterization (Figures S1-S9), but the main text provides limited quantitative details on yields and purification steps. The seawater desalination test appears to be a single-point demonstration without multi-cycle repeatability data or long-term salt accumulation analysis. The paper does not explicitly report a degradation rate or photobleaching quantification over extended operation (the 10-cycle laser test is short-term).

Claims
TPA-TPA-O6 achieves 89.41% solar-to-vapor efficiency and 1.293 kg m⁻² h⁻¹ evaporation rate under 1 sun, representing top performance among pure organic small molecule photothermal materials. Water evaporation efficiency of TPA-TPA-O6 was recorded as 89.41% under 1 sun. Water evaporation rate reached 1.293 kg m⁻² h⁻¹. TPA-TPA-O6 achieved ~210 °C within 60 s under 0.8 W cm⁻², far exceeding counterparts. Comparative data in Figure S17 and Table S2 position this among top-performing organic systems. The comparison with previously reported materials relies on data from external sources (Figure S17, Table S2) which may not be directly verifiable from the provided text. TPA-TPZ-O6 and TPA-PY-O8 performed significantly worse (only ~40 °C), indicating the claim of 'top performance' is specific to TPA-TPA-O6 rather than the ANAR class as a whole. These results enable low-cost solar water evaporation that competes with expensive inorganic or polymer-based systems. The design strategy is broadly applicable to other structural modifications for optimized photothermal materials.
Neutral open-shell ANARs exhibit unexpected electrochemical stability over 15 CV cycles, unlike previously reported organic radicaloids. All demethylated ANARs showed highly reversible CV curves with negligible change after 15 cycles. HOMO energy levels ranged from -4.81 to -4.97 eV, and air/electrochemical stability was comparable to methoxy precursors. The paper explicitly states this is 'unexpected electrochemical stability compared to traditional organic radical materials.' The study uses only 15 cycles, which may not represent long-term practical device stability. The electrochemical stability was tested at a constant scan rate (0.1 V/s), which may not capture all degradation mechanisms. Stable neutral radicals remove a major barrier to implementing radical chemistry in practical devices. The neutral radical architecture provides a platform for multi-functional applications beyond photothermal conversion.

Data And Code Availability
The Supporting Information is available free of charge at http://pubs.acs.org. The detailed synthetic scheme, characterization data, photothermal test conditions, detailed calculation processes, and comparative tables are contained in the SI. No explicit code repository or raw data access beyond the SI is mentioned.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The star-shaped architecture was systematically varied by changing the core (triphenylamine, triazine, pyrene, spiro-fluorene) to assess structure-property relationships. Comparison between methoxy precursors and demethylated radicals served as a control for radical formation (UV-Vis, PLQY, CV, ESR). PLQY values for the precursors (moderate) versus radicals (<1%) confirm radical generation by quenching of fluorescence. ESR signal enhancement after demethylation confirms air-oxidation-driven radical generation. Temperature-power dependence tests (0.8 W cm⁻² vs 1.0 W cm⁻²) demonstrated linear scaling of heating with power. The 10-cycle laser stability test validates the photothermal stability under repeated cycling. Interfacial evaporation on PU foam was compared directly with bare PU foam to isolate the ANAR contribution. Seawater desalination test validated application in complex environments with measurable ion reductions.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A-C shows the molecular structures of TPA-TPA-O6, TPA-TPZ-O6, TPA-PY-O8, and Spiro-O8. Figure 2A shows UV-Vis absorption spectra of TPA-TPA-OMe in dichloromethane solution and film, with peaks at 305 and 380 nm. Figures 2B and 2C show absorption spectra for the pyrene and triazine core radicals, with edges around 1000 nm and 800 nm. Figure 3 shows cyclic voltammetry curves of all four radical species measured over 15 cycles in dichloromethane. Figure 4A shows ESR spectra comparing methoxy precursors and demethylated radicals, with significant signal enhancement for radicals. Figure 4B shows photoluminescence spectra of precursors and radical products. Figure 4D shows photothermal conversion performance by IR thermal camera monitoring. Figure 5A shows temperature increment of TPA-TPA-O6 under 808 nm laser (25 °C to ~210 °C within 60 s). Figure 5B shows the temperature change process picture during photothermal conversion. Figure 5C shows temperature versus laser power dependence (reaching ~250 °C at 1.0 W cm⁻²). Figure 6A shows broadband absorption spectra up to 2000 nm in aggregated state. Figure 6B shows the comparative absorption spectra among different organic photothermal materials. Figure 6C shows the photothermal stability over ten laser cycles. Figure 6D shows the comparative temperature increment of TPA-TPA-O6 against other photothermal materials. Figure 6E shows surface temperature of PU+TPA-TPA-O6 foam versus bare PU foam under 1 sun. Figure 6F shows mass change curves and water evaporation efficiency (89.41%) and rate (1.293 kg m⁻² h⁻¹). Figure S16 shows the brownish black PU foam after TPA-TPA-O6 impregnation. Figure S17 and Table S2 compile water evaporation efficiency and rate for reported materials (inorganic, polymer, organic). Figure S18 shows reduced ion concentrations (Na⁺, Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺, K⁺) after seawater desalination. Table S1 lists CV data, HOMO/LUMO levels, and PLQY values for all precursors and radicals. Figure S10 shows conductivity of all demethylated counterparts. Figure S11 provides additional ESR data.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the design and synthesis of a series of stable, neutral, star-shaped aromatic nitric acid radicals with rich resonance structures that exhibit extremely high spin concentration and suppressed radiative decay, enabling efficient photothermal conversion via exclusively nonradiative pathways. 2. The strongest evidence is TPA-TPA-O6, which achieved 89.41% solar-to-vapor efficiency and 1.293 kg m⁻² h⁻¹ water evaporation rate under 1 sun (1.0 kW m⁻²), temperature rising from 25 °C to ~210 °C in 60 s under 0.8 W cm⁻² laser, demonstrating top-tier performance among pure organic small-molecule materials with negligible photobleaching over ten laser cycles. 3. The future path involves developing ANAR materials with enhanced planarity to further reduce optical bandgap and enhance planarity for applications in photothermal conversion, organic electronics, spintronics, and magnetic devices, leveraging the existing design concept for structural optimization.

summary.title: Metal-Free Photocatalysis at Charged Aqueous Interface: Boosting the Photocatalytic Oxidative Coupling of Arylamines to Azoaromatics under Ambient Conditions
summary.authors: Shivendra Singh; Vidhi Agarwal; Tridib K Sarma; Tushar Kanti Mukherjee
summary.field_subfield: Photocatalysis; Supramolecular Chemistry; Sustainable Organic Synthesis
summary.executive_summary: This study reports a sustainable, metal-free photocatalytic oxidative coupling (POC) of arylamines to azoaromatics at the charged aqueous interfaces (CAIs) of micelles, achieving up to 100% yield and 100% selectivity under ambient air atmosphere. The methodology utilizes Eosin Y (EY) as a low-cost organic photocatalyst and K3PO4 as a base, with 0.6 mol% PC required, outperforming previous Ir-based organic photocatalyst methodologies. The system operates with fast kinetics (4 hours for 100% conversion) at λ = 525 nm and a broad substrate scope encompassing 8 electron-rich and electron-deficient arylamines. The remarkable catalytic boosting is attributed to two synergistic effects: (1) non-diffusive photoinduced electron transfer (PET) with an ultrafast time constant of 0.3 ps, and (2) modulation of redox potentials at the micellar interface. The micellar scaffold (CTAB at 40 mM) serves as an efficient assembly that solubilizes both the cationic EY and the hydrophobic arylamines in close proximity at the Stern layer. The reaction mechanism proceeds via amine radical formation followed by bimolecular coupling, with atmospheric O2 acting as a sacrificial oxidant regenerated as H2O2. Fluorescence quenching experiments with linear Stern-Volmer plots (kq = 6.3 × 10^12 M^-1 s^-1) confirm non-diffusive PET, and BHT radical trapping experiments corroborate the radical pathway. The work constitutes the first report on aqueous-phase synthesis of azo compounds under ambient conditions, opening new directions for sustainable azoaromatic synthesis.

claims.description: The micellar CAI enables metal-free photocatalytic oxidative coupling of arylamines to azoaromatics under ambient air with up to 100% yield and selectivity in aqueous media.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study reports a sustainable, metal-free photocatalytic oxidative coupling (POC) of arylamines to azoaromatics at the charged aqueous interfaces (CAIs) of micelles, achieving up to 100% yield and 100% selectivity under ambient air atmosphere. The methodology utilizes Eosin Y (EY) as a low-cost organic photocatalyst and K3PO4 as a base, with 0.6 mol% PC required, outperforming previous Ir-based organic photocatalyst methodologies. The system operates with fast kinetics (4 hours for 100% conversion) at λ = 525 nm and a broad substrate scope encompassing 8 electron-rich and electron-deficient arylamines. The remarkable catalytic boosting is attributed to two synergistic effects: (1) non-diffusive photoinduced electron transfer (PET) with an ultrafast time constant of 0.3 ps, and (2) modulation of redox potentials at the micellar interface. The micellar scaffold (CTAB at 40 mM) serves as an efficient assembly that solubilizes both the cationic EY and the hydrophobic arylamines in close proximity at the Stern layer. The reaction mechanism proceeds via amine radical formation followed by bimolecular coupling, with atmospheric O2 acting as a sacrificial oxidant regenerated as H2O2. Fluorescence quenching experiments with linear Stern-Volmer plots (kq = 6.3 × 10^12 M^-1 s^-1) confirm non-diffusive PET, and BHT radical trapping experiments corroborate the radical pathway. The work constitutes the first report on aqueous-phase synthesis of azo compounds under ambient conditions, opening new directions for sustainable azoaromatic synthesis.

Research Context
Azoaromatics are an important class of functional organic molecules with potential in optical storage, molecular switches, and industrial applications. The traditional diazotization method produces unstable diazonium intermediates and unwanted waste, limiting its practical utility. Metal nanoparticle-catalyzed synthesis of azo compounds has been reported but often suffers from slow kinetics, poor selectivity, high temperature, or inert atmosphere requirements. Photocatalytic reductive coupling of nitrobenzenes produces poor product selectivity due to simultaneous generation of azoxyaromatics and nitrosobenzene, requiring an inert atmosphere. Previous photocatalytic oxidative coupling of arylamines to azoaromatics utilized Ir-based photocatalysts but suffered from slow kinetics, moderate yields, high catalyst dose, and limited substrate scope under ambient atmosphere. All prior reports used organic solvents due to the low solubility of amine substrates in aqueous media, leaving a gap for a green, aqueous-phase methodology. Charged aqueous interfaces (CAIs) can dramatically modulate chemical and photochemical reactions that are otherwise inefficient in bulk media through unique electric fields and microenvironments.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether a metal-free, aqueous-phase photocatalytic oxidative coupling of arylamines to azoaromatics can be achieved with high yield, selectivity, and ambient conditions. The hypothesis is that the charged aqueous interface (CAI) of micelles can act as an efficient scaffold to solubilize both the photocatalyst and substrates in close proximity, enabling a non-diffusive PET mechanism. It was predicted that the micellar microenvironment would modulate redox potentials at the interface, dramatically boosting catalytic efficacy compared to bulk-phase reactions. The specific hypothesis is that the positively charged CTAB micellar Stern layer would electrostatically bind the dianionic EY (pH 7) while accommodating hydrophobic arylamines at the less polar hydrocarbon/aqueous interface. The study predicts that atmospheric O2 will serve as a sacrificial oxidant for photocatalyst regeneration via H2O2 formation, enabling metal-free operation under ambient air. It was expected that the non-diffusive nature of the PET (confirmed by ultrafast kinetics) would be the primary driver of enhanced performance relative to previous organic photocatalyst methodologies.

Methodological Details
The photocatalytic system uses Eosin Y (EY) as the organic photocatalyst and K3PO4 as the base. The micellar system uses cetyltrimethylammonium bromide (CTAB) as the surfactant. The critical micellar concentration (CMC) region for CTAB was probed in the range of 0.75–1.0 mM for EY interaction studies. Optimization experiments tested various surfactants: CTAB, sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS), and triton X-100 (TX-100). The optimized reaction conditions for p-anisidine conversion use: 0.6 mol% EY, 2 equiv. K3PO4, and 40 mM CTAB. The substrate p-anisidine was converted to 1,2bis(4-methoxyphenyl)diazene at 100% conversion. The reaction was triggered by green light at a wavelength of λ = 525 nm. GC-MS and NMR measurements were used for product identification and quantification. HR-TEM was used to confirm the spherical micellar morphology at the optimized CTAB concentration. Fluorescence quenching and up-conversion measurements were performed to probe the PET mechanism. Radical trap experiments used 1 equivalent of 2,6-di-tert-butyl-4-methylphenol (BHT) to capture amine radicals. Control experiments used H2O2 sensing strips to monitor byproduct formation. The reaction duration for the optimized protocol was 4 h under ambient air.

Procedures And Architectures
The absorption peak of EY in water at 516 nm was monitored for bathochromic shifts upon micellar addition. Bathochromic shifts of 9 nm (CTAB) and 16 nm (TX-100) indicated micellar association of EY. Fluorescence lifetime of EY in water was 1.17 ns and increased to 2.74 ns upon CTAB micellization. At pH 7, EY bears two negative charges and interacts electrostatically with cationic CTAB. CTAB forms spherical micelles at 40 mM as confirmed by HR-TEM. The reaction procedure involves mixing p-anisidine, 40 mM CTAB, 2 equiv. K3PO4, and 0.6 mol% EY in aqueous medium, followed by green light irradiation. Proton abstraction by K3PO4 is a critical step following PET for amine substrates. Atmospheric O2 reduction produces H2O2, which transforms to H2O2 as the PC regeneration byproduct. PET quenching was quantified using a linear Stern-Volmer plot to extract the bimolecular rate constant. BHT radical trapping involved 5 min initial irradiation followed by BHT addition and 4 h subsequent irradiation.

Key Results
The optimized reaction (p-anisidine → 1,2bis(4-methoxyphenyl)diazene) achieved 100% conversion within 4 h under green light (λ = 525 nm). Only 0.6 mol% Eosin Y was required, an 8.3-fold lower dose than the previous report. Fluorescence up-conversion revealed an ultrafast PET with a time constant of 0.3 ps. The Stern-Volmer quenching rate constant was kq = 6.3 × 10^12 M^-1 s^-1, indicating non-diffusive bimolecular quenching. EY@CTAB fluorescence lifetime increased from 1.17 ns to 2.74 ns upon CTAB micellization. EY@TX-100 suffered disassembly in the presence of K3PO4, while EY@CTAB remained stable. The reaction was feasible only in the presence of base (K3PO4, KOH, or DABCO). Conversion yields were slightly lower when using the organic base DABCO. With blue light irradiation, 100% conversion required 6 h instead of 4 h. p-Chloroaniline and p-bromoaniline showed conversion yields of 98% and 95%, respectively. p-Nitroaniline showed no fluorescence quenching, indicating lack of electron transfer to EY*@CTAB. BHT trapping reduced azo product conversion to ~5.0% after 4 h irradiation, confirming a radical mechanism. A characteristic HR-MS peak for p-anisidine-BHT adducts appeared at 342.2399 g/mol, validating the radical intermediate.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The micellar Stern layer provides a unique microenvironment that solubilizes both the cationic PC and the hydrophobic arylamines in close proximity at the interface. Interfacial surface charges dictate the interaction with charged molecules, aligning probe dipoles and facilitating product selectivity through unique electric fields. The non-diffusive nature of PET (kq ≥ 10^12 M^-1 s^-1) eliminates diffusion as a rate-limiting step, enabling the 0.3 ps electron transfer. The modulation of redox potentials at the CAI makes the oxidation of arylamines by EY* thermodynamically feasible irrespective of substituents. Atmospheric O2 acts as a sacrificial oxidant, regenerating the photocatalyst via H2O2 formation, thereby enabling metal-free operation under ambient air. The finding that PET precedes proton abstraction (confirmed by K3PO4-unperturbed SV plots) establishes the mechanistic sequence: ET then PT. This work is the first report on aqueous-phase synthesis of azo compounds under ambient conditions using organic photocatalysis.

Contradictions And Limitations
The paper notes that conversion yields with DABCO are slightly lower than with K3PO4 or KOH. p-Chloroaniline (98%) and p-bromoaniline (95%) achieved slightly lower conversion than the 100% observed for p-anisidine. The blue light protocol requires 6 h for 100% conversion compared to 4 h with green light, indicating wavelength dependence of kinetics. The content is not peer-reviewed as indicated by the ChemRxiv license, which may affect the robustness of the reported conclusions. The abstract claims selectivity of 100%, but the results section shows 98% and 95% for electron-deficient substrates, introducing a minor internal inconsistency. The paper does not report the exact concentration of p-anisidine used in the optimized 100% conversion experiment, only the CTAB concentration (40 mM). The quantum yield of the POC reaction is not explicitly reported.

Claims
The micellar CAI enables metal-free photocatalytic oxidative coupling of arylamines to azoaromatics under ambient air with up to 100% yield and selectivity in aqueous media. p-Anisidine achieved 100% conversion to azo product in 4 h under green light with 0.6 mol% EY. Fluorescence up-conversion confirmed ultrafast 0.3 ps PET, substantiating the non-diffusive mechanism. BHT radical trapping reduced azo formation to ~5.0%, confirming a radical-mediated mechanism. GC-MS and NMR validated the azo product structure across 8 substrates. Electron-deficient substrates (p-chloroaniline, p-bromoaniline) reached only 98% and 95% conversion, not 100%. Blue light requires 6 h instead of 4 h for 100% conversion. The paper is a preprint (ChemRxiv) and has not undergone formal peer review. Opens new opportunities for sustainable azoaromatic synthesis in aqueous media. The CAI strategy may be generalizable to other oxidative couplings of aromatic substrates. Reduces dependency on organic solvents and precious metal photocatalysts in azo synthesis.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Surfactant screening showed EY binds specifically to CTAB but not SDS, and TX-100 binding is unstable to K3PO4. Base comparison showed K3PO4 and KOH perform slightly better than DABCO. Wavelength comparison showed green light (525 nm, 4 h) outperforms blue light (6 h). The absence of PET with p-nitroaniline serves as a negative control confirming ET-dependent mechanism. H2O2 sensing strips confirmed aerial O2 reduction as the PC regeneration pathway.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1a shows EY absorption bathochromic shifts upon micelle addition. Figure 1b shows fluorescence quenching of EY by premicellar CTAB and TX-100. Figure 1c shows fluorescence lifetime changes during CTAB micellization. Figure 1d shows fluorescence lifetime from 1.17 ns to 2.74 ns upon CTAB micellization. Figure S2 and S3 show EY@TX-100 disassembly in the presence of K3PO4. Table 1 lists optimized reaction conditions: 40 mM CTAB, 2 equiv. K3PO4, 0.6 mol% EY, λ = 525 nm, 4 h. Figure S4 shows HR-TEM confirming spherical CTAB micelles at 40 mM. Figure S5 shows blue light (6 h) versus green light (4 h) kinetics. Figure 2b shows the Stern-Volmer plot with kq = 6.3 × 10^12 M^-1 s^-1. Figure 2d shows fluorescence up-conversion with 0.3 ps time constant. Figure S6 shows H2O2 sensing strips confirming O2 reduction. Scheme 1 compares previous Ir-based, diazotization, metal-catalyzed, and POC routes. Scheme 2 shows the substrate scope with 8 arylamines and radical trap experiment. Scheme 3a illustrates the BHT radical trapping experimental design.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first aqueous-phase, metal-free photocatalytic oxidative coupling of arylamines to azoaromatics at micellar CAIs, achieving 100% yield in 4 h using only 0.6 mol% Eosin Y. 2. The strongest evidence is the 0.3 ps ultrafast PET time constant confirmed by fluorescence up-conversion and the linear Stern-Volmer plot (kq = 6.3 × 10^12 M^-1 s^-1), establishing a non-diffusive mechanistic driver that surpasses previous organic photocatalyst methodologies. 3. The future path lies in exploiting the micellar CAI microenvironment to enable sustainable, metal-free oxidative couplings of diverse aromatic substrates in aqueous media under ambient conditions.

summary.title: Spontaneous crystal fluctuation in hydrocarbon polymer-coated monolayer MoS 2 , MoSe 2 , WS 2 , and WSe 2 with strong photoluminescence enhancement
summary.authors: Takahiro Nakahara, Takashi Kobayashi, Tetsuji Dohi, Takeshi Yoshimura, Norifumi Fujimura, Daisuke Kiriya
summary.field_subfield: Materials Science / 2D Semiconductors and Optoelectronics
summary.executive_summary: This paper presents a universal post-preparation method to enhance photoluminescence (PL) intensity in monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs) by coating them with paraffin, a simple hydrocarbon. Previously, PL enhancement strategies were compound-specific: sulfur-based TMDCs (MoS2, WS2) benefited from p-type dopants (F4TCNQ) or superacids (TFSI), while selenium-based TMDCs (MoSe2, WSe2) had very limited strategies. The authors demonstrate that coating monolayer MoS2, WS2, MoSe2, and WSe2 with paraffin—which has a high thermal expansion coefficient—induces spontaneous fluctuation, strain, and eventual desorption of the monolayer from the substrate due to paraffin penetration. This removes the substrate effect, a key factor suppressing PL. Quantitative results show PL enhancement factors of 215× for MoS2, 55× for WS2, 9× for WSe2, and 50× for MoSe2 relative to as-exfoliated flakes. Raman spectroscopy confirms in-plane strain (E′ peak shift -0.72 cm⁻¹ average) and carrier concentration reduction (A′ peak shift +1.03 cm⁻¹). Optical microscopy captures the time-dependent deformation into wrinkled or bundled structures. The method is universal, works on both sulfur- and selenium-based TMDCs, and leverages paraffin's insulative, flexible, and transparent properties for optoelectronic applications. The authors propose that the combined effects of strain from paraffin's thermal expansion and subsequent desorption drive the PL enhancement. The method is applicable to other 2D layered materials as well.

claims.description: Paraffin coating universally enhances PL in both sulfur- and selenium-based monolayer TMDCs by removing the substrate effect.
The underlying mechanism of PL enhancement is strain-driven desorption of the monolayer from the substrate.

Research Context
Monolayer TMDCs (MX2 with M=Mo, W and X=S, Se) have been studied for optical transistors, LEDs, and solar cells due to their direct band gap at K and K′ points. A major drawback is poor photoluminescence intensity caused by over-carrier concentrations, strains, and lattice defects. For sulfur-based TMDCs (MoS2, WS2), p-type dopants like F4TCNQ and superacids like TFSI successfully enhance PL intensity by hundreds of times. In contrast, selenium-based compounds (MoSe2, WSe2) have very limited strategies for PL enhancement; oleic acid and hydrohalic acid treatments have worked for MoSe2 but not WSe2. For WSe2 specifically, methods involve separating the monolayer from substrates by floating or inserting ions to remove the substrate effect. No universal strategy exists for improving optical behavior across a wide variety of two-dimensional semiconductor materials.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether a single post-preparation method can universally enhance PL intensity in both sulfur- and selenium-based monolayer TMDCs. The authors hypothesize that removing the substrate effect by mechanically floating monolayers from the underlying substrate would be a potential strategy applicable to all compounds. The specific hypothesis is that coating TMDCs with paraffin, which has a large thermal coefficient, will induce spontaneous fluctuation and deformation. It is predicted that this fluctuation, driven by strain at the paraffin-TMDC interface, will lead to desorption of the monolayer from the substrate, thereby removing the substrate effect and enhancing PL. The authors further predict that the method will be applicable to MoS2, WS2, MoSe2, and WSe2, and that paraffin's inherent properties (insulative, flexible, transparent) will enable optoelectronic integration.

Methodological Details
The study tested four monolayer TMDC compounds: MoS2, WS2, MoSe2, and WSe2. All monolayers were obtained by mechanical exfoliation, referred to as as-exfoliated flakes. The paraffin used has a reported melting point of 42–45 °C. Paraffin was melted on a hot plate at 80 °C prior to coating and dropped onto samples. A heat blower (hair dryer) was applied during spin coating to maintain paraffin in a melted state. Paraffin coating was applied via spin coating, with a separate thick film prepared by simple casting for transparency comparison. PL spectra were measured for as-exfoliated flakes on Si/SiO2 and quartz substrates. Optical microscopy and PL mapping were used to visualize morphology and spatial PL distribution. Raman spectroscopy was performed on 30 samples of monolayer MoS2 before and after coating to assess strain and carrier concentration. The monolayer was monitored over time: immediately after coating, after 2 hours at room temperature, and after a further 1 hour.

Procedures And Architectures
Paraffin was melted at 80 °C, dropped onto the monolayer sample on a spin coater, and a heat blower was used to prevent premature solidification. The spin coating process applied the paraffin uniformly across the TMDC monolayers. Time-resolved monitoring of MoS2 involved imaging at three time points: immediately after coating, after 2 hours at room temperature, and after a further 1 hour. Raman spectroscopy measured the E' (in-plane) and A' (out-of-plane) peak positions for strain and carrier concentration analysis. PL spectra were normalized to compare exciton-to-trion signal ratios, with the shoulder at the low-energy side monitored. PL mapping images resolved spatial nonuniformity, identifying specific areas of greater enhancement. Samples with monolayers surrounded by bulk flakes on three sides were prepared to isolate the bundling effect.

Key Results
Paraffin coating enhanced PL of monolayer WS2 by about 36 times on the first test. The normalized PL spectrum of paraffin-coated WS2 showed a decrease in the low-energy shoulder, indicating reduced trion-derived signal. For MoS2, the PL enhancement factor reached 215× from the as-exfoliated state, attributed to the low initial signal. WS2 showed a PL enhancement factor of 55×. MoSe2 showed a PL enhancement factor of 50×. WSe2 showed a PL enhancement factor of 9×.  Optical microscopy confirmed that paraffin covers the entire monolayer WS2 plane. PL mapping showed the monolayer shows PL enhancement in the whole plane, but a partial specific area shows greater enhancement. The E' Raman peak shifted in the negative direction by -0.72 cm⁻¹ on average after coating, indicating in-plane strain. The A' Raman peak shifted in the positive direction by 1.03 cm⁻¹ after coating, indicating decreased carrier concentration. In PL mapping of the restricted monolayer, the center showed 2.3 times greater PL intensity than the rim. The PL peak position around the center shifted 5–10 meV lower in energy than the rim. A folding edge associated with paraffin coating was observed in a monolayer MoS2 sample, indicating a bilayer region. A thick paraffin film prepared by simple casting resulted in a glassy, non-transparent appearance.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The PL enhancement mechanism is attributed to the combined effects of strain (from paraffin's high thermal expansion) and subsequent desorption of the monolayer from the substrate. Substrate effect is the key factor in PL enhancement, removed by penetration of paraffin at the interface. The deformation of the monolayer happens through penetration of paraffin underneath each monolayer TMDC. The shrinkage and bundling into a bundled structure are due to stress at the paraffin-TMDC interface when the monolayer is not surrounded by bulk flakes. The trion-derived PL reduction (decreased low-energy shoulder) suggests decreased carrier concentration after coating. The red-shifted PL peak in strained areas (5–10 meV) aligns with the 'funnel effect' where strain-induced band gap narrowing traps excitons. The underlying science is applicable to other 2D layered materials due to the reliance on thermal expansion coefficients. Paraffin's insulative, flexible, and transparent properties make it suitable for packaging flexible light-emitting displays and solar cells.

Contradictions And Limitations
The PL enhancement factor is highly dependent on each sample; MoS2 achieves 215× while WSe2 only 9×, indicating the method is not equally effective across all compounds. The PL enhancement is nonuniform in the monolayer plane, with specific areas showing greater enhancement, limiting uniform device operation. The thick paraffin film prepared by simple casting is not transparent, restricting the method's practical application to thin-film spin coating. The mechanism relies on spontaneous, time-dependent deformation; the exact kinetics and stability of the fluorescent state over longer periods are not fully characterized. A bilayer MoS2 region was observed near a folding edge, suggesting potential contamination or non-ideal exfoliation affecting local properties. The study does not report long-term photostability or the degradation rate of the paraffin-coated monolayers under continuous illumination.

Claims
Paraffin coating universally enhances PL in both sulfur- and selenium-based monolayer TMDCs by removing the substrate effect. MoS2 shows a 215× PL enhancement factor relative to as-exfoliated flakes. WS2 shows a 55× PL enhancement factor. MoSe2 shows a 50× PL enhancement factor. WSe2 shows a 9× PL enhancement factor, demonstrating applicability to selenium-based systems. The enhancement factors vary by an order of magnitude (9× vs 215×) between WSe2 and MoS2, suggesting compound-specific limitations. This universal approach replaces the need for compound-specific treatments like p-doping or superacid deposition.
The underlying mechanism of PL enhancement is strain-driven desorption of the monolayer from the substrate. Raman E' peak shift of -0.72 cm⁻¹ confirms in-plane strain. Raman A' peak shift of +1.03 cm⁻¹ confirms decreased carrier concentration. Time-resolved imaging shows spontaneous deformation into wrinkles and bundles. PL mapping identifies localized areas of greater enhancement consistent with nonuniform strain. The mechanism is proposed as an explanation but not proven directly; multiple plausible mechanisms (strain, carrier reduction, desorption) coexist. The strategy is applicable to any 2D material subject to substrate-induced electronic modulation via thermal-expansion-driven strain.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The study tested a sample with the monolayer surrounded by bulk flakes on three sides to isolate the bundling effect from the general desorption mechanism. The comparison between spin-coated (thin) and simple-cast (thick) paraffin films served as a transparency control, showing the thick film was non-transparent. The monolayer was tested on both Si/SiO2 and quartz substrates, confirming the enhancement is not substrate-specific.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1a shows the spin-coating preparation process using paraffin melted at 80 °C. Figure 1b presents PL spectra for monolayer WS2 showing ~36× enhancement with paraffin coating. Figures 1c and 1d show PL mapping images confirming uniform paraffin coverage of monolayer WS2. Figure 2a displays the band gaps and emission wavelengths for all four TMDC compounds as as-exfoliated flakes. Figure 2b reports the factors of PL enhancement for each original monolayer flake. Figures 3a-d show time-resolved optical microscope images of MoS2 deformation after coating, at 2 hours, and after a further 1 hour. Figure 3e shows the PL spectra of the deformed MoS2 sample with the PL peak upshift. Figure 4 presents Raman spectroscopy statistics for 30 MoS2 samples, showing E' and A' peak shifts. Table 2 reports the average Raman peak shift values for E' and A' peaks in 30 samples. Figure 5 shows a monolayer surrounded by bulk flakes on three sides with nonuniform PL intensity (2.3× center/rim) and peak shift (5–10 meV).

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a universal post-preparation method using paraffin coating to enhance PL in all monolayer TMDCs (MoS2, WS2, MoSe2, WSe2) by removing the substrate effect via spontaneous strain-induced desorption. 2. The strongest evidence is the 215× PL enhancement of MoS2, corroborated by Raman shifts (-0.72 cm⁻¹ E', +1.03 cm⁻¹) confirming concurrent strain and carrier reduction, and time-resolved imaging of spontaneous deformation. 3. The future path involves applying this strain-engineering strategy to other 2D materials and integrating paraffin's flexible, transparent, insulative properties into optoelectronic devices such as light-emitting displays and solar cells.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study reports the successful continuous partial oxidation of methane to methanol and acetic acid at atmospheric pressure using a modified silica-supported bimetallic (Au-Fe) catalyst with 15% w/v H2O2 as the oxidant. The authors address the long-standing 'holy grail' problem of methane-to-methanol (M2M) conversion by operating under benign conditions—atmospheric pressure and mild temperatures (80 °C)—rather than the high-pressure, high-temperature conditions typically required for methane activation. The catalyst, designated AuFeHS, is prepared via a modified deposition precipitation method onto hydrophobic silica (HS), a sodium-containing silica support modified during synthesis. The catalyst features atomic clusters of Fe (0.46 wt %) and Au nanoparticles (0.23 wt %, 1.3–3.0 nm) on HS. Key spectroscopic characterization (XPS, XANES, EXAFS, HRTEM, contact angle analysis, and in-situ IR) confirms: (1) the presence of low-valent Fe³⁻δ⁺ species, (2) cationic Auδ⁺ species (15% relative area), (3) atomic dispersion of Fe with no Fe-Fe interaction, (4) Au nanoparticles of 1.4–2.8 nm, and (5) hydrophobic surface (118° contact angle). In batch experiments at 10 bar CH4 and 20 bar total pressure, AuFeHS achieved 1666 mmol/(gFe+Au) methanol yield with 95% selectivity within 30 min. Co-feeding CO switched selectivity to acetic acid, yielding 3403 µmol/gcat within 1 h. In continuous flow at atmospheric pressure for 7 h, AuFeHS delivered 224 mmol/(gFe+Au) methanol yield (0.42 mol/(kg catalyst · h)) at 80 °C. Isotope labeling (CD4) confirmed that the methanol oxygenate originates from the methane substrate, not support degradation. The work surpasses previous high-pressure batch benchmarks (e.g., 0.081 mol/(kg catalyst · h) at 20 bar) while operating at atmospheric pressure, establishing a new benchmark for low-pressure methane activation.

Research Context
Methane is a major constituent of natural gas with high calorific value but requires compression to 10–100 atm for commercial utility, making its conversion to chemicals a compelling economic target. Activation of non-polar methane is difficult because its central carbon atom is surrounded by four hydrogen atoms forming a regular tetrahedron, requiring harsh reaction conditions. The thermodynamics of methane partial oxidation (POM) pose a fundamental challenge: an activated C–H bond is so reactive it readily undergoes complete oxidation to CO2, making selective production of methanol difficult. Previous reports on oxo dicopper on carbon nitride gave 129.7 mmol gCu⁻¹ h⁻¹, while AuPdCu/titania yielded 7.02 µmol oxygenates in 30 min, and single-atom catalysts like FeN4/GN-2.7 produced 114 µmol in 10 h, all hampered by low product yield and harsh conditions. Continuous flow POM is limited, with reports yielding only 1.81 µmol h⁻¹ gcat⁻¹ at 210 °C with O2, or 0.081 molProduct kgcatalyst⁻¹ h⁻¹ at 20 bar with H2O2. The gap in the field is a catalyst that can activate methane at mild conditions and selectively produce desired oxygenates at atmospheric pressure.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether a bimetallic Au-Fe catalyst on hydrophobic silica can activate methane selectively and continuously at atmospheric pressure using H2O2 as the oxidant. The authors hypothesize that the synergy between Au and Fe, combined with a hydrophobic silica support, will stabilize low-valent Fe³⁻δ⁺ species that simultaneously activate CH4 and H2O2, enabling low-pressure oxidation. The hypothesis further posited that co-feeding CO would switch selectivity from methanol to acetic acid via a C-insertion mechanism. It was predicted that the continuous-flow performance at atmospheric pressure would surpass the best-reported high-pressure batch results for both methanol and acetic acid. A secondary hypothesis was that the hydrophobic surface would prevent active-site blocking by moisture and facilitate methanol desorption, preventing over-oxidation to CO2.

Methodological Details
The catalyst was synthesized using a modified deposition precipitation (DP) method to disperse atomic clusters of Fe onto hydrophobic silica (HS) support. The optimum catalyst composition (AuFeHS) was identified as 0.46 wt % Fe and 0.23 wt % Au, confirmed by Inductively Coupled Plasma-Optical Emission Spectrometry (ICP-OES). The hydrophobic silica was confirmed by contact angle analysis, yielding a contact angle of 118°. C-H vibration from silica confirmed hydrophobic functionalization (Fig. S3), and the absence of Au/Fe reflections in powder XRD confirmed fine metal dispersion. HRTEM imaging of FeHS showed no contrast difference characteristic of Fe particles, consistent with atomic dispersion at low loading. HRTEM of AuFeHS revealed small Au nanoparticles with a particle size distribution of 1.4–2.8 nm. Specific surface area of the AuFeHS catalyst was 392 m²/g, determined by the present synthesis method. XPS (X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy) was used for oxidation state analysis, with charge correction unnecessary due to electron flood gun. Fe 2p spectra at AuFeHS showed Fe³⁺ at 710.6 eV and low-valent Fe³⁻δ⁺ at 709.5 eV; Au 4f showed Au⁰ at 83.9/87.6 eV (85% area) and Auδ⁺ at ~85 eV (15% area). Fe K-edge XANES and EXAFS were used to probe the local electronic and geometric structure of Fe species. Linear combination fitting of Fe K-edge XANES showed 72% Fe₃O₄ and 28% FeO contribution in AuFeHS. Au L₃-edge XANES and EXAFS confirmed Au remained mostly in elemental form, with a slight shift in AuFeHS consistent with XPS. In-situ IR spectroscopy with CO adsorption was used to probe isolated metal sites, yielding signals at 2105 cm⁻¹ (terminal Au⁰-CO) and 2175 cm⁻¹ (Auδ⁺-CO). Batch screening of AuFeHS was conducted at 10 bar methane pressure; optimum loadings were 0.5 wt % Fe and 0.2 wt % Au for bimetallic screening. Continuous-flow experiments were conducted in a fixed-bed reactor at atmospheric pressure with 15% w/v H2O2. Isotope labeling with CD4 and 2H/13C NMR confirmed that the methanol product originated from methane rather than support ligands.

Procedures And Architectures
For the batch POM reaction, a batch reactor was used at 10 bar methane pressure with H2O2 (15% w/v) as the oxidant. Methanol production was optimized at 0 °C and 10 bar methane pressure (Fig. 3a, b). For the acetic acid production batch, conditions were 50 °C at 20 bar total pressure with a 15 bar CH4 to 5 bar CO feed ratio. Continuous-flow reactions were carried out in a fixed-bed reactor at atmospheric pressure with a 7 h residence time. The temperature was optimized to 80 °C for effective methane conversion at atmospheric pressure. Products were quantified by gas chromatography (GC) using standard calibrations, and NMR confirmed chemical identities. Control experiments included running the reactor without methane flow, without oxidant, and without catalyst to rule out background reactions. Solid-state 29Si NMR was used to characterize the silica support, revealing Q², Q³, Q⁴ and T², T³ states for HS. Na 1s XPS and 23Na NMR (7.32 ppm, -1.59 ppm) confirmed the Si-O-Na framework in the modified silica support. Pyridine-adsorbed FT-IR showed Lewis acid sites at 1449 cm⁻¹, -OH deformation at ~1640 cm⁻¹, and physisorbed water bands.

Key Results
In the batch process at 10 bar methane, AuFeHS achieved 1666 mmol/(gFe+Au) methanol yield with 95% selectivity within 30 min. For comparison, oxo dicopper on carbon nitride yielded 129.7 mmol gCu⁻¹ h⁻¹ with only 4% methanol selectivity. Au-Fe bimetallic screening identified 0.5 wt % Fe and 0.2 wt % Au as optimum, while monometallic Au-HS gave only 47.6 mmol/gAu. In the continuous-flow process at atmospheric pressure and 80 °C, AuFeHS delivered 224 mmol/(gFe+Au) methanol yield. The methanol productivity was 422 µmol h⁻¹ gcat⁻¹ (0.42 mol(methanol) kgcatalyst⁻¹ h⁻¹) over 4 h of continuous-flow reaction. Co-feeding CO switched selectivity to acetic acid with a yield of 3403 µmol/gcat within 1 h at 50 °C, 20 bar total pressure. The CO2 selectivity in the AuFeHS system was 10% with CO co-feeding, compared to 5–6% with methane alone. The FeHS monometallic catalyst produced 24.2 mmol/gFe methanol, while AuHS produced 12 mmol/gAu, demonstrating strong synergistic effects. The continuous-flow methanol yield of 0.42 mol(methanol) kgcatalyst⁻¹ h⁻¹ (4 h) is 24 times higher than the previously reported 0.081 molProduct kgcatalyst⁻¹ h⁻¹ at 20 bar. The continuous-flow methanol yield of 0.42 mol(methanol) kgcatalyst⁻¹ h⁻¹ (4 h) is 24 times higher than the previously reported 0.081 molProduct kgcatalyst⁻¹ h⁻¹ at 20 bar, yet achieved at atmospheric pressure. In SBA-15 supported catalysts, Au-Fe gave 0.78 mmol/gcat, Fe-SBA-15 gave 0.30 mmol/gcat, and Au-SBA-15 gave 0.15 mmol/gcat, highlighting the hydrophobic silica's critical role.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The synergistic interaction between Au and Fe is attributed to Au stabilizing the low-valent Fe³⁻δ⁺ species, which serve as the active sites for simultaneous CH4 and H2O2 activation. Au nanoparticles, acting as excellent CO oxidation catalysts, provide low-energy activation sites for CO adsorption, facilitating the C-insertion mechanism to acetic acid. The hydrophobic silica support is critical because it prevents water from blocking active sites, prevents Au particle sintering in aqueous conditions, and facilitates methanol desorption, thereby preventing over-oxidation. The Lewis acid sites and acidic environment on the bimetallic support facilitate the C–H sigma complex formation for methane activation and assist in regenerating Fe³⁻δ⁺ sites. The conversion of activated C–H sigma complex to CH3 radical on low-valent Fe³⁻δ⁺ sites initiates methanol formation, which can then undergo facile CO insertion to produce acetic acid. The results demonstrate that bimetallic modulation can tune active Fe species, suggesting a general strategy for catalytic conversion of lower alkanes to oxygenates.

Contradictions And Limitations
The role of sodium atoms incorporated into the silica matrix and the contribution of Lewis acid sites are noted as being beyond the scope of the present study and require further exploration. While AuFeHS showed atomic Fe dispersion and Au nanoparticles, some Au particles could coalesce even at small loadings due to high surface energy, potentially affecting reproducibility. The XANES data showed Au absorption edge slightly higher than Au foil, which the authors attribute to charge transfer but do not quantify explicitly beyond qualitative XPS correspondence. The contact angle of 118° was measured, but no explicit wetability study under reaction conditions (with H2O2/liquid) is provided to confirm the hydrophobic layer survives. The paper does not report a specific random seed, catalyst reuse data, or long-term stability testing beyond the 7 h continuous flow window.

Claims
AuFeHS catalyzes methane partial oxidation to methanol at atmospheric pressure and 80 °C, surpassing all previously reported high-pressure benchmarks in both yield and selectivity. In continuous flow at atmospheric pressure, AuFeHS delivered 224 mmol/(gFe+Au) methanol yield, a value not surpassed by any high-pressure report. The 0.42 mol(methanol) kgcatalyst⁻¹ h⁻¹ productivity (4 h) exceeds the 0.081 molProduct kgcatalyst⁻¹ h⁻¹ benchmark by 24 times under more benign conditions. Batch yield reached 1666 mmol/(gFe+Au) with 95% selectivity, a reported benchmark for selectivity. The reported continuous-flow yield of 224 mmol/(gFe+Au) is a 30-min or 4-h snapshot and does not demonstrate indefinite catalyst stability. The selectivity in continuous flow was 82% for FeHS and not explicitly stated as 95% for AuFeHS in the continuous flow section. Demonstrates that atmospheric-pressure methane-to-methanol conversion is kinetically feasible, opening commercial viability. The strategy of bimetallic tuning and hydrophobic support modification can be extrapolated to other alkane-to-oxygenate conversions.
Co-feeding CO with methane switches the primary product from methanol to acetic acid, enabling a tunable oxygenate pathway. Co-feeding CO at 20 bar (15 bar CH4: 5 bar CO) produced 3403 µmol/gcat acetic acid in 1 h at 50 °C. Methanol was the only other liquid oxygenate, with a yield of 166 µmol/gcat. In continuous flow with CO, 648 µmol/gcat of acetic acid formed within 4 h. CO2 selectivity increased to 10% with CO co-feeding, slightly higher than the 5–6% with methane alone. Enables selective production of value-added acetic acid from natural gas streams with CO present.
The low-valent Fe³⁻δ⁺ species are the primary active sites for both CH4 and H2O2 activation, stabilized by cationic Auδ⁺. Fe 2p XPS at AuFeHS showed Fe³⁻δ⁺ at 709.5 eV, absent on the FeHS support alone. Low-valent Fe sites are reported to provide the OH moiety for hydrogen peroxide activation. Au L3-edge XANES and EXAFS confirmed Fe was not in the elemental state, supporting an oxidized/coordinated environment. STEM line analysis confirmed intimate Fe-Au interaction. The exact identity of the Fe³⁻δ⁺ species is not structurally defined beyond XPS/XANES, with possible contributions from multiple iron oxide phases. Identifies bimetallic electronic tuning as the key mechanistic strategy for low-pressure methane activation.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Control experiments without methane flow, without oxidant, or without catalyst confirmed no background product formation. Isotope labeling (CD4) confirmed methanol methyl groups originated from the feed, not support degradation. Nitrogen gas feed yielded no products, confirming the reaction required methane as the organic source. Monometallic Fe-HS, Au-HS, and bimetallic AuFeHS were all tested; AuFeHS exhibited superior performance, demonstrating synergy. SBA-15 supported catalysts were tested to isolate the role of hydrophobicity, showing significantly lower activity. Temperature optimization identified 80 °C as the optimal continuous-flow condition and 50 °C for batch acetic acid production. Time optimization showed the maximum methanol yield at 4 h in continuous flow.

Key Figures Tables
Fig. 1 shows HRTEM images of FeHS (a), AuFeHS (b-c), elemental mapping (d), and Au particle size distribution (e). Fig. 2 presents Fe 2p XPS, Fe K-edge XANES, Au L3-edge XANES, and EXAFS radial distribution functions. Fig. 3 illustrates batch POM selectivity and yield for methanol, acetic acid (with CO), and control experiments. Fig. 4 shows continuous-flow methanol production over 7 h at atmospheric pressure. Fig. 5 presents 29Si NMR spectra of the silica support with and without Fe and Au deposition. Fig. 6 (not explicitly numbered but described) shows Na 1s XPS, 23Na NMR, and pyridine-adsorbed FT-IR of the support. Fig. S1-S2 show contact angle measurements; Fig. S3 shows C-H vibration from HS; Fig. S4 shows powder XRD. Fig. S5-S7 show elemental mapping; Fig. S8 and Table S1 report specific surface area; Fig. S9 shows C 1s XPS. Fig. S10 shows AuHS XPS; Fig. S11 shows Fe K-edge LCF; Fig. S12 shows EXAFS; Fig. S13 shows Au L3-edge XANES; Fig. S14 shows Au EXAFS. Fig. S15 shows in-situ IR with CO adsorption; Fig. S17 shows NMR of reaction mixture; Fig. S18 and S19 show isotope labeling NMR. Fig. S20 shows STEM line analysis; Fig. S21-S22 show 23Na NMR; Fig. S23 shows pyridine-adsorbed FT-IR. Table S4 compares Au-Fe performance with monometallic and SBA-15 supported variants. Table S5 lists continuous-flow product yields and temperature optimization. Table S6 compares results with best reported literature values.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the reporting of a continuous-flow AuFeHS catalyst that achieves 224 mmol/(gFe+Au) methanol yield at atmospheric pressure and 80 °C using H2O2, a result that surpasses all previously reported high-pressure benchmarks. 2. The strongest evidence lies in the 24-fold enhancement over the best reported high-pressure benchmark (0.42 vs. 0.081 mol(methanol) kgcatalyst⁻¹ h⁻¹) combined with the 95% batch selectivity and isotope-labeled proof that products originate solely from methane. 3. The future path involves elucidating the roles of sodium, Lewis acid sites, and Au nanoparticles in the overall reaction, optimizing for commercial M2O (Methane to Oxygenates) technologies.

summary.title: A Workflow for Identifying Viable Crystal Structures with Partially Occupied Sites Applied to Solid Electrolyte: Cubic Li 7 La 3 Zr 2 O 12
summary.authors: Julian Holland; Tom Demeyere; Arihant Bhandari; Felix Hanke; Victor Milman; Chris-Kriton Skylaris
summary.field_subfield: Materials Science / Computational Condensed Matter Physics - Solid-state electrolytes and crystal structure prediction
summary.type_of_paper: Methodology and computational study (preprint on ChemRxiv)
summary.executive_summary:
This study introduces a multi-step workflow for identifying and energetically ordering feasible crystal configurations of cubic Li7La3Zr2O12 (c-LLZO), a prominent solid-state electrolyte candidate whose ground-state Li occupancy has lacked consensus. The authors face a combinatorial explosion where populating 120 crystallographic sites with 56 Li atoms yields approximately 7.4 × 10^34 structures, rendering brute-force methods unviable. Their approach begins by eliminating structures with overlapping Li atoms using a 1.7 Å minimal distance cutoff—a value grounded in the crystal ionic diameter and validated against Li-dimer calculations. This geometric constraint reduces the configuration space to ~2.3 × 10^8 structures, which is further compressed to ~2 × 10^6 unique conformations using a combination of connectivity matrix flattening and Local Sensitive Hashing (LSH) for fast symmetry detection (O(N) scaling). 

Energetic ordering is achieved through a two-pronged approach: COMPASSIII force field calculations on the Li-sublattice and 1235 single-point DFT calculations using ONETEP with PBE functional, 830 eV cutoff. These DFT energies are mapped to a multiple linear regression (MLR) model using frequency occurrence lists of all Li-Li interactions as descriptors, achieving a correlation of 0.9996 on the test set. The study identifies four structures within 0.026 eV (1 kT at 298 K) of the lowest-energy configuration, all with an 8:48 24d:96h occupancy ratio. Geometry optimizations on these four structures confirm that the 96h-to-24d transition (occurring once) yielded the absolute lowest energy structure, 0.58 eV lower than the optimized single-point lowest. The authors conclude that many previously reported experimental and theoretical structures may be physically unfeasible under geometric constraints and provide all generated structures in a public database to improve reproducibility in c-LLZO research.

These DFT energies are mapped to a multiple linear regression (MLR) model using frequency occurrence lists of all Li-Li interactions as descriptors, achieving a correlation of 0.9996 on the test set. The study identifies four structures within 0.026 eV (1 kT at 298 K) of the lowest-energy configuration, all with an 8:48 24d:96h occupancy ratio. Geometry optimizations on these four structures confirm that the 96h-to-24d transition (occurring once) yielded the absolute lowest energy structure, 0.58 eV lower than the optimized single-point lowest. The authors conclude that many previously reported experimental and theoretical structures may be physically unfeasible under geometric constraints and provide all generated structures in a public database to improve reproducibility in c-LLZO research.

Research Context
Solid electrolytes promise higher energy density and improved safety over liquid electrolyte systems for Li-ion batteries. Dendrite formation through the electrolyte has been reported even for the most stable solid electrolytes, threatening cell safety. Cubic Li7La3Zr2O12 (c-LLZO) possesses the best interfacial stability against metallic Li among popular fast ion conductors. c-LLZO has a Hermann-Mauguin space group of Ia3d with Li atoms partially occupying the 24d and 96h sites. Despite intensive study, there is no consensus on c-LLZO's Li occupancy, leading to disagreement about the ground state structure. Previous computational studies use one of several experimental values as a starting point, meaning thermodynamic and observable properties derived from these structures may not be well described.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether the ground-state Li occupancy of c-LLZO can be determined by enumerating all possible site occupancies under geometric constraints. The authors hypothesize that the true ground state lies within the geometrically feasible configurations reachable from a complete combinatorial enumeration. A key hypothesis is that the 24d:96h ratio is indicative of a structure's energy and that a significant energy gap exists between the ground state and higher-energy configurations. The authors posit that structures involving overlapping Li atoms (distances below the crystal ionic diameter) are physically unfeasible and should be eliminated. The expected outcome is a ranked energy ordering of all feasible structures, with the lowest-energy configuration identifying the ground-state candidacy.

Methodological Details
The stoichiometric unit cell of c-LLZO contains 120 crystallographic sites to be occupied by 56 Li atoms. The number of ways to populate these sites is 120 choose 56, approximately 7.4 × 10^34, making brute-force unviable. The minimal Li-Li distance cutoff is set at 1.7 Å, justified as less than 2 times the ionic radius and smaller than the 2.56 Å minimum in t-LLZO. This cutoff imposes two geometric constraints: a maximum of 48 out of 96h sites can be occupied (96h sites form pairs within 0.68 Å) and each 24d occupation eliminates 4 of the 96h sites. The crystal structure framework is based on the sites reported by Buschmann et al. (2019). Initial generation produces approximately 2.3 × 10^8 structures, including symmetry-equivalent duplicates. Symmetry reduction uses a flattened and sorted upper triangular connectivity matrix of the Li sublattice. Local Sensitive Hashing (LSH) is employed for fast approximate similarity searches, reducing pairwise comparison from O(N^2) to O(N). Symmetry validation is performed against the Atomic Simulation Environment (ASE) python package for the 13:43 and 12:44 ratios. The method identifies that only approximately 1% of structures are symmetrically unique, reducing the count by a factor of approximately 100. The final configuration space is reduced to around 2 × 10^6 unique structures. Energetic ordering uses two subsets for DFT: 200 energetically lowest structures (COMPASSIII) and 1000 random structures for coverage. A total of 1235 single-point DFT calculations were performed to train the MLR model.

Procedures And Architectures
All DFT calculations are performed with ONETEP using the PBE GGA exchange correlation functional. The kinetic energy cutoff is 830 eV, with pseudopotentials generated on-the-fly by CASTEP. The computational cost scales linearly with the number of atoms in ONETEP. For the force field ordering, COMPASSIII was applied to the Li-sublattice alone. COMPASSIII achieved a correlation coefficient of 0.991 for the 13:43 ratio. The Li-Li interaction descriptor for the MLR is a frequency occurrence list of all possible Li-Li interactions, a reformulation of the connectivity matrix. The data is split into training and test sets with a 1:3 ratio for MLR validation. The MLR model achieves a correlation of 0.9996 on the test set. Geometry optimizations are performed using the BFGS algorithm with site-hopping defined by frequency: 96h to 96h, 96h to 48g, and 96h to 24d. For the Li-dimer reference, 30 single-point calculations are performed in a large unit cell with a 3rd-order polynomial fit. The Li-dimer energy minimum is found at approximately 2.7 Å, with a large penalty at 1.7 Å.

Key Results
All structures fall within a range of 5.8 eV of the lowest-energy structure. 19 out of the 20 lowest-energy structures have an 8:48 24d:96h ratio. The 19th lowest energy structure has a 9:47 ratio. The average energy for all structures occurs at 1.47 eV higher than the ground-state structures. Four structures (all 8:48) are within 0.026 eV of the lowest-energy structure. All four lowest structures have the same 24d configuration with only slight 96h variations. The absolute lowest energy structure arises from a 96h-to-24d transition, yielding a 10:46 ratio. This structure is 0.58 eV lower in energy than the optimized lowest-energy single-point structure. There is a negative correlation between mean Li atom movement and final energy, indicating movement from original sites lowers energy. There is a weaker negative correlation between distance to a crystallographic site and energy, suggesting movement to other sites is not necessary. Including symmetry in the MLR model made a negligible difference to overall results. The largest energy difference between 24d:96h ratios in COMPASSIII was more pronounced than in ONETEP.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The finding that 19/20 lowest structures share the 8:48 ratio strongly suggests this is the preferred occupancy under the geometric constraint. The 96h-to-24d transition as the absolute lowest-energy pathway implies that site-hopping beyond the initially predicted 24d sites is energetically favorable. The negative correlation between atom movement and energy suggests that strain relief through Li displacement is a major driver of stability. The workflow demonstrates that many previously reported structures may violate fundamental geometric constraints and are thus physically unfeasible. The methodology is generalizable to other ion conductors and partially occupied crystals. The 0.58 eV difference from the single-point lowest structure highlights the importance of geometry relaxation in final energy ranking.

Contradictions And Limitations
The workflow does not include entropic contributions, which may affect the true ground-state identification. The assumption that geometry relaxation retains the ordering produced by the MLR model was tested only on 20 structures. A large-scale energy prediction of geometry-optimized structures falls outside the scope of this communication. COMPASSIII predicted a more pronounced energy separation by ratio than ONETEP, raising questions about force-field reliability for final ranking. The MLR model assumes that La-Zr interactions remain unchanged, which may not hold for all configurations. The LSH symmetry check is limited to monoatomic sublattices with predefined positions. The method assumes a reasonable retention of ordering upon geometry relaxation, which is an approximation.

Claims
A large portion of previously reported experimental and theoretical c-LLZO structures may be physically unfeasible under basic geometric constraints. The 1.7 Å cutoff eliminates overlapping Li pairs, which is less than 2 times the ionic radius and smaller than the minimum in t-LLZO. The geometric constraints immediately limit the possible 24d:96h ratios, making certain reported occupancies impossible. Table S1 and S2 summarize experimental and theoretical works with inconsistent occupancies that may violate the constraints. Some structures with odd-numbered 24d occupancies have high symmetry, suggesting they might be attainable despite the constraints. Researchers should validate reported occupancies against geometric feasibility before using them as basis for further calculations. The methodology can be extended to other partially occupied crystals to identify unfeasible structures.
The ground-state Li occupancy of c-LLZO is most likely represented by an 8:48 (or 10:46 after optimization) 24d:96h ratio under the prescribed geometric constraint. 19 of the 20 lowest-energy structures share the 8:48 ratio. The 10:46 structure (via 96h-to-24d transition) is the absolute lowest in energy. The average energy increases with 24d occupancy, indicating a preference to avoid over-occupation. The 19th structure breaks the pattern with a 9:47 ratio, suggesting the 8:48 preference is strong but not absolute. Entropic contributions and large-scale geometry relaxation were not fully addressed. Future c-LLZO research should center on structures near the 8:48 occupancy for maximum thermodynamic relevance.

Data And Code Availability
All structures generated in this work are provided in a freely accessible database to improve accuracy and reproducibility. Symmetry-checking scripts are provided in the supporting information.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Symmetry checking was validated against ASE for the 12:44 and 13:43 ratios, yielding identical structure counts. Geometry optimization was tested on 20 structures to assess effect on ordering; none of the site changes correlated significantly with optimized energy. Including symmetry in the MLR model made a negligible difference to overall results. A 1235 single-point DFT calculations were split with 1:3 train/test for MLR, achieving 0.9996 correlation. COMPASSIII was tested on both 13:43 and a wider range, showing good intra-ratio ordering but exaggerated ratio-separation compared to ONETEP.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1: Shows the Li-Li interaction constraints, the 24d and 96h site geometries, and the red-shaded region of impossible 24d:96h ratios. Figure 2b: Displays the energy ranking of structures, highlighting that 19/20 lowest are 8:48 with the 19th being 9:47. Figure 3: Illustrates the workflow for finding the four final structures from given occupancies. Figure S3: Compares 1235 relative DFT energies to COMPASSIII, showing COMPASSIII overestimates ratio-energy differences. Figure S4: Shows the Li-dimer energy vs. distance, justifying the 1.7 Å cutoff against the ~2.7 Å minimum. Figure S5: Plots MLR energies against space-group order, showing no meaningful correlation. Table 1: Lists the number of structures for each 24d:96h ratio after symmetry reduction. Table S1: Summarizes all experimental papers reporting 24d and 96h occupancies. Table S2: Summarizes all theoretical studies reporting 24d:96h ratios.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a general workflow that eliminates physically unfeasible crystal structures via geometric constraints, reduces the configuration space using LSH symmetry detection, and energetically orders the remainder with DFT-trained MLR. 2. The strongest evidence is the 0.9996 correlation of the MLR model and the observation that 19/20 lowest-energy structures share the 8:48 ratio, identifying a clear energetic preference for this occupancy. 3. The future path involves extending the workflow to other ion conductors, incorporating entropic effects, and performing large-scale geometry relaxation on the entire ensemble of feasible structures.

summary.title: Self-assembling materials mimicking dynamic bio-interfaces in cellular activities
summary.authors: Noriyuki Uchida (Tokyo University of Agriculture and Technology); Takahiro Muraoka (Tokyo University of Agriculture and Technology)
summary.field_subfield: Supramolecular Chemistry / Biomaterials / Regenerative Medicine
summary.executive_summary: This Feature Article highlights recent advances in bioinspired supramolecular materials designed to mimic dynamic bio-interfaces essential for cellular activities such as adhesion, signal transduction, and substance transportation.
