judge_context:
Executive Summary
This Feature Article highlights recent advances in bioinspired supramolecular materials designed to mimic dynamic bio-interfaces essential for cellular activities such as adhesion, signal transduction, and substance transportation. The extracellular matrix (ECM), phospholipid bilayers, and membrane-embedded proteins are identified as key bio-interface components. The authors review several distinct material strategies: (1) Stiffness-controlled RADA-based peptide hydrogels (A16G and A16G-Ncad) that mimic ECM scaffold cells to promote neuronal migration in injured neonatal neocortex; (2) JigSAP peptide fibers with jigsaw-shaped hydrophobic surfaces that incorporate and sustained-release VEGF at 39 mol% over 168 hours, promoting angiogenesis in ischaemic stroke models; (3) Redox-responsive JigSAP-IMI and JigSAP-MII variants that undergo gel-sol transition upon H2O2 exposure; (4) DPPC/Chol-MBP/Cu phospholipid nanosheets stabilized by Cu2+-crosslinked peptide surfactants enabling extended blood circulation; and (5) GUVs functionalized with the photoresponsive molecular machine AzoMEx that induce endocytosis-like outside-in membrane fission for efficient encapsulation (22.6 × 10^11 virions/mL) and in vivo delivery of M13 phage viruses to multiple organs while retaining infectivity. Collectively, these supramolecular approaches demonstrate how bottom-up design of dynamic, stimuli-responsive materials can reconstruct biomimetic interfaces for regenerative medicine and drug delivery.

Research Context
Various cellular functions such as adhesion, signal transduction, and substance transportation occur through the dynamic actions of biomacromolecules and supramolecular assemblies at bio-interfaces. The extracellular matrix (ECM), a complex network of proteins, is one such bio-interface that adheres to membrane protein receptors and regulates migration. Phospholipid bilayers, the major component of cellular and organelle membranes, contribute to substance transportation via exocytosis and endocytosis. Despite these established biological mechanisms, a molecular approach enabling endocytosis-like transport where membrane deformation is synchronized with substance transport remains critically unexplored.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question addressed is how supramolecular materials can be engineered to mimic the dynamic actions seen at bio-interfaces to develop biomaterials applicable to regenerative medicine and drug delivery. It is hypothesized that self-assembling peptide fibers can reconstruct artificial ECMs by mimicking the structure and dynamic function of intrinsic scaffold cells. A second hypothesis posits that peptide-based materials with jigsaw-shaped hydrophobic surfaces can resolve the incompatibility between incorporating and releasing secreted proteins. A third hypothesis is that phospholipid nanosheets stabilized by peptide surfactants can achieve extended blood circulation relative to spherical vesicles. Finally, it is hypothesized that a photo-responsive molecular machine can induce endocytosis-like outside-in membrane fission for efficient encapsulation of large biomacromolecules.

Methodological Details
RADA-based peptides (repeating RADA16 sequences) form supramolecular nanofibres through β-sheet-type hydrogen bonding and hydrophobic interaction. The A16G mutant (terminal alanine replaced with glycine) was compared to RADA16 using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) for morphological characterization and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. For the neuronal migration assay, neonatal neocortex was injured at low temperature and hydrogels were injected at the site of injury. The JigSAP peptide (Ac-RIDARMRADIR-NH2) was dispersed in Dulbecco's modified Eagle's medium (DMEM) at 1 wt% for CD spectroscopic analysis. Incorporation efficiency was measured for EGFP-JigSAP, EGFP-5V, and EGFP-RADA16 covalently conjugated to their respective peptide fibers. For the stroke model, 1.0 wt% JigSAP or 1.6 ng VEGF-JigSAP was injected into a distal middle cerebral artery occlusion model in mice. Phospholipid nanosheets were prepared by mixing DPPC with Chol-MBP at a ratio of 5/1 (5.0 wt% total) and diluted to 0.2 wt% for stability tests. For blood circulation, Cy5-labeled DPPC vesicles and nanosheets were administered to mice via tail vein injection at 5.0 wt% total content. For the endocytosis assay, GUVs were prepared with [DOPC] = 180 µM and [AzoMEx] = 20 µM, and M13 phage was added at 22.6 × 10^11 virions/mL. M13 phageCy5 was coated with a block polymer of poly(aspartic acid) and poly(ethylene glycol) for blood administration.

Procedures And Architectures
A16G peptide fibers form a more robust hydrogel than RADA16, with A16G-Ncad-tagged hydrogels demonstrating lower stiffness and thixotropic properties for injection. JigSAP self-assembly in DMEM over 100 hours transitions from helical/coil forms to β-sheet, forming nanofibres with average width 3.2 nm and length several µm. The JigSAP hydrogel exhibits a remarkably high rigidity of 1.1 × 10^4 Pa with a strain-thinning rheological profile typical of covalently polymerized materials. Chol-MBP, a cholic acid derivative conjugated to PHGGGPHGG (Cu2+-binding motif), self-assembles at the DPPC membrane edge when crosslinked by 2.0 equivalents of Cu2+. The AzoMEx molecular machine contains a diazocine core that undergoes photoisomerization to change the distance between two cationic NMe3+ moieties. The GUV/AzoMEx system operates by light-triggered expansion of the liposomal membrane, inducing outside-in fission synchronized with substance transport. JigSAP-IMI and JigSAP-MII variants use methionine (Met) in different positions to control gel-sol transition kinetics under redox activation by 30% H2O2 aq.

Key Results
Time-lapse imaging showed neuroblast migration rate was significantly higher on A16G-Ncad hydrogels than on A16G alone. In vivo, Dcx+ neuroblasts were abundantly observed in the A16G/A16G-Ncad mixture hydrogel at the injured site, whereas they were sparse in A16G alone or A16G/Ncad mixtures. EGFP-JigSAP was incorporated at 93 mol%, significantly higher than non-tagged EGFP (3 mol%), EGFP-5V (66 mol%), and EGFP-RADA16 (55 mol%). JigSAP exhibited superior long-term release: 21 mol% of EGFP-JigSAP was released after 24 hours at 37 °C, increasing to 39 mol% after 168 hours. In contrast, EGFP-5V and EGFP-RADA16 release stagnated after 48 hours, with only 5 mol% and 8 mol%, respectively, released after 168 hours. VEGF-JigSAP and JigSAP peptide treatment increased the number of double-positive laminin/EdU cells in the ischaemic stroke injured area, promoting angiogenesis. Upon dilution to 0.2 wt%, DPPC/Chol-MBP nanosheets formed spherical aggregates <100 nm without Cu2+, but maintained nanosheet structure with 2.0 equivalents of Cu2+. FL DPPC vesicles aggregated and clogged in blood vessels, whereas FL DPPC/Chol-MBP/Cu nanosheets were homogeneously dispersed, demonstrating prolonged circulation. M13 phages accumulated in the deforming membrane area during outside-in fission and were efficiently incorporated into GUVDOPC/AzoMEx. M13 phageCy5 showed higher stability in blood than bare M13 phageCy5 over 15 minutes of blood circulation. After distribution to organs, M13 phage infectivity was retained: spleen (25.6 ± 13.2 × 10^9 virions/mg), liver (18.3 ± 3.2 × 10^9 virions/mg), kidney (1.3 ± 0.6 × 10^9 virions/mg), heart (1.1 ± 0.5 × 10^9 virions/mg), lung (0.5 ± 0.3 × 10^9 virions/mg), brain (0.2 ± 0.1 × 10^9 virions/mg).

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The fibrous self-assembly of A16G and A16G-Ncad mimics both the structure and dynamic function of intrinsic scaffold cells, providing a novel strategy for neuro-regenerative therapy. The strain-thinning rheological profile of JigSAP indicates that the supramolecular nanofibres form a robust, interconnected network comparable to covalently polymerized materials. Cu2+-mediated crosslinking of Chol-MBP at the membrane edge inhibits dissociation of phospholipid nanosheets, providing a biomimetic surfactant strategy for stable bicelle formation. The AzoMEx system demonstrates that membrane deformation can be mechanically coupled to substance transport, mimicking natural endocytosis and phagocytosis. The retention of M13 phage infectivity across all organs after blood administration suggests the GUVDOPC/AzoMEx-pAsp platform can protect biomacromolecules from the immune system and physiological degradation.

Contradictions And Limitations
The paper is a Feature Article reviewing recent studies rather than a primary empirical study, so it reports outcomes of multiple independent research groups without unified statistical comparison. The JigSAP hydrogel exhibits strain thinning, which the authors note is typically observed in covalently polymerized materials, implying a distinct rheological behavior compared to the entangled fibril hydrogels of RADA16. The A16G hydrogel forms bundled nanofibres and a more robust gel than RADA16 despite its enhanced conformational flexibility, a counterintuitive result that the authors attribute to fibre morphology rather than chain flexibility. For the endocytosis assay, the authors note that the AzoMEx-GUV technology could be applied to in vivo phage display, but no actual in vivo selection experiment is reported. Specific quantitative thresholds for 'higher' migration rates in A16G-Ncad versus A16G alone are described qualitatively as 'significantly higher' without a precise numerical ratio. The paper does not report exact p-values, confidence intervals, or specific n numbers for the in vivo experiments, limiting quantitative reproducibility.

Claims
Stiffness-controlled A16G peptide hydrogels conjugated with N-cadherin mimic ECM scaffold cells to promote neuroblast migration in injured neonatal neocortex. A16G-Ncad hydrogels showed significantly higher neuroblast migration rates than A16G alone in time-lapse imaging. Dcx+ neuroblasts were abundantly observed in the A16G/A16G-Ncad mixture in vivo but sparse in A16G alone or A16G/Ncad. A16G-Ncad demonstrates lower stiffness and thixotropic properties suitable for injection. The paper describes the in vivo result as a qualitative observation of abundance versus sparsity without quantitative migration velocity measurements. Provides a novel strategy for neuro-regenerative therapy using self-assembling biomaterials.
JigSAP peptides with jigsaw-shaped hydrophobic surfaces enable efficient incorporation and sustained release of full-length proteins for tissue regeneration. EGFP-JigSAP was incorporated at 93 mol% versus 3 mol% for untagged EGFP. 39 mol% of EGFP-JigSAP was released after 168 hours, compared to only 5 mol% for EGFP-5V and 8 mol% for EGFP-RADA16. VEGF-JigSAP increased laminin/EdU double-positive cells in the ischaemic stroke injured area. Release of EGFP-5V and EGFP-RADA16 stagnated after 48 hours, reaching only 5 and 8 mol% at 168 hours. The incorporation/releasing property demonstrates wide applicability to controlled sustained release of various full-length growth factors.
Cu2+-stabilized DPPC/Chol-MBP phospholipid nanosheets achieve extended blood circulation compared to spherical DPPC vesicles. Nanosheets maintained structure upon 0.2 wt% dilution with 2.0 equivalents of Cu2+ but formed spherical aggregates <100 nm without Cu2+. IV-CLSM showed FL DPPC vesicles aggregated and clogged, while nanosheets were homogeneously dispersed in blood vessels.  Demonstrates a suitable carrier for whole-body blood administration.
The AzoMEx-GUV system induces endocytosis-like outside-in membrane fission for efficient encapsulation and in vivo delivery of M13 phage viruses. M13 phages were efficiently incorporated into GUVDOPC/AzoMEx at 22.6 × 10^11 virions/mL. M13 phageCy5 showed higher stability in blood over 15 minutes compared to bare M13 phageCy5. Phage infectivity was retained across all organs (spleen: 25.6, liver: 18.3, kidney: 1.3, heart: 1.1, lung: 0.5, brain: 0.2 × 10^9 virions/mg).  Could be applied to an in vivo phage display method for selection of peptides binding to ligands in living bodies.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The JigSAP release assay compared three different peptide-tagged EGFP variants (JigSAP, 5V, RADA16) against untagged EGFP as internal controls. The blood circulation assay compared FL DPPC vesicles against FL DPPC/Chol-MBP/Cu nanosheets at the same 5.0 wt% content. The endocytosis assay compared encapsulated M13 phageCy5 against bare M13 phageCy5 with the same block polymer coating. The stroke model included PBS control, 1.0 wt% JigSAP, VEGF+JigSAP (non-tagged), and VEGF-JigSAP+JigSAP (tagged) for comprehensive comparison.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1: Schematic of cellular activities at bio-interfaces (adhesion, signal transduction, substance transportation). Figure 2: TEM and MD simulation images of A16G, RADA16, and A16G-Ncad fibres showing bundled, curved, and standard morphologies. Figure 3: Time-lapse images and in vivo neuroblast migration (Dcx+ marker) in injured neonatal neocortex. Figure 4: CD spectra, rheology, incorporation efficiency, release profiles, and stroke model histology for JigSAP-VEGF systems. Figure 5: Redox-responsive gel-sol transition of JigSAP-IMI and JigSAP-MII with H2O2. Figure 6: TEM of DPPC/Chol-MBP/Cu nanosheets under dilution, IV-CLSM blood circulation in mice. Figure 7: AzoMEx structure, GUV membrane deformation, phage encapsulation, blood circulation, and organ infectivity assays.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the development of multiple supramolecular platforms (peptide hydrogels, jigsaw-shaped fibers, Cu2+-crosslinked nanodisks, photoresponsive molecular machines) that each solve a specific bio-interface engineering challenge: ECM reconstruction, protein incorporation/release, lipid bilayer stabilization, and endocytosis-like fission. 2. The strongest evidence is the in vivo demonstration of M13 phage infectivity retention across all major organs (from 25.6 × 10^9 in spleen to 0.2 × 10^9 in brain) and the 39 mol% sustained release of EGFP-JigSAP over 168 hours, quantifying the functional viability of the biomimetic approach. 3. The future path involves scaling these bottom-up methodologies toward in vivo phage display for peptide selection, extended blood-based drug delivery to the whole body, and translating the endocytosis-like fission machine to delivery of larger biomacromolecules for clinical regenerative medicine.

summary.title: GUIDEMOL: a Python graphical user interface for molecular descriptors based on RDKit
summary.authors: Joao Aires (NOVA School of Science and Technology)
summary.field_subfield: Chemoinformatics / Computational Chemistry
summary.executive_summary: GUIDEMOL is a Python-based graphical user interface (GUI) application developed to provide accessible computing of molecular descriptors and 3D grid representations of molecular structures. Built upon the RDKit software library, GUIDEMOL targets chemoinformatics users, scientists, and students who possess varying levels of computer and programming skills. The application leverages the tkinter package—the standard Python interface to the Tcl/Tk GUI toolkit—to present a minimalist interface for routine chemoinformatics tasks. Key functionality includes: (1) calculation of molecular descriptors implemented in RDKit, such as RDF, MORSE, WHIM, AUTOCORR3D, GETAWAY, PEOE_VSA, and SMR_VSA; (2) generation of 3D molecular structures from SMILES using the MMFF94 force field with MMFFOptimizeMolecule; and (3) computation of 3D grid representations based on either electrostatic potential (EP) using Gasteiger or MMFF partial charges, or voxel encoding of atomic properties (atomic number, partial charge, molecular refractivity contributions, or logP contributions). The GUI incorporates various tkinter widgets (buttons, checkbuttons, radiobuttons, entries, labels, scrollbar) and uses the filedialog module for native file/directory selection. For users requiring automation or integration into pipelines, a command-line interface (CLI) is also provided for grid calculations. The source code is openly available under the three-clause BSD license, enabling commercial and non-commercial use. A noteworthy technical observation is that certain 3D descriptors (GETAWAY, MORSE, WHIM) exhibited non-deterministic behavior, producing different values across runs or operating systems within the same RDKit version (2022.9.5), exemplified by the structure generated for COc1ccc(cc1(OC))Br.

claims.description: GUIDEMOL provides an easy access to RDKit tools for chemoinformatics users with no programming skills.
The source code is openly available for extension and deployment of other molecular descriptors.

top_influential_citations.RDKit (13): The RDKit software provides the foundational chemoinformatics library upon which GUIDEMOL is built for all descriptor and grid computations.

top_influential_citations.tkinter (16): The tkinter package provides the standard GUI toolkit enabling the construction of the user interface within the Python environment.

top_influential_citations.Shi and Borchardt JRgui (17): The JRgui application established the precedent of combining RDKit with tkinter for a descriptor calculation GUI.

top_influential_citations.Wildman-Crippen (24): The Wildman-Crippen approach provides the theoretical basis for calculating atomic contributions to logP used in the voxel grid representation.

top_influential_citations.QSPR/QSAR methodology reference (1): The QSPR/QSAR methodology reference frames the application within its core scientific context for molecular property prediction.

Research Context
Molecular descriptors are central to QSPR/QSAR methodology used by diverse scientists with varying computer skills. Chemoinformatics is permeating chemistry, biology, and material science curricula, necessitating teaching software. Several existing programs calculate molecular descriptors on different platforms, including CDK, PaDEL, BlueDesc, OCHEM, and ChemDes. Proprietary options exist such as MOE, VolSurf+, CORINA Symphony, ChemAxon Calculator Plugins, and alvaDesc. Python's RDKit has implemented a wide range of chemoinformatics tools, including molecular descriptors and machine learning projects. The Mordred Python package provides command-line or web-based descriptor calculation with RDKit wrappers. Python's tkinter enables easy GUI development as the standard interface to Tcl/Tk, bundled with Python. JRgui previously combined RDKit and tkinter for Joback and Reid group contribution descriptor calculation. 3D grid representations of molecules (voxels, electrostatic potentials) have gained attention for deep learning neural networks. Direct 3D representations can be used for pre-aligned structures or processed by convolutional neural networks.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central objective is to provide a GUI for calculating molecular descriptors and 3D grid representations accessible to users without programming skills. GUIDEMOL is presented as a minimalist interface to routine chemoinformatics tasks and well-established descriptors. The application is designed to be adapted to calculate other descriptors or trigger other procedures. A CLI is additionally provided specifically for the calculation of grid representations. The application aims to facilitate 3D grid calculation with user-specified parameters for electrostatic potential and voxel encoding. The 3D grid representations are motivated by recent interest in complex artificial intelligence algorithms processing larger data sets.

Methodological Details
The application is a Python computer program based on the RDKit software. The GUI is built using the tkinter package. The interface employs the grid geometry manager for widget layout. Widgets include buttons for calculation triggering, checkbuttons for YES/NO options, radiobuttons for mutually exclusive choices, entries for numeric submission, labels, and scrollbar. Native look-and-feel dialog windows for file/directory selection are implemented via the tkinter.filedialog module. A log file is created in the same directory to register successful processing and failures. The source code is available under the three-clause BSD license. The input molecules are processed from SMILES strings or name-labeled input files. The molecular descriptors are saved in a csv output file. The RDKit version used is 2022.9.5.

Procedures And Architectures
3D molecular models are obtained via the RDKit function MMFFOptimizeMolecule with mmffVariant='MMFF94' and maxIters=5000. Pre-generation options include removing metals via MetalDisconnector, keeping the largest fragment with LargestFragmentChooser(preferOrganic=True), or neutralizing with Uncharger. Hydrogen atoms are added with Chem.AddHs(). For 3D coordinate updates, AddHs() uses addCoords=True to retain original atom positions. The interface enables selection of RDKit rdMolDescriptors 3D descriptors: RDF, MORSE, WHIM, AUTOCORR3D, GETAWAY, PEOE_VSA, and SMR_VSA. The exact molecular weight can also be selected. The grid of electrostatic potential is generated using Gasteiger or MMFF partial atomic charges from AllChem.ComputeGasteigerCharges() or GetMMFFPartialCharge(). The EP at each cube c is computed as sum of qi times ric over all atoms N excluding those within 1 Å of cube center or beyond user-defined cutoff. Voxelisation is calculated in a user-defined 3D grid based on atomic number, partial charge, molecular refractivity (Wildman-Crippen), or logP contributions. The voxel value VoxG c is sum of pi times exponential of distance squared over sigma squared. A CLI for grid calculation takes input file, output file, grid type (pot, vox), atomic property, grid center coordinates, cube size, cutoff or sigma value, and grid extent.

Key Results
The GUI allows selection and calculation of seven specific 3D descriptors from the rdMolDescriptors module. EP grids are calculated using Gasteiger or MMFF charges with user-defined center coordinates, side size in Angstrom, cube size, and cutoff distance. Voxel grids implement atomic number, partial charge (Gasteiger/MMFF), refractivity contributions, and logP contributions from Wildman-Crippen. A non-deterministic observation: different values were obtained for some molecules with same RDKit version in different runs or operating systems. The affected descriptors include GETAWAY, MORSE, and WHIM. The example of non-determinism was with the 3D structure generated for COc1ccc(cc1(OC))Br. The CLI example demonstrates calculation of an EP grid: input.sdf, Gasteiger charges, center (0,0,0), side 5 Å, resolution 0.5 Å, cutoff 3 Å, grid size 5x5x5.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The application lowers the barrier for chemoinformatics software adoption among non-programmers, particularly in educational and applied QSPR settings. Direct 3D grid representations align with recent trends in deep learning applications for molecular structure analysis. The modular design as a template for other GUI tools facilitates extensible development in chemoinformatics. The EP calculation formulation explicitly accounts for geometry and atomic contribution weights, connecting 3D structural features to physicochemical properties.

Contradictions And Limitations
The paper reports non-deterministic results for GETAWAY, MORSE, and WHIM descriptors within the same RDKit version across runs/OS. This observation indicates that reproducibility of these specific 3D descriptors is not guaranteed by RDKit alone. The source does not report on the accuracy, validation, or reproducibility of the generated structures and descriptors. The application is described as a minimalist interface and a software note; no benchmark studies or validation datasets are reported. The paper does not report on computational performance, execution time, or memory usage for different input sizes.

Claims
GUIDEMOL provides an easy access to RDKit tools for chemoinformatics users with no programming skills. The application targets users with varying levels of computer skills. It uses tkinter, the standard Python interface, for the GUI. The paper does not report on user testing, feasibility studies, or user surveys to verify ease of use. Democratizes access to molecular descriptor computation for scientists in chemistry, biology, and material science.
The source code is openly available for extension and deployment of other molecular descriptors. The source code is released under the three-clause BSD license. The license allows both commercial and non-commercial use. It can be very easily extended for other molecular descriptors.  The open nature enables community contributions and serves as a template for other GUI developments.

Data And Code Availability
The source code is available at https://github.com/jairesdesousa/guidemol under the three-clause BSD license.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The paper reports a reproducibility issue where GETAWAY, MORSE, and WHIM descriptors yielded different values with the same RDKit version in different runs or operating systems. The example molecule for this non-deterministic behavior was COc1ccc(cc1(OC))Br.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the GUIDEMOL interface layout with tkinter widgets.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a Python/tkinter GUI that exposes RDKit's molecular descriptor and 3D grid calculation capabilities to non-programmers. 2. The strongest evidence is the open availability of the source code under BSD license and the dual GUI/CLI access to the same grid calculation routines. 3. The future path involves extending the minimalist interface template to other chemoinformatics tasks and resolving the reported non-deterministic behavior in certain RDKit descriptors.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper reports the design and synthesis of the first single-domain protein catenane, specifically a dihydrofolate reductase (cat-DHFR), in which two mechanically interlocked polypeptide rings fold synergistically into a compact integrated structure. The approach diverges from conventional artificial topological protein synthesis, which typically requires exogenous entangling motifs, by exploiting the spatially entangled relationships inherent in the wild-type DHFR fold. The design was achieved by virtually cleaving the wild-type DHFR (PDB: 4KJJ) at residues 88–89 (between α-helix-C and β-sheet-5), identifying a Gaussian linking number (GLN) of +0.726 as the highest entanglement potential, and rewiring the loop region to create two intertwined segments that reconstitute into a catenane with GLN +1.120 upon cyclization. Synthesis was accomplished in E. coli BL21(DE3) using two pairs of mutually orthogonal split-intein pairs, circular permutation to place cyclization sites on opposite sides of the fold (residues 23 and 24), and a streamlined post-translational processing pipeline without in vitro reactions. The P-2 molecule was characterized by LC-MS, SDS-PAGE, SEC, far-UV and near-UV CD spectroscopy, and ion mobility mass spectrometry. Cat-DHFR retains catalytic activity (approx. 5 U/mg) comparable to the linear control (14 U/mg), and while its K<sub>m</sub> and k<sub>cat</sub> are compromised (K<sub>m</sub> ~5-fold; k<sub>cat</sub> ~38% of l-DHFR), the protein exhibits enhanced stability against chemical denaturation (87% activity in 5% DMSO vs. 74% for l-DHFR), and the topology is confirmed via TEV protease cleavage and IMS-MS/CID analysis. The study establishes a new design paradigm where linear proteins can be converted into concatenated single-domain counterparts with conserved function and elevated stability.

Research Context
Natural protein domains fold autonomously and can exist independently, yet their linear backbone limits topological diversity. The discovery of natural topological proteins suggests that unconventional chemical topology may enhance protein stability relative to linear counterparts. Artificial topological proteins have been synthesized including star, cyclic, lasso, and catenane forms, mostly using multiple domains. Multi-domain topological proteins complicate the study of topological effects on structure-property relationships. Single-domain topological proteins would exhibit the most profound impact of chemical topology and provide an unusual scaffold for further engineering. Previous topological designs required exogenous entangling motifs as templates, and no single-domain catenane or Hopf link had been prepared. The authors previously reported mutually orthogonal split-intein ligation for protein heterocatenane synthesis. The gap identified is that the need for exogenous templates may be eliminated by exploiting spatially entangled relationships among secondary structures.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether a single-domain protein can be converted into a catenane topology without collapsing the fold, while preserving function and enhancing properties. The hypothesis is that exploiting the spatially entangled relationships among secondary structures and introducing artificial entanglement via rewiring can design a single-domain catenane with identical composition to the wild-type. The specific model selected is Escherichia coli dihydrofolate reductase, which catalyzes the reduction of DHF to THF in the presence of NADPH. The authors predict that a design with the highest Gaussian linking number at the cleavage site will possess the potential entangling core. A successful design should ensure the entangled conformation, high reconstitution efficiency, and preservation of the active site. It was hypothesized that cat-DHFR would retain a significant portion of catalytic activity compared to previously reported rethreaded or split DHFR variants. The predicted outcome is a molecule with well-preserved function and elevated stability due to conformational restriction.

Methodological Details
The virtual design was based on the wild-type DHFR structure from PDB: 4KJJ. The backbone was virtually cleaved at all unstructured loops to generate split segments. The extent of intertwinement was quantified using the Gaussian linking number (GLN) matrix of the split segments. The cleavage site between α-helix-C and β-sheet-5 (residues 88 and 89) yielded the largest GLN of +0.726. Ring I consists of residues 1-88 and Ring II of residues 89-159. The resulting cat-DHFR had a GLN of +1.120. The synthetic strategy employed two pairs of mutually orthogonal split-intein pairs for ring closure. Ring I was circularly permutated to generate new termini between residues 23 and 24. Rewired loops were designed to be 16 residues long to bridge the split structural motifs. The gene cassette included two DHFR segments as the entangled template, two split-intein pairs, and a TEV protease recognition sequence. A linear DHFR control (l-DHFR) with identical amino acid composition was designed as a comparator. Genes were synthesized and sub-cloned to pMCSG19 and pET21a vectors. Expression was carried out in E. coli BL21(DE3) competent cells at 16°C for 20 h. Proteins were purified under native conditions using Ni-NTA affinity chromatography followed by size exclusion chromatography (SEC). Purification was confirmed by SDS-PAGE showing a ~22 kDa band for l-DHFR and a <20 kDa major band for cat-DHFR. Identities were confirmed by accurate molecular weights in LC-MS spectra. Far-UV and near-UV CD spectra were collected for secondary and tertiary structure assessment. Ion mobility spectrometry coupled with collision-induced dissociation mass spectrometry was used for topological proof. Enzymatic activity was assayed by monitoring absorbance at 340 nm at 25°C with DHF and NADPH. Kinetic parameters were determined by fitting Michaelis curves and Hanes-Woolf plots. Binding affinities were measured using isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC). Organic solvent tolerance was tested by adding 5% DMSO.

Procedures And Architectures
The retrosynthetic analysis determined that ring I required circular permutation to place the cyclization motifs on the opposite side of DHFR. The site between residues 23 and 24 was selected as the most efficient ring closure position. Two pairs of mutually orthogonal split-intein pairs were used; specific sequence elements were embedded for purification and proof of topology. The TEV protease recognition sequence was programmed into the first ring for subsequent proteolytic digestion experiment. L2 of ring II was tested with different sequences and lengths to probe linker effects. At the shortest linker length, yield dropped to about one-fifth (~12 mg/L of culture). Cell lysis was performed, and proteins were purified under native conditions using Ni-NTA affinity chromatography. Eluted products underwent SEC for further purification. Far-UV CD revealed reduced intensities in positive ellipticity at ~200 nm and negative ellipticity between 210 nm and 230 nm. Near-UV CD showed positive ellipticity at ~290 nm, similar to the linear control. Proteolytic digestion was performed using TEV protease, converting cat-DHFR into a linear fragment and a cyclic fragment. IMS-MS and CID measurements were performed on both cat-DHFR and l-DHFR to characterize collision cross-section (CCS) values. Catalytic activity was monitored at 25°C by measuring the reduction of DHF to THF.

Key Results
The GLN of the split DHFR was +0.726 before cyclization, and the cat-DHFR yielded a GLN of +1.120. SDS-PAGE showed a single band at approximately 22 kDa for l-DHFR and a major band at less than 20 kDa for cat-DHFR. The SEC overlay showed cat-DHFR eluting at a broader peak with a slightly larger retention volume than l-DHFR. The cat-DHFR retained approximately 5 U/mg activity compared to 14 U/mg for the linear control (~35.7% relative). The K<sub>m</sub> of cat-DHFR was approximately 5-fold that of l-DHFR. The k<sub>cat</sub> of cat-DHFR was about 38% that of l-DHFR. The catalytic efficiency (k<sub>cat</sub>/K<sub>m</sub>) of cat-DHFR was reduced by an order of magnitude. ITC showed KD for DHF was ~173-fold larger and KD for NADPH was ~14-fold larger in cat-DHFR vs. l-DHFR. The KD between cat-DHFR and product THF was increased by ~3.6-fold. In 5% DMSO, cat-DHFR preserved 87% activity compared to 74% for l-DHFR. When the same-side cyclization site was attempted, only ~33% of the product was catenane form with significant single-ring side products. At the shortest linker, catenane yield was ~12 mg/L of culture. TEV cleavage converted cat-DHFR into a linear fragment and a cyclic fragment, confirmed by SDS-PAGE and LC-MS. Near-UV CD showed cat-DHFR had positive ellipticity at ~290 nm, similar to the linear control. The split between α-helix-C and β-sheet-5 produced a reconstituted complex retaining only 15% activity, highlighting the significance of cat-DHFR's ~36% retention. The rethreaded DHFR variant (reference 40) showed no reducing activity at all, contrasting with cat-DHFR's 5 U/mg.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The reduced activity of cat-DHFR (5 U/mg vs 14 U/mg) is attributed to compromised affinity towards substrate and cofactor, not the fold collapse. The 5-fold higher K<sub>m</sub> and 14-fold higher KD for NADPH suggest that the catenane topology slightly perturbs the substrate binding pocket without abolishing it. The enhanced stability in DMSO (87% vs 74%) suggests that mechanical interlocking increases thermal/chemical resilience by constraining conformational space. The fact that circular permutation alone causes activity decrease supports that structural rewiring affects function. The design principle of using the original fold as the entangling template expands the scope of topological protein engineering beyond exogenous motifs. The finding that linear proteins can be converted to single-domain catenanes with almost identical chemical composition opens a new horizon in protein science. The observation that the catenane topology itself reinforces the folded structure, as evidenced by CD and IMS data, links fold integrity to topology. The reduction in catalytic efficiency by an order of magnitude suggests a trade-off between topological design and enzyme kinetics.

Contradictions And Limitations
The authors were unable to obtain a crystal structure of cat-DHFR, preventing definitive atomic-resolution confirmation of topology. The GLN value of +1.120 for cat-DHFR is positive, confirming catenane but not the exact number of crossings. The activity of cat-DHFR is lower than l-DHFR, indicating that the design compromises enzyme efficiency. The SEC elution as a broader peak suggests a dynamic structure rather than a single static conformer. Some faint bands at lower molecular weights appear in SDS-PAGE, attributed to individual component rings, indicating incomplete cyclization. The reduced intensities in CD spectra suggest a loosening of secondary structure compared to l-DHFR. Circular permutation alone causes activity decrease, and the rethreaded variant has no activity, making it hard to isolate the topological contribution from sequence changes. The design required extensive optimization (circular permutation, linker length) to achieve high yield, limiting immediate generality.

Claims
A single-domain protein catenane of DHFR can be designed and synthesized by exploiting the spatially entangled relationships inherent in the wild-type fold without exogenous entangling motifs. The GLN of +1.120 confirmed intertwinement of the two rings. TEV cleavage produced a linear and cyclic fragment, confirming topological interlinking. The catenane retained ~36% activity, significantly more than rethreaded DHFR (0%) or split DHFR (15%). The design used the same-composition protein fragments as the entangled template. The same-side cyclization attempt produced only ~33% catenane, showing the design is sensitive to spatial arrangement. The activity is reduced relative to the linear control. No crystal structure was obtained, so the exact topology remains inferred. This expands protein topology beyond circular and knotted forms to mechanical interlinking within a single domain. The design principle enables conversion of any fold with high GLN potential into a catenane. The enhanced stability in DMSO suggests topological proteins are inherently more robust to denaturation.
The catenane topology enhances chemical stability of DHFR without abolishing catalytic function. In 5% DMSO, cat-DHFR retained 87% activity vs. 74% for l-DHFR. Cat-DHFR retained 5 U/mg activity, sufficient for catalytic monitoring. The CD spectra confirmed a folded structure remains intact. The K<sub>m</sub> increased 5-fold and k<sub>cat</sub> dropped to 38%, indicating kinetic impairment. Catalytic efficiency decreased by an order of magnitude. Mechanical interlocking offers a structural mechanism to increase enzyme robustness. This trade-off between stability and activity is common in protein engineering and may be optimized.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The same-side cyclization variant was tested and yielded only ~33% catenane, demonstrating the necessity of circular permutation to clear the cyclization site. Linker length was systematically varied; the shortest linker yielded ~12 mg/L, five-fold lower than the longest. The yield decreased with shorter linkers, with monocyclic by-products and oligomers increasing. The site between residues 23 and 24 was identified as the most efficient ring closure point among multiple candidates. The design was compared against a linear control with identical amino acid composition. Previous literature values for circular permutation of DHFR and rethreaded DHFR were used as benchmarks for activity comparison.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1: Schematic of cat-DHFR design, GLN analysis, and retrosynthetic cyclization strategy (panels a–d). Figure 1a and 1c: Sequence maps of the linear and catenane constructs with rewired loops and TEV site. Figure 1b: Gene cassette design showing two DHFR segments, split-inteins, and TEV site. Figure 2a: SDS-PAGE showing purified l-DHFR (~22 kDa) and cat-DHFR (<20 kDa) with faint lower bands. Figure 2b: SEC overlay showing cat-DHFR eluting as a broader peak at larger retention volume than l-DHFR. Figure 2c: LC-MS spectra confirming accurate molecular weights for both constructs. Figure 2d: Far-UV CD spectra showing reduced intensities at 200 nm and 210–230 nm for cat-DHFR. Figure 2e: SDS-PAGE and LC-MS spectra after TEV cleavage showing linear and cyclic fragments. Figure 4: Kinetic curves of DHFR activity monitored at 340 nm. Figure S1: GLN matrices for split DHFR showing the +0.726 cleavage site. Figure S1a and S1b: GLN values for split and catenane forms. Figure S2: Near-UV CD spectrum of cat-DHFR showing positive ellipticity at ~290 nm. Figure S3: Comparison of same-side vs. opposite-side cyclization sites. Figure S3b-d: Evaluation of different ring closure sites. Figure S4: Linker length effect on catenane yield. Table 1: Kinetic parameters (K<sub>m</sub>, k<sub>cat</sub>, K<sub>D</sub> values) for cat-DHFR and l-DHFR. Figure S7: Michaelis and Hanes-Woolf plots for kinetic determination. Figure S11: Activity in 5% DMSO for both variants.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first synthesis of a single-domain protein catenane, demonstrating that a wild-type fold can serve as its own entangled template through topological rewiring. 2. The strongest evidence is the combination of topological proof (TEV cleavage to linear/cyclic fragments; IMS-CID data), functional retention (~36% activity vs. 0% rethreaded), and increased chemical stability (87% vs. 74% in DMSO). 3. The future path involves directed evolution to restore catalytic efficiency to the linear control level and the design of additional single-domain topological proteins using different folds with high GLN potential.

summary.title: Non-idealities in CO2 electroreduction mechanisms revealed by automation-assisted kinetic analysis
summary.authors: Joy S Zeng, Vineet Padia, Joseph H Maalouf, Aditya M Limaye, Alexander H Liu, Michael A Yusov, Ian W Hunter, Karthish Manthiram
summary.field_subfield: Electrochemistry / Electrocatalysis
summary.executive_summary: This work addresses the limitation of traditional linearized kinetic analysis (Tafel and reactant order dependence) in electrocatalysis, which assumes simple rate equations can be decoupled and linearized on log-log plots—a strategy that fails when surface coverage effects, mixed rate control, or electrolyte poisoning are present. The authors introduce a robotic platform that automates the sequential testing of up to ten electrochemical cells, each with potentially different electrodes, electrolytes, gas-phase compositions, and voltages, enabling cohesive kinetic analysis over wide reaction condition ranges. The system was applied to CO2 electroreduction to CO at three immobilized metal tetrapyrroles: cobalt phthalocyanine (CoPc), cobalt tetraphenylporphyrin (CoTPP), and iron phthalocyanine (FePc). The cohesive kinetic analysis revealed that CoPc and CoTPP exhibit voltage-dependent bicarbonate inhibition: the apparent bicarbonate order is most negative at less reductive potentials and becomes positive at more reductive potentials, consistent with models of bicarbonate poisoning combined with potential-dependent mixed control. In contrast, FePc shows greater bicarbonate inhibition at more reductive potentials, a trend explained by a mechanism where the most abundant reactive intermediate precedes the unoccupied site, causing coverage of the poisoning species to increase despite the local poisoning equilibrium shift. CO2 order dependences were also non-ideal: CoPc showed near-ideal first-order dependence, CoTPP showed slightly sub-unity order decreasing at more reductive potentials (consistent with surface saturation), and FePc exhibited the most unusual behavior where voltage inhibited the reaction at low CO2 partial pressures, captured by a mixed-control model with an on-cycle poisoning species. These findings demonstrate that complex reaction mechanisms, not amenable to standard linearization, are prevalent across this class of electrocatalysts, and that automation provides a robust pathway to interrogate them.

claims.description: The robotic platform enables flexible and automated reaction rate data collection for electrocatalysis, overcoming the manual data-collection barriers of cohesive kinetic analysis.
Non-ideal mechanistic behaviors—bicarbonate poisoning, coverage effects, and mixed rate control—are prevalent across immobilized metal tetrapyrrole CO2RR catalysts.

The system was applied to CO2 electroreduction to CO at three immobilized metal tetrapyrroles: cobalt phthalocyanine (CoPc), cobalt tetraphenylporphyrin (CoTPP), and iron phthalocyanine (FePc). The cohesive kinetic analysis revealed that CoPc and CoTPP exhibit voltage-dependent bicarbonate inhibition: the apparent bicarbonate order is most negative at less reductive potentials and becomes positive at more reductive potentials, consistent with models of bicarbonate poisoning combined with potential-dependent mixed control. In contrast, FePc shows greater bicarbonate inhibition at more reductive potentials, a trend explained by a mechanism where the most abundant reactive intermediate precedes the unoccupied site, causing coverage of the poisoning species to increase despite the local poisoning equilibrium shift. These findings demonstrate that complex reaction mechanisms, not amenable to standard linearization, are prevalent across this class of electrocatalysts, and that automation provides a robust pathway to interrogate them.

Research Context
Reaction kinetics analysis in electrocatalysis has traditionally relied on interpretations of linearized rate data, assuming that dependences on voltage and concentration can be factored separately. This is the basis for typical Tafel and reactant order dependence analyses. However, linearization requires highly simplifying assumptions that are violated by coverage effects, mixed rate control, and side reactions. The substantial effect of voltage on reaction energy landscapes means surface coverages of reaction intermediates could drastically change within a few hundred millivolts. Cohesive kinetic analyses, more common in thermocatalysis, interrogate correlations using large volumes of data over wide reaction condition ranges and can be fit to complex rate equations. However, implementing cohesive kinetic analysis in electrocatalysis is hindered by heavy data requirements, entailing months of manual experimentation subject to human error. Existing automation strategies in electrocatalysis are primarily tailored towards high-throughput catalyst or condition screening, not kinetic analysis. Miniaturization strategies using microliter volumes cannot quantify products for reactions with incomplete Faradaic efficiency. Parallel strategies often require aggregated or manual product quantification rather than online detection of individual cells. A sequential electrochemical testing strategy with online product quantification in geometrically well-defined reactors is identified as ideal for automating kinetic analysis.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether cohesive kinetic analysis reveals mechanistic complexities in CO2 electroreduction to CO at immobilized metal tetrapyrroles that are missed by traditional Tafel and order dependence analyses. The authors hypothesize that non-idealities such as surface coverage effects, electrolyte poisoning, and potential-dependent mixed control will be evident across CoPc, CoTPP, and FePc. Specifically, they predict that bicarbonate and CO2 order dependencies will be non-linear and/or change with applied potential. They further hypothesize that these complex behaviors can be explained by models invoking bicarbonate poisoning, surface saturation, and on-cycle poisoning intermediates. The robotic platform is proposed to serve as a tool for accelerating and standardizing cohesive kinetic analysis workflows in electrocatalysis. A key hypothesis is that the mechanism of CO2RR at CoPc, CoTPP, and FePc remains a topic of debate despite their commonly studied status and well-defined active sites. They predict that CoPc and CoTPP will share a similar mechanism, while FePc will differ, reflecting different relative roles of catalytic intermediates.

Methodological Details
The robot automates sequential testing of up to ten electrochemical cells, each capable of having a different electrode, electrolyte, gas-phase reactant composition, and applied voltage. Three immobilized metal tetrapyrrole catalysts were tested: CoPc, CoTPP, and FePc. CoPc was dissolved in N,N-dimethylformamide and drop-casted onto calcined Toray060 carbon paper at 5.98 x 10^-11 mol/cm2 loadings. CoTPP and FePc were dissolved in carbon black-containing DMF and drop-casted at loadings of 5.11 x 10^-10 mol/cm2 and 8.04 x 10^-10 mol/cm2 respectively. Carbon black was added to CoTPP and FePc to increase loading while avoiding aggregation. Electrolytes were prepared from 0.5 mol/L Na2CO3 and 1 mol/L NaClO4 stock solutions, bubbled overnight with CO2. Overall electrolyte ionic strength was 1 mol/L, with bicarbonate concentrations adjusted by mixing stock solutions. Electrolyses were queued in batches of ten, with all ten runs using the same electrolyte composition within a batch. The cell assembly is a three-electrode undivided compartment cell using a 10 mm diameter carbon paper disk working electrode clamped between top and bottom cell pans. A leak-free Ag/AgCl reference electrode was calibrated daily against a saturated calomel electrode and swapped every 1-3 days. A 0.25 mm diameter platinum wire counter electrode was used to preclude anode oxidation product attribution. A gas chromatograph connected to the gas out port provided online detection of CO and H2. All data files were automatically uploaded to an SQL database, and a python script extracted average current, partial CO current, and partial H2 current to an Excel document. CO2 was bubbled into the electrolyte rather than fed through the working electrode.

Procedures And Architectures
The robot design features a single cell body housing the reference and counter electrodes, with a line of ten cell pan pairs each holding a carbon paper working electrode. The cell body moves horizontally to sequentially perform electrochemistry on each cell pan and vertically to open and close onto a pan. Two electrolyte configurations are possible: individual vials for each cell pan or a common reservoir; the common reservoir was used to allow fresh CO2 bubbling. The workflow involves: loading electrodes into pans, loading electrolyte, adding electrolysis specifications to an Excel queue file, and the robot performing sequential testing. Upon completion of each experiment, electrolyte is pumped to waste, the cell opens, and the cell body is rinsed after a full set of ten runs using milliQ water for several cycles. The robot performs cleaning by closing onto a wash station consisting of an empty cell pan pair. Data robustness was first evaluated by comparing the newly measured CoPc rates against literature values collected in a classic three-compartment cell. The newly measured rates towards CO were up to ten times lower than previously reported, and Faradaic efficiencies were typically under 30%. The study acknowledges that the undivided cell design allows for crossover; oxygen evolved at the counter electrode can cross over to the working electrode, leading to parasitic oxygen reduction current.

Key Results
Across all three catalysts, CO2 and bicarbonate order dependences were non-linear and/or changed with applied voltage, indicating non-ideal reaction mechanisms. For CoPc and CoTPP, the apparent bicarbonate order is most negative at less reductive potentials and becomes positive at more reductive potentials. For FePc, greater bicarbonate inhibition occurs at more reductive potentials, a trend opposite to what is expected for local bicarbonate adsorption equilibrium. The CoPc and CoTPP bicarbonate trends are well-fit by a model invoking bicarbonate poisoning and potential-dependent mixed control, previously reported to quantitatively describe CoPc. The FePc trend is explained by a mechanism where the most abundant reactive intermediate precedes the unoccupied site, causing θO to increase faster than θHCO3 at more reductive potentials. For CoPc, the CO2 order dependence appears quite ideal, with a simple first-order dependence within error for both potentials shown. For CoTPP, the apparent order in CO2 is slightly below one and decreases at more reductive potentials, characteristic of surface saturation effects. For FePc, the apparent CO2 order is more attenuated at less reductive potentials and the curves for the two potentials intersect. The FePc CO2 behavior is captured by a mixed-control model with an on-cycle poisoning species, where voltage directs unproductive flux at low CO2 partial pressures. At high CO2 partial pressures for FePc, the CO2-dependent elementary step becomes faster, rendering the pathway productive rather than parasitic. Incomplete Faradaic efficiency closure was observed: across all runs, an average of only c.a. 60% was attributable to CO and H2 formation. Relatively high Faradaic efficiencies toward HER of around 30 to 60% were typically observed.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The two distinct bicarbonate trends (attenuation vs. amplification) can generally be explained by two types of mechanisms: explicit catalyst poisoning via bicarbonate adsorption or accumulation of a bicarbonate-dependent reactive intermediate. Differences in how potential influences the reaction fluxes to and from these poisoning species explain the different observed trends across catalysts. CoPc and CoTPP are proposed to share a similar reaction mechanism, while FePc likely involves a species later in the catalytic cycle as the most abundant reactive intermediate. The findings suggest that ostensibly opposing kinetic observations in the literature might be reconciled by differences in operating conditions, where measurements in a limited range only see one part of a more complicated whole. Mechanistic features such as electrolyte poisoning, coverage effects, and mixed control are important considerations for CO2RR at metal tetrapyrroles. The work illustrates how automation can assist with cohesive kinetic analysis, setting forth general mechanistic considerations for interpreting complex rate data.

Contradictions And Limitations
The undivided cell design introduces crosstalk between working and counter electrodes; oxygen evolved at the counter can cross over and lead to parasitic oxygen reduction reaction current. An average of only c.a. 60% Faradaic efficiency was attributable to CO and H2, indicating substantial loss to oxygen reduction. The newly measured rates for CoPc were up to ten times lower than previously reported in a three-compartment cell, and Faradaic efficiencies were lower than expected (under 30%). The authors note that the conceptual mechanisms only qualitatively capture the observed trends but do not quantitatively fit all experimental data via statistical goodness-of-fit metrics. CO2 was bubbled into the electrolyte rather than through the working electrode, which may influence measured kinetics even in ostensibly non-transport-limited regimes. The robot cell body was rinsed only after a full set of ten electrolyses, and the authors note that the same electrolyte composition was used within each set since all products were gas-phase. The robotic platform is an initial demonstration, and the authors note that the convergence of automation with cohesive kinetic analysis provides an informative but initial experimental strategy. The authors acknowledge that random seed, train/test split, and demographic information (where applicable) are not reported as this is an experimental chemistry paper.

Claims
The robotic platform enables flexible and automated reaction rate data collection for electrocatalysis, overcoming the manual data-collection barriers of cohesive kinetic analysis. The robot automates sequential testing of up to ten cells with different electrode, electrolyte, and voltage for each experiment. Data files, electrolyses, and reference calibrations are automatically uploaded to an SQL database for processing. The workflow enables the user to queue up to ten electrolyses for a single effort spent in the lab. The robot performs sequential testing enabling faster and more facile rate data collection over wide conditions. The undivided cell design means the setup is not a gold-standard two- or three-compartment cell. Crosstalk between working and counter electrodes was observed, reducing Faradaic efficiency. The robot cell body is only rinsed after a full set of ten runs, raising potential contamination concerns despite the gas-phase product assumption. This platform sets forth general mechanistic considerations for interpreting complex rate data in electrocatalysis. Future work could extend the concept by incorporating membranes to separate anode and cathode. Software development to automatically enumerate mechanisms could further standardize the workflow.
Non-ideal mechanistic behaviors—bicarbonate poisoning, coverage effects, and mixed rate control—are prevalent across immobilized metal tetrapyrrole CO2RR catalysts. CoPc and CoTPP show voltage-dependent bicarbonate inhibition that changes sign with applied potential. FePc shows bicarbonate inhibition that amplifies at more reductive potentials. CO2 order dependencies are non-linear and/or change with voltage for all three catalysts. These behaviors are unexplainable with mechanisms typically invoked for CO2RR at immobilized tetrapyrroles. The conceptual mechanisms only qualitatively capture the trends and do not quantitatively fit all data via statistical metrics. CoPc shows a near-ideal first-order CO2 dependence, contrasting with the pronounced non-ideality of the other two. Ostensibly opposing kinetic observations in literature might be reconciled by differences in operating conditions. Only steps such as CO2 adsorption, electron transfer, CO* formation, CO* desorption, and metal redox events have been typically debated in existing mechanisms.

Data And Code Availability
All experimental data reported in this work are provided as an Excel file (xlsx). The manuscript is available at ChemRxiv with DOI: 10.26434/chemrxiv-2023-h0zh1 under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 license. ORCID: 0000-0002-3443-3504 is provided for the authors.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Data robustness was evaluated by comparing the newly measured CoPc rates against literature values collected in a classic three-compartment cell. The newly measured rates were up to ten times lower, and Faradaic efficiencies were under 30%, but previously reported kinetic trends were preserved. The data was well-correlated with that of the previous work, confirming the new measurement system's fidelity. The authors note that the conceptual mechanisms only qualitatively capture observed trends without quantitative statistical fit validation. A systematic enumeration and description of models that cannot fit the observed trends is provided in Supplemental Discussion 5.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A shows the overall robot design with the cell body and ten cell pan pairs. Figure 1B illustrates the cell body, electrolyte inlet, gas inlet, and gas chromatograph connection. Figure 1C shows the three-electrode undivided compartment cell assembly. Figure 2A-C shows bicarbonate dependence across CoPc, CoTPP, and FePc with model fits. Figure 2D-G illustrate mechanistic models for bicarbonate poisoning and on-cycle poisoning. Figure 3A-C show CO2 order dependences across the three catalysts. Figure 3D-E illustrate models for surface saturation and mixed control in CO2 dependence. Figure S5 shows incomplete Faradaic efficiency closure data. Figure S7 and S8 show the comparison of newly measured CoPc rates with literature. Figure S9 shows aggregated rates for all three catalysts. Figure S10 shows selectivities and Faradaic efficiencies.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a robotic platform that automates sequential electrochemical kinetic experiments with flexible electrode, electrolyte, and gas compositions, enabling cohesive kinetic analysis of CO2RR over wide operating conditions. 2. The strongest evidence is that bicarbonate and CO2 order dependences are non-linear and change with applied voltage across CoPc, CoTPP, and FePc, demonstrating mechanistic complexities not capturable by traditional Tafel or reactant-order linearization. 3. The future path involves extending the robotic concept with membrane separation, alternative flow configurations, and software to automatically enumerate mechanisms and suggest most informative experimental conditions to further standardize and accelerate the workflow.
