judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper presents the first direct experimental visualization of a π-hole—a π-electron-deficient cavity in a halogen-substituted polyaromatic hydrocarbon—on a single molecule using Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM). The authors investigate 9,10-dichlorooctafluoroanthracene (FCl-An) and compare it to anthracene (An) on an Au(111) surface. The π-hole concept, previously predicted only theoretically, is confirmed by KPFM imaging that reveals a characteristic bow-tie pattern in the local contact potential difference (LCPD) map of FCl-An, which is absent in An. Noncontact atomic force microscopy (nc-AFM) with a CO-functionalized tip was used to structurally resolve the self-assembled rhombic periodic molecular island (one An and two FCl-An molecules per unit cell), with DFT calculations providing a benchmark that unambiguously assigns molecular identities. KPFM imaging, performed with the same CO-terminated tip, captured submolecular LCPD variations that match simulated maps generated from DFT-calculated electrostatic potential maps. Furthermore, specific-site force-distance spectroscopy revealed a 30 pm height difference between An (330 pm) and FCl-An (360 pm) above the Au(111) surface, attributed to the π-hole increasing the ionization potential and suppressing charge induction at the molecule/metal interface. SAPT0 energy decomposition confirmed that while dispersion dominates, the induction energy is significantly larger for An than for FCl-An. This work establishes KPFM as a viable tool for real-space submolecular charge distribution imaging and demonstrates that π-holes fundamentally alter non-covalent electrostatic interactions, affecting both molecular self-assembly and surface adsorption properties.

Research Context
The study of non-covalent interactions, determined by dispersion and electrostatic forces, is fundamental for comprehending supramolecular assembly, ion recognition, and protein stability. In polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, the larger electronegativity of carbon compared to peripheral hydrogen results in an electron-rich delocalized π-bond system that generates a negative quadrupole moment. Substituting peripheral hydrogens with more electronegative substituents such as fluorine or chlorine reverses the electron population to make the π-system electron-deficient, generating a positive quadrupole moment. The π-electron-deficient cavity in the central part of such a molecule is defined as a π-hole. The presence of a π-hole significantly affects non-covalent intermolecular interactions, including intermolecular stacking that stabilizes the helical structure of DNA bases. While the concept has been developed exclusively on a theoretical basis using quantum calculations, a direct experimental observation clearly proving the existence of a π-hole has been lacking so far. Scanning probe microscopy emerges as the most appropriate tool for the direct visualization of π-holes in molecular systems due to the recent development of functionalized probes. The Kelvin probe force microscopy method, which enabled the first resolution of the sigma-hole, is proposed as an ideal imaging tool for real-space observation of the π-hole system.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether the theoretically predicted π-hole can be directly visualized on a single molecule using Kelvin probe force microscopy. The authors hypothesize that FCl-An, bearing halogen substituents, will exhibit a π-hole localized on the carbon skeleton, while anthracene (An), lacking these substituents, will not show such a feature. It is predicted that the presence of a π-hole will significantly alter the local charge distribution and, consequently, affect both the molecular self-assembly pattern and the adsorption height on a metallic substrate. The specific prediction is that a bow-tie pattern in the LCPD map of FCl-An will match DFT-calculated electrostatic potential and reproduce the theoretical expectation of a π-hole. The authors further posit that the π-hole will increase the ionization potential of the molecule, suppressing charge induction at the molecule/metal interface and leading to a larger adsorption height compared to the unsubstituted anthracene. The study aims to demonstrate that KPFM with a functionalized probe can resolve submolecular charge distribution variations that are inaccessible by standard AFM topographic imaging.

Methodological Details
The experiments were conducted at a temperature of 4.2 K using a commercial STM/nc-AFM microscope manufactured by Createc GmbH. Pt/Ir tips, sharpened by focused ion beam (FIB), were cleaned and shaped by gentle indentation of approximately 1 nm in the bare metallic substrate. The nc-AFM employed a qPlus sensor with a resonant frequency of approximately 30 kHz and a stiffness of 1800 N/m, operated in frequency modulation mode with an oscillation amplitude of 200 pm. The Au(111) substrate was prepared by repeated cycles of Ar+ sputtering at 1 keV followed by annealing at approximately 800 K. FCl-An and An molecules were co-sublimated using two Knudsen cells simultaneously in ultrahigh vacuum conditions at room temperature for 15 s on the Au(111) surface. STM topography was acquired in constant current mode with the bias voltage applied to the sample. Both nc-AFM and KPFM images were captured in constant height mode, with a CO-functionalized tip used for both molecular species. LCPD maps were obtained by fitting a parabolic expression to frequency shift versus bias spectroscopies collected on a 64 x 80 pixels rectangular grid covering 3 nm x 5 nm. Each KPFM data point was acquired in approximately 3 seconds, with each parabola containing 600 points over a bias range of (-150, 400) mV. For structural analysis, the Au(111) slab consisted of 4 atomic layers with a surface supercell corresponding to the 6x6 unit cell of the unreconstructed surface. For the supramolecular structure, a √39 x √39 surface cell was constructed and deformed (stretched 1.20% in one direction, compressed 1.06% in another, angle reduced to 56.3°) to match 2 optimal unit cells of the assembly. DFT calculations used the PBE exchange-correlation functional, the light default basis set, and a single k-point (Γ) for surface calculations. For free-standing molecules, hybrid PBE0 functional and tight basis sets were also employed. Van der Waals corrections were applied using the Tkatchenko-Scheffler method with Hirshfeld partitioning, excluding direct Au-Au interactions. KPFM simulations used the Probe Particle (PP) model adapted to a CO-terminated tip with a lateral spring constant of 0.25 N/m. The CO tip was modeled with a dz2-like charge quadrupole of -0.2 e/Å² for the CO termination. SAPT0 calculations were performed on cluster models using the PSI4 program in cc-pVDZ (cc-pwCVDZ-PP for Au) basis sets, with ORCA for orbital and potential map calculations. The cluster model for SAPT0 consisted of a single molecule and a gold layer represented by one layer of 38 gold atoms with (111) orientation.

Procedures And Architectures
Molecules were first co-sublimed to form a self-assembled island, imaged by STM at 4.8 K base temperature to reveal large-scale periodic islands. nc-AFM images at constant height with a CO functionalized tip were acquired to resolve the two molecular species in the assembly. The supramolecular arrangement was identified as a rhombic periodic structure with one An and two FCl-An molecules per unit cell, confirmed by comparison of experimental nc-AFM images with total energy DFT calculations. The assembly arrangement was attributed to attractive intermolecular electrostatic interactions between negatively charged fluorine atoms, a σ-hole on chlorine, and positively charged hydrogen atoms. KPFM was then performed with the same CO-terminated tip, at a tip-sample height chosen close to the Δf minima on both molecules to ensure the absence of tip relaxation. LCPD was extracted by fitting frequency shift versus bias data to the parabolic expression Δf(V) = a × (V − LCPD)² + Δf⁎, where LCPD is the bias at the maximum. To rationalize KPFM images, simulated maps were generated using the PP model with DFT-calculated electrostatic potential and electrical polarizability maps. Specific-site force-distance spectroscopy was performed over the central benzene unit of both molecules and the bare Au(111) surface to measure adsorption heights. For adsorption energy analysis, SAPT0 calculations were carried out on cluster models, providing an interaction energy decomposition scheme including dispersion, electrostatic, and induction terms. DFT-calculated induced electron densities were compared for An and FCl-An on the metallic substrate to interpret the induction term. Molecular orbitals for An and FCl-An were calculated at MP2/cc-pVTZ optimized geometries for potential map generation. Both KPFM and nc-AFM images were processed using WSxM software.

Key Results
nc-AFM at constant height clearly distinguished two molecular species in the assembly, with FCl-An imaged systematically brighter than An due to a topographic effect. The supramolecular assembly was resolved as a rhombic periodic structure with one An and two FCl-An molecules per unit cell, confirmed by the perfect agreement between experimental nc-AFM images and theoretical DFT-calculated structures. KPFM images revealed a characteristic bow-tie pattern in the LCPD signal across the central part of the FCl-An molecule, which is absent in the An molecule. The submolecular variation in the LCPD map of FCl-An matched the distribution of the electrostatic potential calculated for a free-standing FCl-An molecule, confirming the π-hole signature. Δf-z spectroscopy over the central benzene unit revealed a 30 pm difference in the minima position between An and FCl-An, directly corresponding to their relative adsorption heights. The absolute adsorption heights were determined to be 330 pm for An and 360 pm for FCl-An above the bare Au(111) surface. These experimental heights matched reasonably well with DFT total energy calculations of 325 pm for An and 351 pm for FCl-An. DFT calculated induced electron density was significantly larger at the An/Au(111) interface compared to the FCl-An/Au(111) interface, consistent with the π-hole suppressing charge induction. HOMO orbital of An was found close to the Fermi level of metal, facilitating charge induction, whereas the π-hole in FCl-An increased the ionization potential and inhibited charge density induction. SAPT0 energy decomposition showed that the attractive interaction dominates the dispersion energy in all cases, with the induction energy larger for An than for FCl-An. The KPFM images showed no significant distortion or deviation from expected parabolic behavior within the bias range of (-150, 400) mV for either molecule. At large tip-sample distances, KPFM images did not exhibit intramolecular features, while submolecular contrast became increasingly pronounced as the distance decreased, until the regime where tip relaxation causes artifacts.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The experimental detection of the bow-tie LCPD pattern on FCl-An, absent on An, provides direct real-space evidence confirming the theoretically predicted π-electron-deficient cavity (π-hole). The heterogeneous charge distribution of the π-hole is attributed to different electronegativity of fluorine and chlorine modulating charge transfer from the π-system locally. The π-hole increases the ionization potential of the molecule, which elevates the energy barrier for charge transfer to the metallic substrate. The weakened induced electrostatic interaction, quantified by the smaller induction energy in SAPT0 and reduced induced electron density in DFT, explains the larger adsorption height of FCl-An. The finding that dispersion energy dominates the adsorption energy in all cases confirms that non-covalent interactions remain primarily dispersive even in π-hole systems. The study demonstrates that KPFM with a CO-functionalized tip can map submolecular charge distribution at atomic resolution, a capability extended from σ-hole imaging to π-hole visualization. The results imply that π-holes fundamentally govern the electrostatic component of non-covalent interactions, affecting molecular stacking, surface adsorption, and potentially supramolecular architecture.

Contradictions And Limitations
The authors note that AFM images alone do not provide direct experimental evidence of the π-hole, as the carbon skeletons of both molecules show relatively similar contrast and FCl-An is only brighter due to a topographic effect. At shorter tip-sample distances, tip relaxations can noticeably influence the KPFM signal and generate measurement artifacts, causing a deviation from the parabolic LCPD shape. The SAPT0 calculations were performed on a cluster model rather than the full slab model, although the authors state these give very similar results. The DFT calculations used a lightweight setup (PBE, light basis, no k-grid) for surface supercells, which may limit the precision of the absolute adsorption energies compared to more rigorous methods. The study does not report a random seed for the optimization, the specific exchange-correlation functional beyond PBE, or the exact temperature during co-sublimation. The SAPT0 analysis is limited to a single molecule and 38 gold atoms, which may not fully capture the long-range electronic effects of the periodic assembly. The Δf-z spectroscopy was performed only over the central benzene unit, and no specific-site spectroscopy was conducted over the halogen substituents or the chlorine σ-hole region.

Claims
The π-hole in FCl-An is directly observable on a single molecule using KPFM with a CO-functionalized tip, as evidenced by the characteristic bow-tie LCPD pattern. KPFM images reveal a characteristic bow-tie pattern in the LCPD signal across the central part of the FCl-An molecule, absent in An. The submolecular LCPD variation matches the DFT-calculated electrostatic potential map of a free-standing FCl-An molecule. The simulated KPFM images using the PP model reproduce the experimental submolecular LCPD variation very well. The nc-AFM topographic images alone do not provide evidence of the π-hole, as the two species show relatively similar carbon skeleton contrast. The KPFM contrast is highly dependent on tip-sample distance; at large distances, no intramolecular features are visible. KPFM is validated as a tool for submolecular charge distribution mapping, extending beyond σ-hole detection to π-hole systems. The direct visualization enables testing of electronic structure theories in a real-space, molecular-scale context.
The presence of a π-hole increases the adsorption height of the molecule on a metallic surface by suppressing charge induction at the interface. FCl-An adsorbs at 360 pm above Au(111), compared to 330 pm for An, giving a 30 pm height difference measured via Δf-z spectroscopy. DFT-calculated induced electron density is more significant at the An/Au(111) interface than at the FCl-An/Au(111) interface. SAPT0 induction energy is larger for An than for FCl-An, consistent with reduced charge transfer in the π-hole molecule. The HOMO of An is close to the metal Fermi level facilitating induction, whereas the FCl-An π-hole increases ionization potential and inhibits induction. The SAPT0 and DFT calculations give very similar adsorption energies (325 vs 330 pm and 351 vs 360 pm), introducing small uncertainties in the absolute height values. Submolecular charge distributions (like π-holes) can be used to tune the adsorption geometry of molecules on surfaces, important for device fabrication. This provides a mechanistic link between π-electron deficiency and surface bonding strength.
The molecular assembly is a rhombic structure with one An and two FCl-An molecules per unit cell, driven by intermolecular electrostatic interactions. nc-AFM images with CO-terminated tip clearly distinguish the two species and reveal a rhombic periodic structure. The arrangement is dictated by attractive electrostatic interactions between negative fluorine atoms, chlorine σ-hole, and positive hydrogen atoms. Mere deposition of An on the surface does not result in self-organized structures, confirming the driving force requires the co-sublimed FCl-An. DFT-calculated total energy structures match the experimental nc-AFM images unambiguously. The nc-AFM images show FCl-An brighter than An due to a topographic effect, so the contrast difference is not purely electronic. Molecular π-holes direct and control supramolecular architecture, opening design rules for π-hole-mediated self-assembly.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
A tip-sample distance series was conducted, showing submolecular contrast becomes increasingly pronounced as distance decreases, confirming the electrostatic origin of the LCPD signal. The absence of submolecular resolution in Δf⁎ images (maximum frequency shift at compensated LCPD) for both molecules confirms the choice of acquisition height avoids tip relaxation artifacts. For free-standing molecules, hybrid PBE0 calculations with tight basis sets were performed and yielded results without substantial changes in geometry or charge distribution, validating the PBE/light-basis approach. The SAPT0 calculations were carried out on both a single-molecule cluster and a 38-atom gold layer, giving very similar results to the slab model. DFT and SAPT0 calculations gave very similar adsorption energy results (325 vs 351 pm for DFT vs experimental 330 and 360 pm), validating both methods. The CO tip lateral spring constant of 0.25 N/m was used in the PP model, with Pauli repulsion evaluated from DFT-calculated electron densities. The electrostatic potential and electrical polarizability maps were derived from electron density differences in a 0.1 eV/Å external field.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1: Schematic of PAH quadrupole moments, showing carbon's negative quadrupole with hydrogen substituents and positive quadrupole with halogen substituents, illustrating π-hole formation. Figure 2a: STM images at 4.8 K showing large-scale ordered molecular islands of alternating An and FCl-An on Au(111). Figure 2b: High-resolution nc-AFM images in constant height mode distinguishing the two molecular species in the self-assembly. Figure 2c: Topographic view of the rhombic unit cell containing one An and two FCl-An molecules. Figure 2d: Schematic of the attractive electrostatic interactions dictating the assembly arrangement. Figure 3a: KPFM LCPD map of free-standing FCl-An showing submolecular variation. Figure 3b: KPFM LCPD map of free-standing An for comparison (showing absence of π-hole signature). Figure 3c, f: Simulated KPFM images matching experimental LCPD maps of FCl-An. Figure 4a: Δf-z spectroscopy over the central benzene unit of both molecules showing a 30 pm difference in minima position. Figure 4b, c: DFT-calculated induced electron density at the molecule/Au(111) interface for An and FCl-An. Figure 5: Supplemental figure showing KPFM contrast dependence on tip-sample distance. Figure 6: Constant height AFM images showing submolecular contrast emerging first on FCl-An. Table S2: DFT total energy calculations, SAPT0 decomposition, and induced electron density values. Table S3: SAPT0 energy decomposition for all three molecules.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first direct experimental visualization of a π-hole on a single molecule using KPFM with a CO-functionalized tip, confirming the theoretically predicted π-electron-deficient cavity. 2. The strongest evidence is the simultaneous confirmation from three independent techniques: KPFM LCPD maps (bow-tie pattern), nc-AFM structure resolution, and DFT/SAPT0 theoretical verification of the electrostatic potential and energy decomposition. 3. The future path lies in using KPFM for broader submolecular charge distribution imaging to study how π-holes and σ-holes control supramolecular assembly, molecular electronics, and surface-molecule interactions.

summary.title: Machine learning force field ranking of candidate solid electrolyte interphase structures in Li-ion batteries
summary.authors: James M Stevenson; Garvit Agarwal; Leif D Jacobson
summary.field_subfield: Computational Chemistry / Machine Learning for Materials Science
summary.executive_summary: This work presents the first machine learning force field (MLFF) ranking of candidate solid-electrolyte interphase (SEI) structures formed in lithium-ion batteries, combining organic and inorganic components that pose significant simulation challenges. The authors develop a multitask QRNN (Quaternion Recurrent Neural Network) model trained simultaneously on both hybrid (wB97X-D3BJ/def2-TZVPD) and pure (PBE-D3) DFT reference labels, complemented by an organic chemistry dataset (SPICE) to broaden chemical coverage. Data generation employs multiple rounds of active learning enhanced by Artificial Force Induced Reactions (AFIR) and Nudged Elastic Band (NEB) on the QRNN potential energy surface, alongside OPLS4 molecular dynamics with reaction templates in a 1 M LiPF6 in EC solution system. The model is trained with hidden layers of size 256, 224, and 192 across elements, using the Adamax optimizer with decoupled weight decay and a learning rate of 2e-3. The methodology extends prior QRNN applications to complex redox-reactive metalorganic systems, producing stable MD dynamics at 400 K and 1000 atm. The model identifies four sets of candidate SEI structures with 5, 12, 23, and 33 added Li+ ions per box, ranked by mean potential energy over 20 ps MD trajectories. The most lithiated subgroup (33 Li+) is validated against the best available surface reaction energy barriers from Table 1, though experimental metrics like density and diffusivity are unavailable. Statistical bonding analysis reveals that P-F and Li-O bonds correlate with lower energies (more stable structures), while C-O and Li-F bonds correlate with higher energies. The paper emphasizes that this multitask QRNN framework can capture complex reactions characteristic of an SEI and proposes extending the work to multiple electrolyte formulations for property prediction. The authors conclude that while the model is not yet final, it establishes a quantitative baseline for understanding Li-ion battery interphases and sets a foundation for future MLFF-based SEI optimization.

The most lithiated subgroup (33 Li+) is validated against the best available surface reaction energy barriers from Table 1, though experimental metrics like density and diffusivity are unavailable. Statistical bonding analysis reveals that P-F and Li-O bonds correlate with lower energies (more stable structures), while C-O and Li-F bonds correlate with higher energies. The paper emphasizes that this multitask QRNN framework can capture complex reactions characteristic of an SEI and proposes extending the work to multiple electrolyte formulations for property prediction. The authors conclude that while the model is not yet final, it establishes a quantitative baseline for understanding Li-ion battery interphases and sets a foundation for future MLFF-based SEI optimization.

Research Context
The fundamental nature of Li-ion batteries requires the anode to be unstable relative to the cathode but stable relative to the electrolyte, with a solid-electrolyte interphase (SEI) as the passivating layer. Key questions about SEIs, such as whether they are amorphous or crystalline and how Li+ moves through them, remain unanswered, limiting next-generation battery development. An SEI is a complex chemical structure forming over large length and time scales involving conductors, insulators, and redox reactions, with no existing method fully applicable to simulating such systems. Existing pure density functionals underestimate reaction barriers in metallic systems, and hybrid functionals such as wB97X that improve barriers struggle with metals and have poor periodic scaling. Traditional force fields with fixed functional forms are very difficult to fit for complex systems like the SEI. The study positions itself as the most complex redox reactive system simulated using an MLFF or method of comparable accuracy.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether a multitask MLFF can be trained to simultaneously describe the complex organic and inorganic components of an SEI and produce a ranking of plausible candidate structures. The authors hypothesize that multitask learning, combining both pure and hybrid DFT labels with a supplemental organic chemistry dataset, will enhance model capacity without imposing a heavy cost on accuracy. A secondary hypothesis is that adding general organic chemistry data (SPICE) to the training set will broaden chemical applicability without degrading performance on battery-specific tasks. The study also posits that the model can produce stable MD dynamics under extreme conditions (400 K, 1000 atm), enabling reliable structural relaxation and ranking. The authors anticipate that a structure's energetic stability will correlate with specific bonding patterns, which can be analyzed post-simulation.

Methodological Details
The reference level for non-periodic systems is wB97X-D3BJ/def2-TZVPD, and for periodic systems, PBE-D3 in a plane wave basis. To improve information exchange between output heads, a random subset of non-periodic systems was labeled with PBE-D3. Atomic partial charges from GFN1-xTB were found most suitable for SEI training labels, achieving the best compromise between accuracy and convergence. Data generation uses multiple rounds of active learning with AFIR and NEB on the QRNN potential energy surface. The SPICE organic dataset was included using elements H, Li, C, O, F, and P with GFN1-xTB charge labels. The SEI Simulator uses OPLS4 molecular dynamics with reaction templates in a 1 M LiPF6 in EC solution. Each system starts with 700 molecules of EC and 52 ions each of Li+ and PF6-, giving a 1 M solution with 7416 total atoms. Four sets of candidates were defined with 5, 12, 23, and 33 added Li+ ions per box, arising after 40 iterations of the simulator. For periodic DFT, Quantum Espresso was used via Schrodinger Materials Science Suite version 2022-3 with PBE functional and D3 correction, 40 Ry cutoff. The Brillouin zone integration used a 3x3x3 k-point mesh for bulk and 3x3x1 for surface supercells. Gas-phase wB97X-D3BJ/def2-TZVPD used Psi4 v1.6 with dft_basis_tolerance of 1e-10 and ints_tolerance of 1e-10. NEB used lithium surfaces with 54 atoms (6 layers of 9 atoms each) topped with a single EC molecule. Non-periodic cluster extraction chose a radius from 3.0 to 5.2 Å with a 1.2 Å hydrogen buffer. Liquid EC geometries were built with Disordered System Builder and equilibrated via NPT for 1 ns. Solid-liquid interface geometries used a BCC lithium lattice with spacing optimized by the model at 2 Å. Lithium oxide, carbonate, fluoride, and hydroxide were added to the training set in periodic and cluster geometries.

Procedures And Architectures
The model is a multitask QRNN with four output levels: GFN1-xTB, PBE-D3, wB97X-D3BJ/def2-TZVPD, and the SPICE level of theory. The first (GFN1-xTB) and last (SPICE wB97X-D3BJ) heads shaped the latent space and were not used for SEI predictions. The loss function is the energy and atomic force MSE for each level, plus charge MSE with consistent charge labels across all levels. The Adamax optimizer was used with decoupled weight decay and a learning rate of 2e-3. Hidden layers had sizes of 256, 224, and 192 for all elements with a batch size of 64. Weight decay was set at 1e-3 per batch for the final model, reduced from 3e-3 which produced smoother surfaces but suppressed reaction barriers. A validation set of 1% of data, selected uniformly at random, was used since early stopping had little effect. The final model was an exponential moving average of training parameters, averaging every 10 batches with alpha = 0.001. Structural annealing used reactive QRNN NPT MD at 400 K and 1000 atm for 100 ps each. Ranking calculated mean potential energy over 20 ps MD at 300 K and 1 atm. Non-DFT geometries were generated via Disordered System Builder with Van der Waals radius factor of 0.5 to produce steric clashes. No DFT-generated MD, AFIR, or NEB geometries were used as training inputs to avoid test set leakage.

Key Results
Adding SPICE data resulted in no increase in PBE-head validation RMSE and only an 8% increase in hybrid-head RMSE. This 8% cost implies the latent space contains unused capacity for broadening chemical applicability. The QRNN models produced stable dynamics at 400 K and 1000 atm, which is remarkable as many MLFFs fail under extreme conditions. The four candidate sets with 5, 12, 23, and 33 added Li+ per box were generated after 40 iterations. The lowest-energy candidate from the 33-Li subgroup was identified via the wB97X-D3BJ output head. P-F and Li-O bonds were associated with lower total system energies (more stable structures). C-O and Li-F bonds were associated with higher total system energies (less stable structures). Energy and gradient RMSEs are reported but specific numerical values for the final validation are not listed in the main text body. The model was validated against the best available surface reaction energy barriers from Table 1, though no experimental metrics are available. The SEI candidate structures and energies are deposited at https://figshare.com/s/e842ae88023902700e12.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Multitask training with a QRNN, combined with active learning of relevant chemical systems, enables modeling of complex redox reactions characteristic of SEI. The multitask framework shows that latent space in MLFFs can accommodate disparate chemical tasks with minimal interference. The results suggest that P-F and Li-O chemistry is energetically favored in the most lithiated SEI candidates, while C-O and Li-F destabilize the interface. The technique, when extended to multiple electrolyte formulations, will permit property prediction (diffusivity, mechanical properties) as a function of starting formulation. The work demonstrates that MLFFs can reach the accuracy and complexity required for redox-active metalorganic solids, opening a new paradigm for battery interphase simulation.

Contradictions And Limitations
No experimental benchmarks (density, diffusivity, viscosity, elastic modulus) exist for any SEI composition, preventing direct validation. The model was trained with only a single formulation (1 M LiPF6 in EC), limiting generalizability. The scope of the dataset remains small compared to what is required for full SEI characterization; the authors do not regard the model as final. NEB focused on a relatively small part of reactive chemical space (EC decomposition) and did not sample other potential surfaces like Li2O or Li2CO3. There is no unique way to determine cluster boundaries for metalorganic solids, requiring stochastic radius extraction. The probability of being proven wrong by future experimental or theoretical developments is acknowledged as high.

Claims
Multitask training with QRNN combined with active learning enables modeling of complex redox-reactive SEI systems with DFT accuracy. The QRNN models gave stable dynamics at 400 K and 1000 atm, which is often not the case for MLFFs. Only an 8% increase in hybrid-head RMSE was observed when adding SPICE data, implying the latent space has unused capacity. The model was validated against best available surface reaction energy barriers from Table 1. The model was trained on a single electrolyte formulation, limiting its scope to one specific chemical environment. The scope remains small compared to what is required, and the authors do not regard the model as final. The technique can be extended to multiple electrolyte formulations for property prediction and optimization. Future works should include other architectures (Nequip, MACE, CHGNet) and ablation studies on dataset subsets.

Data And Code Availability
SEI candidate structures (seed*.pdb), energies (energies.csv), original electrolyte (initial_EC_1M_LiPF6.pdb), and plotting scripts (*.py) are available at: https://figshare.com/s/e842ae88023902700e12

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The model tested weight decay of 3e-3 per batch but reduced it to 1e-3 for the final model because 3e-3 suppressed reaction barriers relative to reference. A high-priority dataset of periodic and cluster surface reaction subsets was used for 50% of each batch to maintain representation of reactive data. Decoupled weight norms were applied with norms not included in the optimizer for stability. Only 1% of data was used as validation set since early stopping had little effect due to limited model capacity to overfit.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the SEI system composition with 7416 total atoms (700 EC molecules, 52 Li+ ions, 52 PF6- ions). Figure 4 displays bond counts versus total system energy (zero = most stable) for the 33-Li subgroup, showing P-F and Li-O bonds at low energies. Table 1 reports surface reaction energy barriers against which the model was validated (specific values referenced in the paper but not fully listed in the text). The appendix contains details on GFN1-xTB charge label comparisons, SPICE data specifics, and additional training hyperparameters.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a multitask QRNN framework that successfully models complex redox-reactive metalorganic solids at DFT accuracy, producing the first ranked set of candidate SEI structures. 2. The strongest evidence is that the model maintains stable dynamics at 400 K and 1000 atm and captures bonding-energy correlations (P-F/Li-O favored) consistent with thermodynamic expectations, with only an 8% RMSE cost for chemical broadening. 3. The future path involves extending the framework to multiple electrolyte formulations for Li+ diffusivity and mechanical property prediction, using additional architectures like Nequip, MACE, and CHGNet.

summary.title: Biological activity of Ajuga iva extracts against the African cotton leafworm Spodoptera littoralis
summary.authors: Leena Taha-Salaime; Galina Lebedev; Jackline Abo-Nassar; Sally Marzouk; Moshe Inbar; Murad Ghanim; Radi Aly
summary.field_subfield: Agricultural Entomology / Plant-Based Pesticide Discovery
summary.executive_summary: This study investigates the insecticidal potential of crude and purified extracts from Ajuga iva (Lamiaceae) against Spodoptera littoralis, a major pest of cotton, maize, and rice. The authors exploited the presence of phytoecdysteroids—steroid analogs that mimic insect molting hormones—and clerodane diterpenes in A. iva to test green pest management alternatives to synthetic insecticides. Using a combination of larval feeding bioassays, LC-TOF-MS identification, TLC profiling, fluorescence microscopy of gut histology, and weight gain monitoring, the team demonstrated that A. iva crude leaf extract (50-250 µg/µl) significantly increases mortality in both first-instar (25%, 65%, 85%) and third-instar larvae, reduces larval weight gain, suppresses relative growth rate, and prevents successful pupation. A fractionated mixture of three phytoecdysteroids (20-hydroxyecdysone, makisterone A, and cyasterone) was also shown to elicit similar toxic effects. Histological analysis revealed that the extracts cause smaller, abnormally shaped nuclei and reduced actin filament density in larval guts, suggesting direct physiological damage. The study concludes that A. iva phytoecdysteroids and clerodanes offer a promising botanical control agent for S. littoralis, supporting integrated pest management programs with reduced environmental risk compared to traditional insecticides.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigates the insecticidal potential of crude and purified extracts from Ajuga iva (Lamiaceae) against Spodoptera littoralis, a major pest of cotton, maize, and rice. The authors exploited the presence of phytoecdysteroids—steroid analogs that mimic insect molting hormones—and clerodane diterpenes in A. iva to test green pest management alternatives to synthetic insecticides. Using a combination of larval feeding bioassays, LC-TOF-MS identification, TLC profiling, fluorescence microscopy of gut histology, and weight gain monitoring, the team demonstrated that A. iva crude leaf extract (50-250 µg/µl) significantly increases mortality in both first-instar (25%, 65%, 85%) and third-instar larvae, reduces larval weight gain, suppresses relative growth rate, and prevents successful pupation. A fractionated mixture of three phytoecdysteroids (20-hydroxyecdysone, makisterone A, and cyasterone) was also shown to elicit similar toxic effects. Histological analysis revealed that the extracts cause smaller, abnormally shaped nuclei and reduced actin filament density in larval guts, suggesting direct physiological damage. The study concludes that A. iva phytoecdysteroids and clerodanes offer a promising botanical control agent for S. littoralis, supporting integrated pest management programs with reduced environmental risk compared to traditional insecticides.

Research Context
Spodoptera littoralis is a serious pest affecting cotton, maize, rice, alfalfa, potato, tomato, ornamentals, and orchard trees. Current pest control relies primarily on insecticides that pose risks to human health and the environment. Phytoecdysteroids are plant-produced steroid analogs that mimic insect molting hormones, present in 5-6% of plant species. Phytoecdysteroids may cause abnormal larval development, feeding deterrence, and ultimately death by disrupting the endogenous endocrine levels of insects. The authors previously identified and quantified high contents of three phytoecdysteroids and two clerodanes in A. iva growing in Israel. Prior work showed that Ajuga remota extracts containing 20-hydroxyecdysone and cyasterone inhibited ecdysis in Bombyx mori. Ajuga reptans extracts caused 100% mortality in greenhouse whitefly larvae when fed. A dose of 5 μg/ml of pure extracted A. iva ecdysterone significantly reduced fecundity, fertility, and survival of Oligonychus perseae, outperforming commercial ecdysterone at the same dose.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central hypothesis is that crude extract of A. iva leaves, containing the three phytoecdysteroids responsible for molting interference and antifeedant activities, may be a promising pest-control agent. The authors addressed four specific research questions: Does A. iva crude leaf extract affect S. littoralis larvae? Do phytoecdysteroids isolated from the crude leaf extract and commercial standards have different effects on the larvae? Do phytoecdysteroids have a direct effect on the larvae's gut? Does the effect of the crude extract versus the purified phytoecdysteroid fraction differ in magnitude of toxicity? Does the order of exposure (pre-treatment vs. post-treatment) alter the outcome?

Methodological Details
Young and mature leaves and stems of fresh A. iva were collected after blooming (July-November) and oven-dried at 55 °C for 3-4 days. Material was homogenized to a fine powder prior to extraction. For crude extraction, 24 g of leaf and stem powder were soaked in 240 ml of 100% MeOH, homogenized at 2500 rpm for 1 h, and centrifuged. For purified phytoecdysteroids, 100 g of powder was soaked in 300 ml methanol, vacuum-concentrated, and treated with H2O to give 30% aqueous methanol. LC-TOF-MS analysis used an Agilent 1290 Infinity Series LC coupled with an Agilent 6224 Accurate Mass TOF mass spectrometer. TLC was performed on silica gel GF-254 plates (0.25 mm; 20 × 20 cm). The first and third instars of S. littoralis larvae were from a laboratory colony reared on castor bean leaves. For first instar bioassays, 10 larvae were placed on one treated castor bean leaf per treatment in 11 replicates. Treatments included 50, 100, and 250 µg/µl of crude leaf extract with Tween 20 (1.5 mg) added to the aqueous smear. Third instar experiments used 1 or 10 larvae on one leaf for 4 or 8 days. The purified phytoecdysteroid fraction used in the experiments contained ecdysterone, makisterone A, and cyasterone. Gut histology used DAPI and phalloidin staining after 7 days of treatment. Guts were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde, washed in 0.1% Triton X-100, and mounted in hybridization buffer. Imaging was performed using a Leica SP8 and Olympus IX 81 confocal laser scanning microscope. Statistical analyses were conducted with IBM SPSS software v.20 for Windows.

Procedures And Architectures
Crude leaf extract was prepared by dissolving 1.2 g of dried extract powder in 4.8 ml ddH2O and Tween 20 (0.5 mg/ml) for the 250 µg/µl concentration. The 100 µg/µl concentration was obtained by dissolving 0.83 ml of the 250 µg/µl extract in 3 ml ddH2O. The 50 µg/µl concentration was prepared by dissolving 0.67 ml of the 100 µg/µl solution in 3 ml ddH2O. Mature castor bean leaves were smeared with the aqueous A. iva crude leaf extract (1:10 ratio) and dried in a chemical hood for 2 h. For the four-treatment third instar experiment, leaves were fed for 4 days then switched to a second leaf for another 4 days to avoid decayed leaf feeding. Pupation was evaluated for an additional 15 days after the 8-day feeding period. Relative growth rate was calculated as (ln W2 - ln W1) / (t2 - t1). The fractionated phytoecdysteroid mixture was applied at 250 µg/µl on castor bean leaves. A control experiment used a mixture of three commercial standards (ecdysterone, makisterone A, and cyasterone) at a maximum concentration of 100 ppm each.

Key Results
First instar S. littoralis larvae showed significant mortality of 25%, 65%, and 85% at 50, 100, and 250 µg/µl of A. iva crude leaf extract, respectively, compared to 5% in the control. Third instar larvae fed on 250 µg/µl crude leaf extract showed a statistically significant reduction in larval weight gain (F3.104 = 20.334, p < 0.001). All concentrations of crude leaf extract significantly decreased larval RGR compared to the control diet. At the highest concentration, RGR decreased by 0.05 g/g per day on day 6 and 0.20 g/g per day on day 8 compared to control. None of the treated first instar larvae survived more than 8 days for the highest concentration and 10 days for the other concentrations, while all control larvae survived. When larvae were first fed on control leaves and then switched to crude extract, RGR was affected after day 5 (F3.16, 18 = 7.310, p < 0.001) and continued to decrease until the end. When larvae were first fed on crude extract and then switched to control leaves, RGR decreased significantly on days 2-4 at all three concentrations (F3.16, 18 = 4.595, 3.608, and 8.113; p = 0.034, 0.02, and 0.001, respectively). The purified phytoecdysteroid mixture at 250 µg/µl significantly reduced RGR (F2.20, 18 = 6.172, p = 0.001) compared to control. Few larvae survived on leaves treated with the purified phytoecdysteroid fraction (χ²₃ = 11.305, p = 0.04). Larvae fed on 250 µg/µl crude leaf extract or the phytoecdysteroid mixture lost weight, stopped growing, and died; none completed development to adult moths. Larvae with purified phytoecdysteroids had smaller, abnormally shaped nuclei that moved to the edges of the cell and were thinner than normal. Phalloidin staining in treated guts showed actin filaments were smaller and their amount was reduced compared to normal organization in control. Larvae exposed to the 250 µg/µl crude leaf extract or phytoecdysteroid fraction for 8 days were unable to complete pupation after 15 additional days. The commercial mixture of three standards at 100 ppm each for 8 days showed no significant effect on S. littoralis larvae.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The dose-dependent mortality suggests that phytoecdysteroids operate through a concentration-dependent disruption of the endocrine-controlled molting and metamorphosis cycle. The reduced RGR and LWG suggest that phytoecdysteroids or the crude extract components impair the insect's nutritional assimilation and metabolic efficiency. Histological evidence of gut cell destruction (reduced actin fibers, smaller nuclei) indicates that the toxic effects may be mediated through direct damage to the intestinal epithelium. The observation that mortality occurred during molting in smaller larvae and at the prepupal stage in larger larvae supports the endocrine-disruption hypothesis. The fact that the pure 100 ppm commercial mixture showed no effect, while the 250 µg/µl A. iva fraction (containing much higher phytoecdysteroid levels) was highly toxic, suggests that the endogenous levels in A. iva exceed the threshold for toxicity. Phytoecdysteroids may therefore serve as a viable non-chemical pest management tool in IPM programs, leveraging their selective toxicity toward Lepidopterans while being safe for mammals.

Contradictions And Limitations
The authors could not fractionate clerodanes from the A. iva crude leaf extract due to calibration difficulties and high cost of commercial standards, leaving this class of bioactive compounds unexamined. Only a few commercial standards were used because they were very expensive and not feasible as a control treatment, limiting direct comparison of pure compounds at applied concentrations. The commercial mixture was tested at 100 ppm per compound (250,000 ppm total), which is significantly lower than the 250 µg/µl concentration used in the A. iva treatments, confounding direct comparison. The gut morphology experiment was performed at 7 days post-treatment, which may not capture the full progression of histological damage over the entire 8-day exposure period. The study was limited to two larval instars (first and third), leaving the effects on second instar larvae and the full life cycle unexamined. The paper is a preprint (bioRxiv) and has not undergone full peer review at the time of this version. The ecdysone receptor controls development, but the exact mechanism of how A. iva phytoecdysteroids interfere with this pathway in S. littoralis specifically is not delineated.

Claims
Ajuga iva crude leaf extract and its purified phytoecdysteroids are toxic to S. littoralis at the concentrations tested. Mortality reached 85% in first instars at 250 µg/µl. None of the treated larvae survived beyond 8 days at the highest concentration. The purified phytoecdysteroid fraction caused significant RGR reduction (F=6.172, p=0.001). The commercial mixture at 100 ppm showed no significant effect. Phytoecdysteroids from A. iva could be developed into a botanical pesticide.
The toxicity of A. iva extracts is mediated through direct histological damage to the larval gut epithelium. Gut cells showed smaller, abnormally shaped nuclei at the cell edges. Actin filaments in treated guts were smaller and reduced in amount. The gut epithelium showed massive deterioration and destruction of microvilli. It is also hypothesized that the endocrine-disruption mechanism (molting failure) contributes significantly to mortality. Targeted delivery or formulation could be optimized to exploit gut permeability.
A. iva phytoecdysteroids are selective for Lepidoptera and are not toxic to mammals. Ecdysteroids are not toxic to mammals because their structure differs from mammalian steroids. Previous studies showed phytoecdysteroids negatively affect lepidopteran pests but are tolerated by other insect species. Specific toxicity profiles in non-target Lepidopteran species were not tested in this study. A. iva extracts offer a safer alternative to synthetic insecticides for IPM.

Data And Code Availability
No specific statement on data or code availability is provided in the manuscript.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
A four-treatment crossover experiment varied exposure order (control-extract vs. extract-control), demonstrating consistent RGR depression. The purified phytoecdysteroid fraction (ecdysterone + makisterone A + cyasterone) yielded similar toxicity to the crude extract, confirming phytoecdysteroids as the primary active class. Dose-response was demonstrated across three concentrations (50, 100, 250 µg/µl), confirming the effect is not binary but graduated. Replicates (n=11 for first instar mortality; n=20 for RGR; n=10 for weight gain) were used to support statistical comparisons. The commercial mixture control at 100 ppm acted as a negative comparator, highlighting that the A. iva content is supra-threshold for toxicity.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1: TLC profiles showing Rf values of A. iva phytoecdysteroids compared to commercial standards for identification confirmation. Figure 2a: Survival of first instar larvae at 50, 100, and 250 µg/µl crude leaf extract vs. control. Figure 2b: Larval weight gain of third instars on the three crude extract concentrations vs. control. Figure 3a: RGR of third instars over 8 days showing depression starting as early as day 2. Figure 3b: Survival of third instars over 11 days with 100% control survival and zero treated survival after 8–10 days. Figure 4a–d: RGR in crossover experiments showing consistent depression regardless of exposure sequence. Figure 5a–b: RGR and survival comparisons between crude extract, purified phytoecdysteroid mixture, and control. Figure 6a–i: Fluorescence microscopy of larval gut actin (phalloidin) and nuclei (DAPI) in control vs. 250 µg/µl treatments. Figure 7: Pupation outcomes after 15 days showing short limbs, small heads, and incomplete pupation (stomach/chest only).

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution: A. iva crude leaf extract at 50-250 µg/µl significantly increases S. littoralis mortality (up to 85%), reduces growth rates, disrupts gut histology, and prevents pupation, with the effects mediated by phytoecdysteroid and/or clerodane contents. 2. The strongest evidence: Crossover experiments demonstrated consistent RGR depression regardless of exposure order, and fluorescence microscopy revealed direct morphological damage to the gut actin cytoskeleton and nuclei, supporting a direct physiological toxic effect. 3. The future path: Further study is needed to isolate and characterize A. iva clerodanes, determine full life-cycle toxicity in S. littoralis, and evaluate field efficacy to validate A. iva as a viable botanical component for IPM programs.

summary.title: Sorry, we're open: Golden Open Access and inequality in the natural sciences
summary.authors: Russell J Gray
summary.field_subfield: Bibliometrics / Scientometrics; Open Access Policy in Natural Sciences
summary.executive_summary: This study investigates the relationship between Article Processing Charges (APC), Impact Factor (IF), Eigen Factor (EF), citability, and publisher country within the ecosystem of Golden Open Access (GOA) natural science journals. The author collected and cleaned metadata from the Directory of Open Access Journals (DOAJ), starting with a pool of 14,275 records, and filtered for 237 GOA natural science journals after excluding medical and engineering journals with IF > 40. Statistical analysis using Pearson's correlation confirmed that APC is significantly and positively correlated with IF (r = 0.391, p < .001), EF (r = 0.303, p < .001), and total citations (r = 0.323, p < .001). Furthermore, publishers from developed countries exhibited higher mean APC, IF, EF, and citability compared to those from developing countries. The author argues that these findings expose a structural inequality in global science: high-impact, GOA journals create a 'pay-to-play' model where prestige, citations, and credibility are purchased rather than earned, disadvantaging researchers from developing countries, unaffiliated independent scholars, and those in conservation-critical fields. The study highlights the paradox where the very mechanisms of open access (higher citation counts, higher visibility) are gated behind costs that exclude the most resource-constrained contributors, potentially suppressing important research—particularly in tropical ecology and conservation—that cannot access the >1000 USD fees required by prestigious GOA outlets.

Research Context
The rise of Black and Green Open Access (Sci-Hub, ResearchGate) has largely nullified the previous paywall system for journal profit. Many high-impact journals have transitioned to mandatory Golden Open Access to maintain profitability through scientific publication. However, the associated publication costs create a barrier that makes GOA not a viable option for many researchers seeking high-impact outlets. Previous evidence showed that researchers from developing institutions pay full developed-nation prices for high-impact Mega-Journals to gain exposure. The alternative for these researchers is publishing in lower-impact journals, predatory journals, or questionable outlets that may damage manuscript credibility. High-impact journals generate exposure through increased citations, which accelerates career advancement for researchers. Despite the perceived openness, the cost of publishing becomes a bottleneck for researchers without available funding, narrowing options for impactful research.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether links exist between publication costs (APC), impact factor (IF), Eigen Factor (EF), and citability for open-access natural science journals. The author also examines whether country of publisher creates disparities in APC, citability, IF, and EF between developed and developing nations. The hypothesis is that IF, EF, and citability all increase as APC increases within GOA natural science journals. A secondary hypothesis is that publishers from developed countries will exhibit higher metrics (IF, EF, citability) compared to publishers from developing countries. The implicit null hypothesis is that journal metrics are distributed equally across publisher locations regardless of publication costs. The study seeks to identify if the openness of GOA is undermined by cost-related inequality that favors wealthy institutions and nations.

Methodological Details
The data source was the Directory of Open Access Journals (DOAJ), which provided journal name, APC, country of publisher, and currency records. The initial dataset comprised 14,275 records with journal metadata. R statistical software was used for all data analyses with specific packages for each task. The scholar package (Keirstead, 2016) was used to generate impact factors from journal name strings. The quantmod package (Ryan et al. 2019) converted all currencies to USD for standardization. The dplyr and reshape2 packages (Wickham et al. 2015, 2012) were used for data cleaning and selection. The ggplot2 package (Wickham et al. 2016) was used for data visualizations. A subset of 1,047 journals related to biological sciences was queried using keywords such as ecology, conservation, agriculture, species, and forest. Journals with an IF > 40 were excluded to separate natural sciences from medical and engineering fields. Excluded journals were manually checked via keywords and found to relate to oncology, medical, and engineering. The final analyzed dataset consisted of 237 deeply vetted open-access natural science journals. APC was examined in relation to citability (total citation count), IF (general impact), and Eigen Factor (relative importance). Pearson's correlation coefficient was used to analyze relationships between APC, IF, EF, and citability using functions from the ggpubr package.

Procedures And Architectures
APC was examined against three dependent variables: citability (total citation count), IF, and EF. Country of publisher was treated as an additional independent variable examined against APC, IF, EF, and citability to locate disparities. Currency standardization involved converting all APC records to USD using the quantmod package before analysis. IF was generated by passing journal name strings through the scholar package to retrieve values from impact factor databases. Data cleaning involved keyword-based subsetting to isolate biological sciences from the broader DOAJ dataset. The IF > 40 threshold was applied to exclude medical and engineering journals that would skew the natural sciences analysis. A manual keyword audit was performed on excluded journals to ensure no natural science journals were inadvertently removed. Pearson correlations were computed for APC-IF, APC-EF, and APC-citability relationships within the n = 237 dataset. Visualizations were generated using ggplot2 to display trends and country-level distributions.

Key Results
A linear trend was found between IF, EF, and citability in relation to APC within the natural science GOA journal corpus. The mean APC of the 237 analyzed open-access journals was $1344.27 USD. The mean Impact Factor (IF) across the sample was 2.855. The mean Eigen Factor (EF) across the sample was 0.017. The mean total citation count (citability) was 5925.92 across the sample. APC was significantly positively correlated with IF, with a Pearson correlation of r(237) = 0.391 and p < .001. There was a highly significant positive correlation between APC and EF, with a Pearson correlation of r(237) = 0.303 and p < .001. There was a highly significant positive correlation between APC and citability, with a Pearson correlation of r(237) = 0.323 and p < .001. Journal publishers from developed countries were more likely to have higher APC, IF, EF, and citability than those from developing countries (Figure 1). Research published in journals from developing countries is less likely to gain exposure, while journals from developing countries are less likely to generate profit and credibility.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The findings demonstrate that with increasing publishing costs, the impact (IF), importance (EF), and overall citation count in open-access natural science journals also increase, supporting a cost-driven hierarchy of prestige. The data indicates that the majority of journal publishers with the highest metrics are from developed countries, suggesting systemic inequality in global research exposure. The author argues that expensive APC in prestigious journals are not linked to the reliability of the research published in them, citing Brembs (2018). The IF of prestigious journals creates a false perception of reliability in the research they publish (Brembs, 2013). The paradox of GOA journals is that the system prioritizes publisher profit over scientific integrity, creating an environment that favors predatory journals and editorial complacency. The irregular distribution of resources across the world and academia creates a bubble where higher-ranking institutions have greater access to expensive, high-impact journals. The authors from developing countries are forced to pay developed-country prices to access higher-impact outlets, while unaffiliated individual researchers face even narrower options. The authors contend that researchers being pushed to the backburner by cost constraints are no less reliable than privileged institutional researchers. For conservation and ecology, the inequality is particularly acute because most biodiversity hotspots are in the tropics, where authors from developed countries often nullify eligibility for APC funding assistance (Research4Life, 2015). The scientific community must address these issues to create a more inclusive environment where important research is recognized regardless of country or institutional affiliation.

Contradictions And Limitations
The paper does not report the specific countries categorized as developed versus developing, leaving the exact definition of these classifications unclear. The study does not provide the random seed used for data partitioning or the exact criteria for 'deeply vetted' beyond the keyword exclusion. The author admits personal experience with funding rejection (Sumatran elephant study) which may introduce a subjective perspective into the interpretation of the data. The paper does not report the variance or confidence intervals for the mean metrics (APC, IF, EF, citability), only central tendency values. The study is limited to a single journal repository (DOAJ) and a single discipline (natural sciences), so generalizability to humanities or social sciences is not established. The author acknowledges the tension between maintaining prestige as a credible outlet and the profit-driven dynamics of the GOA model.

Claims
Higher Article Processing Charges in GOA natural science journals are positively and significantly correlated with increased Impact Factor, Eigen Factor, and citability. The Pearson correlation between APC and IF was r = 0.391 (p < .001). The Pearson correlation between APC and EF was r = 0.303 (p < .001). The Pearson correlation between APC and citability was r = 0.323 (p < .001). A linear trend was found between IF, EF, and citability in relation to APC. The study does not control for journal age, publication frequency, or editor prestige, which may confound the APC-metrics relationship. Prestige and visibility in the global scientific record are partially purchased rather than solely meritocratic. Researchers from resource-constrained backgrounds face structural disadvantages in achieving the academic currency of career success.
Publishers from developed countries systematically maintain higher journal metrics (APC, IF, EF, citability) than those from developing countries, entrenching global inequality. Journal publishers from developed countries were more likely to have higher APC, IF, EF, and citability. Research from developing countries is less likely to gain exposure while journals from these countries generate less profit and credibility. The study does not provide specific country-level mean comparisons or standard errors to quantify the magnitude of the disparity. A self-reinforcing loop of prestige and funding privileges is created that marginalizes scientific output from the Global South. The Research4Life eligibility criteria may unintentionally penalize international collaborations that could benefit conservation science.
High APC costs in prestigious GOA journals do not correlate with higher research reliability, yet they create a false perception of reliability. Expensive APC in prestigious journals are not linked to reliability of the research published in them (Brembs, 2018). The IF of prestigious journals creates a false perception of reliability (Brembs, 2013). Researchers put on the backburner by cost are no less reliable than privileged institutional researchers. The author acknowledges that high-impact journals have built reputations of credibility that can accelerate careers regardless of content validity. The scientific community must decouple quality metrics from cost-driven prestige to create a more inclusive research environment.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
A manual keyword audit was performed on excluded journals to verify that no natural science journals were incorrectly removed during the IF > 40 filtering. The subsetting procedure used keywords (ecology, conservation, agriculture, species, forest, etc.) to define biological sciences, but the exact full keyword list is not specified. Currency standardization to USD was performed using the quantmod package before correlation analyses.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 displays the relationship between APC and journal metrics (IF, EF, citability) with indicators of country-level disparities. The study reports mean values for APC ($1344.27), IF (2.855), EF (0.017), and total citation count (5925.92) for the n = 237 sample.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is demonstrating that APC is positively and significantly correlated with IF (r = 0.391), EF (r = 0.303), and citability (r = 0.323) in GOA natural science journals, with the largest disparities favoring developed-country publishers. 2. The strongest evidence is the quantitative showing that publishers from developed countries disproportionately hold higher APC, IF, EF, and citability, creating structural barriers for researchers from developing nations and unaffiliated independent scholars. 3. The future path requires structural reform of APC funding eligibility (e.g., Research4Life) and a shift away from cost-driven prestige to ensure important research is recognized regardless of institutional or national resources.

summary.title: Highly sensitive and full-genome interrogation of SARS-CoV-2 using multiplexed PCR enrichment followed by next-generation sequencing
summary.authors: Chenyu Li, David N Debruyne, Julia Spencer, Vidushi Kapoor, Lily Y Liu, Bo Zhou, Utsav Pandey, Moiz Bootwalla, Dejerianne Ostrow, Dennis T Maglinte, David Ruble, Alex Ryutov, Lishuang Shen, Lucie Lee, Rounak Feigelman, Grayson Burdon, Jeffrey Liu, Alejandra Oliva, Adam Borcherding, Hongdong Tan, Alexander E Urban, Xiaowu Gai, Jennifer Dien Bard, Guoying Liu, Zhitong Liu
summary.field_subfield: Molecular Diagnostics / Genomics and Virology / SARS-CoV-2 Surveillance
summary.type_of_paper: Method development and validation (technical paper with mathematical modeling and experimental validation)
summary.executive_summary: This study addresses the limitations of RT-PCR for SARS-CoV-2 diagnosis, where only 47-59% of positive cases were identified due to low viral load, sampling timing, or mutations. The authors developed a multiplex-PCR method using 343 pairs of specific primers (172 in the first pool, 171 in the second overlapping pool) targeting the entire SARS-CoV-2 genome. Mathematical modeling established that while RT-PCR detects 4.8 copies at 95% probability, the single 172-primer panel detects 1.15 copies, and combining both pools yields 0.29 copies at 95% probability. Experimental validation using S and N gene plasmids spiked into human RNA confirmed detection from 8,900 down to 2.8 copies, with electrophoretic visualization of library peaks across a dynamic range. In clinical application, 13 nasopharyngeal swab specimens with viral loads from 8 to 675,885 RNA copies/uL were amplified; approximately 95-99% genome coverage at 100X was achieved. Mutations were identified at seven clustered loci, including the D614G variant in 11/13 specimens. A secondary metagenomic multiplex-PCR method using random hexamer-adapters achieved >96% S and N gene coverage with only ~0.6M reads per library, with no host depletion. No cross-reactivity with MERS-CoV, CoV 229E, CoV OC43, CoV NL63, or CoV HKU1 was observed (0% read alignment).
