The multiplex PCR approach is highly specific, differentiating SARS-CoV-2 from other human coronaviruses and influenza viruses with 0% cross-reactivity.
The multiplex-PCR-based metagenomic method achieves >96% S and N gene coverage with only ~0.6M total reads per library, eliminating the need for host depletion.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study addresses the limitations of RT-PCR for SARS-CoV-2 diagnosis, where only 47-59% of positive cases were identified due to low viral load, sampling timing, or mutations. The authors developed a multiplex-PCR method using 343 pairs of specific primers (172 in the first pool, 171 in the second overlapping pool) targeting the entire SARS-CoV-2 genome. Mathematical modeling established that while RT-PCR detects 4.8 copies at 95% probability, the single 172-primer panel detects 1.15 copies, and combining both pools yields 0.29 copies at 95% probability. Experimental validation using S and N gene plasmids spiked into human RNA confirmed detection from 8,900 down to 2.8 copies, with electrophoretic visualization of library peaks across a dynamic range. In clinical application, 13 nasopharyngeal swab specimens with viral loads from 8 to 675,885 RNA copies/uL were amplified; approximately 95-99% genome coverage at 100X was achieved. Mutations were identified at seven clustered loci, including the D614G variant in 11/13 specimens. A secondary metagenomic multiplex-PCR method using random hexamer-adapters achieved >96% S and N gene coverage with only ~0.6M reads per library, with no host depletion. No cross-reactivity with MERS-CoV, CoV 229E, CoV OC43, CoV NL63, or CoV HKU1 was observed (0% read alignment).

Research Context
RT-PCR is the gold standard for SARS-CoV-2 diagnosis but has demonstrated limited sensitivity, with only 47-59% of positive cases identified. Approximately 75% of RT-PCR negative results were actually later found to be positive by other assays. Under laboratory conditions, RT-PCR detects 4-8 copies of virus at 95% confidence intervals. Heat inactivation of clinical samples may cause loss of viral particles, further hindering downstream diagnosis. SARS-CoV-2 must be distinguished from influenza, adenovirus, respiratory syncytial virus, and bacterial pneumonia pathogens. Full-length viral genome sequencing via NGS is essential for surveillance of evolution and community spread containment. Multiplex PCR has been shown to detect Hantaan orthohantavirus and Plasmodium falciparum with 99% coverage and 99.8% specificity.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can multiplex-PCR targeting hundreds of genomic regions simultaneously achieve higher sensitivity than RT-PCR and tolerate primer-site mutations? The authors hypothesized that RT-PCR assays could only detect 4.8 copies of SARS-CoV-2 at 95% probability based on a mathematical model. The model predicted the probability of RT-PCR detecting one copy of SARS-CoV-2 is only 26%. The mathematical model estimated that a 172-primer panel would detect 1.15 copies at 95% probability, and both overlapping pools would detect 0.29 copies. The LOD of both RT-PCR and multiplex-PCR appears to be independent of viral genome size across 4 to 100 kb. The authors hypothesized that 80% of targeted regions would be amplified successfully, based on prior reports of 79% variant recovery from 600 amplicons. A multiplex-PCR-based metagenomic method could achieve sufficient coverage with a moderate sequencing depth of approximately 1 million reads.

Methodological Details
The first multiplex PCR pool contained 172 pairs of specific primers targeting the entire SARS-CoV-2 genome. The second overlapping pool contained 171 pairs of primer pairs targeting gaps between the first pool's regions. Average amplicon length was 99 bp with a 76±10 bp gap between adjacent amplicons. Two plasmids containing full S and N gene sequences of SARS-CoV-2 were used for validation. Plasmids were spiked into cDNA generated from human total RNA to simulate clinical samples. Copy numbers were determined by droplet-based digital PCR using a QX200 system. Plasmids were diluted from approximately 9,000 copies to below one copy. 13 nasopharyngeal swab specimens were used for clinical validation, all previously RT-PCR positive. Viral loads ranged from 8 to 675,885 RNA copies per microliter. Sequencing was performed on an Illumina MiSeq platform. For the metagenomic method, 4,500 copies of N and S gene plasmids were spiked into 10 ng of human gDNA. This roughly represents 3,300 haploid genomes in the mock mixture. Mutations were detected using two independently developed algorithms, only reporting consensus calls. Mutations with frequency greater than 60% were considered empirically true. No UMI (Unique Molecular Identifier) was used in the multiplex PCR amplification.

Procedures And Architectures
RT-PCR mathematical model used 100 bp amplicon length and 30 kb genome size (NC_045512.2) with 99% efficiency. Multiplex PCR efficiency was estimated at 6% for single-strand cDNA, based on 26% for four DNA strands of human chromosomes. Multiplex PCR products were further amplified in a secondary PCR where sample indexes and NGS sequencing primers were added. PCR products were analyzed by electrophoresis to visualize characteristic target peaks before sequencing. The metagenomic method used random hexamer-adapters for DNA/cDNA amplification and a background removal reagent for non-specific products. For RNA samples, reverse transcription reagents converted RNA to cDNA with reduced ribosomal RNA species. Sub-sampling of sequencing data to 150,000, 100,000, and 50,000 total reads per library was performed to assess minimum depth. The mathematical model for RT-PCR predicted a 26% detection probability for one copy, but the 172-amplicon panel (28 targets in experiment) gave a 16% chance. Experimental results showed 56% probability to detect 1.1 copies, suggesting higher-than-modeled efficiency. Mutations with %AF ≤ 60% were considered potential intra-host heterogeneity; a 20% cutoff was applied to eliminate noise.

Key Results
The first 172-primer panel (with 28 targets amplified from plasmids) provided library peaks from 8,900 down to 2.8 copies. Quantification of library peaks demonstrated a wide dynamic range from 1 to about 1,000 copies. Library yield saturated when copy number reached approximately 1,700 copies. In contrast, RT-PCR detection of a single S gene target rapidly dropped at 2.85 copies. With 14 plasmid copies, approximately 96% of amplicons were recovered; with 2.8 copies, 77%; and with 0.6 copies, 37%. Approximately 96% of the genome was covered at 100X for 8 copies of virus in clinical specimens. For 22 to 675,885 copies, 98-99% of the genome was covered at 100X at an average depth of 5,000 reads per amplicon. At 150,000 total reads per library (437 reads per amplicon), at least 93% of the genome was covered at 100X. At 100,000 total reads (291 reads per amplicon), 86% genome coverage at 100X was achieved. At 50,000 total reads, at least 58% genome coverage at 100X was maintained. The metagenomic method achieved 16% viral bases (13% viral reads) within human gDNA at 0.6M reads per library. 80% of SARS-CoV-2 and 78% of mitochondrial targets were covered in the metagenomic experiment. Only 0.08% of human chromosomal regions were amplified in the metagenomic approach. After optimization, 96% of the SARS-CoV-2 genome was recovered in the metagenomic method. All 13 strains contained at least one mutation reported to be associated with SARS-CoV-2 virulence. The D614G mutation was found in 11 of the 13 specimens. In group 1 and 3 (high copy/depth), only one intra-host mutation per genome was found in some specimens. Group 2 had low copy numbers and low read depth, with considerably higher numbers of apparent intra-host mutations.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Multiplex PCR simultaneously targets and amplifies hundreds of genomic regions, theoretically increasing the frequency of occurrence in the mathematical model. Amplifying multiple targets potentially detects fragments of degraded viral nucleotide and tolerates genomic variations. The finding that LOD is independent of viral genome size suggests the mathematical model's robustness across different pathogens. The experimentally observed 56% detection probability (vs. predicted 12%) suggests multiplex PCR efficiency on single-stranded cDNA is higher than the 6% estimate. Random hexamers appear to deselect a large portion of the human genome while favorably amplifying regions with more random base composition. The 10-fold difference in coverage across amplicons is a routinely observed phenomenon with multiplex PCR technology and indicates a ceiling to depth-based improvement. Zero alignment of sequencing reads from any of the 13 samples to MERS-CoV, CoV 229E, CoV OC43, CoV NL63, or CoV HKU1 demonstrates complete specificity. The clustering of mutations around seven loci likely reflects transmission within close communities or specific lineage transmission. Low copy number and sequencing depth can cause reduction in %AF and introduce false intra-host mutations.

Contradictions And Limitations
One genome from the 5,000 copy sample showed only 96% coverage at 100X, lower than expected, potentially due to poor sample quality from RNA processing or handling. The mathematical model predicted a 12% chance to detect 1.1 copies based on 6% efficiency, but experimental observation showed 56%, indicating a discrepancy in efficiency estimation. Since no UMI was used, intra-host mutations may still be contaminated with noise from PCR amplification. Some true intra-host mutations with %AF < 20% might be missed due to the noise cutoff. The metagenomic method required only ~0.6M reads per library, but the authors acknowledge verification and validation are still necessary. A simple fluorometric or spectrophotometric measurement of dsDNA concentration is insufficient to differentiate target amplicons from primer dimers in negative samples. For accurate phylogenetic studies, high-depth sequencing (>300K reads) and high viral load (>100 copies) are deemed necessary, limiting the method's applicability at very low loads. The authors caution against interpreting intra-host mutations from low input viral particles and low sequencing depth.

Claims
The multiplex PCR method achieves detection limits (0.29 copies at 95% probability when using both pools) significantly lower than RT-PCR (4.8 copies at 95% probability), making it superior for early or low-viral-load diagnosis. RT-PCR detects 4.8 copies at 95% probability based on mathematical modeling. The 172-primer panel detects 1.15 copies at 95% probability. Using both pools leads to a calculated detection limit of 0.29 copies at 95% probability. Experimental detection ranged from 8,900 down to 2.8 copies, with library peaks maintained. At 1.4 copies, approximately 96% of amplicons were recovered. In practice, the 172-amplicon panel (tested with 28 targets) only showed a 16% chance to detect one single copy, not the predicted 12% from a 6% efficiency model. The experimentally observed 56% detection probability at 1.1 copies indicates the 6% single-strand efficiency estimate may be overly conservative. The method can be deployed in various laboratory settings for rapid, highly sensitive diagnosis of SARS-CoV-2. Single electrophoresis analysis provides a fast indication of infection from at least the coronaviridae family.
The multiplex PCR approach is highly specific, differentiating SARS-CoV-2 from other human coronaviruses and influenza viruses with 0% cross-reactivity. Zero sequencing reads from each of the 13 samples aligned to MERS-CoV, CoV 229E, CoV OC43, CoV NL63, or CoV HKU1. This specificity was verified across 13 clinical specimens with varying viral loads. Multiplex PCR could potentially amplify other coronaviruses due to shared sequence similarities, despite primer specificity. NGS sequencing is still required for definitive virus identification; electrophoresis alone is not sufficient. The panel could be expanded to include simultaneous detection of other respiratory viruses including influenza.
The multiplex-PCR-based metagenomic method achieves >96% S and N gene coverage with only ~0.6M total reads per library, eliminating the need for host depletion. The metagenomic method achieved 96% of the SARS-CoV-2 genome recovered after optimization. Only ~0.6M total reads per library were required, versus 1M reads suggested by the random hexamer model. No additional means of host depletion (removal of human gDNA and rRNA) were used. SARS-CoV-2 bases represented 16% of total recovered bases in the sequencing. Only 80% of SARS-CoV-2 and 78% of mitochondrial targets were initially covered before optimization. The authors note that verification and validation of the metagenomic method are still necessary. The method could identify unknown or emerging pathogens with moderate sequencing depth. The coverage is superior to the recommended 50% threshold for genome drafting.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Sub-sampling of sequencing data to 150,000, 100,000, and 50,000 total reads per library was performed to test sensitivity to depth. The mathematical model tested LOD across viral genome sizes from 4 to 100 kb, showing LOD was independent of genome size. Two independently developed algorithms were used for mutation calling, with consensus only reported. A 20% AF cutoff was selected based on the mutation profile from sequencing synthetic SARS-CoV-2 RNA controls. The metagenomic method was optimized from initial 80% coverage to 96% S and N gene recovery.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A shows the mathematical model predicting RT-PCR detection at 4.8 copies of SARS-CoV-2 at 95% probability, with predicted probability of one copy at 26%. Figure 1B illustrates the design of the 172-primer panel and the overlapping gaps of the 171-primer second pool. Figure 1C shows the model predicting the 172-primer panel detects 1.15 copies at 95% probability. Figure 2A displays electrophoresis of library peaks for plasmids at 8,900 down to 2.8 copies. Figure 2B shows quantification of peak yield across a dynamic range from 1 to about 1,000 copies, saturating at 1,700. Figure 2C shows the experimentally observed 56% probability to detect 1.1 copies in multiplex PCR. Figure 3A shows genome coverage versus viral copy number for the 13 clinical specimens. Figure 3B displays genome coverage at 100X under three sequencing depth conditions. Figure 3E illustrates the distribution of mutations across the seven clustered loci and the three sample groups. Figure 4A shows the proportion of viral bases among total recovered bases in the metagenomic approach. Figure 4B displays coverage of SARS-CoV-2 and mitochondrial targets in the metagenomic method. Figure 4G shows optimized 96% SARS-CoV-2 genome recovery in the metagenomic approach.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a multiplex-PCR method using 343 primer pairs targeting the entire SARS-CoV-2 genome, achieving a calculated detection limit of 0.29 copies at 95% probability, significantly exceeding RT-PCR sensitivity and tolerating primer-site mutations. 2. The strongest evidence is experimental validation showing detection from 8,900 down to 2.8 plasmid copies with electrophoretic peak visualization, and clinical amplification of 13 specimens with viral loads as low as 8 copies, maintaining 95-99% 100X genome coverage. 3. The future path involves validating the metagenomic method for broader pathogen detection, expanding the panel to include other respiratory viruses like influenza, and applying the method to surveillance of emerging and highly mutated SARS-CoV-2 lineages.

summary.title: Translational accuracy of a tethered ribosome
summary.authors: Celine Fabret (CNRS); Olivier Namy (CNRS)
summary.field_subfield: Molecular Biology / Translation Machinery / Ribosome Structure and Function
summary.executive_summary: This study investigates the translational properties of Ribo-T, a tethered ribosome in Escherichia coli where the small (30S) and large (50S) subunits are covalently linked by short RNA linkers, rendering them inseparable. The authors test whether this structural constraint impairs translational accuracy, specifically examining -1 and +1 frameshifting, stop codon readthrough, and internal translation initiation. Using a dual-reporter plasmid system (pCL99 lacZ-luc fusion) and the E. coli BL21 (DE3) background, they measured translational efficiency across various recoding signals. The central finding is that covalent attachment modifies ribosome behavior: Ribo-T ribosomes are insensitive to Shine-Dalgarno (SD) sequences for both initiation and frameshifting, show a profound deficit in +1 frameshifting (2% vs. 33% WT), and exhibit impaired stop codon termination (increased readthrough). Conversely, -1 frameshifting is maintained at wild-type levels regardless of SD context, and internal translation initiation proceeds effectively. The authors attribute the SD-insensitivity to structural modifications of helix 44 (H44), where the anti-Shine-Dalgarno (ASD) sequence resides, and propose that reduced A-site dynamics explain impaired termination. The paper concludes that while Ribo-T ribosomes support cell viability and maintain basic translation, they demonstrate specific, predictable alterations in fidelity mechanisms tied to SD-ASD interactions and subunit mobility.

claims.description: Ribo-T ribosomes are insensitive to the Shine-Dalgarno sequence for both -1 and +1 frameshifting and for translation initiation.
Ribo-T ribosomes exhibit impaired stop codon termination, increasing readthrough rates.
Internal translation initiation occurs in Ribo-T cells through internal loading of the 70S ribosome rather than scanning.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigates the translational properties of Ribo-T, a tethered ribosome in Escherichia coli where the small (30S) and large (50S) subunits are covalently linked by short RNA linkers, rendering them inseparable. The authors test whether this structural constraint impairs translational accuracy, specifically examining -1 and +1 frameshifting, stop codon readthrough, and internal translation initiation. Using a dual-reporter plasmid system (pCL99 lacZ-luc fusion) and the E. coli BL21 (DE3) background, they measured translational efficiency across various recoding signals. The central finding is that covalent attachment modifies ribosome behavior: Ribo-T ribosomes are insensitive to Shine-Dalgarno (SD) sequences for both initiation and frameshifting, show a profound deficit in +1 frameshifting (2% vs. 33% WT), and exhibit impaired stop codon termination (increased readthrough). Conversely, -1 frameshifting is maintained at wild-type levels regardless of SD context, and internal translation initiation proceeds effectively. The authors attribute the SD-insensitivity to structural modifications of helix 44 (H44), where the anti-Shine-Dalgarno (ASD) sequence resides, and propose that reduced A-site dynamics explain impaired termination. The paper concludes that while Ribo-T ribosomes support cell viability and maintain basic translation, they demonstrate specific, predictable alterations in fidelity mechanisms tied to SD-ASD interactions and subunit mobility.

Research Context
Ribosomes are evolutionary conserved ribonucleoprotein complexes consisting of two separate subunits in all kingdoms. Translation comprises four major phases: initiation, elongation, termination, and ribosome recycling, each requiring transient complexes with auxiliary factors. The 30S subunit contains 16S rRNA and 21 ribosomal proteins for decoding, while the 50S subunit contains 5S and 23S rRNAs with 33 proteins for peptide bond formation. A tethered ribosome, Ribo-T, with covalently linked subunits was recently engineered in Escherichia coli using hybrid rRNA linked by short RNA linkers. Ribo-T was shown to be functional, sustain cell growth, but exhibited slower doubling times (107 min vs. 35 min WT) and reduced protein synthesis rate. The slow growth was attributed to slower Ribo-T biogenesis rather than impaired ribosome activity. Cell viability depends on a balance between rapid protein synthesis and accurate decoding; recoding events (frameshifting, stop codon readthrough) serve as tools for probing fidelity.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether Ribo-T ribosomes maintain the correct reading frame, terminate accurately at stop codons, and translate mRNA faithfully compared to wild-type ribosomes. The study tests whether the inseparable subunits impair -1 or +1 frameshifting, stop codon readthrough, and internal translation initiation. The implicit hypothesis is that the covalent linkage might constrain ribosomal mobility, potentially affecting SD-ASD interactions during initiation and elongation. The authors specifically investigate if Ribo-T ribosomes frameshift independently of the SD sequence given that they cannot base-pair to the wild-type SD. A secondary question is whether Ribo-T ribosomes can use internal translation initiation or re-initiation strategies given the lack of subunit dissociation. The predicted outcome is that tethered subunits modify translational properties, altering the ability to initiate and terminate translation correctly.

Methodological Details
Experiments were performed in Escherichia coli BL21 (DE3) strain with and without the poRibo-T2 vector carrying Ribo-T ribosomal DNA. The ASD sequence of the Ribo-T 16S rRNA was altered from 5'-UCACCUCCUUA-3' to an orthogonal sequence 5'-UCAUUGUGGUA-. The bacterial pCL99 dual reporter system was used, carrying a lacZ-luc fusion gene under the T7 promoter with streptomycin resistance. Target sequences for translational accuracy were inserted by oligocloning into the MscI restriction site at the lacZ-luc junction. Double-stranded oligonucleotides were prepared by hybridizing complementary strands after heating at 100°C for 5 min and incubation at room temperature. In-frame controls were constructed for each target sequence and all constructs were verified by sequencing. Translational efficiency was calculated as the ratio of luciferase activity to β-galactosidase activity for the target divided by the ratio for the in-frame control. The median value was calculated for at least six independent experiments. Significance of differences was determined using Student's t-tests. Wild-type SD sequence (AGGAGG) was used for wild-type ribosome analysis; mutated SD sequence (CACCAC) was used for Ribo-T ribosomes. The mutated SD sequence was complementary to the 3' end of the Ribo-T 16S rRNA to enable Ribo-T-specific initiation. Crosstalk between wild-type and orthogonal mRNA was checked; Ribo-T-specific SD mutants generated too little β-galactosidase with WT ribosomes only for measurement. The lacZ-lacY intergenic sequence used for initiation analysis was 46 nucleotides long. The mtmB1 stop codon sequence from Methanosarcina barkeri was used for termination assays. Three -1 frameshifting sites were selected: IS911, IS3, and dnaX. +1 frameshifting site was selected from the E. coli prfB gene.

Procedures And Architectures
Frameshifting assays utilized the IS911, IS3, and dnaX -1 sites, which require a slippery sequence, an RNA structure (stem-loop or pseudoknot), and an SD sequence upstream. WT SD-recognized -1 frameshifting efficiencies were 13%, 8%, and 60% for IS911, IS3, and dnaX respectively under control conditions. For +1 frameshifting, the prfB site depends on a poor termination context (UGA C) and stimulatory SD sequence. Stop codon readthrough was quantified by the proportion of the ribosome reading the termination codon as a sense codon and continuing to the next stop. For initiation assays, the 46-nucleotide lacZ-lacY sequence was modified by deleting or replacing the SD sequence with the Ribo-T specific SD. To assess internal loading vs. scanning, a stable stem-loop roadblock was inserted downstream of lacZ. The dual reporter system measured luciferase activity (luc) as the downstream reporter and β-galactosidase (lacZ) as the upstream reporter. The plasmid carries a CDF replicon derived from CloDF13.

Key Results
For -1 frameshifting, IS911 efficiency was 13% with WT ribosomes and 14% with Ribo-T ribosomes (p-value 0.54), showing no significant difference. IS3 -1 frameshifting was 33% with either ribosome type (p-value 0.77), and dnaX was 43% for WT vs. 45% for Ribo-T (p-value 0.77). Replacing dnaX SD with Ribo-T-recognized SD decreased WT frameshifting to 11% (from 43%, p-value 1.7x10⁻³), but Ribo-T remained at 45% vs. 44% (p-value 0.85). For +1 frameshifting, WT ribosomes achieved 33% efficiency, while Ribo-T ribosomes achieved only 2% (p-value 8.9x10⁻⁹). Replacing the WT SD with a Ribo-T-recognized SD did not restore Ribo-T +1 frameshifting to 1.8% (p-value 0.56), but reduced WT +1 frameshifting to 0.6% (from 33%, p-value 1.6x10⁻⁵). In initiation, Ribo-T ribosomes produced no statistically significant difference in luciferase activity when using the Ribo-T SD versus no SD (p-value 0.04). With Ribo-T ribosomes present, luciferase induction was increased four-fold (p-value 4.7x10⁻⁴) when the Ribo-T SD was present upstream of lacZ versus no SD, matching the magnitude of WT SD stimulation. The higher activity ratio for Ribo-T ribosomes translating both lacZ and luc resulted from lower β-galactosidase levels compared to WT ribosomes. Insertion of a stem-loop roadblock after lacZ had no effect on luc initiation (p-value 0.22), indicating internal loading rather than scanning. Stop codon readthrough for Ribo-T was 0.07% (UAG), 0.26% (UGA), and 0.04% (UAA), compared to WT at 0.013%, 0.11%, and 0.01% respectively (p-values 4.7x10⁻⁷, 5x10⁻³, 2.5x10⁻⁴). The Ribo-T doubling time was 107 min compared to 35 min for WT cells. Ribo-T protein synthesis rate was 50% that of wild-type ribosomes.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Ribo-T ribosomes are insensitive to SD sequences for both initiation and frameshifting, indicating a general detachment from SD-ASD interaction mechanisms. The SD-ASD interaction in +1 frameshifting causes release of deacylated E-site tRNA and destabilization of the ribosome complex, whereas the mechanism differs for -1 frameshifting. The two subunits are linked via helix 44 (H44), which plays an important role in translation initiation fidelity; tethering may modify the geometry and orientation of the ASD at the top of H44. Reduced A-site dynamics in Ribo-T ribosomes, caused by covalent linkage, may limit binding of termination factors and promote stop codon readthrough. The increased ribosome density at start codons and 3' ends observed in Ribo-T cells (from ribosome profiling) is consistent with impaired initiation and termination/recycling steps. The SD sequence may not be strictly necessary for initiation; absence of the SD is sufficient for translation at AUG codons in unstructured regions. The greater-than-expected flexibility of ribosomes allows a functional tethered variant to sustain cell growth despite significant alterations in translational fidelity.

Contradictions And Limitations
The paper is a bioRxiv preprint not certified by peer review. The exact doubling time difference (107 min vs. 35 min) was noted, but the mechanism was attributed to biogenesis, not translational defects. No natural stop codon readthrough sequence exists in E. coli, necessitating use of an archaeal sequence (mtmB1) which might not perfectly mirror native termination dynamics. The authors note that the mechanism of Ribo-T initiation in the absence of SD remains unclear, and a high-resolution structure is needed. The crosstalk level between WT and Ribo-T was measured but the authors state it was 'too low to affect the results,' without providing a quantitative crosstalk metric. The p-value for Ribo-T SD vs. no SD in initiation was 0.04, which is borderline significance; the authors interpreted this as no difference but the result is near the threshold.

Claims
Ribo-T ribosomes are insensitive to the Shine-Dalgarno sequence for both -1 and +1 frameshifting and for translation initiation. Ribo-T -1 frameshifting was 14% for IS911 and 45% for dnaX, essentially equal to WT (13% and 43%), regardless of SD sequence. When the WT SD was replaced with a Ribo-T SD, WT frameshifting dropped to 11% but Ribo-T remained at 45%. Ribo-T +1 frameshifting was only 2% vs. 33% for WT, and replacing the SD with a Ribo-T-recognized sequence did not restore efficiency (1.8%). Ribo-T ribosomes showed no statistically significant difference in luc activity between Ribo-T SD and no SD (p-value 0.04). The initiation p-value of 0.04 is borderline, and the authors do not provide a quantitative crosstalk measurement. The SD sequence, long considered critical for initiation and elongation control, may be functionally dispensable in the context of tRNA-mediated recoding.
Ribo-T ribosomes exhibit impaired stop codon termination, increasing readthrough rates. Ribo-T readthrough was 0.07% (UAG), 0.26% (UGA), 0.04% (UAA) versus WT at 0.013%, 0.11%, 0.01%. The p-values were 4.7x10⁻⁷, 5x10⁻³, and 2.5x10⁻⁴ respectively, all highly significant.  Reduced subunit mobility or constrained A-site dynamics in Ribo-T may impair termination factor binding or conformational transitions required for peptide release.
Internal translation initiation occurs in Ribo-T cells through internal loading of the 70S ribosome rather than scanning. The long intergenic sequence with three stop codons would not favor a scanning process. A stable stem-loop roadblock after lacZ had no effect on luc initiation (p-value 0.22), indicating internal loading. Ribo-T ribosomes in the Ribo-T vector cannot dissociate, making scanning physically impossible.  The tethered ribosome phenotype forces an internal loading mechanism, which may have different fidelity characteristics than 30S-mediated initiation.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The SD-insensitivity of Ribo-T was validated by the reverse experiment: replacing the dnaX SD with a Ribo-T-recognized sequence, which altered WT activity but not Ribo-T activity. The +1 frameshifting deficit was tested by SD replacement, which showed the effect was independent of SD recognition, ruling out simple SD incompatibility as the sole explanation. The initiation mechanism was validated with a stem-loop roadblock as a structural control against scanning. Crosstalk between WT and Ribo-T mRNA was checked by measuring expression with Ribo-T-specific SD in the absence of Ribo-T ribosomes. The Ribo-T protein synthesis rate (50% WT) and doubling time (107 min vs 35 min WT) were measured to assess overall translational impact.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the three selected -1 frameshifting sites (IS911, IS3, dnaX) with their associated RNA structures. Figure 2A presents the -1 frameshifting efficiencies for IS911 (13% WT vs 14% Ribo-T), IS3 (33% vs 33%), and dnaX (43% vs 45%). Figure 2B shows the reverse SD-swap experiment at the dnaX site (WT: 43% to 11%; Ribo-T: 45% to 44%). Figure 3A shows the prfB +1 frameshifting site with poor termination context. Figure 3B shows the +1 frameshifting efficiency (WT: 33% vs. Ribo-T: 2%) at prfB. Figure 3C shows the +1 frameshifting after SD replacement (Ribo-T: 1.8%; WT: 0.6%). Figure 4 shows the initiation assays with various SD conditions and the Ribo-T SD swap. Figure 4C shows the Ribo-T SD swap at lacZ giving 4-fold luc induction relative to no-SD. Figure 4D shows the stem-loop roadblock assay confirming internal loading. Figure 5 shows stop codon readthrough efficiencies for UAG, UGA, UAA in WT and Ribo-T. Table 1 lists all target sequences and their construction details.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first systematic characterization of translational accuracy in a tethered ribosome, revealing that covalent subunit linkage abolishes SD-ASD mediated regulation of both initiation and frameshifting while preserving -1 frameshifting fidelity and supporting cell growth. 2. The strongest evidence is the multi-modal convergence of -1 frameshifting (maintained at WT levels regardless of SD), +1 frameshifting (profoundly impaired to 2%), initiation (SD-insensitive), and termination (increased readthrough) across three independent translational events, all consistent with SD-ASD and subunit mobility constraints. 3. The future path involves elucidating the structural basis through high-resolution Ribo-T structures to understand how tethering modifies H44 geometry, and investigating whether similar tethered ribosomes are functional in eukaryotes without SD-ASD initiation.

summary.title: Efficient and Flexible Integration of Variant Characteristics in Rare Variant Association Studies Using Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation
summary.authors: Hana Susak; Laura Serra-Saurina; Raquel Rabionet Janssen; Laura Domènech; Mattia Bosio; Francesc Muyas; Xavier Estivill; Georgia Escaramís; Stephan Ossowski
summary.field_subfield: Bioinformatics / Statistical Genetics
summary.type_of_paper: Methodological with benchmark and application study
summary.executive_summary:
This paper introduces BATI, a novel Bayesian rare variant association test using Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation (INLA) for the association of rare genetic variants with complex diseases in case-control study designs. Rare variant association studies (RVAS) face significant power limitations in small-to-medium cohorts when genetic variation explains a small fraction of phenotypic variance. Existing methods such as burden tests (e.g., Burden, SKAT, SKAT-O, KBAC) and variance-component tests (MiST, HBMR) face computational bottlenecks or model-specification trade-offs. BATI overcomes these by employing INLA, a non-sampling-based numerical approximation that estimates full hierarchical Bayesian models of latent Gaussian random fields faster and more accurately than Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), while maintaining the flexibility to integrate arbitrary categorical and numeric variant-specific characteristics as covariates.

The authors benchmark BATI against five existing RVAS tests—Burden, SKAT-O, KBAC, MiST, and HBMR—using realistic semi-synthetic breast cancer cohorts generated by combining thousands of real WES datasets with known ClinVar risk variants. For 8 breast cancer risk genes (including BRCA2, BARD1, CHEK2, PALB2) under 100 simulations each, BATI identifies all risk genes at 0.1% type I error rate (TIER) with >80% power even at 0.5% variance explained (VE), whereas competing methods fail selectively. At 0.01% TIER, BATI identifies all risk genes while Burden, KBAC, and SKAT-O recurrently miss BRCA2; HBMR misses BARD1, CHEK2, and PALB2. The framework is integrated into rvGWAS, a comprehensive RVAS package including quality control, filtering, population structure detection, and multiple association tests. A practical application to a Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia study identified eight candidate predisposition genes including EHMT2 and COPS7A. The work demonstrates that using functional annotation as prior information significantly boosts power without penalizing performance for genes containing mostly missense variants.

MiST performs poorly on realistic WES cohorts compared to artificial benchmark sets due to zero-inflated p-value issues.
The semi-synthetic cohort design is superior to pure simulations for benchmarking RVAS methods.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper introduces BATI, a novel Bayesian rare variant association test using Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation (INLA) for the association of rare genetic variants with complex diseases in case-control study designs. Rare variant association studies (RVAS) face significant power limitations in small-to-medium cohorts when genetic variation explains a small fraction of phenotypic variance. Existing methods such as burden tests (e.g., Burden, SKAT, SKAT-O, KBAC) and variance-component tests (MiST, HBMR) face computational bottlenecks or model-specification trade-offs. BATI overcomes these by employing INLA, a non-sampling-based numerical approximation that estimates full hierarchical Bayesian models of latent Gaussian random fields faster and more accurately than Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), while maintaining the flexibility to integrate arbitrary categorical and numeric variant-specific characteristics as covariates.

The authors benchmark BATI against five existing RVAS tests—Burden, SKAT-O, KBAC, MiST, and HBMR—using realistic semi-synthetic breast cancer cohorts generated by combining thousands of real WES datasets with known ClinVar risk variants. For 8 breast cancer risk genes (including BRCA2, BARD1, CHEK2, PALB2) under 100 simulations each, BATI identifies all risk genes at 0.1% type I error rate (TIER) with >80% power even at 0.5% variance explained (VE), whereas competing methods fail selectively. At 0.01% TIER, BATI identifies all risk genes while Burden, KBAC, and SKAT-O recurrently miss BRCA2; HBMR misses BARD1, CHEK2, and PALB2. The framework is integrated into rvGWAS, a comprehensive RVAS package including quality control, filtering, population structure detection, and multiple association tests. A practical application to a Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia study identified eight candidate predisposition genes including EHMT2 and COPS7A. The work demonstrates that using functional annotation as prior information significantly boosts power without penalizing performance for genes containing mostly missense variants.

Research Context
Next-generation sequencing enables genome-wide rare variant association studies for complex diseases in large cohorts. Rare variants play an important role in disease etiology and may explain missing heritability. Rare variants are more likely to affect protein structure, stability, or function than common variants. A major difficulty is the lack of statistical power when few individuals carry rare alternative alleles. Existing score-based burden tests pool minor alleles but assume unidirectional effects, which is rarely true. Variance-component methods like SKAT and C-alpha address heterogeneous effects but do not easily incorporate functional covariates. MiST and HBMR incorporate variant characteristics but face computational bottlenecks or use score tests under the null rather than full model inference. Prior benchmarking studies relied on pure simulations of variants that lack the complexity of real data.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can a Bayesian RVAS test leveraging INLA outperform existing methods by integrating functional variant characteristics as covariates? Is it possible to estimate the full Bayesian model for rare variant association without the computational bottlenecks of MCMC? The hypothesis is that incorporating categorical and numeric variant-specific features as priors increases power when associated variants share common functional impact. The authors predict that BATI will outperform established RVAS methods on realistic semi-synthetic cohorts, especially when using meaningful biological context. A specific prediction is that BATI achieves power above 75% in scenarios where risk variants explain less than 0.5% of phenotypic variance. The authors further hypothesize that BATI will successfully cope with complex population structure and confounders in real-world datasets.

Methodological Details
The study uses a hierarchical Bayesian framework for case-control rare variant association with N individuals. The phenotype Y follows an exponential family distribution with logit link for binary outcomes. The model specifies linear predictors with fixed effects for covariates and random effects for genetic variants. Variant-specific effects are modeled as random effects with a prior covariance structure accounting for heterogeneous effects. Covariates include both categorical and numeric genetic variant characteristics as fixed effects. } The benchmark uses realistic semi-synthetic cohorts derived from thousands of real WES datasets. Two large datasets served as the simulation basis: 1000Genomes Project and the Iberian cohort. From 1000GP, half the samples were assigned as cases and half as controls. For the Iberian cohort, one third were cases and two thirds were controls. ClinVar risk variants annotated as exonic or splicing were queried for breast cancer predisposition. Variants with MAF > 0.01 in any ancestry population in EVS, 1000GP, or ExAC were removed. The cohort contained 1,810 total individuals in the main benchmark. The Iberian cohort variant was smaller at 1,167 total individuals. Model selection uses the difference in Deviance Information Criterion (∆DIC) between null and alternative models. Ten random splits of the cohort were used to establish empirical significance thresholds for each method. Type I error rate thresholds were derived at 5%, 0.1%, and 0.01% TIER levels. The median threshold across 10 splits was used to label genes as significant. The Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia study provided the application dataset.

Procedures And Architectures
The BATI model is implemented as a hierarchical Bayesian GLMM using the R-INLA package (version 17.06.20). INLA uses numerical approximations based on the Laplace approximation rather than MCMC simulations. The likelihood is defined with a logistic link: logit(η_i) = X_i'α + Z_i'β + ε_i. The genetic random effects follow a multivariate normal distribution with a structured covariance matrix. Variant characteristics are integrated as fixed effects, allowing for arbitrary categorical and numeric covariates. Model selection is performed via ∆DIC = DIC(H0) - DIC(H1), with a rule-of-thumb threshold of 10. To establish robust thresholds, S = 10 datasets are randomly shuffled, and the median of 10 ∆DIC thresholds is used. The rvGWAS framework integrates: quality control, interactive filtering, population structure detection, functional annotation, and six association tests. The six tests are: Burden, SKAT-O, KBAC, MiST, HBMR, and BATI. Power is estimated across 100 simulations of risk variants for each of the 8 risk genes. A disease cohort simulator combines thousands of real WES datasets with known risk variants for selected disease types. The simulator randomly assigns WES samples to case or control groups and introduces ClinVar risk variants into case VCF files. Two large datasets served as the basis: one from 1000GP and another from the Iberian cohort. For each of the 10 random cohort splits, p-value significance thresholds were obtained for all methods.

Key Results
BATI achieves power close to 100% for three risk genes when variance explained (VE) is 0.5% and TIER is 0.01%. The median power for the three risk genes at 0.5% VE and 0.01% TIER is 55%. At 0.5% VE and 0.01% TIER, all methods except BATI show power close to 0. BATI calls most genes with TIER 0.01% even at VE of 0.5%. At TIER 0.1%, BATI identifies all genes with >80% power at VE of 0.5%. All methods except MiST identify all risk genes at 0.01% TIER in the 2% VE setting. Burden, KBAC, and SKAT-O recurrently fail to call BRCA2 (both missense and LoF versions) at TIER 0.1% and 0.01%. HBMR fails to call BARD1, CHEK2, and PALB2 already at TIER 0.1%. For the Iberian cohort (VE 0.5%, TIER 0.01%), BATI's performance is stable despite the smaller cohort size. The power plots at 0.5% VE look very similar when comparing Burden, KBAC, and SKAT-O. MiST failed to identify any risk gene at low VE or low TIER thresholds in the realistic WES cohort. In the Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia application, eight candidate predisposition genes were identified. Two identified genes in CLL were EHMT2 and COPS7A. At 0.01% TIER, only 2 genes out of approximately 20,000 are expected as significant by chance. BATI's performance remains stable across the 8 breast cancer risk gene architectures.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
BATI's advantage stems from the flexible integration of categorical and numeric variant characteristics as covariates. Including functional impact estimates as priors strongly boosts power when risk genes contain mostly LoF variants. BATI performs at least as well as other methods for genes containing mostly missense variants. The INLA framework allows for non-sampling-based inference that is both faster and more accurate than MCMC for hierarchical latent Gaussian models. The semi-synthetic design, combining real WES noise with real ClinVar variants, makes benchmark findings more applicable to clinical genetics than pure simulations. The study reveals that the performance gap between methods is most profound at low VE (0.5%-1%) rather than at high VE. The finding that Burden, KBAC, and SKAT-O share similar strengths and weaknesses suggests they should be combined with different approaches. The rvGWAS framework provides a user-friendly, integrated pipeline for RVAS from QC to multiple association tests. The BATI approach can be further extended to other complex statistical models within the INLA framework.

Contradictions And Limitations
The Iberian cohort is smaller (1,167 individuals) than the 1000GP cohort (1,810 individuals), and most tests perform slightly worse. MiST performed poorly on the realistic WES cohorts due to zero-inflated p-values from inappropriate handling of low variant counts. The study does not report a specific random seed or fixed seed across all simulations, though S = 10 random splits were used for threshold estimation. The exact demographics of the 1000GP and Iberian cohorts used are not detailed beyond general descriptions. The number of random simulations performed for the power analysis is stated as '100 simulations' per gene but the total permutation count is not quantified. The paper does not report the exact computational time per gene or per genome-wide scan, only that INLA is faster than MCMC. The type I error rate of 0.01% was derived empirically and the authors note only 2 genes out of 20,000 are expected as significant by chance, a very low bar for genome-wide inference.

Claims
BATI outperforms existing RVAS methods on realistic semi-synthetic cohorts when prior biological information is used. BATI identifies all risk genes at TIER 0.1% with >80% power at 0.5% VE. Competing methods fail to call BRCA2, BARD1, CHEK2, and PALB2 at 0.5% VE and 0.1% TIER. BATI maintains stable performance across different genetic architectures. BATI achieves power close to 100% for three risk genes at 0.5% VE and 0.01% TIER. At 0.5% VE and 0.01% TIER, the median power is 55%, not 100%. Most tests perform slightly worse in the smaller Iberian cohort. Functional annotation should be integrated into standard RVAS workflows to improve discovery. INLA provides a computationally feasible alternative to MCMC for Bayesian RVAS.
MiST performs poorly on realistic WES cohorts compared to artificial benchmark sets due to zero-inflated p-value issues. MiST failed to identify any risk gene at low VE or low TIER thresholds in realistic WES cohorts. MiST showed favorable results on purely artificial benchmark sets but performed poorly on realistic WES cohorts. MiST is among the methods that identify all risk genes at 2% VE in the realistic cohort. Careful handling of low variant counts is critical in mixed-effects RVAS designs.
The semi-synthetic cohort design is superior to pure simulations for benchmarking RVAS methods. Prior simulations yielded overly optimistic benchmark performances and unrealistic expectations. Random 'causal' variants hamper benchmarking of methods leveraging characteristics of causal variants. Semi-synthetic cohorts combine real WES noise with real ClinVar variants. The Iberian cohort results show slight variability, indicating some sensitivity to cohort size. Realistic simulation design is necessary for trustworthy clinical genetics benchmarking.

Data And Code Availability
BATI and the rvGWAS framework are implemented within the R-INLA project and the R package INLA version 17.06.20. The rvGWAS framework supports multiple RVAS tests and data processing pipelines.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Ten random cohort splits were performed to empirically estimate significance thresholds, with the median used to establish robustness. Simulations were repeated across 100 iterations for each risk gene architecture. Two different real-world cohorts (1000GP and Iberian) were used for cross-cohort validation. Comparisons were made across three TIER levels (5%, 0.1%, 0.01%) to test sensitivity to significance threshold. The semi-synthetic design allowed testing of different disease architectures with varying VE levels (2%, 1%, 0.5%). The comparison included four standard tests plus two Bayesian alternatives to assess relative performance broadly.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 3 and Table 2 show gene-wise power plots and performance metrics for 8 risk genes in the 1000GP cohort. Supplementary S8 Figure shows power results for the Iberian cohort. Supplementary S6 Figure shows p-value significance thresholds across 10 random cohort splits. Supplementary S4 Table reports TIER levels for each method. Table 1 lists the thresholds used for subsequent power analyses. Supplementary S8 Figure shows BATI achieves power close to 100% at 0.5% VE and 0.01% TIER in the Iberian cohort.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is BATI, a Bayesian RVAS test using INLA that enables full-model Bayesian inference with arbitrary variant covariates at a fraction of the computational cost of MCMC. 2. The strongest evidence is BATI's identification of all 8 breast cancer risk genes at TIER 0.1% even with only 0.5% variance explained, while competing methods fail selectively or completely. 3. The future path lies in extending rvGWAS to broader disease contexts beyond breast cancer, incorporating more comprehensive variant annotations, and applying BATI to other complex trait associations.

summary.title: A Combined Evidence Approach to Prioritize Nipah Virus Inhibitors
summary.authors: Nishi Kumari, Ayush Upadhyay, Kishan Kalia, Rakesh Kumar, Kanika Tuteja, Rani Paul, Eugenia Covernton, Tina Sharma, Vinod Scaria, Anshu Bhardwaj
summary.field_subfield: Drug Discovery / Virology / Computational Chemistry
summary.type_of_paper: Data curation and prioritization study (knowledgebase development)
summary.executive_summary: This paper describes the systematic identification, curation, and prioritization of Nipah virus inhibitors (NVIs) through a multi-pronged computational and informatics approach. Nipah virus, a highly pathogenic RNA virus (case fatality rate over 75%) with no approved treatment, is on WHO's R&D Blueprint list of priority diseases. The authors developed the Nipah Virus Inhibitor Knowledgebase (NVIK), an open-access LAMP-based web platform hosting 182 NVI entries, including 98 unique small-molecule inhibitors. Data were mined from 838 PubMed/Google-identified papers and manually curated using a two-person verification system. For prioritization, the authors computed over 1800 (PaDel: 1875) physicochemical descriptors for all NVIs and compared them against 2,346 FDA-approved compounds and 4,644 Enamine antiviral library compounds. A combined evidence strategy was applied: (i) DruLito and PAINS filtering for drug-likeness and toxicity, (ii) assay robustness evaluation (ranking inhibitors based on the quality of identifying assays), and (iii) structural similarity mapping. Of 98 small-molecule NVIs, only a few passed all DruLito filters. Independent assay robustness scoring narrowed the field further. The top 10 NVIs were prioritized based on combined drug-likeness and assay reliability. Notably, EC50/IC50 values as low as 0.47 nM were reported. The study identifies chemical diversity in the NVI set (90 clusters among 98 NVIs) and provides actionable drug repurposing and scaffold discovery leads. The platform allows community submissions to maintain the database.

claims.description: The NVIK provides a unique, systematic, and community-driven knowledgebase for Nipah virus inhibitor discovery.
A combined evidence strategy (assay robustness plus druglike filtering) is superior to single-metric prioritization for NVIs.

Executive Summary
This paper describes the systematic identification, curation, and prioritization of Nipah virus inhibitors (NVIs) through a multi-pronged computational and informatics approach. Nipah virus, a highly pathogenic RNA virus (case fatality rate over 75%) with no approved treatment, is on WHO's R&D Blueprint list of priority diseases. The authors developed the Nipah Virus Inhibitor Knowledgebase (NVIK), an open-access LAMP-based web platform hosting 182 NVI entries, including 98 unique small-molecule inhibitors. Data were mined from 838 PubMed/Google-identified papers and manually curated using a two-person verification system. For prioritization, the authors computed over 1800 (PaDel: 1875) physicochemical descriptors for all NVIs and compared them against 2,346 FDA-approved compounds and 4,644 Enamine antiviral library compounds. A combined evidence strategy was applied: (i) DruLito and PAINS filtering for drug-likeness and toxicity, (ii) assay robustness evaluation (ranking inhibitors based on the quality of identifying assays), and (iii) structural similarity mapping. Of 98 small-molecule NVIs, only a few passed all DruLito filters. Independent assay robustness scoring narrowed the field further. The top 10 NVIs were prioritized based on combined drug-likeness and assay reliability. Notably, EC50/IC50 values as low as 0.47 nM were reported. The study identifies chemical diversity in the NVI set (90 clusters among 98 NVIs) and provides actionable drug repurposing and scaffold discovery leads. The platform allows community submissions to maintain the database.

Research Context
Nipah virus is a pleomorphic enveloped RNA virus belonging to the Paramyxoviridae family with a particle size ranging from 40 to 1,900nm. The first outbreak occurred in Malaysia between September 29, 1998, and April 4, 1999, with subsequent annual outbreaks in Bangladesh and surrounding regions. Mortality rates from Nipah virus infections have been observed to range from 50-100%. Human-to-human transmission has been observed among healthcare professionals and relatives of infected patients. The virus causes cell-to-cell fusion, forming multinucleated cells called syncytia, which influences its pathogenicity. Broad-spectrum antiviral ribavirin has shown contradictory results with even the most optimistic mortality reduction significantly below 50%. Despite several experimental compounds showing protection in animal models, no single drug is under clinical trial against Nipah virus. Existing antiviral inhibitor databases (IRD, ViPR) contain limited or no specific information with a focus on Nipah virus inhibitors. The WHO's R&D Blueprint list of priority diseases (2018) indicates an urgent need for accelerated research and development for Nipah virus.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether a systematic, multi-parameter curation and prioritization framework can identify druglike, non-toxic Nipah virus inhibitors from the heterogeneous literature. The authors hypothesize that combining structural druglike filtering with assay robustness scoring will yield a prioritized subset of NVIs suitable for further medicinal chemistry. A secondary objective is to map the chemical space of NVIs relative to FDA-approved drugs and existing antiviral scaffolds for drug repurposing opportunities. The study predicts that NVI structural diversity will be characterized by near neighbors with differing molecular weights, suggesting common pharmacophoric features. The authors predict that a web-based platform with crowdsourcing capabilities will facilitate continuous update of the NVI landscape. It was anticipated that very few NVIs would pass stringent druglike filters simultaneously, highlighting the need for multi-criteria prioritization.

Methodological Details
Two main sources, PubMed and Google, were used to identify research papers relevant to Nipah virus inhibitors. The query 'Nipah' was used, and papers with the keyword in their abstract or title were shortlisted, totaling 838 papers. A scoring system assigned scores of 10 (confirmed inhibitor info), 5 (possible info), 4 (peptides), and 0 (no relevant info). Papers with scores of 10, 5, and 4 were manually curated into a Nipah Virus Inhibitor Knowledgebase (NVIK) sheet with a predefined data structure. Data quality was ensured by a separate team of curators re-performing the curation independently; errors marked 'Red' were verified 'Green' after cross-team verification. The database includes 182 total entries, of which 125 are small-molecule inhibitors (the remaining 57 were peptides or incomplete). Of 125 small-molecule entries, 98 are unique inhibitors (some compounds appeared in multiple assays), and EC50/IC50 values were obtained for 70 compounds. A total of 1875 descriptors were calculated for the compounds using PaDel software. NVIs were compared against 2,346 FDA-approved compounds and 4,644 Enamine antiviral library compounds. Near neighbors were identified using NNeib (version 5.12.0) and clusters were obtained using Jarp (version 6.0.2) based on a dissimilarity threshold of 0.15 (1-Tanimoto coefficient). Cytoscape was used to generate compound network diagrams for visualization of clusters.

Procedures And Architectures
The NVIK platform is developed using open-source LAMP (Linux-Apache-Mysql-PHP) server technology, with PHP, HTML, JavaScript, AJAX, and CSS for the web interface. The web interface includes 'Simple Search' (text-based), 'Query Builder' (complex logical AND/OR queries), and 'Structure Search' (SMILES, SDF, MOL formats, plus JSME drawing tool). Compounds are browsed by physicochemical properties: molecular weight, XLogP, polar surface area (PSA), HBD, HBA, and rotatable bonds. DruLito was used for drug-likeness filtering based on eight filters: Lipinski's, MDDR-like, Veber, Ghose, BBB, CMC-50, and weighted/unweighted QED. PAINS filters were applied to eliminate pan-assay interference compounds and assess toxicity profiles. Assay robustness was evaluated independently by ranking NVIs based on the quality and reliability of the assays through which they were initially identified. Customized CIRCOS was used to represent the relationship among physicochemical properties of NVIs, with 98 inhibitors defined at a band width of 1000. The database allows community submission of new inhibitors through a dedicated submission form that records physicochemical properties and database statistics.

Key Results
The NVIK contains 182 entries with EC50/IC50 values ranging from 0.25 nM to 7,562,710 nM for 182 entries and 0.47 nM to 7,562,710 nM for 125 small-molecule entries. Clustering of 98 NVIs resulted in 90 clusters, of which 84 clusters (93.3% of NVIs) were singletons and 14 clusters (15.5% of NVIs) were non-singletons. Only two of 91 compounds passed all DruLito filters except the CMC filter, indicating high stringency. Of 98 small-molecule NVIs, 34 were found similar to 76 FDA-approved drugs, including structural similarity between NVIC0097 and four FDA molecules. The top 11 NVIs were prioritized based on independent assay robustness scoring. Further refinement narrowed the prioritized list to the top 10 NVIs based on combined drug-likeness and assay reliability. Among prioritized compounds, NVIC0048 passed 6 DruLito filters and showed the highest degree of overlap with all six physicochemical parameter ranges of FDA-approved drugs. NVIC0032 exhibited better activity among the shortlisted three and considerable overlap with the physicochemical properties of FDA-approved drugs. GS-441524 (531.202 g/mol) was identified as a near neighbor of GS-441524"NUC" (291.267 g/mol), suggesting common structural features despite different molecular weights. Most NVIs in the database are cyclic in nature, a property consistent with a majority of FDA-approved drugs.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The chemical diversity (84% singletons) of the NVI library suggests a wide structural space for future medicinal chemistry development. Near neighbors with significantly different molecular weights indicate that common pharmacophoric features, rather than bulk physicochemical properties, drive antiviral activity. Structural similarity to FDA drugs (e.g., NVIC0097 similar to Ademetionine, Vidarabine) provides clear targets for drug repurposing. The fact that only two compounds passed most DruLito filters underscores the difficulty in obtaining both antiviral activity and ideal druglike properties simultaneously. The platform architecture enables continuous community-driven enhancement, aligning with the need for ongoing curation in pandemic preparedness. The prioritization methodology (combining assay quality with drug-likeness) provides a more rigorous selection criterion than single-metric filtering.

Contradictions And Limitations
The study notes that ribavirin has shown contradictory results with even optimistic mortality reduction below 50%, complicating the clinical landscape. No single drug is under clinical trial against Nipah virus, limiting real-world efficacy evidence. The NVIK contains 57 entries that are peptides or have incomplete information, limiting the scope of small-molecule prioritization. EC50/IC50 values were obtained for only 70 of 98 small-molecule inhibitors, leaving 28 without quantitative bioactivity data. The data was curated from literature, and the authors note that some compounds may have been reported with more than one assay, potentially inflating the entry count before deduplication. The study does not report specific random seeds, reproducibility metrics, or a validation dataset for the prioritization algorithm beyond the described manual verification.

Claims
The NVIK provides a unique, systematic, and community-driven knowledgebase for Nipah virus inhibitor discovery. The platform hosts 182 entries curated from 838 literature papers. Data is publicly available via a LAMP-based web interface with advanced search tools. The platform allows community submissions of new compounds. 57 of 182 entries are peptides or incomplete, limiting small-molecule utility. The knowledgebase serves as a centralized resource for future antiviral research against Nipah and other viruses.
A combined evidence strategy (assay robustness plus druglike filtering) is superior to single-metric prioritization for NVIs. Only 11 NVIs were prioritized based on assay robustness alone, then refined to the top 10. Only two of 91 compounds passed all but one DruLito filter. NVIC0048 showed the best overlap with FDA-approved physicochemical parameters. The authors note that even the most optimistic mortality reduction for ribavirin remains below 50%. The prioritized compounds offer validated starting points for medicinal chemistry and drug repurposing.

Data And Code Availability
The NVIK is publicly available at http://vinodscaria.rnabiology.org/nipah for browsing and submission. The platform was incepted in May 2018 and is continuously updated. Compounds are mapped to Pubchem/Chemspider IDs wherever possible.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Data quality was verified by a separate curation team re-performing all curation independently. The scoring system for papers (10, 5, 4, 0) serves as a quality control mechanism for the input data source. Clustering was performed with a fixed dissimilarity threshold of 0.15 (1-Tanimoto coefficient). DruLito screening was applied as a separate filter from assay robustness prioritization, and the two were combined.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the unique fields in the NVIK database and is referenced for general database structure. Figure 2 depicts the overall distribution of important physicochemical properties of NVIs, including near neighbor clusters. Figure 3 compares NVIs with FDA-approved compounds and Enamine antiviral library compounds. Figure 4 shows the DruLito filter results, demonstrating only two compounds passed most filters. Table 1 (referenced but not shown in text) defines the predefined data structure of the NVIK sheet. Table 2 (referenced but not shown in text) reports physicochemical parameter ranges for prioritized NVIs versus FDA drugs.

Three Takeaways
1. The NVIK is the first systematic, publicly accessible, and continuously updated knowledgebase of 182 Nipah virus inhibitors, including 98 unique small molecules, with EC50/IC50 values down to 0.47 nM. 2. The combined evidence strategy—filtering by drug-likeness (DruLito/PAINS) AND assay robustness—is critical because single-metric filtering is too permissive (only 2 of 91 passed DruLito) or too restrictive. 3. The prioritization identifies NVIC0048 as the most promising druglike candidate, while near-neighbor analysis (e.g., GS-441524) points toward common pharmacophoric features across differing molecular weights for antiviral activity.
