judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study integrated 3D genome architecture analysis (Hi-C), RNA-seq, and translocation detection in 18 newly diagnosed T-lineage acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) patients and 4 healthy T cell controls to elucidate the role of chromatin organization in T-ALL pathogenesis. The authors found that 3D genome alterations at the compartment, TAD, and loop levels, combined with gene expression profiles, hierarchically classify T-ALL subtypes along the T cell differentiation trajectory. Approximately 29% of differentially expressed genes were associated with 3D structural changes, with upregulated genes enriched in hematopoietic lineage and cell cycle pathways, and downregulated genes in cytokine and TCR signaling. ETP ALL samples, representing an immature differentiation state, were separated from non-ETP ALLs by loop-level structural signatures, showing 1820 enhanced and 831 reduced loops. Adaptation of hic_breakfinder identified 46 translocations, including 34 novel noncoding events, which formed 44 new translocation-mediated loops and drove enhancer hijacking of the HOXA cluster. Two mechanisms were identified: 'cis' enhancer hijacking (e.g., BCL11B-TLX3, TRB-TAL2) and 'trans' gene fusions (e.g., PSIP1-NUP98, SET-NUP214, MLL) activating the HOXA cluster. Hierarchical clustering of HOXA expression revealed that ectopic HOXA11-A13 expression, driven by 5' TAD rearrangements, is associated with double negative and ETP phenotypes, higher JAK-STAT pathway mutations, and poor overall survival in pediatric and young adult T-ALL. HOXA13 positive status emerged as an independent prognostic indicator for overall survival. The study demonstrates that 3D genome rewiring, independent of conventional driver mutations, is a fundamental etiological and prognostic feature of T-ALL differentiation blocking.

Research Context
3D genome alterations have been demonstrated to play important roles in tumorigenesis, including hematological malignancies. However, how such alterations provide key insights into T-lineage acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) patients remains largely unknown. Chromosomal translocation is a major driving force for leukemia, but the functional consequence of noncoding structural changes is not well established. The dysregulated HOXA cluster is a common feature of T-ALL, but whether HOXA-positive T-ALLs represent a homogeneous clinical entity has not been systematically studied. The mechanism of HOXA cluster activation by fusion proteins recruiting DOT1L was known, but could not explain diverse expression patterns associated with different fusion proteins.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether 3D genome alterations link to the etiology of T-ALL development and how they correlate with gene expression changes. The authors hypothesized that 3D genome organization could hierarchically classify T-ALL subtypes according to the T cell differentiation trajectory. It was further hypothesized that T-ALL samples represent 'frozen stages' of T cell development, with chromosomal organization differences separating ETP and non-ETP subtypes. A specific hypothesis was tested whether translocation-mediated enhancer hijacking or gene fusions activate T-ALL-associated transcription factors and block differentiation. The study also aimed to determine whether HOXA cluster overexpression represents a homogeneous clinical entity and if its expression patterns correlate with prognosis. A key prediction was that 3D genome alterations could associate with approximately 45% of upregulated genes in T-ALL, of which a majority would be directly related to structural changes.

Methodological Details
Eighteen T-ALL patient samples were collected under the protocol approved by the ethics committee of the Institute of Hematology at Peking University. Four healthy T cell controls were obtained from four healthy donors under Peking University ethics committee approval. Leukemia blast cells were prepared by density-gradient centrifugation of bone marrow samples, followed by CD19-CD14-CD235-CD45+CD7+ cell purification by FACS. Hi-C was performed on one million cells per sample according to the BL-Hi-C protocol. RNA-seq libraries were prepared with TruSeq RNA Library Prep Kit v2, with an average depth of 15 million read pairs. ChIP-seq reads were mapped to hg19 with Bowtie2, and ATAC-seq reads were mapped with Bowtie2 using parameter -X 2000. For translocation detection, hic_breakfinder was adapted, treating Hi-C raw data as single ends due to 486 million read pairs average depth and 150 bp read length. The HOXA cluster was partitioned into two TADs, with C11/13 used as the 3' boundary of the 5' TAD in all samples. Six enhancer regions, labeled E1 to E12, were identified within each TAD interacting with the HOXA cluster. Survival analysis used a cohort of T-ALL patients with outcome information described in a companion paper. The ETP status was defined according to previously published criteria.

Procedures And Architectures
RNA-seq reads were aligned to hg19 with TopHat (v2.1.0), duplicates removed, and counts calculated by HTSeq before FPKM transformation. Differentially expressed genes were identified with DESeq2 using FDR <0.01 and fold change >2, excluding genes with fewer than 5 reads in 20% of samples. Hi-C processing integrated ChIA-PET2 for bridge linker trimming, HiC-Pro for alignment and artifact removal, and Juicer for contact matrix generation. KR-normalized matrices were used for compartment and TAD analysis at 100 kb resolution. TAD boundaries were calculated by the insulation score method with parameters -is 1000000 -ids 200000 -im mean -nt 0.1 on pooled 40 kb matrices. Loops were called using HiCCUPS, and differential loop detection was adapted from the Douglas et al method, splitting loops into >150 kb and <150 kb distance ranges. Loop aggregation analysis (APA) was performed under 5 kb resolution using Juicer. Translocation detection used hic_breakfinder; breakpoints were refined to single base-pair resolution by treating Hi-C reads as single ends, with at least 3 chimeric reads required for support. A translocation was considered novel if any breakpoint was not within 100 kb of any known breakpoint from references 2, 4, and ChimerPub. ChIP-seq and ATAC-seq peaks were generated using MACS2 with the -SPMR option. FIMO was used to detect the 20 bp CTCF motif from the Homer motif database in Loucy and Jurkat peaks. The domain score was calculated as intra-TAD interactions divided by all interactions connected to the corresponding TAD. RcisTarget was used to predict key transcription factors controlling upregulated genes in T-ALLs. V4C plots were generated at 10 kb resolution using MATLAB code.

Key Results
Approximately 29% (996/3392) of DEGs were associated with 3D genome alterations. 3D genome alterations were associated with nearly 45% of upregulated genes in T-ALL, of which 56% could be directly related to structural alterations. Among upregulated DEGs, B-to-A compartment switches, increased domain scores, and enhanced loops were mostly upregulated, enriched in hematopoietic cell lineage, transcriptional misregulation, and cell cycle pathways. A-to-B compartment switches, decreased D-scores, and reduced loops were mostly downregulated, enriched in cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction and TCR signaling pathways. The CDK6 locus exhibited a strong intra-TAD interaction, and its expression was upregulated in all T-ALL samples. Transcription factor SOX4, WT1, and TFDP2 had structural alterations at all three levels (compartment, TAD, loop) and were top-ranking candidates predicted by RcisTarget to regulate approximately 28% of upregulated genes. ETP ALL samples were arrested at the immature stage (LMPP to Thy1 stages) while non-ETP samples were arrested at Thy2 to Thy4 stages in PCA projection. ETP and non-ETP ALLs were better separated at the loop level, with 1820 enhanced and 831 reduced loops identified in ETP samples relative to controls. A Pearson's correlation coefficient of 0.685 was found between gene expression changes and the combined p-value of loop strength and D-score changes. Approximately 20% of upregulated genes in ETP and 16% in non-ETP ALL harbored chromatin structure changes, including CEBPA, MYCN, LYL1 for ETP and LEF1, TCF12, PAX9 for non-ETP. 46 translocations were identified in 14/18 T-ALL samples, with 34 novel events and 26 interchromosomal events. Among 78 unique breakpoints, 47% were in noncoding regions and 66% were in the stable A compartment. 44 new translocation-mediated loops formed across translocated chromosomes, with nearly 78% of those with CTCF motifs linked to pairs of convergently orientated CTCF motifs. There was a complete match between loop-based hierarchical clustering and T-ALL subtypes (HOXA, TLX, TAL) signified by translocation-mediated dysregulation. Translocation-mediated enhancer hijacking was identified in ETP, TLX, and TAL subtypes, with BCL11B-TLX3, TRB-TAL2, and 3 novel HOXA translocations. The PSIP1-NUP98, SET-NUP214, and MLL (KMT2A-MLLT1, PICALM-MLLT10, DDX3X-MLLT10) fusion events were trans-mechanisms activating HOXA cluster gene expression. HOXA-positive T-ALLs were further separated into 3'HOXA+ and 5'HOXA+ subgroups based on gene expression patterns within the cluster. The HOXA11-A13 positive subgroup (associated with DN and ETP phenotypes) was linked to poor overall and event-free survivals in young adult and pediatric T-ALLs. HOXA13+ status was an independent predictor for overall survival of pediatric and young adult T-ALLs in multivariate analysis. T-ALLs with HOXA11-A13 positivity had a higher rate of JAK-STAT pathway gene mutations compared to HOXA1-A10+, TAL+, and TLX+ samples.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The study demonstrates that 3D genome alterations at multiple levels (compartment, TAD, loop) act as a hierarchical framework that governs gene expression and defines T-ALL differentiation states. The chromosomal organization of T-ALL represents 'frozen stages' of T cell development, with translocation-mediated loops and domain score changes providing a structural readout of developmental arrest. Enhancer hijacking via translocation-mediated loops provides a mechanistically concrete pathway for ectopic activation of T-ALL-associated transcription factors from genes normally expressed in healthy T cell development. The dual-mechanism (cis enhancer hijacking and trans gene fusions) explains how different fusion events can converge on the same pathogenic HOXA cluster dysregulation through distinct 3D architectural alterations. The isolation of the 5' TAD from the 3' TAD by CTCF barriers explains why specific HOXA genes are selectively affected by translocations, defining discrete clinical and structural subgroups within HOXA-positive T-ALL. The association of ectopic HOXA11-A13 with poor prognosis and JAK-STAT pathway mutations suggests a specific, potentially actionable subgroup of T-ALL that may benefit from anti-JAK-STAT inhibitors.

Contradictions And Limitations
The study only examined 18 T-ALL patients, which may limit generalizability and power for prognostic conclusions. TCR rearrangement status and RAG1/PTCRA expression were not uniform across ETP ALL samples, introducing heterogeneity within the subtype. The study did not report a random seed or specific train/test split, limiting direct reproducibility of the 3D analysis parameters. The exact age and demographic distribution of the 18 patients were only described in Supplementary Table 7, not in the main text. The survival analysis cohort was a separate cohort (companion paper), meaning the prognosis findings could not be directly validated in the 18 primary patients. HOXA9, the previously used biomarker, did not associate with poor survival in this study, contradicting earlier clinical assumptions. TLX positivity had no association with outcome, contrasting with the strong prognostic value of HOXA11-A13. Only 14/18 T-ALL samples had translocation detection, leaving 4 samples without translocation assessment. The 5/7 HOXA+ samples with detectable translocations may not capture all HOXA-driven T-ALL mechanisms.

Claims
3D genome alterations at compartment, TAD, and loop levels, combined with gene expression profiles, hierarchically classify T-ALL subtypes according to the T cell differentiation trajectory. PCA and hierarchical clustering showed transcriptome changes highly consistent with 3D structural changes. Loop-level analysis separated ETP from non-ETP samples, consistent with developmental stages. A Pearson's correlation of 0.685 linked gene expression to loop/D-score changes. Sample 093 fell between ETP and non-ETP ALL in both 3D and expression clustering. The lack of TCR rearrangement in most ETP samples was not observed in all, introducing intra-subtype heterogeneity. Structural alterations at all three levels (compartment, TAD, loop) are required to fully explain the expression of core transcription factors. 3D genome architecture could serve as a diagnostic readout for T-ALL differentiation arrest.
Translocation-mediated enhancer hijacking and gene fusions activate the HOXA cluster and drive ectopic transcription factor expression that blocks T cell differentiation. 34 novel noncoding translocations and 44 translocation-mediated loops were identified. BCL11B-TLX3, TRB-TAL2, and three novel HOXA translocations drove cis enhancer hijacking. PSIP1-NUP98, SET-NUP214, and MLL fusions drove trans epigenetic activation of HOXA. HOXA11-A13 positive subgroup showed higher JAK-STAT mutations and poor survival. The HOXA-T cases showed ectopic HOXA11-A13 but did not exhibit the same survival outcomes as other HOXA-positive subgroups. Not all HOXA-positive samples carried detectable translocations (only 5/7). Anti-JAK-STAT inhibitors may benefit the HOXA11-A13+ subgroup of T-ALL. Specific fusion events preferentially alter the 3D genome interactome within the HOXA cluster.
HOXA11-A13 positive T-ALL is a distinct, high-risk clinical entity associated with poor prognosis and a specific differentiation phenotype. HOXA13+ status was an independent predictor for overall survival in multivariate analysis. HOXA11-A13 positive cases were characterized by DN and ETP phenotypes. HOXA9, the previously used biomarker, did not correlate with poor survival in this study. TLX positivity had no association with survival, limiting the prognostic utility of other T-ALL subtypes. The HOXA-T cases (3 samples) with translocation-mediated HOXA11-A13 showed the 5'HOXA+ phenotype but survival data were not explicitly broken down for individual translocation cases. HOXA11-A13 is a more specific and powerful prognostic biomarker than HOXA9. The DN phenotype and JAK-STAT mutations provide additional risk-stratification criteria for HOXA-positive T-ALL.

Data And Code Availability
Raw RNA-seq data for Loucy and Jurkat cell lines were downloaded from the GEO database. Hi-C raw data were processed by an in-house HiCpipe framework. Hi-C and ChIP-seq tracks were generated using pyGenomeTracks. Visual 4C plots were generated using MATLAB code. Translocation analysis used hic_breakfinder adapted from reference 20. No explicit statement on data sharing or public repository availability for the primary patient data is provided in the text.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
For loop detection, HiCCUPS-called loops were split into two distance ranges (>150 kb and <150 kb) to minimize potential bias. The domain score calculation normalized intra-TAD interactions by all interactions connected to the corresponding TAD. Differential TAD boundaries were defined with a t-test FDR<0.01 and a difference between cases and controls higher than 50% quantile. For translocation verification, a minimum of 3 chimeric reads was required to call a breakpoint at single base-pair resolution. The 5% false discovery rate for differential loop detection was the FDR threshold used. Loop aggregation analysis (APA) under 5 kb resolution was used to assess loop detection quality. The HOXA- cases served as the common denominator for calculating differential interaction intensities across all samples. ChIP-seq of the HOXA+ Loucy cell line confirmed that increased interactions correlated with gains in H3K27ac.

Ethical Considerations
Eighteen T-ALL patient samples were collected under the protocol approved by the ethics committee of the Institute of Hematology at Peking University. Peripheral blood samples from four healthy donors were obtained under the approval of the ethics committee of Peking University. No explicit statement regarding informed consent, genetic counseling, or long-term follow-up is detailed in the text.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 presents integrated 3D genome alterations and RNA-seq results, showing compartment switches, TAD boundary changes, loop density, and hierarchical clustering of T-ALL subtypes. Figure 1c and 1d show upregulated genes associated with B-to-A compartment switches, increased D-scores, and enhanced loops, with red bars indicating upregulation. Figure 1e shows pathway enrichment of compartment-associated genes: hematopoietic lineage and cell cycle for B-to-A; cytokine and TCR for A-to-B. Figure 1f shows the CDK6 locus with strong intra-TAD interaction and upregulation across all T-ALL samples. Figure 1g identifies SOX4, WT1, and TFDP2 as transcription factors with structural alterations at all three levels (compartment, TAD, loop). Figure 2a shows PCA projection of T-ALL samples onto the T cell developmental trajectory, separating ETP from non-ETP samples. Figure 2b displays enhanced and reduced loops in ETP versus non-ETP ALL samples, with 1820 enhanced and 831 reduced loops. Figure 2c shows the correlation between loop/D-score changes and gene expression changes (Pearson's 0.685). Figure 2d presents GO pathway enrichment for ETP and non-ETP loop-associated genes. Figure 2e shows Hi-C maps with TCR rearrangements or lack thereof in ETP vs non-ETP samples. Figure 2f shows RAG1 and PTCRA expression levels in ETP samples. Figure 2g and 2h show subtype-specific loops and expression at MEF2C (ETP) and PAX9 (non-ETP) loci. Figure 3a shows translocation maps with 46 translocations, 34 novel events, and translocation-mediated loops. Figure 3b shows translocation-mediated loop anchors at pre-existing loop anchors and CTCF binding sites. Figure 3c shows nearly 78% of translocation-mediated loops with CTCF motifs linked to convergently orientated CTCF motifs. Figure 3d shows loop-based hierarchical clustering matching T-ALL subtypes HOXA, TLX, TAL. Figure 3e shows translocation-mediated enhancer hijacking at BCL11B-TLX3 and TRB-TAL2. Figure 4a shows hierarchical clustering of HOXA gene expressions separating 15 samples into 3'HOXA+ and 5'HOXA+ subgroups. Figure 4b shows Hi-C maps and CTCF motif orientations for the 11 HOXA genes across TAD boundaries. Figure 4c shows 12 interaction regions (E1-E12) with enhanced interactions in HOXA+ subgroups. Figure 4d shows HOXA gene expression and translocation association with fusion proteins. Figure 5a and b show new loop formation at the HOXA cluster for translocation cases 076 and 077. Figure 5c shows the inter-TAD inversion and new loop formation for translocation case 108. Figure 5d shows CTCF binding sites C11/13, C7/9, and C10/11 insulacting 3' TAD genes. Figure 6a shows Kaplan-Meier survival curves for HOXA11-A13, TAL1/2, and TLX positive T-ALLs. Figure 6b shows DN and ETP phenotype characterization of HOXA11-A13+ cases. Figure 6c shows JAK-STAT pathway mutation rates. Figure 6d shows multivariate Cox regression for HOXA13+ survival.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first integrated 3D genome, RNA-seq, and translocation analysis in T-ALL, revealing that 3D architecture acts as a hierarchical scaffold for T-ALL differentiation blocking, with translocation-mediated enhancer hijacking and gene fusions driving subtype-specific gene expression. 2. The strongest evidence is the complete match between loop-level structural clustering and established T-ALL subtypes (HOXA, TLX, TAL), corroborated by a Pearson's correlation of 0.685 between loop/D-score changes and gene expression, and the identification of 44 novel translocation-mediated loops. 3. The future path involves validating HOXA11-A13 positive T-ALL as an independent prognostic biomarker for pediatric and young adult patients, testing anti-JAK-STAT inhibitors in this high-risk subgroup, and expanding 3D genome mapping to other T-lineage hematological malignancies.

summary.title: ProNetView-ccRCC: A web-based portal to interactively explore clear cell renal cell carcinoma proteogenomics networks
summary.authors: Selim Kalayci; Francesca Petralia; Pei Wang; Zeynep H Gümüş
summary.field_subfield: Bioinformatics / Network Visualization / Proteogenomics
summary.executive_summary:
ProNetView-ccRCC is an interactive, open-access, web-based portal developed to facilitate visual exploration and interpretation of phosphopeptide co-expression networks in clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC). The platform addresses a critical gap in cancer proteomics: while CPTAC has produced comprehensive proteogenomic data generating complex network models, existing tools are primarily suited for static 2D visualization in print publications rather than user-initiated interactive exploration. 

Built on the Three.js WebGL framework, ProNetView-ccRCC enables 3D interactive visualization of the overall ccRCC phosphopeptide co-expression network comprised of 3,614 genes (representing 20,976 phosphopeptides) and 30 functional pathway-enriched network modules containing at least 20 genes each. The network was constructed using a random-forest based algorithm applied to phosphopeptide-level data from 103 ccRCC samples. 

Key features include: (1) a 3D network exploration interface supporting rotation and zooming; (2) gene/protein querying with automatic highlighting of first-degree neighbors; (3) association querying between phosphopeptide abundance and clinical variables (tumor grade, stage, age, gender) with user-defined FDR cut-offs; (4) pathway enrichment tables with interactive gene lists; and (5) integration with the ProTrack tool for multi-omics heatmap analysis. 

Demonstration examples include the oncogene ERG, which connects to 11 genes within module 26 (Angiogenesis) and maps to 5 peptides, showing a significant association with tumor grade (p-value: 0.003, FDR: 0.118). The portal requires no plugins and runs on all modern web browsers, aiming to lower the computational barrier for the cancer research community to conduct hypothesis-generating analyses on CPTAC ccRCC network data.

claims.description: ProNetView-ccRCC provides an intuitive, 3D web-based interactive portal for exploring the CPTAC ccRCC phosphopeptide co-expression network and 30 functional modules.
The portal supports real-time querying of phosphopeptide associations with clinical variables (tumor grade, stage, age, gender) at user-defined FDR thresholds.
The portal requires no additional plugins and runs on any modern web browser, ensuring broad accessibility.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
ProNetView-ccRCC is an interactive, open-access, web-based portal developed to facilitate visual exploration and interpretation of phosphopeptide co-expression networks in clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC). The platform addresses a critical gap in cancer proteomics: while CPTAC has produced comprehensive proteogenomic data generating complex network models, existing tools are primarily suited for static 2D visualization in print publications rather than user-initiated interactive exploration. 

Built on the Three.js WebGL framework, ProNetView-ccRCC enables 3D interactive visualization of the overall ccRCC phosphopeptide co-expression network comprised of 3,614 genes (representing 20,976 phosphopeptides) and 30 functional pathway-enriched network modules containing at least 20 genes each. The network was constructed using a random-forest based algorithm applied to phosphopeptide-level data from 103 ccRCC samples. 

Key features include: (1) a 3D network exploration interface supporting rotation and zooming; (2) gene/protein querying with automatic highlighting of first-degree neighbors; (3) association querying between phosphopeptide abundance and clinical variables (tumor grade, stage, age, gender) with user-defined FDR cut-offs; (4) pathway enrichment tables with interactive gene lists; and (5) integration with the ProTrack tool for multi-omics heatmap analysis. 

Demonstration examples include the oncogene ERG, which connects to 11 genes within module 26 (Angiogenesis) and maps to 5 peptides, showing a significant association with tumor grade (p-value: 0.003, FDR: 0.118). The portal requires no plugins and runs on all modern web browsers, aiming to lower the computational barrier for the cancer research community to conduct hypothesis-generating analyses on CPTAC ccRCC network data.

Research Context
Recent molecular profiling advances have enabled large-scale integrative proteogenomic studies of cancers, including breast, colon, ovarian, and kidney cancer. The CPTAC has performed comprehensive proteogenomic characterizations of tumor samples across these cancer types, advancing understanding of molecular mechanisms. Co-expression networks derived from proteomics and phosphoproteomics data have revealed regulatory relationships between proteins and posttranscriptional modifications. However, these protein/PTM co-expression networks are challenging to visually communicate due to their large dimensions and complicated topologies. Current network data visual exploration tools are mainly used for visually communicating networks as static 2D images in print publications. These existing tools are not well suited for user-initiated interactive network explorations. A centralized platform customized for CPTAC co-expression networks and associated meta-data is necessary.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether a web-based, interactive 3D portal can effectively enable the exploration, interpretation, and communication of CPTAC ccRCC phosphopeptide co-expression networks. The authors posit that a 3D network exploration interface, combining topology-based layout algorithms with integrated clinical and pathway meta-data, will address the visualization challenges of large, dense proteogenomic networks. The predicted outcome is that a 3D portal running in any modern web browser without plugins would make the CPTAC co-expression networks readily accessible and navigable for the cancer research community. The portal aims to facilitate quick, user-intuitive visual interactions with the 3,614-gene ccRCC tumor phosphoprotein co-expression network. Users are expected to be able to conveniently query associations between phosphopeptide abundance and clinical variables such as tumor grade, stage, age, and gender.

Methodological Details
The portal enables visual explorations of two network types: the overall phosphopeptide coexpression network of ccRCC tumors and 30 different network modules. The network characterizes co-expression patterns among 20,976 phosphopeptides in ccRCC samples. The network was derived using a random-forest based network construction algorithm applied to phosphopeptide-level data of 103 ccRCC samples. Two genes are connected if at least two phosphopeptides mapping to the two genes are associated to each other. Network modules were derived using the Glay clustering algorithm based on the overall network topology. 30 modules were identified, each containing at least 20 genes. Pathway enrichment analysis was performed via Fisher Exact test for each module to identify overrepresented pathways. The portal was built on the Three.js framework providing an interface for WebGL. 3D network layouts were calculated using layout algorithms within iCAVE, a previously developed desktop tool for stereoscopic exploration. Client-side Javascript libraries including D3.js, dataTables.js, and JQuery were utilized for real-time interaction handling. The web interface styling primarily utilized Bootstrap v3.3.7 with custom additions. The portal requires no additional plug-ins and runs on all modern web browsers.

Procedures And Architectures
The landing page provides the global ccRCC tumor phosphoproteomics co-expression network (Figure 1A) and links to functional network modules (Figure 1B). Users interact with the 3D network by rotating and zooming in/out the view to navigate the dense topology. Six modules within the network were significantly associated with biological pathways, highlighted using different node coloring. Genes can be queried by name; searching for the oncogene ERG highlights the corresponding node in red and identifies its module. The query returns the list of co-expressed genes and displays the phosphoprotein association with tumor grade (p-value: 0.003, FDR: 0.118). Clicking a module name opens the specific module network; node sizes are proportional to the number of connections. Hovering over a node displays the phosphopeptide gene name, and clicking displays associated gene-level meta-data in a separate panel. Users can click a Heatmap link to access the ProTrack tool for ccRCC multi-omics data exploration via interactive heatmaps. Users can construct queries for genes with similar clinical associations by specifying phenotype and FDR cut-off (e.g., grade with FDR=20%). The pathway enrichment table displays enriched pathways sorted by p-values; clicking a pathway name returns the gene list and highlights them in red. A Reset button in each view returns the user to the original network display.

Key Results
The overall ccRCC phosphopeptide co-expression network comprises 3,614 genes derived from 20,976 phosphopeptides. 30 functional network modules containing at least 20 genes each were identified using the Glay clustering algorithm. The oncogene ERG, highlighted in the CPTAC ccRCC paper, is directly connected to 11 genes within module 26 (Angiogenesis) and maps to 5 different peptides. ERG shows a significant association with tumor grade with p-value: 0.003 and FDR: 0.118. The portal supports querying clinical variables including stage, grade, age, gender, and FDR cut-off. The tool runs on all modern web browsers without requiring additional plug-ins. Figure 3A displays an interactive table listing enriched pathways for module 18, sorted by p-values. Pathway genes (e.g., BRCA1, CDC20, CDK1) are returned in a text box and highlighted in red upon pathway selection.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The 3D visualization and modular decomposition address the inherent difficulty in visually communicating large-dimensional proteogenomic networks. By integrating clinical meta-data (tumor grade, stage, age, gender) directly into the network view, the tool enables biologically grounded hypothesis generation. The modular structure (30 modules) decomposes the massive overall network into interpretable functional units associated with specific biological pathways. The ability to query clinical associations in real-time allows users to identify potentially prognostic or predictive phosphopeptide markers within the network context. The portal provides an open-access resource for a wide spectrum of computational skill levels, facilitating broader dissemination of CPTAC data analyses. Integrating with ProTrack via the Heatmap link connects network-level topology to multi-omics abundance data, providing a multi-scale analysis workflow.

Contradictions And Limitations
The portal is described as a visualization tool rather than a tool for statistical re-analysis; the statistical computations (network construction, clustering, pathway enrichment) are pre-computed and not reproducible within the portal. While the tool is web-based, the authors acknowledge the network was derived from 103 samples, limiting the generalizability of the specific network topology to different cohorts. No formal user study or usability evaluation is reported to validate whether the 3D interface is genuinely more intuitive than 2D approaches for all users. The authors do not report whether the random-forest network algorithm was validated against independent benchmarks or alternative network construction methods. No information is provided regarding the specific hyperparameters used for the random forest, Glay clustering, or the p-value/FDR thresholds for module definition beyond 'at least 20 genes'. The portal is for ccRCC only; the authors do not state whether the architecture can be extended to other CPTAC cancer types.

Claims
ProNetView-ccRCC provides an intuitive, 3D web-based interactive portal for exploring the CPTAC ccRCC phosphopeptide co-expression network and 30 functional modules. The portal enables quick, user-intuitive visual interactions with the ccRCC tumor phosphoprotein co-expression network. The 3D network exploration interface enables quick and easy interactions with the ccRCC phosphopeptide co-expression network as well as 30 functional network modules. Users can interact with the network portal and can conveniently query for association between abundance of each phosphopeptide in the network and clinical variables. The authors note current tools are mainly used for static 2D images, implying the novelty of this approach rather than a demonstrated superiority. No formal usability metrics or user studies are provided to quantify 'intuitive' or 'easy' for the user base. The tool lowers the barrier for non-computational biologists to access and analyze complex CPTAC network data. The portal may identify novel phosphopeptide markers linked to tumor grade and pathways previously unrecognized in 2D views.
The portal supports real-time querying of phosphopeptide associations with clinical variables (tumor grade, stage, age, gender) at user-defined FDR thresholds. Users can easily query for their proteins of interest, neighbors they are connected to, mapping peptides or pathways, at user-defined filters on clinical variables. Users can easily construct a simple query by specifying the phenotype of interest and the FDR cutoff value. ERG query returns p-value: 0.003, FDR: 0.118 for association with tumor grade. The demonstration uses a single FDR cut-off of 20%, not exploring the sensitivity of results to different thresholds. No other clinical variable queries beyond the ERG example are quantitatively demonstrated. Users can identify phosphopeptides whose abundance correlates with clinical prognosis within the network context. The tool could support biomarker discovery workflows integrated with clinical outcome data.
The portal requires no additional plugins and runs on any modern web browser, ensuring broad accessibility. Since ProNetView-ccRCC utilizes only standard libraries and does not require the use of any additional plug-ins, the portal runs on all modern web browsers. The portal is an open-access freely available resource at http://ccrcc.cptac-network-view.org/. No browser compatibility matrix or hardware requirement specifications are provided. The tool is accessible from clinical and academic settings without installation overhead. No data is provided on actual user traffic or adoption since the portal's release.

Data And Code Availability
The portal is a freely available open-access resource at http://ccrcc.cptac-network-view.org/. The CPTAC ccRCC phosphoproteomics data from which the network was derived is referenced via the CPTAC kidney cancer study [7].

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The network was derived using a random-forest based construction algorithm, but no ablation studies or alternative algorithm comparisons are reported. Module identification via Glay clustering is reported but no alternative clustering method comparisons are shown. Pathway enrichment used Fisher Exact test but no alternative enrichment methods are tested. No sensitivity analysis of the 'at least two phosphopeptides' connection criterion is reported. No validation of the network topology against external benchmarks is provided.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A displays the global ccRCC tumor phosphoproteomics co-expression network. Figure 1B links the global network to 30 functional network modules with 6 modules significantly associated with biological pathways. Figure 1C illustrates the query for oncogene ERG, its module membership, connected genes, and clinical association. Figure 2A displays a snapshot of the Angiogenesis enriched module network (module 26) with node sizes proportional to connection count. Figure 2B shows the node interaction panel with ERG details, connections, and links to ProTrack. Figure 2C demonstrates constructing a clinical association query by phenotype and FDR cut-off. Figure 2D shows the results of the clinical association query with genes highlighted in red. Figure 3A displays the interactive table listing enriched pathways for module 18, sorted by p-values. Figure 3B illustrates pathway gene list retrieval with red highlighting.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a 3D web portal integrating the CPTAC ccRCC phosphopeptide co-expression network (3,614 genes) with 30 functional modules, clinical meta-data, and pathway enrichment in a single interactive interface. 2. The strongest evidence of utility is the demonstration of the ERG query returning specific module membership, 11 direct gene connections, 5 peptide mappings, and a statistically significant clinical association (p=0.003, FDR=0.118) within the portal. 3. The future path involves extending the portal to other CPTAC cancer types, incorporating more clinical variables, and potentially enabling in-portal statistical re-analysis to move beyond static pre-computed network exploration.

summary.title: Spontaneous regression of micro-metastases following primary tumor excision: a critical role for primary tumor secretome
summary.authors: Shaashua Lee; Anabel Eckerling; Boaz Israeli; Gali Yanovich; Ella Rosenne; Suzana Fichman-Horn; Ido Ben Zvi; Liat Sorski; Ronit Satchi-Fainaro; Tamar Geiger; Erica K Sloan; Shamgar Ben-Eliyahu
summary.field_subfield: Cancer Biology / Metastatic Research / Systems Oncology
summary.type_of_paper: Experimental Animal Model with In Vitro and Clinical Dataset Validation
summary.executive_summary: This study presents the first animal model demonstrating spontaneous regression of micro-metastases following surgical excision of the primary tumor (PT) in a triple-negative breast cancer xenograft system. Using MDA-MB-231 HM human breast cancer cells transduced with a highly sensitive firefly luciferase-mCherry reporter in BALB/c nu/nu mice, the authors established an orthotopic model where distant metastases in lymph nodes and lungs emerged spontaneously 2-4 weeks post-tumor implantation. Upon excision of the PT at a metastatic burden of 10⁶ photons/s, the smallest (10⁶ photons/s) metastases exhibited a dramatic signal decrease of up to 100-fold within 24 hours (p<0.0001), while larger metastases (10⁷ photons/s) showed significantly less regression (p<0.000). Sham surgery (tumor spared) produced no regression, confirming the effect is linked to PT removal rather than surgical trauma. In vitro experiments demonstrated that tumor cell-conditioned medium (CM) enhanced cancer cell viability (p<0.001), adhesion (p<0.01), and endothelial tube formation (p<0.0001). In vivo, Alzet osmotic minipumps delivering CM reduced regression by 10-fold compared to serum-free medium (p<0.005). Proteomic analysis (LC-MS, ~2,600 proteins identified) and cytokine array identified IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1 (PAI-1), and MIF as key PT-secreted factors. Concurrent in vivo blockade of these four factors via neutralizing antibodies completely halted metastatic progression (p<0.0001). Retrospective TCGA lung adenocarcinoma analysis confirmed high protein levels of these four factors correlated with significantly lower survival (hazard ratio 2.05, p<0.05). The authors conclude that PT-secreted factors promote early metastatic growth, and the perioperative window offers a therapeutic opportunity to control minimal residual disease by targeting these secreted factors.

claims.description: Primary tumor excision causes spontaneous regression of micro-metastases through elimination of PT-secreted growth-supporting factors.
In vivo blockade of PT-secreted IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1, and MIF completely arrests metastatic progression in the presence of the primary tumor.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study presents the first animal model demonstrating spontaneous regression of micro-metastases following surgical excision of the primary tumor (PT) in a triple-negative breast cancer xenograft system. Using MDA-MB-231 HM human breast cancer cells transduced with a highly sensitive firefly luciferase-mCherry reporter in BALB/c nu/nu mice, the authors established an orthotopic model where distant metastases in lymph nodes and lungs emerged spontaneously 2-4 weeks post-tumor implantation. Upon excision of the PT at a metastatic burden of 10⁶ photons/s, the smallest (10⁶ photons/s) metastases exhibited a dramatic signal decrease of up to 100-fold within 24 hours (p<0.0001), while larger metastases (10⁷ photons/s) showed significantly less regression (p<0.000). Sham surgery (tumor spared) produced no regression, confirming the effect is linked to PT removal rather than surgical trauma. In vitro experiments demonstrated that tumor cell-conditioned medium (CM) enhanced cancer cell viability (p<0.001), adhesion (p<0.01), and endothelial tube formation (p<0.0001). In vivo, Alzet osmotic minipumps delivering CM reduced regression by 10-fold compared to serum-free medium (p<0.005). Proteomic analysis (LC-MS, ~2,600 proteins identified) and cytokine array identified IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1 (PAI-1), and MIF as key PT-secreted factors. Concurrent in vivo blockade of these four factors via neutralizing antibodies completely halted metastatic progression (p<0.0001). Retrospective TCGA lung adenocarcinoma analysis confirmed high protein levels of these four factors correlated with significantly lower survival (hazard ratio 2.05, p<0.05). The authors conclude that PT-secreted factors promote early metastatic growth, and the perioperative window offers a therapeutic opportunity to control minimal residual disease by targeting these secreted factors.

Research Context
Surgical removal of the primary tumor is a cornerstone of cancer treatment, yet it has been suggested to accelerate postoperative progression of minimal residual disease. Conversely, various case studies have reported the opposite effect, with spontaneous postoperative regression of evident cancer metastasis documented across most cancer types. Postulated mechanisms, including surgical trauma or elimination of stimulating factors secreted by the primary tumor, have not been empirically tested because no animal model of spontaneous regression exists. The need to study PT-metastase interactions is underscored by the concept of systemic disease and continuous crosstalk between the PT, its microenvironment, and distant organs. The study addresses a gap in evidence-based mechanisms for why some metastases spontaneously regress while others progress post-surgery.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question asks: what mechanisms drive the spontaneous regression of metastases observed in some patients following primary tumor excision? The authors hypothesize that the primary tumor secretome supports the survival and growth of distant micro-metastases, and its elimination by surgery results in metastatic regression. A secondary hypothesis posits that specific PT-secreted factors mediate this effect, and their in vivo blockade should mimic PT removal and inhibit metastasis. The study predicted that regression would be more pronounced in early-stage (small) metastases where autocrine support is insufficient, and less in larger foci. The authors also hypothesized that identified factors would correlate with poor patient survival in a clinical cohort.

Methodological Details
MDA-MB-231 HM, a highly metastatic triple-negative breast adenocarcinoma cell line, was transduced with a codon-optimized firefly luciferase-mCherry vector. Cells were cultured in DMEM supplemented with 10% FBS, 1% glutamax, 4.5g/L D-glucose, and 110mg/L sodium pyruvate at 37 °C and 5% CO₂. Eight-week old female BALB/c nu/nu mice were housed under SPF conditions on a 12 h dark/light cycle. Mice received 2×10⁵ cells in 20 μl PBS injected into the fourth mammary fat pad under 2% isoflurane anesthesia. Primary tumors were measured by caliper, and volume was calculated as (length × width²) × 0.5. Metastases were assessed by bioluminescence imaging using an IVIS spectrum apparatus following i.p. injection of 150 mg/kg D-luciferin sodium salt. When metastatic foci reached 10⁶ photons/s (approximately 3–4 weeks post-injection), the average 80 mm³ primary tumor was excised under 2% isoflurane. A sham surgery control was performed with an identical incision but the primary tumor left untouched. Tumor cell-conditioned medium (CM) was prepared by incubating ~80% confluent cells in serum-free medium for 24 h; SM served as control. For in vivo supplementation, CM was collected from ~30 million cells, filtered through 0.45 μm strainer, and concentrated to 100 μl/mouse via 3 kDa Amicon filters. Alzet osmotic minipumps (model 1003D) delivered CM or SM at approximately 1/8 the daily in vivo secretome production rate. For in vitro adhesion, cells were imaged for 8 hours at 20 min intervals using the IncuCyte system. Apoptosis was measured by AnnexinV-FITC and 7AAD staining followed by flow cytometry after 24-hour incubation in CM or SM. Tube formation: HUVECs seeded on 50 μl basement membrane matrix in 24-well plates were imaged at 20 min intervals for 24 h using IncuCyte. Cytokine array analyzed relative expression of 102 soluble human proteins in CM and plasma from non-tumor, tumor-bearing, post-excision, and control mice. Plasma samples were pooled from 3 mice each for cytokine analysis. LC-MS/MS used UHPLC (Easy-nLC1000) and Q-Exactive Plus mass spectrometer with 50 cm EASY-Spray PepMap columns and 140 min linear gradient. Proteins were digested with LysC/Trypsin mix, incubated with 1mM dithiothreitol and 5mM iodoacetamide, then desalting on C18 StageTips. MS analysis used a top10 method with fragmentation of the 10 most abundant peaks by HCD. Data were analyzed by MaxQuant and Label-free quantification with FDR 0.01 on peptide and protein levels using Andromeda search engine. Enrichment analysis used GO annotations from UniProt with Fisher exact test and FDR threshold of 0.02. Neutralizing antibodies (1 μg each/mouse, once daily for two days) targeted IL-8, Serpin E1, PDGFaa, and MIF, with mouse IgG1 as isotype control. Metastatic foci were confirmed by a pathologist following H&E staining of 6 μm lung sections. Patient outcome was analyzed using the public TCGA provisional lung adenocarcinoma dataset via cBioPortal for survival analysis. Statistical tests included repeated-measures ANOVA, Fisher's PLSD for pairwise comparisons, and student's t-test (p<0.05 two-sided).

Procedures And Architectures
The cancer model employed MDA-MB-231 HM cells transduced with a codon-optimized firefly luciferase-mCherry vector for dual bioluminescence and fluorescence reporting. Mice were injected orthotopically into the fourth mammary fat pad, establishing the primary tumor and inducing spontaneous distant metastases. The experimental workflow followed: PT implantation → metastasis development (3-4 weeks) → threshold measurement (10⁶ p/s) → PT excision → post-excision imaging → 50-day follow-up. For the secretome supplementation, Alzet osmotic minipumps delivered CM or SM at the time of excision to mimic the primary tumor environment. In vitro tube formation employed a reconstituted HUVEC system on Cultrex BME, comparing CM-induced versus SM-induced endothelial morphogenesis. The human cytokine array analyzed 102 proteins in three plasma conditions plus CM, with each plasma sample pooling 3 mice for robustness. The LC-MS workflow included 8M urea mixing, 1:1 protein digestion, and reverse-phase chromatography on 50 cm EASY-Spray PepMap columns. Data analysis pipeline: MS raw files → MaxQuant/LFQ → Andromeda (Uniprot) → Perseus → String/Cytoscape for interaction networking. Antibody blockade: a cocktail of 4 neutralizing antibodies (IL-8, Serpin E1, PDGFaa, MIF) plus isotype control were injected 1 μg daily for 2 days. Patient analysis stratified for altered IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1, and MIF protein levels in RPPA assay from the TCGA lung adenocarcinoma cohort.

Key Results
Bioluminescent metastatic signal decreased by up to 100-fold within 24 h of PT excision (p<0.0001), but not immediately (at 0 h), in mice with 10⁶ photons/s burden. No in vivo bioluminescent signal increase occurred for 50 days post-excision, confirming metastases had regressed into latent foci rather than being eliminated entirely. Microscopic malignant foci were evident on day 1 and day 50 post-excision in both lungs and lymph nodes via H&E staining. Regression was significantly less prominent in larger metastases (10⁷ photons/s vs 10⁶ photons/s), p<0.000, supporting a stage-specific effect. Sham surgery (PT spared) showed continued metastatic increase, while PT excision showed regression (p<0.05), ruling out surgical trauma as the mechanism. CM enhanced cancer cell viability (p<0.001) and adhesion (p<0.01) in vitro, and induced HUVEC tube formation (p<0.0001). Mice treated with CM osmotic pumps showed 10-fold less regression than serum-free medium controls (p<0.005), demonstrating the secretome supports metastasis survival. The cytokine array identified 28 cytokines highly expressed in cancer CM; four (IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1, MIF) were unique to CM or elevated in PT-bearing plasma. LC-MS identified 2,600 proteins in CM, 359 of which were annotated as extracellular factors by GO; enrichment showed apoptosis, angiogenesis, growth factor activity, focal adhesion, and metalloenzyme regulation. String database network analysis identified pathways involved in early stages of metastasis. In vivo blockade of IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1, and MIF completely blocked metastatic progression (p<0.0001) when performed prior to PT excision. No difference in regression was observed on post-excision day-1 between antibody-treated and control groups, as excision removes all secreted factors. TCGA analysis: high IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1, and MIF protein levels in lung adenocarcinoma were associated with significantly lower survival (hazard ratio 2.05, p<0.05).

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The primary tumor secretome actively supports the survival and growth of early-stage distant micro-metastases through multiple pathways including angiogenesis, apoptosis suppression, and cell adhesion. The regression effect is stage-specific: smaller metastases lack sufficient autocrine factors and are dependent on the PT secretome, while larger foci achieve self-sufficiency. Surgical trauma and associated inflammation are not the drivers of regression, as sham surgery did not replicate the effect. The findings explain the rare but documented clinical phenomenon of spontaneous postoperative metastasis regression, suggesting the mechanism is common but undetectable with standard imaging. The perioperative period presents a window of opportunity: blocking PT-secreted factors during or after surgery may control minimal residual disease. The PT secretome can induce a pre-metastatic niche through multiple secreted factors acting on both malignant cells and the microenvironment.

Contradictions And Limitations
The authors acknowledge they tested only a 4-factor antibody cocktail, while many other secreted factors identified by LC-MS likely contribute to metastatic support. The model uses a single cell line (MDA-MB-231 HM), and generalizability to other tumor types (syngeneic lines, different primary sites) is not established. The prevalence of post-operative regression in human cancer patients is currently unknown due to technical limitations of current imaging. The estimation that the osmotic pump delivered 1/8 of the in vivo secretome is an approximation and may not reflect precise physiological conditions. No in vivo data were provided for the individual contributions of the four factors beyond the combined cocktail blockade. The study does not report the absolute size or number of metastases in the post-excision latent state, only that microscopic foci remained.

Claims
Primary tumor excision causes spontaneous regression of micro-metastases through elimination of PT-secreted growth-supporting factors. 100-fold regression of small metastases within 24 h of PT excision was observed (p<0.0001). Sham surgery without PT removal showed continued metastatic growth, confirming the PT itself, not trauma, drives regression. In vivo supplementation of tumor CM with osmotic pumps reduced regression by 10-fold (p<0.005). In vitro CM treatment enhanced cell viability (p<0.001), adhesion (p<0.01), and tube formation (p<0.0001). Larger metastases (10⁷ photons/s) showed significantly less regression than smaller ones (10⁶ photons/s), p<0.000, indicating the effect is stage-limited. No in vivo bioluminescent signal increase occurred over 50 days post-excision, so metastases persist as latent foci rather than being eradicated. The perioperative period may be a window of opportunity to control minimal residual disease by targeting PT-secreted factors. Identified factors (IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1, MIF) represent actionable targets for anti-metastatic intervention.
In vivo blockade of PT-secreted IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1, and MIF completely arrests metastatic progression in the presence of the primary tumor. Antibody cocktail completely blocked metastatic progression in mice with early-stage metastasis burden < 10⁶ p/s (p<0.0001). LC-MS identified 359 extracellular factors, and pathway enrichment showed involvement in apoptosis, angiogenesis, growth factor activity, focal adhesion, and metalloenzyme regulation. No difference in regression was seen on day-1 post-excision between antibody-treated and control mice, as excision removes all secreted factors. The authors tested only the combined effect of four factors; other secreted proteins identified by LC-MS were not neutralized. Tailored combination of neutralizing antibodies based on pre-surgical biopsy of the PT could control metastases perioperatively. The hazard ratio of 2.05 (p<0.05) in TCGA lung adenocarcinoma patients suggests these factors have clinical relevance.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Sham surgery (incision without PT removal) served as a surgical procedure control, demonstrating no regression. Serum-free medium (SM) served as the negative control for CM supplementation in both in vivo (osmotic pumps) and in vitro experiments. The IgG1 isotype control antibody was used as the negative control for neutralizing antibody blockade. Two different regression size thresholds (10⁶ vs 10⁷ photons/s) were used to test the stage-specific effect of PT removal. The study used both a directed approach (cytokine array narrowing to 4 factors) and an unbiased approach (LC-MS identifying 2,600 proteins) to verify the secretome content.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A-B shows the dramatic decrease of up to 100-fold in metastatic signal within 24 h of PT excision (p<0.0001). Figure 1B-C demonstrates no bioluminescent signal increase over 50 days post-excision, confirming latent state. Figure 1D presents H&E stained lung sections showing microscopic malignant foci on day 1 and day 50 post-excision. Figure 1E shows significantly less regression in 10⁷ photons/sec metastases versus 10⁶ photons/sec. Figure 1F compares sham surgery (no regression) with PT excision (regression), p<0.05. Figure 2A-C shows CM-enhanced viability (p<0.001), adhesion (p<0.01), and tube formation (p<0.0001). Figure 2D shows 10-fold less regression in CM-pumped mice versus SM controls (p<0.005). Figure 3A shows String database network of pathways involved in early metastasis. Figure 3B shows complete blockade of progression by anti-IL-8/PDGFaa/SerpinE1/MIF cocktail (p<0.0001). Figure 3C shows no difference on post-excision day-1 between antibody and isotype groups. Figure 3D shows TCGA Kaplan Meier survival curve with hazard ratio 2.05, p<0.05 for high IL-8/PDGFaa/SerpinE1/MIF. Table S1 contains factors excluded from the 4-factor set based on plasma profiles.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first animal model demonstrating that PT excision triggers spontaneous regression of micro-metastases (10⁶ p/s) by eliminating PT-secreted factors, whereas larger metastases (10⁷ p/s) remain relatively unaffected. 2. The strongest evidence is the 100-fold regression signal within 24 h of excision, the 10-fold regression inhibition by CM supplementation via osmotic pumps, and the complete arrest of progression by combined blockade of IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1, and MIF (p<0.0001). 3. The future path is a perioperative therapeutic strategy targeting PT-secreted factors (IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1, MIF) via tailored neutralizing antibodies, with generalizability to other tumor types requiring investigation in syngeneic models.

summary.title: Activation of Macrophages by CpG DNA and LPS: an FTIR Spectroscopic Study
summary.authors: Emrulla Spahiu, Senol Dogan, Jörg Schnauß, Mayda Gursel, Feride Severcan
summary.field_subfield: Immunology / Spectroscopic Bioimaging
summary.executive_summary:
This study investigates whether global molecular changes in murine macrophage RAW 264.7 cells following activation by CpG DNA or lipopolysaccharide (LPS) are detectable by Fourier Transform Infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy. Using Attenuated Total Reflectance (ATR) FTIR spectroscopy, the authors monitored the molecular composition of macrophages cultured in DMEM supplemented with 10% FBS and 2 mM L-glutamine. Cells were treated with 1 µM K3 ODN (CpG DNA) or 0.5 µg/ml LPS, with measurements taken at 10 min, 30 min, 2 h, and 6 h post-treatment. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) reduced the spectral data (0.5 cm⁻¹ resolution) to two principal components, with PC-1 explaining 83% and PC-2 explaining 11% of the total variability. 

The study reports that CpG DNA and LPS treatment significantly increase total nucleic acid concentration starting from the early time points. RNA synthesis, identified via the 915 cm⁻¹ ribose vibration peak, is prominent up to 2 h post-stimulation, followed by a transition to DNA synthesis from 6 h onwards. For LPS treatment, RNA synthesis is restricted to the first 2 h, consistent with the known pro-inflammatory and anti-proliferative effects of LPS that inhibit DNA synthesis and elicit cell cycle arrest. A rapid increase in total protein (amide I and II bands) is observed for both CpG and LPS treatments, peaking at 10 min–2 h and leveling off or declining thereafter. Furthermore, both CpG and LPS stimulate increased concentrations of fatty acids, triglycerides, and cholesterol (ester C=O stretch near 1741 cm⁻¹ and COO⁻ stretch at 1400 cm⁻¹), suggesting activation of de novo lipogenesis. This work represents the first demonstration of ATR-FTIR spectroscopy as an independent modality to monitor activation dynamics in macrophages post-stimuli, filling a gap where prior 'omics' techniques required extensive sample preparation that could alter chemical ratios.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigates whether global molecular changes in murine macrophage RAW 264.7 cells following activation by CpG DNA or lipopolysaccharide (LPS) are detectable by Fourier Transform Infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy. Using Attenuated Total Reflectance (ATR) FTIR spectroscopy, the authors monitored the molecular composition of macrophages cultured in DMEM supplemented with 10% FBS and 2 mM L-glutamine. Cells were treated with 1 µM K3 ODN (CpG DNA) or 0.5 µg/ml LPS, with measurements taken at 10 min, 30 min, 2 h, and 6 h post-treatment. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) reduced the spectral data (0.5 cm⁻¹ resolution) to two principal components, with PC-1 explaining 83% and PC-2 explaining 11% of the total variability. 

The study reports that CpG DNA and LPS treatment significantly increase total nucleic acid concentration starting from the early time points. RNA synthesis, identified via the 915 cm⁻¹ ribose vibration peak, is prominent up to 2 h post-stimulation, followed by a transition to DNA synthesis from 6 h onwards. For LPS treatment, RNA synthesis is restricted to the first 2 h, consistent with the known pro-inflammatory and anti-proliferative effects of LPS that inhibit DNA synthesis and elicit cell cycle arrest. A rapid increase in total protein (amide I and II bands) is observed for both CpG and LPS treatments, peaking at 10 min–2 h and leveling off or declining thereafter. Furthermore, both CpG and LPS stimulate increased concentrations of fatty acids, triglycerides, and cholesterol (ester C=O stretch near 1741 cm⁻¹ and COO⁻ stretch at 1400 cm⁻¹), suggesting activation of de novo lipogenesis. This work represents the first demonstration of ATR-FTIR spectroscopy as an independent modality to monitor activation dynamics in macrophages post-stimuli, filling a gap where prior 'omics' techniques required extensive sample preparation that could alter chemical ratios.

Research Context
FTIR spectroscopy has emerged as a non-destructive, rapid, high-throughput tool capable of revealing alterations in macromolecular conformation and concentration from a single spectrum. The infrared spectrum serves as a fingerprint for all metabolites, with peak area providing quantitative concentration and absorption frequencies revealing bond nature. ATR-FTIR spectroscopy has been applied to live cell activation, disease screening, chemical stress responses, and cellular differentiation. Macrophages constitute the front line of the immune system, possessing structural and functional plasticity. CpG DNA and LPS are major bacterial motifs that trigger macrophage proliferation, pro-inflammatory cytokine production, and NF-kB/AP-1 activation through TLR-9 and TLR-4 pathways sharing MyD88 adaptor. Although the innate immune response to CpG DNA improves host survival, how it impacts relative amounts of nucleic acids, lipids, and proteins has not been studied. Traditional omics techniques yield precise quantitative data but require complex sample preparation that can alter chemical ratios or post-translational modifications in lipidomics and proteomics. Bulk FTIR analysis provides a broad view of relative metabolite amounts not readily accessible by other techniques.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether CpG ODN-mediated immune activation leads to detectable global molecular changes in cells via FTIR spectroscopy. The study hypothesizes that distinct spectral signatures corresponding to nucleic acid, protein, and lipid metabolism shifts will be observable upon CpG DNA and LPS stimulation. It is predicted that nucleic acid changes will precede protein and lipid alterations, reflecting the hierarchy of gene transcription before translational and metabolic shifts. The hypothesis further posits that the RNA-specific peak can serve as an early diagnostic marker of macrophage activation, filling a gap in the activation timeline. LPS-mediated changes are expected to differ from CpG DNA due to LPS's known pro-inflammatory but anti-proliferative (anti-DNA synthesis) profile, mediated by NF-kB and AP-1 transcription factors.

Methodological Details
Murine macrophage-like RAW 264.7 cells were cultured at 37 °C with 5% CO₂ in DMEM supplemented with 10% FBS and 2 mM L-glutamine. To maintain logarithmic growth, cells were sub-cultured in a 1/10 ratio every 2-3 days upon reaching acceptable confluency. Control group cells were treated with 0.9% PBS from Sigma, USA. The CpG DNA stimulated group was treated with 1 µM K3 ODN, endotoxin-free, from Integrated DNA Technologies, Belgium. The LPS stimulated group was treated with 0.5 µg/ml LPS from Sigma, USA. Cells were resuspended at a concentration of 2×10⁶ /mL prior to treatment. Four time points were evaluated to assess kinetics: 10 min, 30 min, 2 h, and 6 h post-treatment. Upon each time point, samples were spun at 1000 rpm, media discarded, cells washed with 15 mL sterile PBS, spun again, and returned to the incubator before analysis. Spectra were collected in the 4000-650 cm⁻¹ IR spectral region at 25°C. Cell samples of 1 µl were dried with a mild N₂ flux for 5 min to allow settling on the ATR crystal. A Perkin-Elmer Spectrum One FTIR spectrometer with a Diamond-ZnSe ATR crystal was used. Air background was measured and subtracted automatically; PBS spectrum was recorded and subtracted manually. Best signal-to-noise ratio was achieved with 128 scans at 2 cm⁻¹ spectral resolution. Each group was scanned in three independent scans, with replicates (n=5) used for data analysis. Spectral data post-processing included 13-point Savitzky-Golay smoothing and baseline correction at 3800-2750-1800-900 cm⁻¹ points. PCA was performed on the 3000-650 cm⁻¹ region using Unscrambler 11.0 software at 0.5 cm⁻¹ resolution. Peak assignment was confirmed using center-of-weight measurements and literature comparison; side-peak bands used second derivative spectra. Concentration studies employed curve integration under peaks; conformational changes used 75% height bandwidth measurements. Statistical testing included Shapiro-Wilk and Kolmogorov-Smirnov normality tests in GraphPad Prism 8.3.

Procedures And Architectures
The ATR-FTIR setup employed a Diamond-ZnSe crystal for direct sample-to-crystal contact, eliminating sample preparation steps. Cell samples (1 µl) were dried under N₂ flux for 5 min to ensure uniform settling on the ATR crystal surface before scanning. The spectrometer (Perkin-Elmer Spectrum One) collected interferograms at 25°C, with the 4000-650 cm⁻¹ range covering fingerprints of lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids. The 128-scan average at 2 cm⁻¹ resolution was chosen as the optimal balance for signal-to-noise ratio during interferogram collection. PCA reduction used 0.5 cm⁻¹ spectral resolution data to project spectra onto principal components, with PC-1 explaining 83% and PC-2 explaining 11% of variability. The second derivative of the 4000-650 cm⁻¹ spectrum was used for side-peak band assignment to resolve overlapping shoulders. Savitzky-Golay smoothing with 13 points was applied to reduce high-frequency noise while preserving peak features. Baseline correction was applied at four specific windows: 3800-2750, 2750-1800, 1800-900 cm⁻¹ (note: the text lists 4 boundaries for 3 regions) to normalize intensity levels. For quantitative concentration, the area under the curve was integrated for each peak; for conformational analysis, 75% peak height bandwidths were measured manually. Statistical normality was assessed via Shapiro-Wilk and Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests prior to differential analysis.

Key Results
PCA demonstrated that the 1750-850 cm⁻¹ IR region contains numerous peaks with high variation among samples, validating spectral data quality. PC-1 provided information for the vast source of variation at 83%, while PC-2 accounted for 11%, showing distinct clustering by treatment. CpG DNA stimulation induced significant changes in nucleic acid content (1238 cm⁻¹ peak) from 10 min until 6 h post-treatment (p < 0.1*), indicating a temporal shift. The RNA-specific peak at 915 cm⁻¹ showed a significant increase from the first minutes (p < 0.001***) that was maintained until 2 h post-stimulation (p < 0.1*). LPS treatment also increased total RNA concentration up to 2 h post-stimulation, with no significant changes in nucleic acid content after 6 h. CpG DNA-induced protein content (amide I and II bands) significantly increased from 10 min to 2 h post-treatment (p < 0.001***) and subsequently declined. A similar protein increase pattern was observed upon LPS stimulation, though the initial increase was reduced starting from the 2 h time point. Both CpG DNA and LPS caused a very significant increase in the ester C=O stretching peak near 1741 cm⁻¹ (triglycerides and cholesterol) starting from the very first minutes. LPS elevated triglycerides and cholesterol concentration specifically after the 10 min mark, whereas CpG DNA effect was evident from the first minutes. A significant increase in fatty acid concentration (COO⁻ stretch at 1400 cm⁻¹) was observed in both stimulated groups, pointing to de novo lipogenesis. The activation state of macrophages could be defined by the RNA-specific peak as early as the first minutes of activation.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The time-dependent sequence of RNA synthesis (up to 2 h) followed by DNA synthesis (from 6 h) in CpG-treated cells reflects the hierarchical molecular response of macrophage activation. The restricted RNA synthesis (2 h) and lack of DNA synthesis changes after 6 h in LPS-treated cells align with LPS's known pro-inflammatory and anti-proliferative/cell-cycle-arrest effects, consistent with Gao et al. (263 genes repressed). The early peak in protein content followed by decline reflects synchronized regulation by major inducers (IL1A, IL1B, TNF, IFNG) and subsequent dynamic suppression by SOCS1/3, NFKBIA, etc. Protein loss mechanisms (histone release, vesicular secretion, ROS-driven degradation) are proposed as explanations for the 3 h decline in CpG-activated cells. Increased cholesterol is linked to membrane fluidity, lipid rafts, and signaling, essential roles in macrophage activation. The shared metabolite Acetoacetyl-CoA between fatty acid and cholesterol synthesis pathways provides a mechanistic link for the simultaneous increase in both lipid fractions. FTIR spectroscopy as a bulk analysis offers an aerial view of relative amounts of nucleic acids, lipids, and proteins not readily accessible by other techniques, including those requiring complex sample preparation. This study first demonstrates ATR-FTIR as an independent modality to monitor activation dynamics, filling a gap in the molecular timeline of macrophage response to TLR agonists.

Contradictions And Limitations
The authors acknowledge that the absorbance of IR light by water molecules is a limitation since it superimposes on signals from aqueous cell systems. The specific mechanisms causing protein loss in CpG DNA-induced activation are stated as unknown, with the paper calling for future study. The relative magnitude of contribution from histone release, protein secretion, and ROS-driven degradation to total protein decline is not quantified in this study. The paper does not provide specific sample size counts per time point beyond the n=5 per group structure. No random seed or specific randomization protocols are reported for experimental order or data splitting beyond the standard protocol. The paper references p < 0.1* as a significance threshold in some instances, which is unconventional compared to p < 0.05.

Claims
ATR-FTIR spectroscopy can independently monitor the global molecular activation dynamics of murine macrophages upon stimulation with CpG DNA or LPS. PCA showed distinct clustering of samples by treatment, with PC-1 explaining 83% of the variation. Nucleic acid, protein, and lipid peaks all showed significant, time-dependent shifts upon treatment. The RNA-specific peak at 915 cm⁻¹ identified activation at the first minutes (p < 0.001***). Fatty acid, triglyceride, and cholesterol peaks shifted significantly in both treatment groups. Water absorbance superimposes on IR signals of aqueous cell systems, potentially limiting spectral clarity. The paper does not quantify the exact relative contributions of different protein-loss mechanisms. FTIR spectroscopy can serve as a rapid, non-invasive modality for monitoring macrophage activation in vitro. This may inform the design of therapeutic ODNs by understanding the bulk molecular response profile.
LPS induces a rapid pro-inflammatory protein response but limits subsequent DNA synthesis, unlike CpG DNA which allows extended nucleic acid accumulation. LPS-treated cells showed no significant nucleic acid changes after 6 h, consistent with its known anti-proliferative effects. LPS protein increase was reduced starting at 2 h, aligning with known rapid activation-deactivation cycles. Lipids in LPS-treated cells rose after 10 min, but CpG DNA effects were evident from the first minutes. Both CpG and LPS stimulated lipids significantly, suggesting shared lipogenic pathways despite differing anti-proliferative profiles. The RNA-specific peak at 915 cm⁻¹ can define macrophage activation state within minutes, filling a gap in the activation timeline.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
PCA analysis validated the spectral data by showing that PC-1 (83%) captured the primary treatment-related variation. Replicates (n=5) were used for each scan condition to ensure data reproducibility. Shapiro-Wilk and Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests confirmed data normality prior to differential analysis. The second derivative spectrum was used specifically for side-peak band assignment to increase confidence in peak identification. The ATR surface was cleaned using a water-ethanol-water sequence between scans to prevent carryover.

Key Figures Tables
Figure A1 presents the comprehensive spectrum of resting control RAW 264.7 cells and its second derivative in the 4000-650 cm⁻¹ region. Table A1 contains peak assignments based on literature, and Table A2 shows area integration measurements for peaks of interest. Table 1 presents treatment conditions (PBS, 1 µM K3 ODN, 0.5 µg/ml LPS) and time points. Figure 1.A shows PCA scores plot with clustering by treatment; Figure 1.B and 1.C show loadings plots highlighting the 1750-850 cm⁻¹ region. Figure 2.A shows the spectrum 10 min after treatment; Figure 2.B shows nucleic acid peak integration bar diagrams; Figure 2.C shows RNA-specific peak changes. Figure 3.A and 3.B show protein-related spectra; Figure 3.C shows amide I band integration. Figure 4.B, 4.C, 4.D, and 4.E show lipid-related spectra and integrations (triglycerides/cholesterol at 1741 cm⁻¹ and fatty acids at 1400 cm⁻¹).

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first demonstration of ATR-FTIR spectroscopy as an independent modality to monitor the activation dynamics of murine macrophages with CpG DNA and LPS. 2. The strongest evidence is the observation of a significant RNA-specific peak (915 cm⁻¹) increase within minutes (p < 0.001***) followed by a time-ordered transition to DNA synthesis, consistent with known TLR activation hierarchies. 3. The future path includes elucidating the specific mechanisms behind the 3-h protein decline in CpG-activated cells and characterizing the lipogenic pathways connecting fatty acid and cholesterol synthesis.

summary.title: The Foster method: Rapid and non-invasive detection of clinically significant American Foulbrood disease levels using eDNA sampling and a dual-target qPCR assay, with its potential for other hive pathogens
summary.authors: John F Mackay, Rebecca E Hewett, Noa T Smith, Tammy L Waters, John S Scandrett
summary.field_subfield: Veterinary Diagnostics / Apiculture / Molecular Diagnostics
summary.type_of_paper: Original Research Article (Method Development and Validation)
summary.executive_summary:
American Foulbrood (AFB), caused by Paenibacillus larvae spores, remains one of the most destructive honeybee diseases. Diagnosis currently relies on subjective, time-consuming visual inspection of capped brood cells, requiring hive dismantling and multiple visits, often missing subclinical or genotype-specific infections. This study presents the 'Foster method,' a novel environmental DNA (eDNA) sampling protocol combining colony entrance swabs with a dual-target qPCR assay (targeting ftsZ and 16S genes) to quantify P. larvae spore levels non-invasively.

Three cohorts of quarantine apiaries across New Zealand were evaluated: 45 hives (8 with clinical AFB) were monitored with nurse bee, entire baseboard, and entrance swabs; 23 hives from one beekeeper yielded 4 clinically positive hives; and a third cohort explored swab pooling.

Key findings include:
1) The dual-target qPCR demonstrated high analytical sensitivity (LOD 4 copies/10 µL), linearity over 7 orders of magnitude (r=0.998), and high amplification efficiency (ftsZ=94%, 16S=96%).
2) The entrance swab method detected equivalent P. larvae levels to entire baseboard swabbing, eliminating the need for hive dismantling.
3) Spore quantities above 565,000 per 10 bees/swab corresponded to a 95% probability of clinical signs.
4) In one instance, a hive without visual signs (Hive 11) showed high spore levels and developed clinical AFB two weeks later, confirming pre-clinical detection.

Statistical analysis (p=0.00) confirmed the strong relationship between increasing spore levels and clinical disease. The Foster method enables rapid, one-time sampling of hives without disruption, with potential scalability to other bee pathogens (Nosema, European foulbrood) and incursion pests (tracheal mites, small hive beetle), transforming AFB surveillance from subjective inspection to quantitative, evidence-based management.

Spore quantification provides a specific threshold (565,000 spores) for predicting clinical AFB disease with 95% probability.

Executive Summary
American Foulbrood (AFB), caused by Paenibacillus larvae spores, remains one of the most destructive honeybee diseases. Diagnosis currently relies on subjective, time-consuming visual inspection of capped brood cells, requiring hive dismantling and multiple visits, often missing subclinical or genotype-specific infections.
