Research Context
Extracellular glycans such as glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) provide essential regulatory components for tissue development and maintenance. GAGs harbor binding sites for a range of growth factors and help establish gradients in the extracellular matrix. However, their structural complexity and compositional heterogeneity make establishing structure-function relationships difficult. Recent advances in synthetic and recombinant technologies have produced increasingly large numbers of chemically well-defined HS structures. Arrays comprising HS structures immobilized on glass are used to profile the specificity of HS-binding proteins. Multiplexed, on-array analysis of HS-dependent cellular signaling would significantly streamline biomaterial discovery. Early examples include studying MAPK pathway activation by FGF2 in Swiss 3T3 cells on HS oligosaccharide arrays.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether HS-protein conjugates arrayed on polyacrylamide hydrogels can generate stable ECM-mimetic microenvironments for stem cell signaling analysis. A secondary question concerns whether NHS-crosslinking of heparin to gelatin preserves protein-binding specificity while ensuring retention on the array. The authors hypothesized that the selectivity of FGF2 binding and activity in these microenvironments would be defined by the chemical composition of the HS polysaccharides. It was further hypothesized that Ext1-/-ESCs, lacking cell-surface HS, would isolate the effects of arrayed GAGs on FGF2 signaling from endogenous HS contributions. The expected outcome was that FGF2 stimulation would activate the MAPK pathway only when HS was present, either immobilized on the array or added as a soluble supplement.

Methodological Details
A polyacrylamide hydrogel thin film was deposited on glass according to a method by Brafman et al. The substrates were spotted with a gelatin solution at 500 µg/mL in PBS to support ESC growth. Heparin (12 kDa) was added to the gelatin solution at concentrations of 50-750 µg/mL as a model HS glycan. Covalent crosslinking of heparin was achieved by activating carboxylic acid groups as NHS esters with EDC in HEPES buffer at 4°C for 18 hours. Purification was performed via size exclusion on a PD10 column to remove small molecule reagents. Low levels of crosslinking (~15% carboxylic acid crosslinks per chain) were targeted to retain GAG in the hydrogel without compromising GF-binding. For the cell model, murine ESCs lacking Exostosin 1 (Ext1) expression were used, which are unable to engage HS-dependent GFs including FGF2. Cells were seeded at increasing densities, with 40,000 cells/cm² producing consistent monolayers of Ext1-/-ESCs. The last 24 hours of culture were carried out under serum-free conditions to establish a signaling activity baseline. The array was probed with FGF2-AF647 (AlexaFluor 647 labeled) to detect immobilized heparin and assess retention. For signaling quantification, a microarrays scanner was used, with fluorescence microscopy validation.

Procedures And Architectures
Hydrogel arrays were generated by printing and physisorption of GAG polysaccharides chemically crosslinked with extracellular matrix proteins onto polyacrylamide hydrogel substrates. The heparin was activated by treatment with NHS in HEPES buffer (100 mM, pH = 7.4) with EDC, then purified by size exclusion. GAG specificity was tested using a panel of CS, DS, and HA, plus heparin treated to remove 6-O-, 2-O-, and N-sulfates. For signaling assays, Ext1-/-ESCs (40,000 cells/cm²) were seeded on spots with gelatin (500 µg/mL) with or without NHS-crosslinked heparin (500 µg/mL). Cells were grown for 48 hours under optimized embryonic culture and starvation conditions, then stimulated with 0.5 ng/mL FGF2 for 15 min at 37°C in serum-free media. Following stimulation, cells were fixed, permeabilized, and immunoassayed for Erk1/2 and pErk1/2. MAPK activity was quantified by the ratio of phosphorylated ERK1/2 (pERK, green) to total ERK1/2 (ERK, red) signals. A positive control was soluble heparin (s-Hep, 5 µg/mL), known to restore MAPK activity in Ext1-/-ESCs.

Key Results
Covalently linked heparin showed superior FGF2 binding compared to non-covalently immobilized heparin, with NHScrosslinked heparin providing ~5-to 10-fold higher signal. After initial decrease during the first 18 hours, heparin arrays remained stable with ~40% of FGF2 binding activity retained after 48 hours of ESC culture. FGF2 bound most strongly to fully sulfated heparin; removal of 6-O-, 2-O-, and N-sulfates resulted in progressive loss of binding activity. CS56 and HABP exhibited high specificity for CS and HA, respectively, confirming that crosslinking did not alter protein-binding specificity. While ERK1/2 protein levels were similar across all conditions, only Ext1-/-ESCs stimulated with FGF2 in the presence of immobilized or soluble heparin showed significant increase in Erk1/2 phosphorylation. FGF2 stimulation of Ext1-/-ESCs on gelatin spots with increasing immobilized heparin (0-500 µg/mL) showed a heparin dose-responsive ERK1/2 phosphorylation. Somewhat lower levels of MAPK activity were observed on the arrayed heparin compared to its soluble form, attributed to limited FGFR accessibility. Seeding at 20,000 cells/cm² resulted in slow growth and irregular colonies, while 100,000 cells/cm² led to rapid proliferation and spot overgrowth. Monolayers of Ext1-/-ESCs retained high levels of Oct4 expression and showed no obvious differentiation (Nestin negative) after optimization.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The results confirm that HS-protein conjugates can be retained on hydrogel surfaces during cell culture without altering their native protein-binding specificity. The reduced signaling on immobilized versus soluble heparin is interpreted as a consequence of limited FGFR accessibility to the array surface, reflecting the spatial constraints of the cell-matrix interface. The platform demonstrates that engineered glycan microenvironments can directly drive intracellular signaling in live stem cells, validating the use of arrays for biological activity assessment. The method enables systematic interrogation of structure-function relationships for GAGs, bridging the gap between defined glycan chemistry and functional biological activity in biomaterials. By using Ext1-/-ESCs, the system successfully isolates the arrayed GAG contribution, confirming that the detected signaling originates from the engineered components rather than endogenous cell-surface glycans.

Contradictions And Limitations
The array-derived MAPK signal was lower than the soluble heparin benchmark, which may introduce a quantitative limitation when comparing array-based and traditional assays. The authors note that ~40% FGF2 binding was retained after 48 hours, indicating some gradual degradation or loss of the glycan-protein complex during extended culture. The study is restricted to a single glycan (heparin) and a single growth factor (FGF2); broader coverage of the GAG and GF repertoire is needed to fully validate the platform's versatility. Only one cell line (Ext1-/-ESC) was tested; the platform's generalizability to other stem cell types or differentiated cells is not demonstrated. The optimal seeding density and serum-free conditions were empirically determined, but the exact thresholds for scalability to larger arrays or different materials are not specified. The study does not report random seeds, replicate numbers for quantitative measurements, or specific imaging acquisition parameters, limiting direct reproducibility.

Claims
The hydrogel-GAG microarray platform enables direct, rapid, and multiplexed profiling of ECM glycan activity on stem cell signaling. Dose-responsive Erk1/2 phosphorylation was observed across increasing immobilized heparin concentrations (0-500 µg/mL). Protein-binding specificity of crosslinked GAGs was preserved, confirming the array faithfully represents chemical structures. Ext1-/-ESCs showed significant phosphorylation only in the presence of immobilized or soluble HS. Marked MAPK activity was lower on the array than with soluble heparin, potentially affecting quantitative comparisons. Only ~40% of FGF2 binding was retained after 48 hours, suggesting time-limited assay windows. The platform could accelerate development of bioactive glycomaterials for stem cell-based therapies by providing high-throughput structure-function data.
NHS-crosslinking of heparin to gelatin preserves protein-binding specificity while ensuring glycan retention on the hydrogel surface during cell culture. Crosslinked heparin provided 5-to 10-fold higher FGF2 binding signal than non-covalently immobilized heparin. FGF2 bound most strongly to fully sulfated heparin and decreased upon stepwise removal of specific sulfate groups. CS56 and HABP showed high specificity for CS and HA, confirming native binding motifs were intact. The authors note that 15% crosslinking was targeted to avoid compromising GF-binding, implying excessive crosslinking could abolish binding. A stepwise decrease in signal was observed, indicating that the immobilization strategy does not eliminate, but modulates, accessibility. This enables the creation of stable, chemically defined glycan arrays that maintain biological functionality during stem cell culture.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Multiple surface passivation strategies were screened (Figure S1), and polyacrylamide-gelatin was found to best support ESC growth in well-separated colonies. Gelatin concentrations were optimized: 500 µg/mL in the hydrogel supported monolayers, while higher densities led to spot overgrowth. Heparin concentrations were tested from 50-750 µg/mL, with 500 µg/mL identified as the optimal concentration for the functional array. The crosslinking density was targeted at ~15% per chain to balance retention versus accessibility. Cell seeding was tested at 20,000, 40,000, and 100,000 cells/cm², with 40,000 identified as optimal. MAPK activity was validated by: (1) comparing with soluble heparin, (2) fluorescent microscopy imaging, and (3) Image J analysis of co-localization. The signaling response was probed with soluble heparin (5 µg/mL) as a positive control and benchmark.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the general array concept: ESC culture on gelatin hydrogels with GAGs, and the structure/sulfation patterns of major GAG classes. Figure 2A demonstrates that covalently linked heparin has ~5-to 10-fold higher FGF2 binding than non-covalently immobilized heparin. Figure 2B shows FGF2 retention on the array surface for 48 hours under ESC culture conditions at 37°C, 5% CO2. Figure 2C validates protein-binding specificity using FGF2, CS56, and HABP against a panel of GAGs with removed sulfate groups. Figure 3A-B shows optimized cell seeding at 40,000 cells/cm² with Oct4 and Nestin characterization, and Figure 3C confirms growth on heparin spots. Figure 4A-D presents the FGF2 signaling assay: (A) cell morphology, (B) pERK/total ERK ratio by microarray scanner, (C) fluorescence microscopy validation, and (D) dose-responsive ERK1/2 phosphorylation. Figure S1 shows screening of surface passivation strategies, and Figure S2 shows Image J co-localization analysis.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a polyacrylamide hydrogel microarray platform that integrates chemically crosslinked GAG-protein conjugates to enable multiplexed, on-array assessment of growth factor signaling in live stem cells. 2. The strongest evidence is the demonstration of dose-responsive Erk1/2 phosphorylation in Ext1-/-ESCs upon FGF2 stimulation, only in the presence of immobilized or soluble HS, with preservation of known sulfate-dependent binding specificities. 3. The future path involves utilizing this platform to profile the wider repertoire of synthetic and chemoenzymatic HS structures to accelerate development of functional glycomaterials for regenerative therapies.

summary.title: Robust Brain State Decoding using Bidirectional Long Short Term Memory Networks in functional MRI
summary.authors: Anant Mittal (University of Maryland); Priya Aggarwal (Indraprastha Institute of Information Technology); Luiz Pessoa (University of Maryland); Anubha Gupta (Indraprastha Institute of Information Technology)
summary.field_subfield: Neuroscience / Deep Learning (Brain-computer interface, fMRI analysis)
summary.type_of_paper: Methodology and validation study with experimental results
summary.executive_summary:
This paper proposes and validates a bidirectional Long Short Term Memory (bi-LSTM) network architecture for decoding brain states from functional MRI (fMRI) data, specifically addressing the temporal dynamics of the Blood Oxygen Level Dependent (BOLD) response. Conventional LSTM models capture information only from past time points, but due to inherent latency and BOLD response dynamics, the authors argue that future temporal context is also critical. The proposed bi-LSTM processes fMRI time-series in both forward and reverse directions, collating hidden activations to form a dual-directional 'memory' that predicts brain states at every time instance without requiring pre-processing delay adjustments. The framework was validated on working memory task fMRI data from the Human Connectome Project (HCP), using 400 participants performing a 2-back task across four stimulus categories (tools, places, faces, body parts) and a 0-back control. Data was preprocessed into 360 cortical regions of interest, yielding 405 time-points per scan, yielding S=9 brain states (including fixation blocks labeled as 'others'). The bi-LSTM model (two hidden layers with 256 units each) was compared against a unidirectional LSTM (same specifications) and a three-layer feed-forward neural network. Using inter-subject 10-fold cross-validation (N=360 for training, N=40 for testing), the bi-LSTM-c (vector concatenation) achieved 0.84 ± 0.02 accuracy, compared to 0.66 ± 0.18 for the unidirectional LSTM, an absolute improvement of 0.18 (approximately +27% relative). The bi-LSTM required no time-delay adjustment for BOLD response synchronization, unlike prior methods that assumed a constant response delay across all voxels. The study concludes that future temporal context contains useful information for BOLD dynamics and that the bi-LSTM framework provides a robust, delay-free solution for brain-state decoding in fMRI.

Key findings indicate that the bi-LSTM consistently outperforms its unidirectional counterpart across all brain states, with the unidirectional model exhibiting higher misclassification rates. The highest confusion for both models occurred for the 'Others' (fixation) class, and the second-highest confusion involved mislabeling stimulus-specific tasks as the base task. The model also occasionally confused 'body' and 'tools' stimuli. Limitations noted include the fixed windowing approach, the remaining challenge of class imbalance, and the need for further analysis of cortical regions confused between stimuli categories. The work establishes the bi-LSTM as a viable alternative to traditional univariate and multivariate decoding methods in sequential brain-state analysis.

The bi-LSTM framework does not require hard-coded time-delay adjustment for BOLD response synchronization.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper proposes and validates a bidirectional Long Short Term Memory (bi-LSTM) network architecture for decoding brain states from functional MRI (fMRI) data, specifically addressing the temporal dynamics of the Blood Oxygen Level Dependent (BOLD) response. Conventional LSTM models capture information only from past time points, but due to inherent latency and BOLD response dynamics, the authors argue that future temporal context is also critical. The proposed bi-LSTM processes fMRI time-series in both forward and reverse directions, collating hidden activations to form a dual-directional 'memory' that predicts brain states at every time instance without requiring pre-processing delay adjustments. The framework was validated on working memory task fMRI data from the Human Connectome Project (HCP), using 400 participants performing a 2-back task across four stimulus categories (tools, places, faces, body parts) and a 0-back control. Data was preprocessed into 360 cortical regions of interest, yielding 405 time-points per scan, yielding S=9 brain states (including fixation blocks labeled as 'others'). The bi-LSTM model (two hidden layers with 256 units each) was compared against a unidirectional LSTM (same specifications) and a three-layer feed-forward neural network. Using inter-subject 10-fold cross-validation (N=360 for training, N=40 for testing), the bi-LSTM-c (vector concatenation) achieved 0.84 ± 0.02 accuracy, compared to 0.66 ± 0.18 for the unidirectional LSTM, an absolute improvement of 0.18 (approximately +27% relative). The bi-LSTM required no time-delay adjustment for BOLD response synchronization, unlike prior methods that assumed a constant response delay across all voxels. The study concludes that future temporal context contains useful information for BOLD dynamics and that the bi-LSTM framework provides a robust, delay-free solution for brain-state decoding in fMRI.

Key findings indicate that the bi-LSTM consistently outperforms its unidirectional counterpart across all brain states, with the unidirectional model exhibiting higher misclassification rates. The highest confusion for both models occurred for the 'Others' (fixation) class, and the second-highest confusion involved mislabeling stimulus-specific tasks as the base task. The model also occasionally confused 'body' and 'tools' stimuli. Limitations noted include the fixed windowing approach, the remaining challenge of class imbalance, and the need for further analysis of cortical regions confused between stimuli categories. The work establishes the bi-LSTM as a viable alternative to traditional univariate and multivariate decoding methods in sequential brain-state analysis.

Research Context
Decoding brain states via learning discriminative feature representations has gained significant interest in brain-computer interface applications. Advances in non-invasive neuroimaging methods such as fMRI are proving helpful in determining cognitive or perceptual states in motor decoding, attention classification, and brain reading. Conventional decoding methods involved massive univariate analysis measuring activity from thousands of brain locations separately, failing to integrate distributed spatial information. Multivariate analysis was developed to integrate distributed but overlapping information across the spatial domain simultaneously. Recent advances in time-sensitive machine learning frameworks, particularly RNN variations like Echo-state Networks and LSTM models, have shown to perform better than conventional decoding models for dynamic fMRI information. The BOLD response in fMRI exhibits a time-lag relative to neuronal activation, typically not synchronized with stimulus presentation. Prior approaches assumed all fMRI voxels have the same response delay and adjusted each time point accordingly before model training. LSTMs store past information as contextual memory for feature learning but are not encoded to capture future temporal context.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether information from future BOLD response instances can be effectively utilized to improve brain-state decoding accuracy without requiring prior delay adjustment. The authors hypothesize that bidirectional LSTM architecture, which acquires information from both past and future time instances, will produce more robust brain state representations than unidirectional LSTM. A secondary hypothesis is that the bi-LSTM framework eliminates the need for explicit time-delay adjustment, simplifying the preprocessing pipeline. The predicted outcome is that bi-LSTM will outperform the unidirectional LSTM in predicting brain states across the HCP working memory task. The study also predicts that the LSTM model will consistently underperform the bi-LSTM-c variant across all individual brain states, as evidenced by confusion matrix analysis.

Methodological Details
The study used task fMRI data from the Human Connectome Project (HCP) working memory dataset. N = 400 participants were randomly selected from the N = 1200 HCP data release for the final analysis. Participants performed a working memory 2-back task comparing current stimulus to one presented two stimuli before, and a 0-back control condition. The task combined category representation with four stimulus types: tools, places, faces, and body parts, separated by fixation periods. Data were collected in two runs per participant, each with 8 task blocks for every task/stimuli combination, each lasting 27.5 seconds. Each scan consisted of 4 fixation blocks of 15 seconds each after every two task blocks, resulting in a 405 time-points sequence per run. Preprocessing included field-map based distortion correction, functional-to-structural alignment, and intensity normalization. Motion-related variables (6 translation parameters and derivatives) were regressed out using 3dDeconvolve with 'ortvec' in AFNI. Low-frequency signals were regressed out using 3dDeconvolve with 'polort'. Cortical data only was used, available as a surface representation from the HCP preprocessing pipeline. Brain areas were separated using cortical parcellation, generating 360 cortical regions of interest (ROIs) by averaging individual voxels. The region-averaged time-series served as the input feature vector, creating a 360 by 405 2D-tensor. No stimuli and brain-state synchronization was performed for BOLD response delay adjustment. Each time-point in task blocks was labeled by brain-state, and fixation blocks were labeled 'others', yielding S = 9 brain states.

Procedures And Architectures
The bi-LSTM architecture consists of two hidden layers with each LSTM cell having 256 hidden activations. Input activations x_t are extracted from 360 brain ROIs at each time point. The model processes the time-series in both forward and backward directions using separate hidden layers. The forward hidden activation h^f_t computes temporal dependency on preceding time points up to t-1. The backward hidden activation h^b_t computes temporal dependency on future points from t+1 onward. The two hidden activations are collated to generate hidden cell state features; three merging schemes were tested: vector concatenation (bi-LSTM-c), element-wise addition (bi-LSTM-a), and element-wise averaging (bi-LSTM-μ). Input to subsequent LSTM layers are the hidden activations of the previous layer. The final layer is a fully-connected layer with S = 9 neurons and softmax activation, mapping learned features to brain states. The model was implemented in the Keras deep learning framework. Training was performed on a GeForce GTX 980 GPU with a batch size of 32, using the ADAM optimizer with a learning rate of 0.001. The model was trained for 100 epochs with no early stopping. A dropout of 0.3 was applied in LSTM layers during training to prevent overfitting. The full-length training data was windowed into overlapping segments of size w = 40 with an overlap of 10 points. Inter-subject 10-fold cross-validation was employed: 360 subjects for training and 40 subjects for testing. The training set (9 folds) was further split into 80-20 training-validation sets for hyperparameter tuning. Class imbalance was addressed by computing weights inversely proportional to class frequency using Sklearn's 'compute_class_weight' and applying them during loss calculation.

Key Results
The bi-LSTM model (bi-LSTM-c variant) achieved an overall classification accuracy of 0.84 ± 0.02. The unidirectional LSTM model achieved an accuracy of 0.66 ± 0.18. The bi-LSTM improved accuracy by an absolute 0.18 points compared to the unidirectional LSTM. The misclassification rate was highest for both models in the 'Others' class, representing fixation blocks. Mean normalized confusion matrices confirmed that for every brain state, the LSTM model misclassified to a larger extent than the bi-LSTM-c. The second highest confusion occurred when participants were stimulated with 'faces' and 'places', misclassified as the 0-back or 2-back task while stimuli were detected correctly. The model also exhibited confusion between 'body' and 'tools' stimuli. The feed-forward neural network (ff-NN) was used as a baseline with the same number of layers and units, discarding temporal dependencies. The bi-LSTM outperformed the ff-NN baseline, though exact ff-NN accuracy numbers are not explicitly quantified in the main text.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The superior performance of bi-LSTM indicates that future BOLD response dynamics contain predictive information relevant for brain-state classification. The results suggest that BOLD response latency is not a simple constant shift that can be fully corrected by static time-alignment, as future context holds complementary information. The architecture demonstrates that dual-directional temporal modeling can capture the full dynamics of BOLD response without explicit pre-processing delay adjustments. The persistence of confusion between 'body' and 'tools' stimuli suggests overlapping or adjacent neural representations for these categories in the cortical regions analyzed. The finding that BOLD response dynamics require both past and future context challenges conventional approaches that view BOLD as a delayed, purely forward-in-time representation of underlying activity.

Contradictions And Limitations
The largest class ('Others') dominates the dataset, and even with class weighting, it remains the primary source of confusion for both models. The fixed window size (w=40, overlap=10) was used without tuning, which may not be optimal for all runs or stimuli types. The model was evaluated on only one task (working memory, 2-back) and one parcellation scheme, limiting generalizability. No specific random seed or train-test split details (beyond the 80-20 validation split) are reported for the training process. The exact ff-NN accuracy value is not explicitly stated, making the relative improvement over the temporal baseline less quantifiable. The 10-fold cross-validation reports a relatively wide confidence interval for the unidirectional LSTM (±0.18), suggesting high variability in performance.

Claims
Bi-directional LSTM architecture provides superior brain-state decoding accuracy compared to unidirectional LSTM by incorporating future temporal context. The bi-LSTM-c accuracy was 0.84 ± 0.02 while unidirectional LSTM was 0.66 ± 0.18. Mean normalized confusion matrices showed LSTM misclassified to a larger extent for every state. The bi-LSTM performed 18% better than its unidirectional counterpart. The unidirectional LSTM had a very wide confidence interval (±0.18), indicating unstable performance across subjects. Future fMRI brain-state decoding pipelines should consider bidirectional temporal modeling to capture full BOLD dynamics.
The bi-LSTM framework does not require hard-coded time-delay adjustment for BOLD response synchronization. The bidirectional processing inherently handles BOLD dynamics without prior time-shifting. The paper explicitly states no stimuli and brain-state synchronization was performed. The authors acknowledge that class imbalance still requires more sophisticated handling, suggesting the method isn't a complete solution. This simplifies preprocessing for fMRI decoding as voxel-specific delay estimates are no longer necessary.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Three merging schemes were compared: vector concatenation (bi-LSTM-c), element-wise addition (bi-LSTM-a), and element-wise averaging (bi-LSTM-μ). The model was compared against a unidirectional LSTM with the same hidden layer counts and unit sizes. A three-layer feed-forward neural network served as a temporal-independent baseline with equivalent depth and width. A dropout of 0.3 was used to assess robustness against overfitting during training. Inter-subject 10-fold cross-validation provided estimates of generalization performance.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 provides a schematic illustration of the Bidirectional LSTM architecture processing time-series in both directions. Figure 2 presents mean normalized confusion matrices comparing miss-classifications of LSTM and bi-LSTM-c across all nine brain states. Table details regarding the specific 360 ROIs and parcellation are available via the HCP reference [8].

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the application of a bidirectional LSTM architecture to fMRI brain-state decoding, enabling explicit modeling of both past and future BOLD response dynamics without requiring pre-processing delay adjustments. 2. The strongest evidence is the absolute accuracy improvement of 0.18 (from 0.66 ± 0.18 to 0.84 ± 0.02) over the unidirectional LSTM, demonstrated through inter-subject 10-fold cross-validation on 400 HCP participants. 3. The future path involves tuning window sizes and overlaps for time-series chunking, developing more sophisticated class imbalance handling, and neuroanatomical analysis of cortical regions confused between stimuli categories.

summary.title: Phylogenetic study of thermophilic genera Anoxybacillus, Geobacillus, Parageobacillus, and proposal of a new classification Quasigeobacillus
summary.authors: Carling, Blom, Georges, Berenice Talamantes Becerra
summary.field_subfield: Microbial Genomics / Bacterial Phylogenomics
summary.executive_summary: This study presents a comprehensive phylogenomic reassessment of three closely related thermophilic genera within the family Bacillaceae—Anoxybacillus, Geobacillus, and Parageobacillus—using 113 publicly available whole-genome sequences. The primary methodological framework integrated three complementary phylogenomic metrics: a maximum-likelihood core-gene tree derived from 662 orthologous genes, Average Nucleotide Identity (ANI), and Average Amino Acid Identity (AAI) dendrograms. The core gene tree revealed a fundamental phylogenetic split into two main clades: Clade I, containing all Geobacillus, all Parageobacillus, and a subset of Anoxybacillus species; and Clade II, containing the majority of Anoxybacillus species. Clade I was further resolved into three distinct sub-clades corresponding to Geobacillus, Parageobacillus, and a third clade (I-c) composed of Anoxybacillus tepidamans and one unnamed genomospecies. The authors propose that clade I-c be elevated to the new genus Quasigeobacillus gen. nov., supported by 6 unique coding sequence (CDS) identifiers and a position consistently distinct from the three established genera across all three phylogenetic methods. Two Anoxybacillus species (A. vitaminiphilus and A. amylolyticus) showed inconsistent positioning and remain unresolved. The study concludes that taxonomical circumscription based on isolated genus analysis is insufficient; closely related genera must be considered together in phylogenomic workflows to avoid incongruent taxonomic assignments for new strains.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study presents a comprehensive phylogenomic reassessment of three closely related thermophilic genera within the family Bacillaceae—Anoxybacillus, Geobacillus, and Parageobacillus—using 113 publicly available whole-genome sequences. The primary methodological framework integrated three complementary phylogenomic metrics: a maximum-likelihood core-gene tree derived from 662 orthologous genes, Average Nucleotide Identity (ANI), and Average Amino Acid Identity (AAI) dendrograms. The core gene tree revealed a fundamental phylogenetic split into two main clades: Clade I, containing all Geobacillus, all Parageobacillus, and a subset of Anoxybacillus species; and Clade II, containing the majority of Anoxybacillus species. Clade I was further resolved into three distinct sub-clades corresponding to Geobacillus, Parageobacillus, and a third clade (I-c) composed of Anoxybacillus tepidamans and one unnamed genomospecies. The authors propose that clade I-c be elevated to the new genus Quasigeobacillus gen. nov., supported by 6 unique coding sequence (CDS) identifiers and a position consistently distinct from the three established genera across all three phylogenetic methods. Two Anoxybacillus species (A. vitaminiphilus and A. amylolyticus) showed inconsistent positioning and remain unresolved. The study concludes that taxonomical circumscription based on isolated genus analysis is insufficient; closely related genera must be considered together in phylogenomic workflows to avoid incongruent taxonomic assignments for new strains.

Research Context
DNA-DNA hybridization had long been considered the gold standard for bacterial taxonomy but was being superseded by genomic approaches. 16S rRNA gene sequencing provides lower resolution in bacterial taxonomy due to high sequence similarities at the genus level. Average Nucleotide Identity (ANI) and Average Amino Acid Identity (AAI) offer higher resolution for detecting relatedness among bacterial genomes. The authors note that bioinformatic tools calculating ANI alone are insufficient without alignment of orthologous core genes. Anoxybacillus, Geobacillus, and Parageobacillus are moderate thermophiles in the family Bacillaceae with spore-forming capabilities. Anoxybacillus was proposed in 2000 as a new genus with 24 validly described species. Geobacillus was split from Bacillus in 2001 and currently contains 16 validly described species. Parageobacillus was defined in 2016 by reassigning a clade from Geobacillus. Prior taxonomic revisions (e.g., G. galactosidasius to P. galactosidasius) were based on partial core gene trees and GC content.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether the current taxonomic circumscription of Anoxybacillus, Geobacillus, and Parageobacillus is consistent when all three genera are phylogenomically analyzed together. The authors hypothesize that examining closely related genera simultaneously will reveal phylogenetic incongruencies not visible when genera are studied in isolation. The study aims to test whether a third distinct clade within the Geobacillus-Parageobacillus-Anoxybacillus complex warrants recognition as a separate genus. The authors predict that the 7 newly isolated Australian thermophile strains can be preliminarily placed within the existing or proposed genera. The hypothesis is further tested by identifying genes unique to clade I-c to support the proposal of Quasigeobacillus. A key predicted outcome is that the core gene tree topology will match the ANI/AAI dendrograms in resolving the three major sub-clades.

Methodological Details
A total of 113 genome assemblies were selected from the RefSeq database. Thirty-two Anoxybacillus strains and seventy-three Geobacillus strains provided complete genome assemblies. Parageobacillus was represented by one genome assembly per species across the seven validly described species. An additional group of two Anoxybacillus, four Geobacillus, and one Parageobacillus strains from an Australian thermophile study was included. The included assemblies comprised 31 chromosome-level assemblies, 33 scaffold genomes, and 49 genomes at the contig level. Anomalous genome assemblies (chimeric, contaminated, or frameshifted) with suppressed RefSeq status were excluded. The core genome was identified using EDGAR 2.0 with Geobacillus thermodenitrificans NG80-2 as the starting reference. Bacillus subtilis spizizenii TU-B-10T was included as the outgroup. During core gene discovery, 5 assemblies with low CDS counts were excluded, and one exact duplicate was removed. The 662 orthologous core genes were concatenated and aligned using MUSCLE. A maximum-likelihood phylogenetic tree was constructed using FastTree. ANI was calculated using the ani.rb script and AAI using aai.rb, with 100 N bases introduced between contigs in draft genomes. Dendrograms were generated using the DendroUPGMA web server with UPGMA clustering. GC content and genome size were calculated for all genomes.

Procedures And Architectures
Core gene identification employed an iterative BLAST comparison against all assemblies, retaining CDS from the reference for which orthologs existed in all other assemblies. Maximum-likelihood tree inference used FastTree for the 662-gene concatenated alignment. Two-way ANI matrices were computed with default parameters in the enveomics package. Two-way AAI matrices were computed similarly with the aai.rb script. Clustering for dendrograms used unweighted pair group with arithmetic mean (UPGMA). Trees were visualized and plotted using the Interactive Tree Of Life web tool. Genes unique to clade I-c were identified via BLASTn of CDS from Anoxybacillus tepidamans PS2 against all assemblies in NCBI RefSeq and nt databases. The relaxed BLASTn filtering criteria for unique gene identification were 30% identity, bitscore 10, and 1% overlap. Unique genes were defined as present in all clade I-c members and absent from all clade I-a, I-b, and Clade II members.

Key Results
The core gene set comprised 662 orthologous genes per genome across the 114 analyzed assemblies. The maximum-likelihood tree resolved into three major groups: the outgroup, Clade I (87 genomes), and Clade II (24 Anoxybacillus genomes). Clade I was further partitioned into three subclades: Geobacillus, Parageobacillus, and the third clade (I-c). Clade I-c contained two species: Anoxybacillus tepidamans and one unnamed genomospecies. Exactly 6 CDS were found to be unique to clade I-c across all members. The ANI of Anoxybacillus sp. EFIL was 97.99%, Geobacillus sp. MMMUD3 was 97.14%, and Geobacillus sp. DSP4a was 97.64% against their closest relatives. Anoxybacillus sp. CHMUD showed the most distant ANI of 95.03% and AAI of 95.81%. The mean ANI and AAI values indicated that clade I-c is somewhat more closely related to Parageobacillus than to Geobacillus or Anoxybacillus. Two Anoxybacillus species (A. vitaminiphilus and A. amylolyticus) showed inconsistent positioning across the ML tree, ANI, and AAI trees and could not be resolved. The 7 newly isolated Australian strains were preliminary placed among the established or proposed taxa.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The primary finding is that considering closely related genera together reveals phylogenetic structure that is obscured when genera are analyzed in isolation. The consistent distinctiveness of clade I-c across three independent phylogenomic methods supports its elevation to Quasigeobacillus gen. nov. The incongruous positioning of A. vitaminiphilus and A. amylolyticus suggests that existing classification schemes may not fully capture the true phylogeny of these lineages. The study demonstrates that the genome-level taxonomy of thermophilic Bacillaceae requires a broader phylogenetic context for accurate genus-level assignment of new strains. The finding that clade I-c was previously assigned to Anoxybacillus and in one case to Geobacillus, but actually falls outside both, underscores the potential for misclassification. The use of a core gene tree supplemented by ANI and AAI provides a robust multi-pronged validation for taxonomic delimitation.

Contradictions And Limitations
Two Anoxybacillus species (A. vitaminiphilus and A. amylolyticus) showed inconsistent positioning across all three trees and could not be clearly resolved into any genus. Five assemblies with low CDS counts had to be excluded, and one exact duplicate was removed, reducing the available genomic information. The study relied on publicly available RefSeq genomes, which may introduce biases related to sequencing platform, assembly quality, and representation. The 7 newly isolated Australian strains received only preliminary placement, not definitive taxonomic assignment. The study was published as a preprint and was not certified by peer review at the time of the text. The proposed name Quasigeobacillus is provisional and awaits formal publication and validation.

Claims
The clade comprising Anoxybacillus tepidamans and one unnamed genomospecies should be elevated to the new genus Quasigeobacillus gen. nov. Clade I-c was consistently distinct from Geobacillus, Parageobacillus, and Clade II across ML tree, ANI, and AAI methods. Six CDS were identified as unique to all members of clade I-c and absent from all other taxa. The structure of all three phylogenetic trees reaffirms the consistent separation of this clade. Two of the 113 genomes showed inconsistent positioning that could not be resolved, suggesting some phylogenetic uncertainty remains. The proposal is preliminary and the full genomic context of the unnamed genomospecies is not detailed in the core text. Acceptance of the new genus will require formal publication and validation by the International Journal of Systematic and Evolutionary Microbiology. Existing strains of A. tepidamans and the unnamed genomospecies must be reclassified, impacting database entries and ecological studies.
Taxonomic assignment of new thermophilic isolates based on isolated genus phylogeny is prone to error; a multi-genus circumscription is required. The clade I-c genomes were previously assigned to Anoxybacillus and in one case to Geobacillus, but the combined analysis revealed their true distinctiveness. When the two genera are considered together, the phylogeny changes in a way that would be missed if analyzed separately. For many strains, current classifications may still hold as the broader analysis is still in progress. Taxonomic pipelines for thermophilic isolate classification must be updated to include simultaneous analysis of multiple closely related genera. Bioinformatic workflows should mandate ANI/AAI and core-gene tree comparisons across a circumscribed genus-complex.

Data And Code Availability
The ANI and AAI Ruby scripts used for similarity calculations are publicly available in the enveomics package. Genomes used in the study were sourced from the NCBI RefSeq database. The authors note the assemblies are listed in Supplementary Tables S1 and S2.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The results were validated using three independent methods: ML core gene tree, ANI dendrogram, and AAI dendrogram. The unique gene identification used relaxed BLASTn criteria (30% identity, bitscore 10, 1% overlap) to maximize sensitivity. Six unique CDS were cross-validated by BLASTn alignment against all members of clade I-c, confirming they are present in all members. The authors note that if the two clade I-c species were merged with Parageobacillus, the evidence would support Parageobacillus merging with Geobacillus, indicating a nested hierarchical relationship.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 presents the core gene maximum-likelihood phylogenetic tree splitting into the outgroup, Clade I, and Clade II. Figure 2 shows the two-way ANI UPGMA dendrogram with 114 genomes. Figure 3 presents the two-way AAI UPGMA dendrogram with 114 genomes. Table 1 reports mean ANI and AAI values separating the candidate new genus from the existing three genera. Table 2 shows comparative content (presumably GC content) supporting closer affinity to Parageobacillus. Table 3 details specific ANI and AAI values for individual genome pairs. Table 4 lists the 6 CDS unique to clade I-c with descriptions and products. Table 5 contains DNA sequences for each of the 6 unique CDS. Table 6 shows BLASTn alignment results of the unique CDS against all clade I-c members. Table 7 shows the best hit BLASTn results for the unique CDS.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a combined phylogenomic framework (ML core gene tree, ANI, AAI) that demonstrates how multi-genus circumscription reveals taxonomic incongruencies hidden within single-genus analyses. 2. The strongest evidence for the new genus Quasigeobacillus is the consistent clustering of clade I-c across all three independent methods, supported by six unique coding sequences identified via relaxed BLASTn. 3. The future path requires formal publication of the Quasigeobacillus genus, resolution of the two incongruous Anoxybacillus species, and broader adoption of multi-genus phylogenetic workflows for bacterial taxonomy.

summary.title: The structural basis for regulation of the glutathione transporter Ycf1 by regulatory domain phosphorylation

summary.executive_summary: This study provides two cryo-EM structures of endogenously phosphorylated Saccharomyces cerevisiae Ycf1 (a glutathione transporter of the ABC-C subfamily) at 3.4Å and 4.0Å resolution, capturing previously unobserved ordered states of the intrinsically disordered regulatory R-domain (residues 901-935) in two inward-facing conformations (IFwide and IFnarrow). The R-domain, phosphorylated at S908, T911, and S914, is shown to be helical at its C-terminus (residues 920-929) and forms extensive electrostatic and hydrophobic interactions with NBD1 (spanning three buried hydrophobic sites) and the lasso domain. Biochemical data, including ATPase assays, in-gel phosphoprotein staining, limited proteolysis, and LC-MS/MS, confirm that R-domain phosphorylation reorganizes the Ycf1 architecture and is required for maximal ATPase activity. The dephosphorylated state shows a more complete protease digestion pattern and drastically reduced ATPase activity, consistent with cellular phenotypes where S908 and T911 mutations impair cadmium detoxification. The R-domain encircles NBD1 in both structures, with the IFwide-to-IFnarrow transition involving a rigid body movement of the R-domain/NBD1 complex relative to NBD2 and a reconfiguration of the ATP-binding sites, including partial occlusion of the non-functional ATP site in NBD1. The R-domain phosphorylation sites align with PKA-like (RRAS) and CKII kinase recognition motifs. A conserved inhibitory phosphosite at S251 (lasso domain) is identified in proximity, poised to disrupt the R-domain interaction via electrostatic repulsion. These findings challenge existing models of R-domain disordered-to-ordered transition and provide mechanistic insights for the ABCC transporter family, with clinical relevance to CFTR and lumacaftor binding.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study provides two cryo-EM structures of endogenously phosphorylated Saccharomyces cerevisiae Ycf1 (a glutathione transporter of the ABC-C subfamily) at 3.4Å and 4.0Å resolution, capturing previously unobserved ordered states of the intrinsically disordered regulatory R-domain (residues 901-935) in two inward-facing conformations (IFwide and IFnarrow). The R-domain, phosphorylated at S908, T911, and S914, is shown to be helical at its C-terminus (residues 920-929) and forms extensive electrostatic and hydrophobic interactions with NBD1 (spanning three buried hydrophobic sites) and the lasso domain. Biochemical data, including ATPase assays, in-gel phosphoprotein staining, limited proteolysis, and LC-MS/MS, confirm that R-domain phosphorylation reorganizes the Ycf1 architecture and is required for maximal ATPase activity. The dephosphorylated state shows a more complete protease digestion pattern and drastically reduced ATPase activity, consistent with cellular phenotypes where S908 and T911 mutations impair cadmium detoxification. The R-domain encircles NBD1 in both structures, with the IFwide-to-IFnarrow transition involving a rigid body movement of the R-domain/NBD1 complex relative to NBD2 and a reconfiguration of the ATP-binding sites, including partial occlusion of the non-functional ATP site in NBD1. The R-domain phosphorylation sites align with PKA-like (RRAS) and CKII kinase recognition motifs. A conserved inhibitory phosphosite at S251 (lasso domain) is identified in proximity, poised to disrupt the R-domain interaction via electrostatic repulsion. These findings challenge existing models of R-domain disordered-to-ordered transition and provide mechanistic insights for the ABCC transporter family, with clinical relevance to CFTR and lumacaftor binding.

Research Context
ABC transporters regulate diverse molecules for lipid homeostasis, ion transport, and detoxification. Ycf1 transports glutathione into vacuoles upon oxidation to maintain redox balance or after heavy metal conjugation. Approximately half of human ABC transporters are phosphorylated on intrinsically disordered regulatory domains. The R-domain in Ycf1 and CFTR has been predicted unstructured by circular dichroism, estimating as low as 5% helical content. Previous cryo-EM structures of CFTR and Ycf1 reveal a mostly disordered R-domain without assigned sequence for phosphorylation sites. To date no structure of an intact R-domain with the NBDs has been determined in any state. The regulatory mechanism of phosphorylation remains poorly understood, limiting understanding of R-domain interactions.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is how phosphorylation of the intrinsically disordered R-domain regulates the activity of the ABCC transporter Ycf1. The hypothesis is that phosphorylation at the R-domain induces an ordered conformation that stabilizes interactions with NBD1 and the lasso domain, thereby promoting ATPase activity. The authors predicted that the R-domain would be ordered and phosphorylated in the structures, contrary to previous models of complete disorder. It was predicted that the R-domain interactions would be related by rigid body movements between the inward-facing conformations. Biochemical data were expected to show that phosphorylation reorganizes Ycf1 architecture and is required for maximal ATPase activity. The study aimed to provide structural and biochemical details of phosphorylation-dependent regulation of Ycf1.

Methodological Details
Ycf1 was expressed as N-terminal Flag and C-terminal decahistidine tagged fusion protein in S. cerevisiae. The DSY-5 strain was transformed and grown in SC-His media at 30°C, followed by induction with 2% galactose. Two forms were purified: wild-type and the NBD2 Walker B mutant E1435Q to enable structural studies. Cryo-EM grids were prepared in apo conditions, and only the E1435Q dataset yielded homogenous particles for structure determination. Data processing used RELION 3.0/3.1, cisTEM, MotionCor2 for drift correction, and CTFFIND4.1 for CTF estimation. Particle picking used an automated approach guided by a 6.0Å reference free 2D classification map. Model building used SWISS-MODEL for an initial model with 6jb1 as template, COOT for manual building, and Phenix for refinement. Evolutionary couplings were analyzed using 13,723 sequences from Uniref90 via JackHMMR and PLMC. ATPase assays were conducted at 30°C in buffer containing 0.01% LMNG and 0.001% CHS, using an enzyme-coupled method. Each reaction contained 6.45 µg protein with 10 mM MgCl2, 1 mM PEP, and ATP at varying concentrations. Substrate-stimulated activity used GSSG at 1 mM ATP, with basal activity subtracted before fitting. Phosphorylation was confirmed by in-gel phosphoprotein staining (Pro-Q Diamond) and LC-MS/MS using Scaffold Q+S. Dephosphorylation was achieved by Lambda phosphatase treatment for 45 min at 4°C, followed by SEC. Limited proteolysis used trypsin at concentrations of 0–15 µg/mL incubated for 30 min on ice. The substrate binding cavity volume was calculated with a 2.5Å probe size, excluding NBDs.

Procedures And Architectures
The E1435Q NBD2 Walker B mutant substantially lowered ATPase activity (Vmax 18633 ± 474.7 nmol/sec/mg), trapping inward-facing conformations. Two structures were solved to 3.4Å (IFwide) and 4.0Å (IFnarrow) resolution, both in inward-facing open conformations. The resolved R-domain covers residues 901-935, with a helical C-terminal segment (920-929) and disordered other regions. The R-domain is stabilized by contacts along a basic groove of NBD1, intracellular loop 4, and the lasso domain. Phosphorylation sites were assigned to S908, T911, and S914 based on additional electron potential density. Three buried hydrophobic surfaces connect R-domain to NBD1: site 1 (I621-L802-I902-I904), site 2 (F917-I1123-L1120), and site 3 (L912-I915-I1154). The IFwide-to-IFnarrow transition involves a change in angle between G913, G918, and G932 from 130º to 137.5º. In NBD1, the non-functional ATP binding site is rotated to occlusion in IFnarrow, while the active NBD2 site remains open. The NBD1 X-loop and GRD motif are brought into contact upon transition to IFnarrow. A third, less well-resolved state labeled IFtransition was identified with weaker cryo-EM density in NBD2.

Key Results
The E1435Q mutant showed substantially lowered ATPase activity with Vmax 18633 ± 474.7 nmol/sec/mg compared to WT. Two inward-facing conformations were determined to 3.4Å and 4.0Å resolution, identifying IFwide and IFnarrow states. The R-domain is ordered and helical in its C-terminal segment (residues 920-929), aligning with CFTR partial models. Mass spectrometry and phosphostaining confirmed phosphorylation at S908, T911, and S914 in both WT and E1435Q. Phosphates make contacts with R716 (NBD1) and R206 (lasso domain) via hydrogen bonding or charge-charge interactions. The R-domain/NBD1 interface buries ~523Å² in IFnarrow and ~480Å² in IFwide specifically between NBD1 and R-domain. Total surface area buried along the entire R-domain is ~1530Å² in IFnarrow and ~1338Å² in IFwide. Dephosphorylated Ycf1 shows substantially changed trypsin digestion patterns with a clear increase in protease accessibility. ATPase assays show a drastic activity reduction in dephosphorylated Ycf1, suggesting R-domain interactions drive architecture for ATP hydrolysis. GSSG stimulates ATPase activity at physiologically relevant (µM) concentrations in WT and E1435Q. The R-domain encircles NBD1 in both IFwide and IFnarrow, with interactions nearly constant between structures. The IFwide-to-IFnarrow transition rotates the NBD1 non-functional ATP site to occlusion while NBD2 site remains open. The R-domain/NBD1 interaction includes cation-pi coordination of Ycf1 F713 (CFTR delF506 equivalent) with R765 and R1150.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The ordered R-domain architecture is stimulatory, challenging the widely held model of R-domain release upon phosphorylation. R-domain phosphorylation provides a transmission clutch: it engages a motor but does not perform work itself. The multiple phosphate binding interactions explain the well-known robustness to loss of any single R-domain phosphorylation site. The R-domain/NBD1 interaction increases ATPase rate in a manner consistent with CFTR R-domain phosphorylation potentiating ATP binding and hydrolysis. The inhibitory role of S251 phosphorylation in the lasso domain is explained by electrostatic repulsion disrupting the R-domain interaction network. The finding of a single defined binding site for the conserved R-domain may provide a basis for allosteric modulation of transporter function broadly. The proximity of mutations like F713 and lumacaftor binding site to the R-domain binding site rationalizes clinically relevant ABCC dysfunction. Ycf1 serves as a powerful protective function against metals and ROS, both electrophiles that attack DNA, proteins, and the cell membrane.

Contradictions And Limitations
The E1435Q mutation traps conformations but substantially lowers ATPase activity, making it difficult to assess full physiological turnover. The IFtransition state was insufficiently detailed to enable model building, and NBD2 remains less ordered with weaker cryo-EM density. Phosphates themselves may block protease accessibility to some sites, potentially confounding the dephosphorylation-dependent digestion interpretation. The R-domain is only partially resolved; the C-terminal segment is helical but the other regions lack secondary structure. The structures are in apo conditions; substrate-bound (GSSG) structures were not solved directly. The dephosphorylated state was not solved structurally, limiting direct comparison of ordered vs disordered R-domain positions. The NBD2 density is relatively weaker in both states, complicating assignment of NBD2-specific interactions.

Claims
Phosphorylation of the Ycf1 R-domain at S908, T911, and S914 induces an ordered conformation that stimulates ABCC transporter ATPase activity. Mass spectrometry and phosphostaining confirm phosphorylation at S908, T911, and S914 in both WT and E1435Q. ATPase assays show a drastic activity reduction in dephosphorylated Ycf1 compared to endogenously phosphorylated Ycf1. The R-domain/NBD1 interface buries ~523Å² in IFnarrow, providing thermodynamic driving force for R-domain binding. The C-terminal helix of the R-domain aligns with CFTR partial models, confirming conserved folding. The structures do not rule out an inhibitory role for the unphosphorylated state. Phosphates themselves may block protease accessibility, potentially confounding the dephosphorylation interpretation. The ordered R-domain architecture challenges the widely held model of R-domain release upon phosphorylation in CFTR activation. The R-domain acts as a transmission clutch, only engaging a motor but not performing work itself.
The IFwide-to-IFnarrow transition rotates NBD1 to occlude the non-functional ATP site while maintaining an open NBD2 site, priming the transporter for transport. The NBD1 non-functional ATP site rotates to occlusion in IFnarrow while NBD2 site remains open. The angle between G913, G918, and G932 changes from 130º to 137.5º during the transition. The X-loop and GRD motif are brought into contact upon transition to IFnarrow. NBD2 is the less ordered of the two NBDs with weaker cryo-EM density in both states. The IFtransition state is insufficiently detailed to enable model building or precise mechanistic mapping. The architectural changes resemble substrate-bound and substrate-free states of MRP1. The R-domain phosphorylation helps stabilize NBD1 to recruit other domains into a primed, active state.
The lasso domain phosphorylation site S251 acts as a negative regulator by disrupting R-domain interactions via electrostatic repulsion. S251 is accessible to the surface and poised to disrupt R-domain interactions through electrostatic repulsion. The R-domain and lasso domain are clustered, placing S251 in close proximity to R-domain phosphosites. Phosphorylation at S251 was not observed in the cryo-EM structures. This provides a plausible explanation for the inhibitory role of lasso domain phosphorylation on Ycf1 function. The clustering of R-domain and lasso domain domains provides a mechanism for allosteric inhibition.

Data And Code Availability
The study used RELION 3.0/3.1 for EM map generation, and the data processing workflow is detailed in Figs S2-5. Evcouplings was used for evolutionary coupling analysis, with software available at the authors' GitHub repository. No explicit data sharing statement or code repository link is provided in the text.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Two forms of Ycf1 (WT and E1435Q) were purified and used for comparison in ATPase assays and structural studies. Lambda phosphatase treatment was used to generate dephosphorylated Ycf1 for ATPase and proteolysis assays. Three technical replicates were used for ATPase kinetic parameter generation. LC-MS/MS used Bayesian statistics to identify spectra and required a minimum of two peptides with 95% confidence. JackHMMR and PLMC were used to calculate evolutionary couplings across 13,723 sequences with a 80% similarity cutoff for clustering. A probe size of 2.5Å was used for cavity volume calculations, consistent with previous bacterial glutathione transporter assessments.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A-C shows two inward-facing conformations (IFwide and IFnarrow) at 3.4Å and 4.0Å resolution with labeled domain regions. Figure 1D shows ATPase activity of WT and E1435Q Ycf1, with E1435Q substantially lower. Figure 1E shows the unoccluded substrate binding cavities in both IFwide and IFnarrow states. Figure 1F shows substrate-stimulated ATPase activity with GSSG at 1 mM ATP. Figure 2A-D illustrates R-domain contacts with NBD1, intracellular loop 4, and the lasso domain. Figure 2E shows pronounced additional electron potential density at S908, T911, and S914. Figure 2F shows in-gel phosphoprotein staining confirming phosphorylation at the three R-domain sites. Figure 2G shows increased protease accessibility in dephosphorylated Ycf1. Figure 2H shows a drastic ATPase activity reduction in dephosphorylated Ycf1. Figure 2C quantifies the buried surface area at the R-domain/NBD1 interface. Figure 3 shows the hydrophobic interaction sites between R-domain and NBD1. Figure 3E shows the X-loop and GRD motif contacting each other in IFnarrow. Figure 4A-C shows the rigid body movements and the occlusion of the NBD1 ATP site in the transition. Figure 4D shows the inhibitory role of S251 phosphorylation via electrostatic repulsion. Supplementary Table S1 lists evolutionary coupling results for R-domain residues. Supplementary Table S2 reports mass spectrometry and phosphostaining data. Figure S7E shows evolutionary coupling analysis of co-evolving residues. Figure S8A-F shows substrate-bound and substrate-free states of MRP1 for comparison. Figure S1A shows the Flag/His-tagged Ycf1 expression construct.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first determination of an ordered, phosphorylated R-domain (S908, T911, S914) in inward-facing Ycf1 conformations (3.4Å and 4.0Å), revealing an extensive electrostatic and hydrophobic interaction network with NBD1 and the lasso domain that stabilizes the R-domain in a stimulatory architecture. 2. The strongest evidence is the combination of cryo-EM visualization of every R-domain regulatory element with biochemical confirmation: dephosphorylated Ycf1 shows increased protease accessibility and drastic ATPase activity reduction, while GSSG stimulates ATPase activity in both WT and E1435Q at physiological µM concentrations. 3. The future path lies in applying the identified R-domain binding site to explain allosteric regulation and mutational dysfunction across the ABCC transporter family, including CFTR, and in structural studies of substrate-bound (GSSG) Ycf1 to directly confirm the primed-active transport state.

summary.executive_summary: This study evaluated the interaction between seed treatment with plant growth regulators (PGRs) and nitrogen fertilization on the germination, dry matter yield, and physiological composition of Brachiaria decumbens cv. Basilisk. The experiment was conducted in two stages: (1) a germination and initial growth assay (30 DAS) using coated versus conventional seeds with four PGR levels (0, 8, 16, 24 mL·kg⁻¹), and (2) a growth and fertilization experiment with four N application methods. Coated seeds exhibited higher germination percentages and speed index regardless of PGR treatment. A quadratic effect of PGR on germination identified 10.3 mL·kg⁻¹ as the optimal concentration for germination, while 12.8 mL·kg⁻¹ optimized root dry mass. A significant interaction between seed type and PGR level was found for leaf and pseudostem dry mass; coated seeds performed best at 0 and 8.0 mL·kg⁻¹ (optimal at 8.85 and 9.57 mL·kg⁻¹ respectively), while conventional seeds required higher concentrations (15.5 and 18.1 mL·kg⁻¹) for comparable yields. Soil N-fertilization consistently increased dry mass of all plant structures and root volume, with the highest yields achieved when PGR and soil fertilization were combined. Root dry mass increased only under combined PGR and multiple fertilization. Chlorophyll a was significantly increased by PGR, and foliar N-fertilization increased chlorophyll a, b, total chlorophyll, and carotenoids. The study concludes that low-level PGR treatment in coated seeds and soil N-fertilization are effective strategies for enhancing Brachiaria establishment, with PGR acting via hormonal signaling networks and N-fertilization maximizing photosynthetic rates.

Soil N-fertilization consistently increased dry mass of all plant structures and root volume, with the highest yields achieved when PGR and soil fertilization were combined. Chlorophyll a was significantly increased by PGR, and foliar N-fertilization increased chlorophyll a, b, total chlorophyll, and carotenoids. The study concludes that low-level PGR treatment in coated seeds and soil N-fertilization are effective strategies for enhancing Brachiaria establishment, with PGR acting via hormonal signaling networks and N-fertilization maximizing photosynthetic rates.

Research Context
Shortened planting windows due to adverse climatic factors reduce time for recovering degraded pastures. Greater seed efficiency in germination and emergence speed is necessary for timely pasture recovery. Synthetic growth promoters (auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins) act through signaling networks that activate plant growth genes. High-level gibberellin applications (>5-10 g·ha⁻¹) can reduce forage mass, making them uneconomical. PGRs have shown potential under stress by regulating genes linked to growth, water use, and mechanical impedance in dry soils. Nitrogen expands the vegetative phase and increases photoassimilate production for post-defoliation recovery. Nitrogen is essential for amino acids, proteins, and nucleic acids, stimulating cell division and elongation. The gap is the need for independent cross-evaluation of hormonal actions in pasture establishment under stress.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether seed treatment with PGRs combined with different N fertilization methods affects growth, germination, and physiological composition of Brachiaria decumbens cv. Basilisk. It is hypothesized that PGRs will increase germination percentage and mass yields of plant structures through organogenesis activation. It is predicted that soil N-fertilization will increase dry mass productions of leaf, stem, shoot, and root as well as root volume. The hypothesis states that rates of photoassimilate will be increased by the combination of soil fertilization and PGRs. The study predicts a significant interaction between seed type and PGR levels on leaf and pseudostem mass. The specific hypothesis is that coated seeds will perform better at lower PGR levels than conventional seeds.

Methodological Details
Experiments were performed at UESB, Itapetinga-BA, between June and September 2017 in a greenhouse and LAFIEP laboratory. Germination was carried out under hermetic storage in a Mangelsdorf germination chamber (MA-401) at 28°C with a 12h photoperiod. The soil used for the greenhouse experiment was collected at 0-20 cm depth and passed through a 4-mm sieve. Each pot in the greenhouse was filled with eight liters or 12 kg of dry soil for area productivity estimation. The first experiment used a 2 x 4 factorial scheme in a completely randomized design (CRD). Two commercial seed types (coated and conventional) and four PGR levels (0, 8, 16, 24 mL·kg⁻¹) were applied. PGR composition was auxin (0.05 mg·L⁻¹), cytokinin (0.09 mg·L⁻¹), and gibberellin (0.05 mg·L⁻¹). Seeds were wrapped in filter paper moistened with distilled water, 25 seeds per replicate, four replicates per treatment. After seed imbibition (approx. 2 hours), sowing was done in a seedling tray with 32 cells per replicate, two replicates per treatment. The second experiment used 8 treatments: untreated/treated seeds (0 and 24 mL·kg⁻¹) crossed with four N fertilization methods. Four plants per replicate and four replicates per treatment were used in the second experiment. N fertilization rates were 75 kg·ha⁻¹ N for soil and 3 L·ha⁻¹ for foliar, following the Minas Gerais 5th Approximation. The foliar fertilizer contained N (1.37%), P (2.5%), 2O₅ (15%), Mg (1.0%), S (1.5%), Zn (3.0%), Mn (2.0%), Cu (0.3%), B (0.2%), Mo (0.1%), Co (0.1%). Statistical analysis used the MIXED procedure of SAS, Tukey test, with significance at P ≤ 0.05. Pigment analysis used DMSO (5 mL) with 200 mg fresh mass per aliquot, adjusted to mg·g⁻¹ fresh mass. Readings were taken at 665, 649, and 480 nm using absorption spectrophotometry after 72 hours. Daily germination counts were performed for 14 days. At 30 DAS, a standardization cut with average residue height of 15 cm was performed. Two additional 28-day periods followed the standardization cut for data collection.

Procedures And Architectures
The PGR was applied after seed imbibition for approximately two hours, followed by wrapping in filter paper moistened with distilled water. The growth regulator formulation was a combination of auxin (0.05 mg·L⁻¹), cytokinin (0.09 mg·L⁻¹), and gibberellin (0.05 mg·L⁻¹). Initial growth assessments were conducted at 30 days after sowing in seedling trays with sterilized coconut residue substrate. The second experiment design crossed seed type (treated/untreated) with four N methods: no fertilization, soil fertilization, foliar fertilization, and multiple fertilization (soil + foliar). Fertilization was performed after the standardization cut at 30 DAS. The foliar spray composition included 1.37% N, 2.5% P, 15.0% 2O₅, and trace minerals from the manufacturer. Whole-plant yield was determined at the end of each period, followed by desiccation to separate root, stem, and leaf components. The third fully expanded leaf of each repetition was collected at 10 a.m. for pigment extraction. Samples were wrapped in aluminum foil during the 72-hour DMSO extraction period. Linear and quadratic contrast statements were constructed to analyze PGR effects, and the maximum point was estimated from regression equations. PGR, Fertilization, and their interaction were analyzed as fixed effects for all measurements in the second experiment.

Key Results
The interaction between seed type and PGR levels was not significant for germination percentage or germination speed index (GSI). A quadratic effect of PGR levels on germination was found regardless of seed type. Regression estimated that treatment with 10.3 mL·kg⁻¹ PGR promoted the greatest germination percentage. Coated seeds exhibited higher germination percentages and GSI than conventional seeds (Table 2). For number of leaves, tillers, and root dry mass, the interaction between seed type and PGR was not significant. The number of leaves and tillers were influenced by seed type, but root dry mass production was not affected by seed type. Based on the regression equation, 12.8 mL·kg⁻¹ PGR resulted in the highest root dry mass production (Table 3). A significant interaction existed between seed type and PGR on leaf and pseudostem dry mass production. Coated seeds had higher leaf dry mass at 8.85 mL·kg⁻¹ and pseudostem dry mass at 9.57 mL·kg⁻¹. Coated seeds performed best at absence of treatment (0 mL·kg⁻¹) or at the lowest tested level (8.0 mL·kg⁻¹). Leaf and pseudostem dry mass did not differ between seed types at 16.0 and 24.0 mL·kg⁻¹. Conventional seeds required higher PGR levels: 15.5 mL·kg⁻¹ for leaf and 18.1 mL·kg⁻¹ for pseudostem dry mass (Table 4). The interaction between PGR and N fertilization methods was significant for leaf, stem, shoot, and root dry mass. Dry mass of stem, leaf, and shoot was greater when PGR and soil fertilization were combined, but soil fertilization produced higher yields overall. PGR reduced leaf, stem, and shoot production when combined with multiple fertilization (soil + foliar), differing from absence of PGR. PGR increased root dry mass only when combined with multiple fertilization; no influence was observed for other fertilization types (Table 5). The interaction between PGR and N fertilization was not significant for chlorophyll a, b, total chlorophyll, carotenoids, and chlorophyll a/b ratio. PGR had a significant effect on chlorophyll a levels alone. N fertilization methods influenced chlorophyll a, b, and carotenoid levels (Table 6).

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Exogenous hormones increase auxin, cytokinin, and gibberellin levels within 24 hours of imbibition, altering hormonal balance and metabolite biosynthesis. Increased exogenous gibberellin enhances intracellular transport of intermediates to bioactive gibberellin, which activates genes for germinative characteristics. Gibberellin overcomes mechanical barriers by weakening structures covering the radicle and reduces abscisic acid, the main dormancy promoter. Seed coating provides mechanical protection and nutrients to the embryo, favoring radicle and seedling emergence. Auxin in the PGR composition increases rhizogenesis by stimulating stem cell multiplication and accumulating in quiescent centers. The interaction between auxin and cytokinin regulates organ-forming genes and meristem maintenance. Higher root dry mass with soil fertilization reflects greater N supply combined with PGR-accelerated cellular metabolism. Increased chlorophyll a with PGR, combined with mass yields, suggests PGR functions in the signaling network of photosynthetic processes. Higher chlorophyll a promotes photophosphorylation and ATP synthesis in chloroplasts, providing more substrate for plant development. Foliar N fertilization may participate in cytokinin synthesis, promoting chlorophyll synthesis and delayed senescence.

Contradictions And Limitations
PGR did not increase the number of leaves or tillers, contrary to expectations in some hormonal growth studies. PGR reduced leaf, stem, and shoot production when combined with multiple fertilization, a counterintuitive result that required interpretation. Coated seeds required lower PGR levels for optimal response, suggesting that seed purity affects hormone use efficiency. The paper notes that little is known about the role of auxins and cytokinins in regulation of photosynthetic processes. The effect of auxin on chloroplast movement remains inconclusive. PGRs in the form of plant herbicides act by blocking photosynthetic electron flux, a potentially detrimental effect not explicitly quantified here. No random seed or genetic variation control is explicitly detailed beyond 'coated and conventional' seed types. The study was confined to a single location (UESB) and a single cultivar (Basilisk), limiting generalizability.

Claims
PGR seed treatment enhances germination and structural growth of Brachiaria decumbens cv. Basilisk, with optimal effects at specific low concentrations. 10.3 mL·kg⁻¹ PGR promotes the greatest germination percentage. Coated seeds exhibited higher germination and GSI than conventional seeds. Coated seeds achieved peak leaf dry mass at 8.85 mL·kg⁻¹ and pseudostem at 9.57 mL·kg⁻¹ when combined with lower PGR. 12.8 mL·kg⁻¹ PGR resulted in the highest root dry mass. PGR did not affect the number of leaves or tillers. PGR reduced leaf and shoot production when combined with multiple N fertilization. Lower PGR levels are sufficient for coated seeds, reducing input costs. Coated seeds should be prioritized in pasture establishment for better germination.
Soil N-fertilization is the most effective nitrogen management practice for maximizing dry matter yield and chlorophyll content in Brachiaria decumbens. Soil fertilization resulted in higher yields for all evaluated structures regardless of PGR. The combination of PGR and soil fertilization produced the highest stem, leaf, and shoot dry mass. Foliar N-fertilization increased chlorophyll a, b, total chlorophyll, and carotenoids. Foliar fertilization alone showed no specific effect on mass yield compared to soil. Multiple fertilization (soil + foliar) showed reduced yields when combined with PGR. Soil N-application should be the primary fertilization strategy for pasture establishment. PGR and N-fertilization can be combined strategically for enhanced growth.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The study used a 2 x 4 factorial design with four replicates per treatment in the main experiment, providing adequate statistical power. Single-degree-of-freedom contrast statements were constructed to analyze linear and quadratic effects of PGR levels. Regression equations were used to estimate optimal PGR concentrations for germination and root mass. Interaction effects were explicitly tested across all growth structures, identifying specific combinations of seed type × PGR and PGR × N. The foliar fertilizer composition was sourced from the manufacturer to ensure standardization.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows greenhouse conditions (average, minimum, maximum temperatures and relative humidity) recorded with a digital thermo-hygrometer. Table 1 details the foliar spray composition: 1.37% N, 2.5% P, 15.0% 2O₅, 1.0% Mg, 1.5% S, 3.0% Zn, 2.0% Mn, 0.3% Cu, 0.2% B, 0.1% Mo, 0.1% Co. Table 2 reports germination percentage and GSI by seed type and PGR level, showing coated seeds had higher values. Table 3 reports number of leaves, tillers, and root dry mass by seed type and PGR, identifying 12.8 mL·kg⁻¹ as optimal. Table 4 reports leaf and pseudostem dry mass by seed type and PGR, showing 8.85 and 9.57 mL·kg⁻¹ for coated seeds and 15.5/18.1 for conventional. Table 5 reports dry mass of stem, shoot, and root by PGR and N fertilization, showing PGR×N interaction. Table 6 reports chlorophyll and carotenoid contents by PGR and N fertilization, showing significant PGR effect on chlorophyll a.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is demonstrating that low-dose PGR seed treatment (8-12.8 mL·kg⁻¹) in coated seeds, combined with soil N-fertilization (75 kg·ha⁻¹), optimizes germination, root development, and dry matter yield in Brachiaria decumbens cv. Basilisk. 2. The strongest evidence is the quadratic PGR effect identifying 10.3 mL·kg⁻¹ for germination and 12.8 mL·kg⁻¹ for root dry mass, and the significant interaction on leaf dry mass where coated seeds peaked at 8.85 mL·kg⁻¹ and conventional at 15.5 mL·kg⁻¹. 3. The future path involves evaluating Pure Live Seeds (PLS) to improve hormone use efficiency in conventional seeds and clarifying the role of auxins and cytokinins in photosynthetic regulation to better predict physiological responses.

summary.authors: Jihun Ahn; Byounggeol Choi; Yeon Choi; Jae Kyeong Byun; Ahmed Mashaly; Kareem Abdelshafi; Yoonjee Park; Young Jang; Woohyeun Kim; Eunjin Park; Jin Oh Na; Cheol Ung Choi; Eungju Kim; Chang Gyu Park; Hongseog Seo; Dongjoo Oh; Jinsu Byeon; Sangho Park; Hyeyon Yu; Seung-Woon W Rha
