summary.executive_summary: This prospective registry study investigated whether chronic total occlusion (CTO) lesion length significantly affects six-month angiographic and two-year clinical outcomes following successful percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) with drug-eluting stents (DES). A total of 235 consecutive CTO patients undergoing successful DES PCI between November 2004 and October 2010 at Korea University Guro Hospital were divided into long CTO (≥30mm, n=159) and short CTO (<30mm, n=76) groups. The study aimed to determine if lesion length serves as a prognostic factor in the DES era, given prior evidence that long coronary lesions correlate with worse PCI outcomes. Baseline characteristics were similar except for higher prior PCI in the long group and more frequent bifurcation lesions in the short group. In-hospital complications were similar except for more frequent intimal dissection in the long group. At six months, angiographic outcomes, including binary restenosis (19.1% vs. 8.8%, p=0.12) and in-stent restenosis (33.3% vs. 26.6%, p=0.42), showed no statistically significant difference between groups, though a numerical trend toward worse outcomes in long CTO was observed. At two years, hard clinical endpoints—total death (3.1% vs. 5.2%, p=0.43), cardiac death (1.2% vs. 2.6%, p=0.45), MI (1.8% vs. 2.6%, p=0.71), and MACE (21.3% vs. 13.1%, p=0.13)—were statistically similar. However, the long CTO group had significantly higher repeat PCI (18.8% vs. 7.8%, p<0.05) and TVR (16.3% vs. 6.5%, p<0.05). Multivariate logistic regression identified long CTO as a significant independent predictor for repeat PCI (OR 4.26; CI 1.53-11.9; p=0.006) and TVR (OR 4.23; CI 1.52-11.8; p<0.05). The authors conclude that while long CTO lesion length predicts higher revascularization rates, it does not translate into worse hard endpoints in the DES era, and long-term, larger-scale studies are needed to confirm.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This prospective registry study investigated whether chronic total occlusion (CTO) lesion length significantly affects six-month angiographic and two-year clinical outcomes following successful percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) with drug-eluting stents (DES). A total of 235 consecutive CTO patients undergoing successful DES PCI between November 2004 and October 2010 at Korea University Guro Hospital were divided into long CTO (≥30mm, n=159) and short CTO (<30mm, n=76) groups. The study aimed to determine if lesion length serves as a prognostic factor in the DES era, given prior evidence that long coronary lesions correlate with worse PCI outcomes. Baseline characteristics were similar except for higher prior PCI in the long group and more frequent bifurcation lesions in the short group. In-hospital complications were similar except for more frequent intimal dissection in the long group. At six months, angiographic outcomes, including binary restenosis (19.1% vs. 8.8%, p=0.12) and in-stent restenosis (33.3% vs. 26.6%, p=0.42), showed no statistically significant difference between groups, though a numerical trend toward worse outcomes in long CTO was observed. At two years, hard clinical endpoints—total death (3.1% vs. 5.2%, p=0.43), cardiac death (1.2% vs. 2.6%, p=0.45), MI (1.8% vs. 2.6%, p=0.71), and MACE (21.3% vs. 13.1%, p=0.13)—were statistically similar. However, the long CTO group had significantly higher repeat PCI (18.8% vs. 7.8%, p<0.05) and TVR (16.3% vs. 6.5%, p<0.05). Multivariate logistic regression identified long CTO as a significant independent predictor for repeat PCI (OR 4.26; CI 1.53-11.9; p=0.006) and TVR (OR 4.23; CI 1.52-11.8; p<0.05). The authors conclude that while long CTO lesion length predicts higher revascularization rates, it does not translate into worse hard endpoints in the DES era, and long-term, larger-scale studies are needed to confirm.

Research Context
Long coronary artery lesions are established as worse prognostic factors after percutaneous coronary intervention. Despite DES development, procedural success rates for CTO remain lower than for non-CTO patients. Long-term CTO outcomes are affected by both clinical risk factors and baseline lesion characteristics. No definite answers exist regarding CTO PCI outcomes according to lesion length specifically in the DES era. Previous studies established that treatment of non-CTO disease with DES is affected by lesion length as a major predictor of MACE.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether CTO lesion length significantly impacts six-month angiographic and two-year clinical outcomes following successful DES PCI. The investigators predicted adverse clinical outcomes, including MACE and angiographic outcomes, would be more frequent in the long CTO group. Two specific mechanisms were hypothesized to drive worse outcomes in long CTO: worse clinical risk factors (prior MI, prior PCI) and dominant use of paclitaxel-eluting stents in long CTO versus newer DES in short CTO. The study hypothesizes that the difference between hard endpoints and revascularization rates in long CTO can be explained by less myocardial viability and well-developed collateral channels. The study was powered to compare hard clinical endpoints (death, MI, MACE) and major revascularization events (repeat PCI, TVR, TLR) between length cohorts.

Methodological Details
A total of 235 consecutive CTO patients underwent successful PCI with DES from November 2004 to October 2010 at Korea University Guro Hospital, Seoul. The study protocol was approved by the institutional review board at Korea University Guro Hospital. All patients provided informed consent to participate in the study. CTO was defined as complete coronary obstruction with TIMI flow grade 0, estimated duration ≥3 months, with or without visible collateral flow. Only de novo lesions were included; CTO due to in-stent restenosis was excluded. The long CTO group included patients with angiographic lesion length ≥30mm (n=159). The short CTO group included patients with angiographic lesion length <30mm (n=76). Loading doses: clopidogrel (300-600mg) and aspirin (200-300mg) before the index procedure. Maintenance: aspirin (100mg) and clopidogrel (75mg), with clopidogrel encouraged for at least 1 year. Adjunctive cilostazol: 200mg post-loading then 100mg twice daily for at least one month at physician discretion. Procedural success defined as reduction in final angiographic diameter stenosis to <30% and TIMI grade ≥2. QCA parameters measured before PCI, immediately after PCI, and 6 months after index procedure at Korea University Guro Hospital. Primary angiographic endpoint: incidence of binary restenosis at 6-12 months. Secondary angiographic endpoints: in-stent restenosis, mean diameter stenosis, minimal luminal diameter, and late loss at 6 months. Primary clinical endpoint: major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), defined as composite of total death, recurrent MI, and revascularization (PCI and CABG). Secondary clinical endpoints: death, MI, repeat PCI, TLR, TVR, non-TVR; MACE subdivided into TLR-MACE and TVR-MACE. Q-wave MI defined as new pathological Q-waves in ≥2 contiguous leads with or without elevated CK-MB fraction level. Continuous variables: Student's t-test (mean ± standard deviation); Categorical: χ2 or Fisher's exact test. Logistic regression with adjustment for sex, age, hypertension, DM, chronic kidney disease, prior PCI, and bifurcation lesion. Statistical significance set at p < 0.05 (2-sided), analyses performed using SPSS 20.

Procedures And Architectures
PCI procedures were performed using standard techniques with various available guidewires to cross CTO lesions. A variety of atheroablative devices were not utilized; mostly simple pre-dilation with balloon was performed to get adequate luminal diameter for stent accommodation. Adjunctive balloon dilatation was performed only if necessary to achieve optimal outcome. All PCI used DES; stent type was decided by the operator during the procedures. Follow-up angiography was not routinely performed; it depended on ischemic symptoms or physician discretion regardless of symptoms. Vessel size: short CTO group 3.11 ± 0.43 mm versus long CTO group 2.92 ± 0.42 mm (p < 0.05), both categorized as small vessel diameter.

Key Results
In-hospital complications were similar between groups except intimal dissection was more frequent in the long CTO group. Total death at 2 years: 3.1% in long CTO vs. 5.2% in short CTO (p = 0.43). Cardiac death: 1.2% vs. 2.6% (p = 0.45). MI: 1.8% vs. 2.6% (p = 0.71). MACE at 2 years: 21.3% in long CTO vs. 13.1% in short CTO (p = 0.13). Repeat PCI: 18.8% in long CTO vs. 7.8% in short CTO (p < 0.05). Target vessel revascularization (TVR): 16.3% in long CTO vs. 6.5% in short CTO (p < 0.05). Angiographic data available for 99/159 (62%) long CTO and 45/76 (59%) short CTO patients. In-stent restenosis (ISR) at 6 months: 33.3% in long CTO vs. 26.6% in short CTO (p = 0.42). Binary restenosis at 6 months: 19.1% in long CTO vs. 8.8% in short CTO (p = 0.12). Late loss (LL) at 6 months: 0.65 ± 0.82 mm in long CTO vs. 0.46 ± 0.56 mm in short CTO (p = 0.13). Multivariate logistic regression identified long CTO as an independent predictor for repeat PCI with OR 4.26 (CI 1.53-11.9; p = 0.006). Multivariate logistic regression identified long CTO as an independent predictor for TVR with OR 4.23 (CI 1.52-11.8; p < 0.05).

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Hard endpoints (death, MI, MACE) were not significantly different between length groups, suggesting that in the DES era, long CTO lesion length does not worsen overall procedural safety or mortality. The discrepancy between higher TVR in long CTO (no significance in hard endpoints) may be explained by less myocardial viability and well-developed collateral channels lessening the physiologic impact of restenosis. Well-developed collaterals and myocardial viability in long CTO lesions may act as cardioprotective mechanisms against revascularization events. The numerical trend toward worse angiographic outcomes in long CTO (binary restenosis 19.1% vs. 8.8%) suggests that with longer follow-up and larger sample size, the difference may become significant. Even though vessel diameter was smaller in short CTO (3.11 mm vs. 2.92 mm; p < 0.05), both groups met the criteria for small vessel diameter and this did not significantly affect outcomes.

Contradictions And Limitations
The study is not a randomized controlled trial but a prospective registry; baseline clinical and lesion characteristics differed between groups. Newer generation DES was frequent in the short CTO group, while first generation stents were frequently used in the long CTO group, confounding the DES-era comparisons. Follow-up angiography was not routinely performed for all patients; it depended on ischemic symptoms or physician discretion, introducing potential selection bias. Well-developed collaterals and myocardial viability may have influenced ischemic symptoms, confounding the angiography decisions. The sample size was relatively small and the study did not have strong power to prove differences in angiographic outcomes. The two-year follow-up period was not long enough to evaluate long-term safety and efficacy. Despite strict statistical adjustment, unmeasured confounders and analytical bias could not be ruled out. Only 62% of long CTO and 59% of short CTO patients completed 6-month angiographic follow-up, limiting the angiographic analysis.

Claims
Long CTO lesion length is a significant independent predictor of repeat PCI and TVR but not for hard clinical endpoints in the DES era. Repeat PCI incidence was significantly higher in long CTO: 18.8% vs. 7.8% (p<0.05). TVR incidence was significantly higher in long CTO: 16.3% vs. 6.5% (p<0.05). Multivariate regression: Long CTO OR 4.26 for repeat PCI (CI 1.53-11.9, p=0.006). Multivariate regression: Long CTO OR 4.23 for TVR (CI 1.52-11.8, p<0.05). MACE p-value 0.13, cardiac death p=0.45, MI p=0.71: no statistical difference in hard endpoints. Angiographic data was only available for ~60% of patients in each group, limiting the angiographic claim's generalizability. The numerical trend in binary restenosis (19.1% vs. 8.8%) reached only p=0.12, not statistically significant. Long CTO patients require more frequent revascularization surveillance but may not be at higher risk for immediate mortality after DES PCI. Clinical management should consider longer-term angiographic monitoring for long CTO lesions even if DES is successfully deployed.
The lack of difference in hard clinical endpoints between long and short CTO groups in the DES era suggests that DES has equalized safety profiles across CTO lengths. Cardiac death 1.2% vs 2.6% (p=0.45); MI 1.8% vs 2.6% (p=0.71); total death 3.1% vs 5.2% (p=0.43). Safety profile and angiographic outcomes were similar between two groups at 6 months. The results suggest DES PCI in long CTO is as safe as in short CTO. A lot of data shows newer DES has superior outcomes; first-generation DES use in long CTO group may have attenuated differences. The study is single-center, prospective registry without randomization, limiting causal inference. CTO lesion length may not be a primary determinant of procedural or short-term clinical success in the DES era. Larger registry studies are needed to confirm if DES equalizes outcomes across CTO lengths over longer durations.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Multivariate logistic regression was used for sensitivity analysis to adjust for sex, age, hypertension, DM, CKD, prior PCI, and bifurcation lesion. The study reports that despite strict statistical adjustment, unmeasured confounders and analytical bias could not be fully ruled out. No explicit subgroup analyses beyond the long/short CTO split and multivariate regression are reported. The paper notes that the difference in vessel diameter (3.11 vs 2.92 mm, p<0.05) did not significantly affect outcomes.

Key Figures Tables
Table 1 demonstrates baseline clinical and angiographic characteristics for long (n=159) and short (n=76) CTO groups. Table 2 reports procedural and in-hospital complications, noting more frequent intimal dissection in the long CTO group. Table 3 summarizes 2-year clinical outcomes including total death, cardiac death, MI, and MACE. Table 4 shows predictors for repeat PCI and TVR from multivariate logistic regression, including ORs and CIs. Table 5 presents six-month angiographic outcomes including ISR, binary restenosis, and late loss for long (n=99) and short (n=45) follow-up patients.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution: Long CTO lesion length is a significant independent predictor of repeat PCI and TVR (OR 4.26) in the DES era, but does not affect 2-year hard clinical endpoints (death, MI, MACE). 2. The strongest evidence: Multivariate regression confirmed long CTO as an independent predictor for repeat PCI (p=0.006) and TVR (p<0.05) while all hard clinical endpoints showed no statistical difference between groups (p > 0.10). 3. The future path: Long-term follow-up (beyond 2 years) with a larger, multicenter randomized population is required to clarify the ultimate clinical impact of CTO lesion length.

summary.title: Synthesis, Biological Activity and Molecular Docking of New Tricyclic Series as α-glucosidase Inhibitors
summary.authors: Hatem A Abuelizz, Azman N I Nor, Iwana, Rohaya Ahmad, Anouar El-Hassane, Mohamed Marzouk, Rashad Al-Salahi
summary.field_subfield: Medicinal Chemistry / Antidiabetic Drug Discovery
summary.type_of_paper: Original research article reporting synthesis, biological evaluation, and molecular docking
summary.executive_summary: This study reports the design, synthesis, biological evaluation, and molecular docking of 25 new tricyclic 2-phenoxypyrido[3,2e][1,2,4]triazolo[1,5-a]pyrimidin-5(4H)-one hybrids as potential α-glucosidase inhibitors for type II diabetes management. The authors identified two compounds, 6h and 6d, that exhibited potent inhibitory activity surpassing the reference drug acarbose. Compound 6h achieved the highest inhibition with an IC50 of 104.07 mM, significantly lower than the IC50 of acarbose (which is not explicitly quoted but implied as the benchmark). The synthesis proceeded via a convergent route starting from 1,2,4-triazole intermediate B, yielding the core scaffold 1, which was further converted through thionation (compound 3), chlorination (compound 5), and subsequent nucleophilic displacement reactions. In vitro screening using α-glucosidase from Baker's yeast showed that 8 out of 25 compounds exceeded 50% average inhibition. Molecular docking studies using PDB code 3W37 revealed that compound 6h forms a stable ligand-enzyme complex with a binding energy of -10.55 to -10.56 kcal/mol, establishing three hydrogen bonds with residues Ala234, Arg552, and Asp469, while Trp329 directs the ligand orientation. judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study reports the design, synthesis, biological evaluation, and molecular docking of 25 new tricyclic 2-phenoxypyrido[3,2e][1,2,4]triazolo[1,5-a]pyrimidin-5(4H)-one hybrids as potential α-glucosidase inhibitors for type II diabetes management. The authors identified two compounds, 6h and 6d, that exhibited potent inhibitory activity surpassing the reference drug acarbose. Compound 6h achieved the highest inhibition with an IC50 of 104.07 mM, significantly lower than the IC50 of acarbose (which is not explicitly quoted but implied as the benchmark). The synthesis proceeded via a convergent route starting from 1,2,4-triazole intermediate B, yielding the core scaffold 1, which was further converted through thionation (compound 3), chlorination (compound 5), and subsequent nucleophilic displacement reactions. In vitro screening using α-glucosidase from Baker's yeast showed that 8 out of 25 compounds exceeded 50% average inhibition. Molecular docking studies using PDB code 3W37 revealed that compound 6h forms a stable ligand-enzyme complex with a binding energy of -10.55 to -10.56 kcal/mol, establishing three hydrogen bonds with residues Ala234, Arg552, and Asp469, while Trp329 directs the ligand orientation. The study concludes that the aminobridge substitution at position 4 of the pyrimidine ring is key to potency, and the new scaffold offers a non-sugar-mimetic alternative to carbasugar-based inhibitors, potentially reducing the gastrointestinal side effects associated with acarbose.

Research Context
Diabetes prevalence has surged globally, increasing from 108 million in 1980 to 422 million according to the WHO 2014 report. The prevalence among people over 18 years old rose from 4.7% in 1980 to 8.5% in 2014. α-glucosidase inhibitors such as acarbose, miglitol, and voglibose delay carbohydrate hydrolysis but cause flatulence and diarrhoea as gastrointestinal side effects. Acarbose acts by mimicking the oxocarbenium ion-like transition state, but most produced compounds were sugar mimetics requiring tedious synthesis. Previous work demonstrated that pyridine, triazole, and pyrimidine scaffolds incorporated in various compounds displayed antimicrobial, antiviral, anticancer, anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and anticonvulsant activities. Pyrido[3,2-e][1,2,4]triazolo[1,5-a]pyrimidin-5(4H)-ones have been reported as effective fungicidal agents. There is a high demand for effective antidiabetic agents that overcome the side effects associated with sugar mimetic agents.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question was whether modifying well-accepted medicinal chemistry scaffolds (pyridine, triazole, pyrimidine) could yield potent α-glucosidase inhibitors that overcome the side effects of sugar mimetics. Two series of phenoxypyrido-triazolo-pyrimidinones were designed to be evaluated for α-glucosidase inhibitory activity. The hypothesis was that significant inhibitory activity would be observed, with IC50 values lower than acarbose for at least two compounds. It was predicted that the aminobridge substitution at position 4 of the pyrimidine ring would contribute to strong inhibitory activity. Molecular docking was anticipated to provide insights into the binding modes and identify the critical residues responsible for inhibition.

Methodological Details
25 tricyclic 2-phenoxypyrido[3,2e][1,2,4]triazolo[1,5-a]pyrimidin-5(4H)-ones hybrids were synthesized and evaluated. In vitro screening used α-glucosidase type 1 from Baker's yeast. The enzyme was treated with equal concentrations of 100 µg/mL of each compound, with the test repeated three times for each. The α-glucosidase enzyme solution was prepared at a concentration of 0.125 unit/mL in 12 mL of cold phosphate-buffered saline at pH 6.5. The p-NPG substrate was prepared as a 20 mM solution. Compound concentrations for screening were prepared at 200 µg/mL in 100% dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO). Two-fold serial dilutions gave final concentrations of 100, 50, 25, 12.5, 6.25, 3.13, and 1.56 µg/mL. Acarbose served as the positive control, prepared at 200 µg/mL in 100% DMSO. The inhibitory activity was determined based on the method described by Ahmad et al., 2011. The relative standard deviation of the binding energy of the formed complex was less than 2.34 kcal/mol. The protein structure used for docking was PDB code 3W37. Molecular docking was performed using the Autodock software package.

Procedures And Architectures
Starting material A was reacted with diphenoxy-Ncyanoimidocarbonate (5 mmol) in ethanol (20 mL) with triethylamine (20 mmol) at room temperature overnight. The mixture was acidified with conc. HCl under ice cooling, heated for 1-2 h at 80 °C, and the product obtained as a white amorphous powder (78%). 1,2,4-triazole intermediate B was treated with conc. HCl initially at room temperature followed by heating. Compound B was reacted with alkyl or heteroalkyl halides in DMF with K2CO3 to give products 2a-l in 45-83% yields. Target 1 was treated with phosphorous pentasulfide in absolute pyridine to give compound 3 (90% yield). Compound 3 was converted to 4 in basic medium using benzyl bromide. Compound 1 was treated with POCl3 in boiling benzene followed by saturated basic solution to give imidoyl chloride 5. Compound 5 was reacted with aromatic amines in pyridine in a 1:5 molar ratio to give compounds 6a-d in 60-68% yields. Compound 5 was reacted with hydroxylamine HCl in a 1:2.5 molar ratio in boiling pyridine to give 6e in 63% yield. Compound 5 was treated with isoniazid in boiling toluene to give 6i in 74% yield. Hydrazinolysis of 5 in boiling ethanol followed by treatment with aldehydes gave hydrazone derivatives 6g and 6h. For the assay, 10 µL of 5% DMSO, 10 µL of stock, 20 µL of enzyme, 40 µL of PBS pH 6.5, and 20 µL of water were mixed in 96-well plates. The mixture was pre-incubated at 37 °C for 10 min before 10 µL of 20 mM p-NPG was added. Reaction was incubated for 30 min at 37 °C, and absorbance was measured at 405 nm. Molecular docking detailed steps were reported by Abuelizz and collaborators.

Key Results
Out of 25 tested compounds, 8 exhibited more than 50% average percent inhibition. Compounds 3, 6c, and 6d showed average percent inhibition of more than 60%. Compounds 2a, 2d, 6a, 6b, and 6h showed average percent inhibition between 50% and 60%. The average percent inhibitions of 2a and 2d were 50.36% and 57.48%, respectively. Compound 3 at 100 µg/mL exhibited 60.38% inhibition. The IC50 of compound 3 was 167.82 µM. The IC50 values of compounds 2a and 2d were 304.13 µM and 173.83 µM, respectively. Compound 6h exhibited the highest inhibition with an IC50 of 104.07 mM. The binding energy of docked 6h was -10.55 to -10.56 kcal/mol, the lowest among the docked derivatives. The binding energy of compound 6a was -9.76 kcal/mol and 6b was -9.17 kcal/mol. Compound 2a has a free binding energy of -8.12 kcal/mol. Acarbose can establish 10 hydrogen bonds with Asp232, Ala234, Asn237, Asp357, Arg552, Asp568, and His626. Compound 6h establishes hydrogen bonds with Ala234, Arg552, and Asp469. Acarbose shows two hydrophobic interactions with Phe601 and Trp329. Trp329 forms hydrophobic bonds with 2a and 6h, responsible for binding conformation. Compound 2a forms only one hydrogen bond between the nitrogen on the triazole ring and Arg552.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The aminobridge substitution of the pyrimidine ring at position 4 is responsible for the strong inhibitory activity. The derivation of 2a and 2d at position 4 had no significant effect on inhibitory activity. The inhibitory activity of acarbose correlates with the number of hydroxyl groups and the number of established hydrogen bonds. The maximal inhibition activity of 6h is mainly attributable to its binding energy and the stability of the ligand-α-glucosidase complex. Trp329 plays a significant role in directing the ligand in the binding site of the α-glucosidase enzyme. The study provides a new structural insight for the development of novel α-glucosidase inhibitors that differ from commonly employed carbasugars. The new scaffold can eventually be transformed into new clinical drugs for the treatment of type II diabetes.

Contradictions And Limitations
The paper does not explicitly state the IC50 of acarbose in µM or mM for direct comparison. Compound 6h's IC50 is reported as 104.07 mM, which is unusually high for a potent inhibitor; a discrepancy between mM and µM units may exist in reporting. The specific PDB structure 3W37 is for α-glucosidase but the paper doesn't explicitly state the source organism of the enzyme model (though Baker's yeast is used for the assay). The paper does not report a full dose-response curve for all 25 compounds, only IC50s for those with >50% inhibition. No explicit cytotoxicity or in vivo studies are performed to validate the safety of the potent compounds. The molecular docking is performed in silico only; no crystallographic evidence confirms the predicted binding mode. No solubility or pharmacokinetic data are provided for the synthesized compounds. The abstract mentions 

Claims
Compounds 6h and 6d possess the highest α-glucosidase inhibitory activity among the synthesized series, surpassing acarbose. Compound 6h exhibited an IC50 of 104.07 mM, the lowest reported value in the series. Compounds 6d and 6h showed significant inhibitory activity with lower IC50 values than acarbose. Compound 2a and 2d had IC50 values of 304.13 µM and 173.83 µM, which are numerical values in a different magnitude than 104.07 mM. The abstract states 6h is the highest, but the docking data shows 6h binding energy is -10.55 kcal/mol while 6a is -9.76 kcal/mol, yet 6h is described as having 'maximal inhibition'. These compounds represent a non-carbasugar scaffold for α-glucosidase inhibition, potentially reducing gastrointestinal side effects. The aminobridge substitution at position 4 is identified as a critical structural feature for potency.
The binding of compound 6h is stabilized by three hydrogen bonds with Ala234, Arg552, and Asp469, and directed by Trp329. 6h can establish hydrogen bonds with Ala234, Arg552, and Asp469. Trp329 plays a significant role in directing the ligand in the binding site. The binding energy of docked 6h was -10.55 to -10.56 kcal/mol. Acarbose establishes 10 hydrogen bonds while 6h establishes only three, which is a significant difference in binding network complexity. Compound 2a only forms one hydrogen bond with Arg552, highlighting the dependence of stability on the number of interactions. Future optimization should focus on increasing the number of hydrogen bonds to approach acarbose levels.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The study tested 25 compounds with different substitutions to explore the SAR of the pyrimidino-triazolo-pyrido scaffold. Derivatization at position 4 (N-substitution) was explored by comparing compounds 2a-2l against 6a-6i. Compounds 6a, 6b, 6c, 6d, and 6h were compared to assess the effect of varying aromatic and aliphatic groups at the amino bridge. Three hydrogen bonds vs. one hydrogen bond (2a) demonstrated the importance of multiple interactions for stability. Compounds 6a and 6b differ only at the amino group substitution, allowing direct comparison of the aromatic vs. aliphatic benzyl effect.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 illustrates the general structure of acarbose, its mechanism of action, and examples of other α-glucosidase inhibitors. Figure 2 illustrates the synthetic route towards fused pyrimidine derivatives, showing intermediate B, scaffold 1, and products 2a-l, 3, 5, 6a-i. Figure 3 compares the average percent inhibition of compounds 6a-6i against 2a-2l, highlighting the effect of aminobridge substitution. Figure 4 shows the IC50 values of compounds 3, 2a, 2d, 6a-d, 6h compared to acarbose. Figure 5 displays binding energies, number of hydrogen bonds, and hydrophobic interactions for the docked complexes. Table 1 reports the detailed molecular docking parameters: binding energies, number of hydrogen bonds, closest amino acid residues, and RMSD.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the synthesis of 25 tricyclic 2-phenoxypyrido[3,2e][1,2,4]triazolo[1,5-a]pyrimidin-5(4H)-ones and identification of two compounds (6h and 6d) with α-glucosidase inhibitory activity superior to acarbose. 2. The strongest evidence for the mechanism is the molecular docking data showing compound 6h's lowest binding energy (-10.55 kcal/mol), three hydrogen bonds with key residues (Ala234, Arg552, Asp469), and hydrophobic directing by Trp329. 3. The future path involves structural optimization to increase the number of hydrogen bonds, in vivo pharmacological testing, and potential clinical development as a non-carbasugar antidiabetic agent.

summary.title: Major concerns with the integrity of the mitochondrial ADP/ATP carrier in dodecyl-phosphocholine used for solution NMR studies
summary.authors: Martin S King; Paul G Crichton; Jonathan J Ruprecht; Edmund R S Kunji
summary.field_subfield: Biochemistry / Structural Biology / Membrane Protein Biophysics
summary.executive_summary:
This paper is a critical rebuttal by King et al. against a bioRxiv preprint by Brüschweiler et al. regarding the mitochondrial ADP/ATP carrier (AAC3) of yeast. Brüschweiler et al. claimed that AAC3 could be refolded from Escherichia coli inclusion bodies to homogeneity in the detergent dodecyl-phosphocholine (DPC) and maintained in a folded, active state for ITC and NMR studies. King et al. systematically refute these claims using thermostability assays, ITC, and functional reconstitution experiments. They demonstrate that DPC, rather than stabilizing AAC3, causes immediate loss of tertiary structure and inactivation upon isolation from the inner mitochondrial membrane. 

Key evidence includes: 1) ITC measurements showing a CATR binding Kd of ~15 μM for DPC-refolded AAC3, versus 72 nM for native AAC3 in dodecyl-maltoside/tetraoleoyl cardiolipin (a 200–2000-fold difference); 2) thermostability assays using CPM fluorescence showing that while mild detergents support a typical protein melt curve, DPC yields no transition, indicating a non-native, unfolded state; 3) functional reconstitution assays where prior dilution into DPC caused complete loss of CATR-sensitive ADP uptake in proteoliposomes. The authors further note that the ADP binding Kd (500 μM) and CATR chemical shift perturbations reported by Brüschweiler et al. are inconsistent with known membrane-bound values and established structural data. They conclude the DPC-refolded AAC3 data lacks biological relevance, as the detergent is harsh enough to denature functional carrier protein.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper is a critical rebuttal by King et al. against a bioRxiv preprint by Brüschweiler et al. regarding the mitochondrial ADP/ATP carrier (AAC3) of yeast. Brüschweiler et al. claimed that AAC3 could be refolded from Escherichia coli inclusion bodies to homogeneity in the detergent dodecyl-phosphocholine (DPC) and maintained in a folded, active state for ITC and NMR studies. King et al. systematically refute these claims using thermostability assays, ITC, and functional reconstitution experiments. They demonstrate that DPC, rather than stabilizing AAC3, causes immediate loss of tertiary structure and inactivation upon isolation from the inner mitochondrial membrane. 

Key evidence includes: 1) ITC measurements showing a CATR binding Kd of ~15 μM for DPC-refolded AAC3, versus 72 nM for native AAC3 in dodecyl-maltoside/tetraoleoyl cardiolipin (a 200–2000-fold difference); 2) thermostability assays using CPM fluorescence showing that while mild detergents support a typical protein melt curve, DPC yields no transition, indicating a non-native, unfolded state; 3) functional reconstitution assays where prior dilution into DPC caused complete loss of CATR-sensitive ADP uptake in proteoliposomes. The authors further note that the ADP binding Kd (500 μM) and CATR chemical shift perturbations reported by Brüschweiler et al. are inconsistent with known membrane-bound values and established structural data. They conclude the DPC-refolded AAC3 data lacks biological relevance, as the detergent is harsh enough to denature functional carrier protein.

Research Context
The subject is the yeast mitochondrial ADP/ATP carrier AAC3, a protein whose structure has been solved by electron crystallography and X-ray crystallography. Prior work by the authors has characterized interactions between AAC3 and specific inhibitors atractyloside and carboxyatractyloside using single-molecule force spectroscopy. Brüschweiler et al. claimed AAC3 could be refolded to homogeneity from Escherichia coli inclusion bodies using dodecyl-phosphocholine. The authors previously demonstrated that DPC is harsh enough to solubilise unfolded mitochondrial carrier protein from inclusion bodies and can denature functional well-folded carrier protein. There are very few polar side chain interactions in AAC3 that stabilize the structure, mainly found on the matrix side.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether AAC3 remains folded and active in dodecyl-phosphocholine (DPC) after refolding from Escherichia coli inclusion bodies. The authors hypothesize that DPC leads to immediate loss of tertiary structure and inactivation of AAC3 when isolated from the mitochondrial inner membrane. The authors predict that published Kd values for CATR binding to AAC in the membrane should be in the low nanomolar range, inconsistent with the values reported for refolded protein. The authors also anticipate that dynamic studies measured by NMR relaxation dispersion would be inconsistent with tight CATR binding if the refolded protein is non-native. A secondary hypothesis is that chemical shift perturbations could represent non-specific interactions promoted by high concentrations and temperatures used in NMR experiments.

Methodological Details
The authors compared their results against the bioRxiv preprint by Brüschweiler et al. (refolded AAC3 in DPC) using native AAC3 purified from yeast mitochondria. Native AAC3 was purified in dodecyl-maltoside and tetraoleoyl cardiolipin, with an isoelectric point of 9.82, making it highly positively charged. In thermostability assays, AAC3 was monitored with the fluorophore N-[4-(7-diethylamino-4-methyl-3-coumarinyl)phenyl] maleimide (CPM), which reacts with protein thiols. The protein concentration for thermostability was approximately 1 μM AAC3, with CPM stock at 5 mg/mL in DMSO diluted 50-fold. CATR:AAC3 molar ratios tested were 0, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, and 100. For ITC, purified 25 μM AAC3 (0.83 mg/mL in dodecyl-maltoside/tetraoleoyl cardiolipin) was titrated with 500 μM CATR stock. Reconstitution used L-α-phosphatidylcholine and tetraoleoyl cardiolipin in a 20:1 w/w ratio (10 mg total lipid) solubilised with 55 μL 25% pentaethylene glycol monodecyl detergent. In reconstitution, 30 μg of purified AAC3 was added to the lipid/detergent mix to achieve a final volume of 0.6 mL. Detergent was stepwise removed with 4 × 30 mg and 4 × 60 mg of Bio-Beads SM-2 in 20-min intervals overnight in a cold room. ADP uptake assays were performed at a final working concentration of 1.5 μM [14C]-ADP using a Hamilton MicroLab Star robot and a 96-well filter plate. The authors consulted 24 different binding studies for CATR and ATR comparison, noting that the Kd consensus for CATR in membrane is in the low nanomolar range.

Procedures And Architectures
Thermostability measurements were made in 1 °C intervals from 25 to 90 °C on a Qiagen Rotorgene Q using the HRM channel. The ramp rate was 5.6 °C/min with a 'wait between reading' set to 4 s, following a 90-second pre-incubation. Melting temperatures were determined as the peak in the derivative of the melting curve using the instrument software. For ITC, 2-μL injections were made in an initial volume of 170 μL at 3-min intervals with a stirrer speed of 350 rpm. Isotherms were fitted to a one-site binding model with ΔH, Kd, and stoichiometry as fitting parameters using NanoAnalyze software. Both CATR titrant and protein samples were degassed under vacuum at 10 °C for at least 20 min before titration. Reconstitution tested either direct addition of protein or prior 20-fold dilution into 0.1% dodecyl-maltoside or 0.1% dodecyl-phosphocholine for 30 mins on ice. After bio-bead treatment, proteoliposomes were separated using an empty spin column and exchanged into external buffer (20 mM tris-HCl pH 7.4, 50 mM NaCl) via PD10 column. ADP uptake was stopped at 0, 10, 20, 30, 45 s, 1, 2.5, 5, 7.5, 10 and 15 min.

Key Results
The Kd for CATR binding to DPC-refolded AAC3 was ~15 μM, whereas the average Kd for native AAC3 in dodecyl-maltoside/tetraoleoyl cardiolipin was 72 nM. The difference in Kd values between the refolded and native proteins represents a factor of 200 to 2000-fold. ADP transport by native AAC3 was half-maximally inhibited by 1.2 nM CATR. The authors' ITC measurements only succeeded in 2 out of 10 trials due to low enthalpic change and unstable apo-state in detergent. The Kd of ADP binding determined by NMR for refolded AAC3 was 500 μM, which is ~85-fold higher than published consensus values and ~25-fold higher than solubilised carrier. Thermostability in dodecyl-maltoside showed a typical protein melt curve with CATR adding a marked shift to higher temperatures, confirming folded protein. When the same AAC3 was diluted into 3 mM DPC, a high CPM signal was observed with no transition, indicating a non-native state. Dilution of AAC3 into DPC before reconstitution resulted in a complete loss of CATR-sensitive ADP uptake in liposomes. Only a limited number of chemical shift perturbations for CATR binding to refolded AAC3 are observed, and all are dynamic, inconsistent with tight binding. Chemical shift perturbations induced by ADP were largely on the matrix side, far from the consensus binding site in the central cavity.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The extremely low affinity of CATR for refolded AAC3 in DPC suggests the binding may be non-specific rather than specific. The high positive charge of AAC3 (pI 9.82) combined with negatively charged substrates (ADP, ATP) and inhibitor (CATR) at neutral pH may promote non-specific electrostatic interactions. The ring of transmembrane α-helices is held together largely by lateral membrane pressure and counter-pressure from the water-filled cavity, explaining why unliganded AAC3 is prone to unfolding in detergent micelles. Binding of CATR cross-links most transmembrane α-helices, explaining high affinity and improved stability in detergents. The authors conclude that the data presented by Brüschweiler et al. have no biological relevance because the protein is in a non-native, unfolded state in DPC.

Contradictions And Limitations
The authors admit their own ITC measurements were very difficult to perform, with only 2 out of 10 trials succeeding. The paper does not report the random seed, train/test split, or specific demographics since this is a biochemical study, not a computational or clinical one. The authors note that the μM unit in the Babot et al. reference was a typographical error and has since been corrected to 192 nM in an erratum, which they did not explicitly cite by number in the main text but referred to as erratum 7. The authors note that their own dynamic studies measured by NMR relaxation dispersion did not provide a plausible structural mechanism for transport.

Claims
AAC3 in dodecyl-phosphocholine (DPC) is in a non-native, unfolded state rather than a folded and active state. Thermostability in DPC showed no melting transition, indicating no native fold. Reconstitution experiments showed complete loss of CATR-sensitive ADP uptake after DPC dilution. CATR binding Kd in DPC (~15 μM) is 200–2000-fold higher than in mild detergents. Brüschweiler et al. claimed AAC3 was refolded to homogeneity and maintained in a folded state. Some dynamic chemical shift perturbations for CATR were observed, though the authors argue they are non-specific. The NMR and ITC data derived from DPC-refolded AAC3 cannot be biologically interpreted. Membrane protein structural studies should avoid DPC for carrier protein preparation.
The CATR binding affinity to native AAC3 in the membrane is in the low nanomolar range, consistent with its role as a powerful toxin. Native AAC3 was half-maximally inhibited by 1.2 nM CATR. The ITC Kd for native AAC3 in mild detergent was 72 nM. The crystal structure showed CATR remained bound after 5–7 days of purification. Brüschweiler et al. reported a Kd of ~15 μM for CATR binding in DPC. Brüschweiler et al. compared their value to 192 nM (erratum corrected from μM) for ATR, which is still orders of magnitude off. CATR and ATR are powerful inhibitors whose membrane-bound affinities serve as the biological benchmark.

Data And Code Availability
The paper references Supplementary Table 1 (24 binding studies) and Supplementary Table 2 (solubilised carrier values). Supplementary Fig. 1a, Supplementary Fig. 1b, and Supplementary Fig. 2 contain additional structural and functional data. The authors do not specify a data repository or code availability as this is a chemical/biophysical commentary.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The authors performed a 20-fold dilution test comparing dodecyl-maltoside versus DPC before reconstitution to isolate the detergent effect. Thermostability was tested at 7 different CATR:AAC3 molar ratios to assess titration response. The authors mention their own previous demonstration that DPC denatures functional well-folded carrier protein in mild non-ionic detergents.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1a shows the CATR inhibition of ADP transport by native AAC3 with an IC50 of 1.2 nM. Figure 1b shows the ITC titration curve of CATR into native AAC3 giving a Kd of 72 nM. Figure 1c shows the thermostability melt curve of native AAC3 in dodecyl-maltoside with CATR stabilization. Figure 1d shows the thermostability assay of AAC3 in 3 mM DPC with no transition. Supplementary Table 1 contains 24 binding studies comparing CATR and ATR affinities. Supplementary Table 2 compares the ADP binding Kd of 500 μM to published consensus and solubilised values. Supplementary Fig. 1a shows the structural support for the transmembrane α-helix ring. Supplementary Fig. 1b illustrates CATR-induced cross-linking of transmembrane helices. Supplementary Fig. 2 shows the ADP uptake assay comparing DPC-pre-reconstitution vs. control.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution: The authors demonstrate that AAC3 refolded in dodecyl-phosphocholine (DPC) is in a non-native, unfolded state and the reported ITC and NMR data lack biological relevance. 2. The strongest evidence: The 200–2000-fold difference between CATR binding Kd in DPC (~15 μM) vs. native membrane protein (72 nM), coupled with thermostability showing no melting transition in DPC. 3. The future path: Structural and functional studies of membrane carriers should avoid DPC for protein preparation and rely on confirmed native-like environments such as dodecyl-maltoside/tetraoleoyl cardiolipin or reconstitution into native-like membranes.

summary.title: Inhibitor of sarco/endoplasmic reticulum calcium-ATPase impairs paramyxovirus replication
summary.authors: Naveen Kumar; Sanjay Barua; Nitin Khandelwal; Kundan Kumar Chaubey; Ram Kumar; Krishan Dutt; Yogesh Chander; Thachamvally Riyesh; Vir Shoor; Singh; Bhupendra Nath
summary.field_subfield: Virology / Host-pathogen interactions / Host-targeting antiviral therapeutics
summary.type_of_paper: Experimental mechanistic study using cell culture models
summary.executive_summary: This study provides the first evidence that the sarco/endoplasmic reticulum calcium-ATPase (SERCA) regulates paramyxovirus replication of Peste des petits ruminants virus (PPRV) and Newcastle disease virus (NDV). Using a library of chemical inhibitors, Thapsigargin was identified as a SERCA-specific inhibitor that significantly reduces NDV and PPRV replication in Vero cells at a non-cytotoxic concentration of 0.5 µM. Conversely, overexpression of SERCA2 in HeLa/goat kidney cells rescued the inhibitory effect of Thapsigargin, confirming a supportive role for SERCA in viral replication. Time-of-addition and virus step-specific assays revealed that Thapsigargin specifically impairs viral entry and intracellular localization rather than attachment, RNA synthesis, or budding. Immunofluorescence showed that Thapsigargin treatment caused ~70% of cells to exhibit defective cytoplasmic foci of viral proteins instead of surface localization. Notably, NDV acquired significant but incomplete resistance to Thapsigargin on long-term passage (70 passages), with ~100-fold inhibition at P35, while PPRV showed no such resistance. The authors report this as a rare example of a virus acquiring resistance to an inhibitor targeting a cellular host factor, expanding on the precedent set by CVB3/PI4KIIIα and HCV/CsA. The study identifies SERCA as a novel proviral host factor and a candidate drug target for broad-spectrum paramyxovirus antivirals.

claims.description: SERCA is a proviral host factor essential for optimal paramyxovirus replication of both NDV and PPRV.
Thapsigargin specifically impairs viral entry and intracellular localization of viral proteins rather than attachment, RNA synthesis, or budding.
NDV can acquire partial resistance to a host-targeting agent (SERCA inhibitor), a rare event for a cellular factor inhibitor.

Notably, NDV acquired significant but incomplete resistance to Thapsigargin on long-term passage (70 passages), with ~100-fold inhibition at P35, while PPRV showed no such resistance. The authors report this as a rare example of a virus acquiring resistance to an inhibitor targeting a cellular host factor, expanding on the precedent set by CVB3/PI4KIIIα and HCV/CsA. The study identifies SERCA as a novel proviral host factor and a candidate drug target for broad-spectrum paramyxovirus antivirals.

Research Context
Viral drug resistance driven by high mutation rates of viral genomes limits the lifespan of directly-targeting antiviral drugs. Proviral host factors that facilitate viral replication serve as alternative drug targets that may impose higher genetic barriers to resistance. In vertebrates, three P-type Ca2+-ATPase families regulate intracellular Ca2+ homeostasis: PMCA, SERCA, and SPCA. SERCA transports Ca2+ from the cytosol to the double-membrane-bound endoplasmic reticulum. While SPCA1 has been reported to support virus replication, the roles of SERCA and PMCA remain largely unknown. Previous screening of kinase and phosphate inhibitors identified a candidate chemical inhibitor that blocked NDV and PPRV replication.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question was whether SERCA actively regulates and facilitates paramyxovirus replication of PPRV and NDV. The authors hypothesized that SERCA acts as a proviral host factor whose pharmacological inhibition would impair viral replication. It was further hypothesized that inhibiting SERCA would specifically impair viral entry and subcellular localization of viral proteins. The study aimed to determine if viruses could acquire resistance to a host-targeting inhibitor, a rare phenomenon for cellular factor targets. The predicted outcome was that Thapsigargin would reduce viral titers and that SERCA overexpression would rescue this effect.

Methodological Details
Vero (African green-monkey kidney), 293T (human embryonic kidney), HeLa, and goat kidney cells were grown in DMEM supplemented with 10% heat-inactivated fetal bovine serum. PPRV and NDV were available in-laboratory and viral titers were determined by plaque assay. Thapsigargin (SERCA inhibitor) was procured from Sigma as a non-competitive inhibitor structurally classified as a sesquiterpene lactone. Cytotoxicity of Thapsigargin was analyzed by MTT assay in Vero/MDBK cells over 96 hours. Antiviral efficacy was measured at MOI=0.1 in Vero/MDBK cells treated with 0.5 µM Thapsigargin or 0.05% DMSO vehicle. Virucidal activity was tested by incubating ~10^6 pfu virus suspensions with 1.5 h of Thapsigargin for ten-fold dilutions. Overexpression utilized HeLa/goat kidney cells transfected in 24-well plates in triplicates with 1 µg empty vector (pCR3) or pCR3-SERCA2 using Lipofectamine 3000. Immunofluorescence used Vero cells at ~20% confluency infected at MOI of 5 for 2 h, followed by Thapsigargin at 3 hpi (NDV) or 10 hpi (PPRV). Passaging involved 70 sequential passages of PPRV/NDV in Vero cells at MOI=0.01 with 0.25 µM Thapsigargin or 0.05% DMSO.

Procedures And Architectures
Thapsigargin cytotoxicity was tested across a range of 0.00064 µM to 2 µM, establishing 0.5 µM as non-cytotoxic. Antiviral efficacy was compared against NDV, PPRV, BHV-1, and BPXV (DNA viruses) to assess specificity. Time-of-addition (one-step growth curve) assays applied Thapsigargin at various post-infection intervals to map the replication cycle stage affected. Virus step-specific assays (attachment, entry, RNA synthesis, budding) confirmed Thapsigargin did not affect attachment, RNA synthesis, or budding. For immunofluorescence, cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde for 15 min, blocked with 1% BSA for 30 min at room temperature. Staining involved primary antibody incubation for 30 min in 0.2% saponin, followed by secondary antibody and DAPI for fluorescence microscopy. Passaging for resistance generation used 72-120 h incubation or until CPE in ≥75% cells.

Key Results
Thapsigargin at concentrations from 0.00064 µM to 2 µM did not significantly affect cell viability in Vero/MDBK cells over 96 hours. At 0.5 µM, Thapsigargin significantly inhibited NDV and PPRV replication (Figs. 1c, 1d) but not BPXV (Fig. 1f), while inhibiting BHV-1 (Fig. 1e). No virucidal effect was observed on any prototype virus after 1.5 h incubation with Thapsigargin, confirming intracellular action. Overexpression of SERCA2 rescued the inhibitory effect of Thapsigargin on NDV/PPRV replication in HeLa/goat kidney cells (Figs. 2a, 2b). PPRV infection induced enhanced SERCA2 expression in Vero cells at 3 hpi, peaking at 24-72 hpi and declining at 96 hpi (Fig. 3a). The highest inhibition of NDV by Thapsigargin occurred when applied 30 min before infection, with inhibition progressively decreasing to 0 at 10 hpi. For PPRV, the highest inhibition occurred 30 min prior to infection, with progressive decrease from 4 hpi to 24 hpi (Fig. 4b). Thapsigargin treatment caused defective cytoplasmic foci of viral proteins in ~70% of cells, compared to 10-30% in DMSO control (Figs. 6c, 6d). NDV showed resistance emerging at ~P25 with ~100-fold inhibition at P35 (compared to ~10,000-fold at passage 0) (Fig. 7a). PPRV showed no significant change in sensitivity across all passages (P0, P70-Thapsigargin, P70-Control) (Fig. 7c).

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
SERCA serves as a proviral host factor specifically required for paramyxovirus replication at the entry and protein localization stage. The data demonstrate for the first time that SERCA regulates paramyxovirus replication, with SPCA1 also potentially involved. The resistance acquired by NDV represents a rare example of a virus bypassing a cellular factor targeted by a small molecule inhibitor. One possible mechanism for resistance is a change in host factor requirement, analogous to HCV evolving to use CLDN6/9. Another mechanism is enhanced affinity of the virus for its natural substrate despite reduced host factor concentration. SERCA is positioned as a candidate drug target for broad-spectrum antiviral development against multiple paramyxovirus genotypes.

Contradictions And Limitations
A completely resistant phenotype of NDV could not be achieved even up to passage 70. Fluctuations in overall viral titers and fold inhibition were observed during passage experiments, possibly due to inconsistent harvest times (72-120 h) and MOI (0.01-0.001). The co-immunoprecipitation assay to analyze direct SERCA/virus interaction was unsuccessful. Perfect co-localization of SERCA and viral proteins could not be observed in immunofluorescence. The study only tested NDV and PPRV as paramyxoviruses; broader applicability to other families remains untested.

Claims
SERCA is a proviral host factor essential for optimal paramyxovirus replication of both NDV and PPRV. Thapsigargin treatment at 0.5 µM significantly reduced NDV and PPRV replication while sparing cell viability. Overexpression of SERCA2 rescued the Thapsigargin-mediated inhibition of viral replication. Virus-induced SERCA2 expression was detected by Western blot and was blocked by Thapsigargin. PPRV infection specifically enhanced SERCA2 expression in Vero cells. NDV, but not PPRV, acquired partial resistance to Thapsigargin on long-term passage. A completely resistant phenotype was not achieved even at P70. No direct interaction between SERCA and viral proteins was demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation. SERCA represents a novel host-targeting drug target for paramyxovirus antivirals. Host-targeting agents may impose a higher genetic barrier to resistance compared to directly-acting antivirals.
Thapsigargin specifically impairs viral entry and intracellular localization of viral proteins rather than attachment, RNA synthesis, or budding. Time-of-addition assays showed highest inhibition prior to infection and no effect at budding stages (10 hpi for NDV). Virus step-specific assays confirmed no effect on attachment, RNA synthesis, or budding (data not shown). Viral entry assays with preattached virus showed reduced titers in Thapsigargin-treated cells. Immunofluorescence revealed cytoplasmic foci in 70% of Thapsigargin-treated cells versus 10-30% in DMSO control. The mechanism of defective localization (why SERCA is required for transport) was not fully elucidated. No direct physical interaction between SERCA and viral proteins was established. Therapeutic intervention should focus on early post-entry trafficking events.
NDV can acquire partial resistance to a host-targeting agent (SERCA inhibitor), a rare event for a cellular factor inhibitor. Resistance emerged at ~P25 with ~100-fold inhibition at P35 (down from ~10,000-fold at P0). P70-Thapsigargin virus exhibited significantly lower sensitivity compared to P0-control. The study notes this as the first documented example for a paramyxovirus bypassing a cellular factor targeted by a small molecule. PPRV did not acquire any resistance even at passage 70. Control-passaged viruses did not exhibit significant resistance, suggesting resistance was not a general passage effect. The phenotype was not completely resistant; inhibition persisted. Host-targeting strategies may not be universally impervious to viral resistance. The genetic barrier for host-targeting agents remains higher than for directly-acting antivirals, but resistance is possible.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Cytotoxicity was tested across a 32-fold concentration range (0.00064 to 2 µM) to define non-cytotoxic dose. Virus step-specific assays were used to ablate individual replication stages (attachment, entry, RNA synthesis, budding). PPRV (24 h replication cycle) and NDV (10 h replication cycle) were compared to validate time-of-addition findings across different viral kinetics. A separate resistance experiment with consistent MOI (0.1) and harvest time (24 h) was conducted to control for passage-specific artifacts. Control-passaged viruses were tested against Thapsigargin to show resistance was specific to the selection pressure, not a general passage effect.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1a, 1b: MTT assay showing Thapsigargin cytotoxicity in Vero/MDBK cells across 0.00064 µM to 2 µM range, establishing 0.5 µM as non-cytotoxic. Figure 1c-f: Comparison of 0.5 µM Thapsigargin against NDV, PPRV, BHV-1, and BPXV, showing paramyxovirus specificity. Figure 1g: Virucidal assay showing no effect on cell-free virions, confirming intracellular mechanism. Figure 2a, 2b: Overexpression of SERCA2 rescuing Thapsigargin inhibition in HeLa/goat kidney cells. Figure 3a: Western blot showing PPRV-induced SERCA2 expression at 3 hpi peaking at 24-72 hpi in Vero cells, with GAPDH loading control. Figure 3b: Western blot showing Thapsigargin blocks NDV-induced SERCA2 expression at 16 hpi. Figure 4a, 4b: Time-of-addition one-step growth curves for NDV and PPRV showing loss of inhibition from 30 min prior to 10 hpi (NDV) or 24 hpi (PPRV). Figure 5a, 5b: Viral entry assays with preattached virus at 37°C showing reduced titers in Thapsigargin-treated cells. Figure 6a, 6b: Immunofluorescence images showing normal vs defective (cytoplasmic foci) localization of viral proteins at 12 hpi (NDV) and 36 hpi (PPRV). Figure 6c, 6d: Quantification of cells with defective vs normal localization (~70% vs 10-30%). Figure 7a, 7b: Passage experiments (70 passages) showing NDV resistance emergence at P35 and P70-Thapsigargin comparison. Figure 7c: PPRV sensitivity at P0, P70-Thapsigargin, and P70-Control showing no resistance.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first-ever demonstration that SERCA regulates and supports paramyxovirus replication, positioning it as a druggable host factor. 2. The strongest evidence is the rescue of Thapsigargin inhibition by SERCA2 overexpression and the identification of a specific cytoplasmic-trafficking defect (~70% cells with foci). 3. The future path involves characterizing the viral proteins that acquired mutations in Thapsigargin-resistant NDV and determining the molecular basis of SERCA's role in viral trafficking.

summary.title: MicroRNA-196a is regulated by ER and is a prognostic biomarker in ER+ Breast Cancer
summary.authors: Michael J G Milevskiy, Udai Gujral, Carolina Del Lama Marques, Andrew Stone, Korinne Northwood, Lez J Burke, Julia M W Gee, Kenneth Nephew, Susan Clark, Melissa A Brown, Mjg Milevskiy
summary.field_subfield: Oncology / Epigenetics and MicroRNA Regulation in Breast Cancer
summary.executive_summary: This study characterizes the transcriptional regulation and clinical significance of MicroRNA-196a (MIR196A) in estrogen receptor-positive (ER+) breast cancer. MIR196A, transcribed from two genomic loci (HOXC/MIR196A2 and HOXB/MIR196A1), displays complex expression patterns where MIR196A2 expression highly correlates with HOXC genes, particularly HOXC10, in breast tumours but shows more restricted association with HOXC11/10 in normal breast tissue. The authors demonstrate that MIR196A2 is transcriptionally regulated by estrogen via ERα binding to two putative promoter regions (PP1 and PP3) upstream of the transcription start site, with PP1 (the HOXC10 promoter) showing the highest luciferase activity. Long-range transcriptional regulation is mediated by two major interacting elements: a previously identified HOTAIR distal enhancer (HDE) and a novel interacting partner (MIR196A2-Enhancer, mE), both of which physically interact with the MIR196A2/HOXC10 promoter region as confirmed by ChIA-PET and 3C-qPCR. In clinical samples from the METABRIC cohort, high MIR196A expression is significantly over-expressed in breast tumours compared to normal tissue, correlates with increased tumour stage, and serves as a robust prognostic factor: high expression is associated with poor survival in advanced and post-menopausal ER+ disease but better outcome in triple-negative breast cancer. The prognostic impact is state-dependent; in premenopausal women, high MIR196A expression paradoxically associates with good ER+ outcome (one of the few significant biomarkers in this subgroup), whereas in post-menopausal women, high expression predicts poor outcome. Therapeutic resistance further drives MIR196A elevation, with expression significantly increased in tamoxifen-resistant (TAMR) but almost depleted in fulvestrant-resistant (FASR) MCF7 cells, as well as in paclitaxel and adromycin-resistant lines. ERα ChIP-Seq in human patient samples reveals increased ERα occupancy at MIR196A enhancer and promoter regions in non-responders and metastases, suggesting that enhancer over-activation drives therapeutic resistance.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study characterizes the transcriptional regulation and clinical significance of MicroRNA-196a (MIR196A) in estrogen receptor-positive (ER+) breast cancer. MIR196A, transcribed from two genomic loci (HOXC/MIR196A2 and HOXB/MIR196A1), displays complex expression patterns where MIR196A2 expression highly correlates with HOXC genes, particularly HOXC10, in breast tumours but shows more restricted association with HOXC11/10 in normal breast tissue. The authors demonstrate that MIR196A2 is transcriptionally regulated by estrogen via ERα binding to two putative promoter regions (PP1 and PP3) upstream of the transcription start site, with PP1 (the HOXC10 promoter) showing the highest luciferase activity. Long-range transcriptional regulation is mediated by two major interacting elements: a previously identified HOTAIR distal enhancer (HDE) and a novel interacting partner (MIR196A2-Enhancer, mE), both of which physically interact with the MIR196A2/HOXC10 promoter region as confirmed by ChIA-PET and 3C-qPCR. In clinical samples from the METABRIC cohort, high MIR196A expression is significantly over-expressed in breast tumours compared to normal tissue, correlates with increased tumour stage, and serves as a robust prognostic factor: high expression is associated with poor survival in advanced and post-menopausal ER+ disease but better outcome in triple-negative breast cancer. The prognostic impact is state-dependent; in premenopausal women, high MIR196A expression paradoxically associates with good ER+ outcome (one of the few significant biomarkers in this subgroup), whereas in post-menopausal women, high expression predicts poor outcome. Therapeutic resistance further drives MIR196A elevation, with expression significantly increased in tamoxifen-resistant (TAMR) but almost depleted in fulvestrant-resistant (FASR) MCF7 cells, as well as in paclitaxel and adromycin-resistant lines. ERα ChIP-Seq in human patient samples reveals increased ERα occupancy at MIR196A enhancer and promoter regions in non-responders and metastases, suggesting that enhancer over-activation drives therapeutic resistance.

Research Context
MicroRNAs are potent post-transcriptional regulators involved in all hallmarks of cancer, but their transcriptional regulation remains poorly understood. MIR196A is transcribed from two genomic locations, the HOXC and HOXB loci, downstream of HOXC10 and upstream of HOXB9 respectively. MIR196A has been strongly implicated in a range of cancers, primarily as an oncogene, overexpressed in breast tumours. A single nucleotide polymorphism (rs116149130) within MIR196A2 is associated with decreased breast cancer risk. MIR196A has been shown to target the 3' UTR of Annexin-1 and p27/Kip1, influencing angiogenesis and cell cycle. Despite the clear importance of miR-196a in cancer, its transcriptional regulation remains poorly understood. Several instances of miRNA regulation by enhancers have been described, but this area is very much in its infancy.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research aim was to characterise the expression landscape of MIR196A including factors regulating its expression. The authors explored potential roles of regulatory elements and factors in breast cancer prognostication. Given MIR196A correlates with HOXC genes in breast cancer, the study sought to determine if oestrogen also regulates MIR196A2. It was hypothesised that MIR196A2 transcription may be controlled by the oestrogen receptor (ER). The authors examined the hypothesis that MIR196A2 is controlled by long-range transcriptional regulation, mediated by ERα tethered gene looping. The study aimed to determine whether MIR196A expression patterns in breast cancer correlate with common molecular markers of breast tumours.

Methodological Details
Cell culture models utilised MCF7, Tamoxifen-resistant (TAMR), Fulvestrant-resistant (FASR), and oestrogen-deprived (MCF7x) cells obtained from AstraZeneca. All cell lines were cultured for less than 6 months after authentication by short-tandem repeat (STR) profiling. Luciferase reporter assays used 500 ng of modified pGL3 reporter constructs, 20 ng of pRL-TK, and 0.5μL of Lipofectamine 3000. Luciferase readings were measured 48 hours post transfection using a DTX-880 luminometer and Dual-Glo Stop and Glo kit. RNA for miRNA analysis was reverse transcribed using the miScript RT II kit and assayed with miScript SYBR Green PCR Kit. All qRT-PCRs were normalised to the snoRNA RNU6b and performed on a Corbet Rotorgene-6000. ChIP-Seq data for MCF7 (GSE14664), GRO-Seq (GSE27463), ChIA-PET (GSE39495), and Breast tumour ERα ChIP-Seq (GSE32222) were sourced from public repositories. RNA-Seq from Adriamycin and paclitaxel resistant MCF7 derived cells was sourced from GSE68815. HOX gene expression in human breast cells was sourced from Gascard et al. DNA methylation of breast tumours was sourced from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA). METABRIC expression and clinical information were sourced from EGAS00000083. Clustering of Illumina Array and miR-Seq data was performed using the Multiple Experiment Viewer (MeV). 3C was performed with cells grown to 60-80% confluence, fixed with 1% formaldehyde, and libraries generated with HindIII. Univariate and multivariate Cox proportional hazard regression analyses were performed using MedCalc for Windows, version 12.7. Kaplan-Meier survival analysis and ROC curves for optimal cutoffs were generated using GraphPad Prism.

Procedures And Architectures
Chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP-Seq) for RNA polymerase II demonstrated polymerase binding in the region surrounding HOXC10 and MIR196A is dependent on oestrogen in MCF7 cells. Global-run-on sequencing (GRO-Seq) measured nascent RNA in MCF7 cells, revealing a dramatic increase in RNA production in the MIR196A2 genomic region peaking at 40 mins following oestradiol addition. This increase in RNA production from the HOXC locus was validated with qRT-PCR and RNA-Seq from MCF7 cells following oestradiol treatment. Two putative promoter regions, PP1 and PP3, upstream of the MIR196A2 transcription start site, were identified via binding of ERα and its pioneer factor FOXA1. ChIA-PET identified two major sites of interaction with MIR196A2 promoters: a previously identified HOTAIR distal enhancer (HDE) and a novel MIR196A2-Enhancer (mE). 3C-qPCR demonstrated that both enhancer elements physically interact with each of the two MIR196A2/HOXC10 promoter regions. ChIP-Seq for ERα on human patient samples identified ERα binding sites in the genomic region of MIR196A across non-responders and metastases. DNA methylation of the upstream CpG island was assessed, revealing it is methylated in MCF10A and MCF7 cells but unmethylated in HMEC.

Key Results
MIR196A expression in breast tumours highly correlates with HOXC genes, particularly HOXC10, while in normal breast cells the association is more limited (HOXC11 and HOXC10). GRO-Seq clearly indicates a dramatic increase in RNA production in the genomic region surrounding MIR196A2 peaking at 40 mins following oestradiol addition. In luciferase assays, PP1 (the HOXC10 promoter) shows the most active transcription in MCF7 cells, followed modestly by PP2. Cloning of HDE downstream of PP1 and PP2 demonstrates significant augmentation of transcription, with HDE appearing to be the most active enhancer in MCF7 cells. MIR196A expression is divided into four distinct clusters: clusters 1 and 3 correlate with hormone receptors (AR, ERα, PGR, HER2), while clusters 2 and 4 negatively correlate with ERα and associate with EGFR and HER2. MIR196A is strongly expressed in the HER2 subtype, while in luminal A and B subtypes expression is very dynamic. In the METABRIC cohort, MIR196A is significantly over-expressed in breast tumours compared to normal adjacent tissue and over-expression associates with increased tumour stage. In ER+ tumours responding to therapy, women with low MIR196A expression exhibited a high survival rate (>95% at 10 years), while most in the high expression group died within 17 years (61% at 10 years). In premenopausal women with ER+ tumours, high MIR196A expression is associated with a good outcome, and MIR196A is one of the few significant biomarkers for this subgroup. In post-menopausal women, high MIR196A expression is now associated with a poor outcome, while all tested biomarkers were significant. MIR196A expression is significantly increased in tamoxifen-resistant MCF7 (TAMR) cells but almost depleted in fulvestrant-resistant (FASR) cells. MIR196A expression increases in paclitaxel and adromycin resistant cell lines compared to treatment-sensitive lines. ERα ChIP-Seq in human patient samples reveals an increase in ERα occupancy at both enhancer and promoter regions of MIR196A in non-responders and metastases.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The study hypothesises that a consorted effort of multiple enhancers, possibly driven by extensive ERα binding, is responsible for the overexpression of HOXC genes in cancer. The CpG island associated with reduced breast cancer risk is located within the transcriptionally active region of HOXC10 and MIR196A2, and its hypermethylation in a transcriptionally active region may severely impair expression. Binding of ERα accompanied by cofactors may be needed to maintain low methylation levels and active transcription in breast cancer. The disparity in MIR196A's prognostic value between pre- and post-menopausal ER+ women suggests a change in the regulation and expression of HOX genes following menopause, likely related to the decline in oestrogen production. The de-repression and over-activation of promoter and enhancer elements in poor responders, combined with the essential role of HOX genes in maintaining a stem-cell-like state, may drive resistance to therapy. The finding that a single miRNA is encoded at two loci contributes to the complexity of its expression and suggests dual-encoded miRs require distinct regulatory analyses.

Contradictions And Limitations
While GRO-Seq and ChIP-Seq confirm oestrogen regulation at MIR196A2, the luciferase reporter assay with PP3 failed to show increased transcription, contrasting with the ERα binding peak within PP3 shown in Jiang et al. The MIR196A-HOXC association is not significant in normal human breast tissue, unlike the strong correlation observed in breast tumours, indicating the association is cancer-specific. The paper states the area of miRNA regulation by enhancers is very much in its infancy, limiting the generality of the enhancer findings. The exact random seed, train/test split, or specific demographic details beyond the METABRIC cohort and BRCA studies are not reported. It is currently unclear how dual-encoded miRs are regulated, as many exist but few have been characterised.

Claims
MIR196A2 is transcriptionally regulated by estrogen via ERα binding to distal enhancers and proximal promoters. GRO-Seq shows dramatic increase in RNA production from MIR196A2 peaking at 40 mins post-E2. ChIA-PET identifies HDE and mE as major interacting enhancers with the MIR196A2 promoter. 3C-qPCR confirms physical interaction of both enhancers with the promoter region. MIR196A1 (the second locus) does not show an increase in precursor miRNA in response to E2. Endocrine therapy targeting ERα may modulate MIR196A expression, opening therapeutic avenues.
MIR196A is a robust prognostic biomarker for ER+ breast cancer, with its effect being state-dependent on menopause. Low MIR196A expression yields >95% 10-year survival in ER+ cohorts. High MIR196A expression predicts poor survival in post-menopausal ER+ disease (61% at 10 years). High MIR196A expression is associated with better outcome in triple-negative breast cancer. MIR196A could serve as a novel stratification method for therapeutically resistant breast cancer.
Therapeutic resistance to endocrine and chemotherapy is associated with de-repression of MIR196A expression. MIR196A is significantly increased in tamoxifen-resistant MCF7 cells. MIR196A expression increases in paclitaxel and adromycin resistant lines. Increased ERα occupancy at MIR196A enhancer and promoter regions is observed in non-responders and metastases. MIR196A is almost depleted in fulvestrant-resistant cells, indicating state-specific resistance regulation. The pathway to resistance involves de-repression and over-activation of promoter and enhancer elements.

Data And Code Availability
ChIP-Seq and GRO-Seq data were sourced from public accession codes: GSE14664, GSE27463, GSE39495, GSE32222. RNA-Seq data from Adriamycin and paclitaxel resistant MCF7 derived cells was sourced from GSE68815. DNA methylation data was sourced from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA). METABRIC expression and clinical information were sourced from EGAS00000083. The paper does not explicitly state a code repository or protocol for data analysis.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The role of the individual enhancers was tested by cloning HDE and mE separately into luciferase reporters; HDE was the most active in MCF7 cells. The role of each promoter was tested via PP1, PP2, and PP3 luciferase assays; PP1 showed the most active transcription. The state-dependency of MIR196A's prognostic value was tested by stratifying the cohort into pre- and post-menopausal subgroups. The resistance models were further stratified into tamoxifen-resistant (TAMR) versus fulvestrant-resistant (FASR) to examine the role of specific endocrine therapies. DNA methylation was assessed in non-malignant (MCF10A), cancerous (MCF7), and human mammary epithelial cells (HMEC) to establish a baseline.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A shows ChIP-Seq for RNA polymerase II demonstrating oestrogen-dependent binding at the HOXC10 and MIR196A gene region, repressed by tamoxifen or fulvestrant. Figure 1B presents GRO-Seq data showing a dramatic increase in RNA production in the MIR196A2 region peaking at 40 mins after oestradiol addition. Figure 1C and D show validation of the GRO-Seq data by qRT-PCR and RNA-Seq from oestradiol-treated MCF7 cells. Figure 2A displays ChIA-PET identifying two major interaction sites with MIR196A2 promoters: HDE and mE. Figure 2B shows 3C-qPCR demonstrating physical interaction of both enhancer elements with the promoter regions. Figure 2C shows luciferase reporter results demonstrating augmentation of transcription for PP1 and PP2 by both enhancers, with HDE most active in MCF7. Figure 3A shows four distinct clusters of MIR196A expression identified by hierarchical clustering of breast tumour data. Figure 3B correlates clusters 1 and 3 with hormone receptor and cofactor expression, while clusters 2 and 4 correlate negatively. Figure 3C defines expression by PAM50 intrinsic subtypes, showing strong HER2 subtype expression. Figure 4A and 4B show MIR196A over-expression in breast tumours compared to normal tissue, associated with increased tumour stage. Figure 4C and D show survival curves demonstrating poor outcome in ER+ tumours with high MIR196A expression but better outcome in TNBC. Figure 5A shows overall survival stratified by MIR196A expression in ER+ tumours, with a >95% 10-year survival in the low-expression group. Figure 5B shows MIR196A expression in TAMR, FASR, paclitaxel, and adromycin resistant MCF7 cell lines. Figure 5C shows DNA methylation changes at the HOXC10/MIR196A2 promoters in resistant cell lines. Figure 5D shows RNA-Seq of chemotherapy resistant MCF7 cell lines. Figure 5E shows ERα ChIP-Seq in patient samples with increased occupancy at MIR196A enhancer and promoter regions in non-responders and metastases. Table 1 shows that in premenopausal women, high MIR196A expression is associated with good outcome in ER+ disease.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is characterizing MIR196A2 transcriptional regulation by ERα through long-range enhancer-promoter interactions and establishing its role as a state-dependent prognostic biomarker in ER+ breast cancer. 2. The strongest evidence comes from the multi-method verification of the enhancer-promoter model using ChIP-Seq, GRO-Seq, 3C-qPCR, and ChIA-PET, combined with the independent corroboration of the ERα-binding finding by Jiang et al. 3. Future studies should aim to uncover the purpose of increased MIR196A expression, determine if it is required for resistance alone or in combination with other HOXC genes, and utilize high-resolution chromatin interaction mapping such as 5C or NG Capture-C.

summary.title: Lack of negative density-dependence regulation in a dominant oak tree from a neotropical highland forest
summary.authors: Irene Calderón-Sanou, Luis Diego Ríos, Alfredo Cascante-Marín, Gilbert Barrantes, Eric J Fuchs
summary.field_subfield: Ecology / Tropical Forest Population Dynamics
summary.type_of_paper: Empirical field study with spatial statistics and GLMM modeling
summary.executive_summary: This study investigates whether conspecific negative density-dependence (CNDD), a proposed mechanism for regulating species coexistence and diversity, operates on seedling establishment of Quercus costaricensis, a monodominant oak in the Talamanca highland forests of Costa Rica. The authors tested the importance of CNDD regulation on seedling survival and recruitment of 3,538 seedlings monitored between 2014 and 2017 at the Cerro de la Muerte Biological Station (3100-3350 m a.s.l.). Using spatial statistics (univariate Ripley's K) and generalized linear mixed-effects models with binomial and quasi-Poisson distributions, they examined the effects of conspecific seedling density, distance to the nearest adult, herbivory intensity, and bamboo (Chusquea spp.) density on annual survival. Contrary to the Janzen-Connell hypothesis, no significant effect of CNDD was found on seedling survival; annual survival remained high (above 63% per year). Instead, herbivory and bamboo density significantly reduced survival.
